Name: The Hybrid Work Trends That Will Shape 2027 [Webinar]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Here’s a pair of numbers that should make any workplace team pause. Since early 2024, required office days in the US have gone up about 12%. Attendance has gone up 1% to 3%.
Post body:
Here’s a pair of numbers that should make any workplace team pause. Since early 2024, required office days in the US have gone up about 12%. Attendance has gone up 1% to 3%.

Meanwhile, a lot of people quietly started saving a full workday a week with AI. Most of them have no idea what they’re supposed to do with that time.

If you plan the office, all of this lands on you in 2027. The desks, the rooms, the budget, and the policy your CEO wants by Q1.

So we’re putting three hybrid work leaders who study this for a living on one (virtual) stage to argue it out. Kate Lister from Global Workplace Analytics, Debbie Lovich from BCG, and Ryan Anderson from MillerKnoll join us for The Hybrid Work Trends That Will Shape 2027, a live webinar on Tuesday, December 8, at 11 AM ET.

Each of them places a bet on 2027. Then we dig into the 4 trends we think will matter most for facilities, HR, and IT.

Save your spot here.

Meet the experts placing the bets

Kate Lister has tracked distributed work for more than 20 years as Founding Principal of Global Workplace Analytics. If a trend has no data behind it, she’ll tell you.

Debbie Lovich is a Managing Director and Senior Partner at BCG, where she works with CEOs and boards on how work gets done. Her new book, Make Work Work, comes out November 17, so expect a few ideas from it on the day. One of her findings: employee-centric companies are 7 times as likely to be AI-mature.

Ryan Anderson runs global research and planning at MillerKnoll and hosts the About Place podcast. He just published The Relational Office, based on a survey of 2,050 office workers aged 21 to 29 across 7 countries.

Crispin Piney, OfficeRnD’s Managing Director for the UK and Ireland, hosts.

4 trends we’ll dig into

1. Why office mandates aren’t filling the office

66% of US firms with a set schedule now ask for 3 office days a week. A year ago it was 53%. California moved about 109,000 state workers to 4 days in July, and Canada’s federal public service followed.

Kate takes this one on. Does the gap close in 2027, or do companies start rewriting policies around how people work? Debbie jumps in with what a policy looks like when employees help write it.

2. That extra day a week AI gives people back

In BCG’s survey of 11,749 workers, 42% of regular AI users said they save at least a full workday a week. About 2 in 3 get little or no guidance on what to do with it.

Debbie has strong views on where that day should go. Kate then asks the question facility and IT leaders care about: where is AI saving real time in workplace management today, and which promises should you be skeptical of?

3. What makes the commute worth it

US office visits are still 25.5% below 2019 levels (Placer.ai, September). In Ryan’s survey, half of young professionals said working with their team is the main reason they come in. A quarter said there’s nowhere to just talk.

Ryan shares 1 change you can make in Q1 without a full refit. Kate adds what facilities, HR and IT should connect (booking, visitors, badges, calendars) so the office day goes smoothly for whoever shows up.

4. Full on Tuesday, empty on Friday

CBRE puts average office utilization at 53%, with peaks at 80%. So you size the space for the Tuesday crowd and pay for it all week.

Kate covers which numbers earn a workplace team a seat at the leadership table, and what to bring to your 2027 budget meeting (badge swipes alone won’t do it). Ryan takes the lease question: plan for the peak, the average, or somewhere in between? And what on earth do you do with Friday?

We’ll finish with a lightning round: 1 thing each speaker says you should start, stop or keep doing in Q1 2027. Then it’s your turn, with 15 minutes of live Q&A.

Your free copy of the 2027 trends report

70+ minutes goes fast. So every registrant gets the full PDF report on 2027 hybrid work trends, even if you can’t make it live.

It goes deeper on every trend, with the data and sources behind it, and each one is expanded by the speaker behind it: Kate, Debbie, or Ryan.

Save the date

  • What: The Hybrid Work Trends That Will Shape 2027, a live webinar
  • When: Tuesday, December 8, 2026, 11 AM ET (4 PM GMT, 5 PM CET)
  • How long: about 70 minutes, including 15 minutes of Q&A
  • Where: live online
  • Who it’s for: facility and workplace managers, HR leaders, and IT teams getting ready for 2027

Got a question your leadership keeps asking you? Bring it along. We’ll get through as many as we can.

Why it’s worth an hour of your December

Your 2027 plans are probably taking shape right now: the budget, the lease renewal, the policy update. This is a chance to test them against 3 people who track this for a living, before Q1 starts.

Registering costs nothing. You get a live seat, a chance to put your own question to the panel, the recording, and the full PDF report.

Name: Webinar: the coworking and flex space trends to watch in 2027
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Workthere’s latest operator survey puts global flex occupancy at a record 85%. In the same year, IWG reported record half-year revenue and a 44% drop in operating profit. Full buildings and thinner margins, at the same time: that’s the market flex operators are taking into 2027.
Post body:
Workthere’s latest operator survey puts global flex occupancy at a record 85%. In the same year, IWG reported record half-year revenue and a 44% drop in operating profit. Full buildings and thinner margins, at the same time: that’s the market flex operators are taking into 2027.

On Monday, December 14, we’re putting 3 people who see that market from very different places on 1 panel: a global flex advisor, an operator with 20 years in hospitality who runs 8 canal-house buildings in Amsterdam, and the head of Sweden’s coworking association. They’ll tell you which trends will shape 2027 and what they’d act on first.

When and how to join

The panel goes live on Zoom on Monday, December 14, 2026, at 11:00 AM ET (4:00 PM London). It runs about 80 minutes: the panel discussion, a short product session, and an open Q&A with all the speakers.

Save your spot here.

Everyone who registers gets a PDF report with the extended version of the trends from the panel.

Meet the people you’ll hear from

All 3 panelists spoke at Coworking Europe 2026 in Paris in November, so they’ll come to December 14 with a month of fresh conversations with operators, brokers and landlords.

Cal Lee is Global Head of Workthere and Co-head of Savills Flex. Workthere runs Flexmark, one of the largest operator surveys in the sector, and Cal tracks flex demand across markets from London to Singapore.

Maudy Westerveld is Director of EBC Amsterdam, which has rented flexible offices for nearly 50 years and now runs 8 historic buildings on the Keizersgracht. She joined EBC 14 years ago as a temp while finishing her degree, worked her way up to running it, and led the acquisition of EBC’s 8th location in 2024. In Paris, she facilitated a panel on which business models work for flex in tier 2 cities, suburbs and regional markets, and spoke on another about hiring and keeping the right people in flex teams. She’ll bring the operator’s view: what clients ask for at the front desk, often before it shows up in a report.

Pernilla Ytterbring has run SOCK, the Swedish association for coworking and serviced offices, since January 2026. She also chairs Quick Office, which she led as CEO from 2022 to 2025, and she specializes in pre-opening projects and change management. In Paris, she facilitated 2 sessions: one on whether small, local and independent coworking spaces can compete with scale, and one, with Cal on the panel, on how brokers can speed up flex deals. That first question is the one she’ll open on December 14.

Crispin Piney, Managing Director, UK & I at OfficeRnD, will be the host, and Ivailo Ivanov, VP of Product at OfficeRnD, leads the short technology section.

What we’ll talk about

1. Why members are staying for years

Workthere’s Flexmark 2026 survey found corporate occupiers stay in flex space for 3.9 years on average, against 2.6 years for start-ups and SMEs. The panel will discuss what those members pay for when they stay that long, and whether “flex” still describes what operators sell.

A member who stays 4 years renews at least once or twice. If nobody reviews the contract 60 to 90 days before the end date, a 6-person office can stay on its 2023 rate into 2027.

2. Which jobs to hand to AI, and which to keep

In our 2026 Flex Space Tech Stack Report, 18% of 334 flex operators said they use AI tools and 51% said they’re considering them. The 2026 question was worded more strictly than in 2025, so the 2 years don’t compare directly. The panel will cover which jobs in a flex space to hand to AI first and which to keep with your team.

Don’t switch on an AI agent until your inventory and prices in the system are correct. It will quote a wrong rate to a prospect at 9 pm on a Friday, and nobody will see it until Monday.

If you want to see how that plays out in practice, here’s what happened when a 2-site operator let AI answer its enquiries.

3. How people find and book space now

More prospects now start their search by asking an AI assistant. SOCi’s 2026 Local Visibility Index, which covered more than 350,000 business locations, found ChatGPT recommends only 1.2% of local business locations.

The panel will discuss how occupiers find and shortlist space today, and how far self-serve booking can go, from selling day passes and meeting rooms online to private offices.

4. What it takes to stay independent when margins get tight

Large operators are growing revenue faster than profit. IWG’s H1 2026 results showed revenue up 6% to a record $2.0 billion and operating profit down 44% to $38 million.

Our own platform data points the same way. Across more than 3,500 flex locations on OfficeRnD, our FlexIndex benchmark shows RevPAD (revenue per available desk, which counts empty desks too) rising from $362.46 in Q1 2025 to $379.98 in Q4 2025, up 4.8%. Desk occupancy moved 0.27 percentage points to 73.05%. In 2025, the operators who earned more did it through pricing and revenue capture, with occupancy almost flat.

Pernilla will open this topic: is independence an advantage or a liability in 2027, and what do landlords and investors ask an independent operator for first?

After the panel: a look at what we’re building

After the panel, Ivailo Ivanov will spend 15 to 20 minutes on the OfficeRnD Flex roadmap and how it answers the trends the panel raised. That includes OfficeRnD AI Hub, which already runs an AI agent that answers web chat around the clock.

The last 15 minutes are open Q&A with all speakers.

A report for everyone who signs up

Every registrant receives a PDF report with the extended version of the trends discussed on the webinar: the data behind each trend, the speakers’ views, and what operators can act on in Q1 2027. It goes to everyone who signs up, so register even if December 14 doesn’t work for you.

See you on December 14

Save your spot to leave with the first moves 3 flex leaders would make in 2027 on pricing, AI, online sales, and margin, plus the extended trends report as a PDF, even if you can’t join live.

Name: Desk and Parking Booking in One Flow | OfficeRnD Workplace
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Booking a desk was never the whole commute. For anyone who drives to the office, the day starts in the car park, and until now that part has been left to luck. Parking was a separate booking step that was easy to forget. And when the car park was full, there was no way to know when a spot opened up again.
Post body:
Booking a desk was never the whole commute. For anyone who drives to the office, the day starts in the car park, and until now that part has been left to luck. Parking was a separate booking step that was easy to forget. And when the car park was full, there was no way to know when a spot opened up again.

Starting today, OfficeRnD Workplace closes that gap. Parking now sits right inside the desk booking flow. And when every spot is taken, employees can join a waitlist instead of circling the block or refreshing the Dashboard.

The result is fewer surprises at the barrier, fewer “can you hold me a spot?” messages for facility teams, and an office day that starts the way it should.

What’s new in OfficeRnD Workplace

Two new parking features close the gap between “I booked a desk” and “I made it to my desk.”

  • Combined desk and parking booking. Book a desk, and Workplace offers you a free parking spot for the same time. One click and both are yours.
  • The parking waitlist. When every spot is taken, join the waitlist. Workplace lets you know the moment a spot frees up, so you can stop refreshing the Dashboard.

Both are available now on the Pro plan.

Book your desk and your parking in one move

Until now, drivers had two things to remember: book a desk, then go somewhere else in the product and book parking. Forget the second step, and you find out at the barrier.

Combined booking folds parking straight into the desk booking flow. When an employee books a desk and a parking spot is free for the same time, Workplace offers it right there. They confirm in a click, or dismiss it and carry on with their day.

It works wherever people already book:

  • From the Dashboard or the office map
  • With Quick Book or the full More options dialog

And it knows when to stay quiet. If someone already has a spot for that day and time, or no spot is free, there’s no prompt. No noise, no dead ends.

Parking also stands on its own. Employees who only need a spot can see how many are free on the Dashboard and book one directly, no desk required. Reserved spots get their own color and icon, so everyone can tell at a glance what they’ve booked.

Not everyone drives, of course. Employees can switch the parking offer off in their profile settings, so it only shows up for the people who need it.

Car park full? Get in line, not in your car

Every office has that one day when the car park is fully booked. Until now, a full car park left drivers with two bad options: keep refreshing the Dashboard in case someone cancels, or give up and pay for parking down the road.

The parking waitlist gives them a third option. When every spot is booked, employees join the waitlist for the period they need. If a spot frees up during that period, say because a colleague cancels, Workplace notifies them.

Employees can join wherever they are:

  • From the Dashboard, right where it shows that no spots are free
  • While booking a desk, when no parking is free for the same time, so the waitlist covers exactly the hours they’ll be in
  • In Microsoft Teams, through the OfficeRnD Workplace app

The waitlist follows how your parking is set up. If spots are booked by the day, people wait for a day. If they’re booked by the hour, people wait for a time range.

One thing to know: the waitlist doesn’t book the spot automatically. It tells employees a spot is free, and they book it in a couple of clicks. That keeps the decision with the person who’s actually driving in, and keeps spots from going to someone whose plans have already changed.

Why it matters for your team

Facility managers: stop being the human parking waitlist

You know the messages. “Can you hold a spot for me Thursday?” “Let me know if anything opens up.” Every one of them ends up in your inbox or on a sticky note. Now the system keeps the queue. Employees join the waitlist themselves and hear about free spots without you in the middle, so you can get back to running the workplace instead of guarding the car park.

See how Chaos replaced a car park where spots went to whoever arrived first with a booking system that gives employees certainty before they commute.

HR and People teams: the office day starts at the gate

You’ve worked hard to make the office worth the trip. But the experience doesn’t begin at reception. It begins when someone pulls in, and a stressful ten minutes in the car park can undo a lot of good intentions. Booking desk and parking together, and getting a heads-up when a spot opens, makes the first moments of the day calm and predictable.

IT: nothing new to roll out

There’s no new app to deploy and no new tool to learn. Parking lives in the same Workplace product employees already use, on the same office maps, and the waitlist is available in Microsoft Teams. Setup takes a few clicks in the Admin Portal.

Get started in minutes

If you’re on the Pro plan, you can switch parking on today:

  1. In the Admin Portal, go to Settings > Advanced Settings > Resource Types.
  2. Click Add Parking.
  3. Choose a Booking Mode: Time for hourly bookings, or Date for full days.
  4. Add Parking Spot resources to an office map, the same way you add desks.

That last step matters. Employees see parking offers and the waitlist only once at least one spot is live on a map.

A tip from our team: if most of your people drive, add enough parking spots to roughly match your desk capacity. A parking offer that never has anything to offer quickly becomes one people ignore.

No more surprises at the barrier

With desk and parking booked together, and a waitlist for the busy days, drivers walk in on time and in a good mood. Facility teams stop handling parking requests by hand. And the office becomes a little easier to say yes to.

That’s the whole idea: a commute with no surprises, and an office day that starts the way it should.

Already on OfficeRnD Workplace? If you’re on the Pro plan, parking is ready to switch on in your Admin Portal today.

New to OfficeRnD? See how Workplace makes limited parking work for everyone, or book a meeting with our team to see how OfficeRnD Workplace can help you manage your office better.

Quick answers

Does the waitlist book a spot for me? No. It lets you know when a spot is free, and you book it yourself from the Dashboard.

Do I have to book a desk to get parking? No. You can book a parking spot directly from the Dashboard.

What if no spot is free when I book a desk? You won’t see a parking offer. You can join the waitlist for the same time instead.

Name: 6 Skedda Alternatives Priced at 3 Office Sizes (2026)
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Looking for Skedda alternatives?
Post body:
Looking for Skedda alternatives?

You likely know what Skedda does well. It books almost anything with a calendar attached, from desks and meeting rooms to labs and parking, and its rules engine gives admins very tight control.

The reasons to look elsewhere tend to be specific: the bill grows with every space you add, or the office now runs on hybrid planning (who’s coming in, which team sits where) more than on booking shared resources.

We’ve built workplace software at OfficeRnD since 2015, and we’ve spent those years configuring booking policies, sitting in IT security reviews, and watching how offices book in practice. Every tool here gets a fair look, including the cases where it’s the better pick and the cases where staying on Skedda makes sense.

You’ll get a side-by-side table, pricing checked on each vendor’s own page in October 2026, what each tool costs at 3 office sizes, and what to pay attention to in a demo or trial before you sign.

TL;DR

Here are the most popular Skedda alternatives:

  • OfficeRnD Workplace: best for hybrid offices that want desks, rooms, parking, and attendance policies in 1 tool people use from Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar or Slack. Desks and meeting rooms are priced separately, from $99/month billed annually, and G2 reviewers rate its quality of support at 95%. Time to go live could be 2 hours for small organizations.
  • Robin: best for enterprises running several floors or buildings that want space planning, room services, and visitors on 1 platform. Pricing is quote-only and billed annually, and Robin says it’s built for companies with 500 or more employees.
  • YAROOMS: best for Microsoft-heavy offices that want a flat monthly price, from about $79/month for 10 users on yearly billing. The Teams app, Outlook sync, and SSO start on the Business plan, from about $319/month, and parking booking is Enterprise-only.
  • deskbird: best for multi-location teams that want per-user pricing with desks, rooms, and parking in the base plan. Business costs $3.75 per active user per month billed annually, from 25 users, while SAML and SCIM sit in a paid add-on.
  • desk.ly: best for companies that want desk booking tied to their HR system, such as Personio or Workday. It’s free for up to 15 users and starts at about $1.90 per user per month, but Outlook sync, SCIM, and HRIS integrations need the custom-priced Enterprise Plus plan.
  • Dibsido: best for small and mid-size teams that want to pay only for the resources they book. It sells desk, parking, and room booking as separate plans, or all 3 in an All-in-One plan at $2.70 per user per month billed yearly, with a free plan for up to 10 users.

How I compared the Skedda alternatives

In case you haven’t noticed yet, OfficeRnD Workplace is our product. It went through the same scorecard as every other tool here, no vendor paid for a spot, and its review names where it falls short. I also scored Skedda itself, so every alternative is measured against the tool you’re leaving.

The scorecard

Each tool was scored out of 100 across 8 criteria. The weights reflect why teams leave Skedda: the bill, and the shift from booking shared resources to planning hybrid office days.

Also, if your priorities differ, re-weight the table. A university with dozens of lab resources would put booking rules first, and the ranking would shift.

Where the information came from

As usual, G2 was the main source for user feedback. I read rating, review count, and recency together, and read the reviews themselves for repeated praise and complaints. Where a review base needed context (most reviews from 1 month, or mostly from years ago), the tool’s section says so. G2 figures were checked in October 2026. I also looked at Capterra and Trustradius.

Pricing comes from each vendor’s own pricing page, checked in October 2026. When a third-party site disagreed with the vendor, the vendor’s page won. Prices are shown in USD on yearly billing.

Where a vendor’s page opens on monthly prices (YAROOMS, Dibsido), we switched to its yearly view. Skedda prices differ by region, so we show both its US and EMEA plans. desk.ly only publishes euro prices, which we converted at the exchange rate on October 16, 2026.

When that was possible, I also tested some of the products myself to get a better understanding of their performance.

Last but not least, the article was fact-checked by product experts Ivaylo Ivanov, VP of Product at OfficeRnD, and Momchil Blaskov, Principal Product Manager at OfficeRnD.

How our own office data fits in

We run our Sofia office on OfficeRnD Workplace, and a year of that data (13,024 desk bookings from August 2025 to August 2026) shaped how we judged pricing models.

Mondays averaged 73.3% desk utilization. Fridays averaged 36.2%. Under per-space pricing, you pay for every desk every day, whether the floor is three-quarters full or a third full. That’s why the scorecard looks at what each pricing model charges for, and at cost across 3 office sizes, before the starting price.

It’s 1 office of 54 to 60 desks, so I treat it as a worked example, not an industry benchmark.

#1 OfficeRnD Workplace: best for mid-sized organizations where teams plan their office days together

OfficeRnD Workplace is built around the employee’s week. People book desks, rooms, and parking from Microsoft Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar or Slack, see which teammates are coming in, and plan their office days around them.

Facilities gets utilization data from those bookings, and IT gets SSO and automated user provisioning on the Professional plan.

Skedda was built to control access to shared resources. Once employees choose when to come in, the daily problem becomes coordination: people need to find their team when they show up. OfficeRnD Workplace is designed for that.

Booking happens in the tools people already use

If only a third of the office books through the tool and the rest walk in, your utilization reports cover only that third. OfficeRnD Workplace has a native Teams app and Outlook room booking. It also offers desk booking and weekly planning inside Slack, Google Calendar sync and a Chrome extension.

Skedda also offers booking inside Teams and two-way sync with Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace, so for Teams-first companies the 2 are close.

In every demo, ask the vendor to book a desk inside your own Teams or Slack while you watch. We’d weigh that test above any feature checklist, because a booking that needs another login gets skipped on busy mornings.

Coordination is part of the product

In our Sofia office, 76.2% of attendance across 13,024 desk bookings over 12 months came from one-off bookings. People decided week by week, around colleagues, meetings and projects.

The product is built for that. Employees can see when teammates plan to come in, get suggested office days, and invite their team to collaboration days. On Professional, attendance policy reports sit next to utilization, so HR and Facilities work from the same numbers.

Desks and rooms are priced separately

OfficeRnD Workplace charges 1 rate for desks and other resources and a separate rate for meeting rooms. Skedda charges every desk, room, parking spot, and locker at the same rate.

Take a 120-person office with 60 desks, 10 parking spots, and 6 meeting rooms. On OfficeRnD’s Start plan, that’s $188 a month on annual billing (70 resources at $2, 6 rooms at $8). On Skedda, the same office counts as 76 spaces, more than double the 35 included in the US Plus plan, so you’d need a quote.

Headcount works the other way. Skedda allows unlimited users on every plan, while OfficeRnD’s Start plan covers up to 150 users. See the full Workplace pricing breakdown.

Onboarding and support

Professional includes guided onboarding and training, priority support, and a monthly Q&A session. Enterprise adds a dedicated Customer Success Manager.

I’d schedule a policy review for week 6 of any rollout. That’s usually when people start ignoring the first rule, and fixing it then costs far less than relaunching the policy months later.

78.8% of OfficeRnD’s G2 reviewers come from mid-market companies. They praise ease of use and the mobile app. Their most common request is a way to switch desks without cancelling and rebooking.

Why it ranks first despite Skedda’s higher G2 scores

The G2 gaps are 0.1 to 0.3 points. Skedda’s score also includes studios, clubs, and community venues, which are different buyers from a hybrid office.

If you’re reading this, you already use Skedda, and you’re looking because of something those scores don’t measure: a bill that grows with every parking spot, or people who come in to find their team at home. OfficeRnD Workplace is built around those 2 problems.

Pros

  • Booking inside MS Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar, and Slack
  • Team coordination and attendance policy reports built in
  • Desks and rooms priced separately
  • Stellar onboarding and support
  • Time to go live is around 2 hours for small organizations

Cons

  • Less suited to very small organizations. The $99 monthly minimum and the 150-user cap on Start fit mid-sized offices best.

When OfficeRnD Workplace fits better than Skedda

  • Your employees choose their office days, and the main complaint is coming in to an empty floor
  • You’re adding parking or desks, and per-space billing keeps pushing you into the next tier
  • HR needs attendance against policy in the same reports Facilities uses
  • You want resource booking and facility requests, like a broken chair or a room that’s too cold, handled in the same tool

Stay on Skedda if your main job is controlling access to labs, studios, or classrooms with strict quotas and approvals. Its rules engine goes further there.

#2 Robin: best for enterprises running several floors or buildings

Robin is a workplace platform for large offices. Desk, room, parking and locker booking sit next to space planning tools: a drag-and-drop map editor, office neighborhoods, scenario planning and move management. Visitors, deliveries, room displays and employee surveys are part of the same platform.

Robin says it’s designed for companies with 500 or more employees, with at least a third using the office regularly. Its pricing page also lists 150+ hybrid employees and multiple floors, offices, or buildings as signs you’re a fit.

How it differs from Skedda

If you’re on Starter, anything older than 12 months may already be gone, so export what’s left now, even if the switch is months away.

Export by month or quarter if you have several years of data. Ask Skedda how long it keeps your data after cancellation, and ask the new vendor whether it can import that history into its reports or only keep it as a file. OfficeRnD’s onboarding team helps import your bookings and floor plans during setup, so ask the same question of every vendor on your list.

Unpair room calendars before you connect the new tool

Skedda’s two-way sync links its spaces to your Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace room calendars. Your new tool will want write access to the same room calendars.

If both tools write to 1 room calendar at the same time, a booking made in 1 can overwrite or duplicate a booking made in the other. The result shows up on a Monday morning as 2 teams outside the same boardroom.

Plan the cutover in this order:

  1. Export your booking history from Skedda.
  2. List every recurring booking that runs past the cutover date. Recurring bookings don’t move between tools on their own.
  3. Unpair Skedda’s room sync for each room.
  4. Connect the new tool and grant its calendar permissions in Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace.
  5. Recreate the recurring bookings, or ask the new vendor to import them.
  6. Run 1 week with Skedda in read-only mode before you close the account.

The permissions step needs an admin who can approve app access in Microsoft 365, often a Global Administrator, so book that person’s time before the cutover date. If you’re rolling it out across Microsoft 365, the same admin will approve the Teams app.

Security reviews

Each vendor publishes its own security and compliance documents, and those are what IT should read, not a comparison article.

Ask every vendor on your shortlist for 3 things before the demo: its completed security questionnaire, where your data is hosted, and which subprocessors handle it.

For OfficeRnD, those documents are in our security and compliance documentation.

What to check in a demo or trial

A vendor’s demo shows the product working on the vendor’s office. Your switch depends on how it works on yours: your floor plan, your Teams tenant, your busiest Tuesday. Before the call, send the vendor your floor plan, 1 week of your Skedda export and the tests below, so they set up a demo account that looks like your office.

You’ll probably be the only person on the first call, so run it from 3 points of view: the employee booking from a phone, the admin who’ll maintain the floor plan, and IT. Do the IT tests in the security call, and ask 2 or 3 colleagues to try the employee tests in the trial or pilot, on their own phones.

The employee’s side

Start by booking a desk from inside your own Teams, Slack or Outlook. It should take under a minute, with no new login and no jump to another app. If it needs a separate app, expect people to skip it on busy mornings.

Then pick up a phone. Book a desk, check in, and move to a different desk. Count the taps for the desk change. On OfficeRnD, it means cancelling and rebooking, and G2 reviewers mention it, so you’ll want to see how each tool handles it.

Next, find out which day a named teammate plans to come in, and book the desk next to them. You should see that from the booking screen, without messaging the teammate first.

Last, book a room or parking spot for 1 hour, from 14:00 to 15:00. Some tools book desks only by half or full day, which works for hot desking and breaks for a car park.

The admin’s side

Ask to make floor plan changes yourself: move 3 desks, rename a neighborhood and block 1 desk for a week. If any of that needs a support ticket, picture doing it every time a team grows or shrinks.

Book a desk, don’t check in, and watch what happens. The desk should go back to the pool after the window you set.

This test matters more than it looks. In our Sofia office, across 13,024 desk bookings over 12 months, 9.1% were booked and never checked into, and auto-cancel released them. That’s about 4.5 desks a day, or roughly 8% of office capacity. Without check-in, those desks show up in your reports as used, and your next space decision starts from the wrong number.

Then ask for last month’s utilization report. It should separate booked desks from checked-in desks, and the vendor should tell you how many months of history your plan keeps. Finally, hand over your Skedda CSV export and ask whether it goes into their reports or stays a file you keep on the side.

IT’s side

Sign in through your own identity provider in the trial or demo account, and ask which plan includes SCIM. Then pair 1 test room calendar and book it twice, once from Outlook and once from the tool. The booking should show up in both places within a minute, with no duplicate.

Questions for the pricing call

The demo tests the product. These 4 questions test the bill:

  1. What exactly counts toward the price? Per-user tools define an active user differently, and the answer decides whether part-timers, contractors, and people who book twice a year all cost a full seat. Ask for an example invoice.
  2. Which plan puts me where I’ll be in 24 months? Bring your expected headcount, number of offices, desks plus rooms, and whether parking is coming. Tier caps on users, locations and spaces are where most surprise upgrades come from.
  3. Which add-ons will I need in year 1, and what do they cost? Visitor management, room displays, extra analytics history, SSO and setup services are priced separately on most tools here.
  4. What happens to my data if I leave? Ask how you export bookings and check-ins, in what format, and how long the vendor keeps your data after the contract ends.

Trials and demos on this list

Skedda, deskbird and Dibsido offer free trials with no credit card. desk.ly has a free plan for up to 15 users with every Enterprise feature, which works as an open-ended trial. OfficeRnD, Robin, and YAROOMS run demos instead.

If you’d like to look around before a call, you can click through a product tour of OfficeRnD Workplace, and YAROOMS has a recorded platform tour.

On any demo, including ours, ask the vendor to share control or let you name each click. A demo where the vendor drives shows you the path the vendor picked.

See OfficeRnD Workplace on your own office

If your Skedda bill grows with every parking spot, or people come in to find their team working from home, OfficeRnD Workplace is built for those 2 problems. Employees book desks, rooms, and parking from Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar, or Slack. They can also see who’s coming in and plan their week around their team. Facilities gets utilization from check-ins, and the bill grows with your desks and rooms.

Bring your floor plan and a month of your Skedda export to the call. We’ll show you how your busiest weekday looks in OfficeRnD Workplace, book a desk inside your own Teams or Slack, and price your exact count of desks, rooms, and parking spots.

Every hybrid office we’ve worked with reaches the same question sooner or later: how much space do we need? A lease renewal is coming up, or headcount is growing, and the only evidence on the table is a spreadsheet of desk bookings nobody trusts.

The best space management software answers that question with numbers you can defend in a budget meeting. It does 3 jobs. It runs bookings and rules for desks, rooms, and parking.

It measures how that space gets used. And it turns those measurements into planning decisions. A few tools cover all 3 well. Most are strong in 1 or 2.

I’ve spent years helping workplace, facilities, and IT teams choose and roll out these tools. For this guide, I compared 14 platforms using G2 ratings, vendor pricing and documentation, hands-on testing where I had it, and a full year of booking data from our own office.

And before you cringe – full disclosure: OfficeRnD Workplace is our product. I explain how I kept the ranking fair in the methodology section.

The best space management software for most hybrid offices in 2026 is OfficeRnD Workplace. People book desks, rooms, and parking inside from Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, or Slack, and check-in with auto-release keeps utilization data accurate. Built-in workplace analytics then show utilization by day, booking and no-show patterns, and attendance against your hybrid policy. It holds a 4.6/5 rating from 158 G2 reviews (as of September 2026) and is a G2 Leader in Space Management for Mid-Market, Fall 2026.

Other picks for specific needs:

  • Skedda, for detailed booking rules. Quotas, booking windows, and approval flows go deeper than most tools, and pricing is per space, so adding employees doesn’t raise the bill.
  • OfficeSpace Software, for space planning and moves. It adds move management, asset tracking, and maintenance requests to desk and room booking.
  • Spaceti, for sensor-based occupancy data. It pairs booking with occupancy sensors and environmental monitoring, which suits teams that need desk-level measurement.
  • Gable, for hybrid offices with remote staff. It runs desk, room, and visitor booking for your offices, and an add-on gives remote employees access to 17,000+ coworking spaces.
  • Floor Plan Mapper, for the tightest budget. It starts at $28 a month for 2 floor plans with unlimited users and desks, and $148 a month covers unlimited floors. The trade-off is lighter booking and reporting

Review Methodology

First, OfficeRnD Workplace went through the same scorecard as every other tool on this list. No vendor paid for placement, and I named where our own product falls short in its review.

The 3 layers I scored against

Space management software does 3 jobs, and I judged every tool on each one:

  1. Booking and rules: desks, rooms, parking, and other resources, with booking policies, check-in, and auto-release of no-shows.
  2. Measuring use: how the tool knows who showed up, through check-ins, Wi-Fi, badge data, or sensors.
  3. Planning: utilization trends, peak-day reporting, and the data behind moves, sizing, and lease decisions.

The comparison table below shows which layers each tool covers.

Measurement and planning carry 34 points combined, more than in our desk booking software guide or hybrid work software guide. That’s deliberate. A space decision is only as good as the utilization data behind it. If your priorities differ, re-weight the table and the ranking will shift with you.

Where the information came from

G2 was my primary source. I weighed rating, review count, and recency together, so a 4.8 from 75 reviews reads differently to me than a 4.6 from 260.

I also read the reviews for recurring praise and complaints, and flagged review bases that needed context, such as incentivized reviews or large clusters from a single month. Every G2 number was checked in September 2026.

Next came each vendor’s own pages: product, pricing, documentation, integrations, and security. Where sources conflicted, the vendor’s pricing page won. Where I couldn’t verify something, the review says so.

I also tested several tools hands-on, and each review states whether it was tested. Last but not least, the article was fact-checked by product experts Ivan Guberkov – CEO and former Chief Product Officer at OfficeRnD, and Ivaylo Ivanov, VP of Product at OfficeRnD.

How our own data fits in

We run our own office on OfficeRnD Workplace, and a year of that data (13,024 desk bookings from August 2025 to August 2026) shaped how I judged measurement features.

9.1% of those bookings were ghost bookings, auto-canceled when nobody checked in. A tool without check-in would have counted every one of them as a used desk. So when a vendor says it reports utilization, the first thing I check is how it knows someone showed up.

Also, I know it’s one office, so I use it as a reference point for evaluating features, not as an industry benchmark.

#1 OfficeRnD Workplace: best space management system overall

Best for: Hybrid offices that want one platform to book space, see how it’s used, and make space decisions with data they can trust.

OfficeRnD Workplace is a full workplace management platform for hybrid offices. Desk, room, and parking booking, visitor management, an internal helpdesk, and workplace analytics run in one system, and employees use it from Microsoft Teams and Outlook, Google Calendar and Chrome, or Slack.

Key space management features

  • Booking and rules. Desks, rooms, parking, and custom resources such as lockers or labs, on interactive floor plans with team neighborhoods and admin-set booking policies. You can also book desks and parking spots in one flow.
  • Space usage tracking. Mandatory check-in, automatic release of no-shows, QR check-in, and Wi-Fi auto check-in, so reports count people who showed up.
  • Workplace analytics. Utilization by resource and day, booking and no-show patterns, and attendance against your hybrid policy, with custom dashboards and scheduled email reports.
  • Space setup and operations. Spaces built from created or imported resources, a helpdesk for office requests, and Visitor Hub for guests and deliveries (add-on).
  • Team coordination. Employees see when teammates plan to come in, save favorite colleagues, and get suggested office days.

Why I rank it #1

Every space decision depends on knowing which booked desks were used, and OfficeRnD Workplace gets that number right without hardware. Check-in and auto-release remove no-shows from the data, and Wi-Fi auto check-in confirms presence without anyone tapping a button.

The coordination features keep that data complete. Employees see when teammates plan to come in and get suggested office days, so teams come in on the same days and book through the system to find each other.

Complete booking data is what makes the analytics worth trusting, and the reports put space use and policy attendance side by side, so Facilities and HR work from the same numbers. If you want to see it before talking to sales, OfficeRnD Workplace has an interactive product tour you can click through yourself.

From our own office: We run our Sofia office on OfficeRnD Workplace with check-in required for every desk booking. Over 12 months and 13,024 bookings, 9.1% were auto-canceled as no-shows and 25.6% were canceled ahead of time.

Auto-release alone returned about 4.5 desks a day to the pool, roughly 8% of the office. When we moved offices, the same data helped us size the new one. See the full 12-month breakdown.

Customers use it the same way. Tavistock Restaurant Collection moved its corporate staff to a Tuesday-to-Thursday hybrid policy and gave up excess office space by sharing offices with its parent company.

It replaced Excel-based booking with OfficeRnD Workplace inside Microsoft Teams and manages the shared office and a corporate apartment in one system.

We built Workplace analytics on the bookings people make and the check-ins they confirm. When we moved offices, that was the data we used to decide how many desks we needed. – Ivaylo Ivanov, VP Product, OfficeRnD

What real users think

On G2, reviewers consistently mention ease of use and the Teams and Outlook integration, and several say they were up and running within a few hours. The most common requests are more customization options and better calendar synchronization.

  • Start: from $99/mo (annual), $2 per bookable resource, $8 per meeting room, up to 150 users
  • Professional: from $399/mo (annual), $3 per resource, $10 per meeting room, up to 1,000 users

  • Analytics tied to policy: space use and attendance in the same reports
  • Stellar onboarding and support
  • Pricing follows space: more employees than desks doesn’t raise the bill
  • Strong security: SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, GDPR, CCPA

  • No lease or move planning: large portfolios may need an IWMS too

  • Space usage tracking. Check-in with auto-release, plus Wi-Fi presence detection through a desktop app for Mac and Windows.

Why it’s on the list

Skedda has one of the deepest rules engines in this category, and I think that matters more than most buyers expect.

Once an office has fewer desks than people, the rules decide how space gets shared: who gets priority, how far ahead people can book, and how many days each person gets. Most of the booking complaints I hear from workplace teams are rules problems in disguise.

What users think

Should you choose OfficeSpace Software?

Robin covers more of the office day than most tools here, from the desk booking to the catering order for the meeting room.

For an enterprise running dozens of sites, fewer point tools means fewer contracts and one data set. Robin’s own pricing page says it’s designed for companies with 500+ employees and more than 150 hybrid employees using the office, and I’d take that guidance at face value.

I took Elia’s product tour, which is gated: you have to leave an email address to start it. The design is good and intuitive, and the booking flow is easy to follow. The analytics felt basic, though, and overall the tour showed fewer features than I expected.

The pricing page is consistent with that: Basic includes “basic reports and analytics,” and custom reports need Business at twice the price. If reporting will drive your space decisions, Kadence, OfficeRnD Workplace, or WorkInSync go further on the plans most mid-sized offices buy.

What users think

G2 reviewers praise ease of use, the floor plan, fast setup with Microsoft 365, and responsive support.

Complaints include occupancy analytics that sometimes undercount busy days, data that can’t be extracted, clunky floor plan edits, and permissions that are hard to manage. Almost all 40 reviews arrived within a few weeks in July 2026, so treat the score as early.

Pricing and onboarding

  • Pricing model: per plan, capped by bookable places, unlimited users
  • Basic: 500/mo monthly), up to 250 places, basic reports, SSO, Microsoft 365
  • Business: 1,000/mo monthly), up to 1,000 places, custom reports and dashboards, user provisioning, account manager
  • Enterprise: custom; AI analytics, API, audit logs, SLAs
  • Hardware: desk sensor $50, room sensor $500, gateway $300, room display $1,100, kiosk $5,000

Unlimited users is a fair model for hybrid offices, much like OfficeRnD’s and Skedda’s per-space pricing.

The entry point is high for a small office, though. A 30-desk office pays the same $5,000 a year as a 250-desk one, which is more than Eden or OfficeRnD Workplace would charge at that size.

Pros

  • Own sensors at published prices
  • Full French and English interface
  • Unlimited users on every plan

Cons

  • Basic analytics on the entry plan
  • High entry price for small offices
  • Floor plan edits and permissions can be clunky

Should you choose Elia?

Yes, if you want an easy booking tool with the option to add sensors later, particularly if your teams work in French. If you need deeper reporting at a mid-market price, compare OfficeRnD Workplace or Kadence. If sensors are the main requirement across a large campus, Spaceti goes further.

# 13 Roomzilla: best space management tool for meeting rooms

Best for: Offices, coworking spaces, and multi-tenant buildings where meeting rooms are the main shared resource, and a landlord or building team manages booking for several companies.

G2 rating4.3 / 5 (212)
PricingPer resource. Free up to 3 resources; Standard $10/resource/mo; Business $17/room and $10/desk/mo (annual)
StandoutRoom-first booking with tablet displays, guest access, and paid guest reservations for shared buildings
Best fitSmall businesses and shared buildings
Space usage trackingCheck-in with auto-cancelation of no-shows, QR check-in, and check-in from room tablets

Roomzilla focuses on meeting rooms and does that job well. The software also handles desks and equipment. Users book from a web timeline, an interactive map, QR codes, or tablets outside each room, with Google Workspace and Outlook calendar sync.

Key space management features

  • Space booking. Rooms, desks, and equipment on a timeline or interactive map, with amenity filters, room photos, recurring bookings, and an approval queue.
  • Space usage tracking. Check-in with automatic cancelation of no-shows, QR codes for ad-hoc bookings, and check-in or on-the-spot booking from paired room tablets.
  • Shared-building controls. Guest read-only access, guest reservations, public sign-up with a trusted-domain allowlist, and payments for guest bookings.
  • Booking rules. Daily, weekly, and monthly limits, max simultaneous bookings, and different limits per team.

Why it’s on the list

Roomzilla is the most room-focused tool here, and it’s built for buildings where several companies share the same rooms. Its customers include innovation centers such as CIC and LabCentral, and many G2 reviewers are tenants booking rooms their landlord manages. Paid guest reservations are rare on this list and useful if you rent rooms to outside groups.

I took the free trial and explored the features. The product is quite basic, but intuitive enough, and the design is good. A few G2 reviewers call it dated; I found it clean. The simplicity makes sense for a room-focused tool, and I think people who only manage rooms will appreciate it. The booking flow is intuitive, but in my view not as smooth as some other tools on this list.

The analytics are limited, yet they give you what matters for rooms: booking history and usage data you can export. Reports sit on the Business plan. If you need attendance trends or desk utilization, Kadence, OfficeRnD Workplace, or WorkInSync go much further.

What users think

G2 reviewers praise ease of use, the quick booking flow, and room tablets that show how much time is left in a meeting. Recurring complaints are the mobile experience (there’s no native app, so booking runs in the mobile browser), calendar sync issues, a design some find dated, and room filters that could go deeper. Most recent reviews are organic.

Pricing and onboarding

  • Free: up to 3 resources, with check-in and QR codes
  • Standard: $10/resource/mo annual ($12 monthly); adds calendar sync
  • Business: $17/room and $10/desk/mo annual ($20 and $12 monthly); adds reports, team-level limits, guest payments, and room tablets
  • Trial: 14 days, no card needed; discounts above 30 resources

Room pricing is fair for a small office: 10 rooms on Business cost $170 a month. Desks get expensive fast. Adding 50 desks raises that to $670 a month, while Eden starts at $2.25 per desk and OfficeRnD Workplace at $2 per resource.

Pros

  • Clean, simple room booking
  • Built for shared and multi-tenant buildings
  • Free plan and card-free trial

Cons

  • Limited analytics, reports on Business only
  • No native mobile app
  • Expensive per desk

Should you choose Roomzilla?

Roomzilla is for you if meeting rooms are your main shared resource, especially in a coworking space or multi-tenant building. If desks are a big part of your office, Eden and Skedda cost less per desk, and OfficeRnD Workplace or Kadence add team coordination and deeper reporting.

  • Space booking. Desks and rooms on the floor plan, by the hour, day, week, or on a recurring basis, with email reminders.
  • Seating plans and directory. Drag-and-drop seating, employee profiles and photos synced from Active Directory, Office 365, or Entra ID, and automatic seat assignments from Office 365.

Why it’s on the list

Floor Plan Mapper is by far the cheapest tool here. Every plan includes every feature, and even the unlimited plan costs $148 a month for any number of users, desks, and rooms.

For a law firm or campus that mainly needs people to find colleagues, rooms, and printers, that price is hard to argue with. G2 reviewers, many of them IT admins, praise how well it syncs with Active Directory. Like YAROOMS, it also offers an on-premise version.

I took the free trial. I liked that it comes with a good setup and administration guide. But I’d prefer an interactive demo or tour that shows what each option means, as other tools on this list do.

In Floor Plan Mapper, you have to do the work to get a feel for the platform: create or upload a map, then configure a lot of settings before anything is bookable. That takes time. I prefer tools where everything is preconfigured, and you can start testing right away, as with the product tours from Robin or OfficeRnD Workplace, for example.

I didn’t find an analytics feature during the trial, and I think analytics are a must-have for space management. Floor Plan Mapper’s office management page says it tracks occupancy and usage trends from logins and bookings, with visual reports, but reporting isn’t listed in any pricing plan. One G2 reviewer names the lack of reporting as a dislike, while another mentions downloading reports from the data. If utilization data drives your decisions, ask for a live walkthrough of the reports before buying, or look at OfficeRnD, Kadence, or OfficeSpace.

What users think

G2 reviewers praise ease of use, the Active Directory and Entra integration, low cost, and responsive support. Recurring complaints are printing maps, desk edits that are disabled while directory sync is on, slow floor plan uploads, and no way to assign one person to more than one desk.

Pricing and onboarding

  • Medium: $42/mo, 3 to 6 floor plans
  • Medium to large: $72/mo, 7 to 10 floor plans

Pros

  • Lowest price on this list
  • Strong Active Directory and Office 365 sync
  • Cloud or on-premise hosting

Cons

  • No clear analytics or check-in
  • Setup takes work before you can test
  • Printing and desk editing are clunky

So, should you choose Floor Plan Mapper?

Choose Floor Plan Mapper if you want an affordable, always-current seating chart and staff directory, and desk booking is a secondary need.

If you need to measure how space is used, OfficeRnD Workplace, Kadence, or Skedda can give you check-in and usage data. For moves and stack planning, OfficeSpace goes much further.

Honorable Mentions

These 3 space management tools score well in G2’s Space Management category and are worth a demo if none of the main 14 fits. G2 figures were checked October 2, 2026.

deskbird

G2: 4.5 (310) | Pricing: from $3.75 per active user/mo, billed annually

Swiss-built deskbird covers desks, rooms, parking, visitors, and workplace ticketing, with native Teams and Slack apps. A free Starter plan covers up to 15 users. On Professional and above, its deskbird Dock app checks people in from their laptop. G2 reviewers like how simple booking is. Their most common complaints are notifications and default booking times. Our OfficeRnD Workplace vs deskbird comparison covers how the two differ.

Archie

G2: 4.9 (244) | Pricing: desk booking from $159/mo (Starter) and $249/mo (Pro)

Montreal-based Archie has the highest G2 score of any tool in this article. It sells desk booking, room scheduling, and visitor management as separate products, plus software for coworking operators. It charges per desk or room, with no per-user fee. Reviewers praise ease of use. The most common complaint is tight check-in windows with no location-based check-in. If you run a flex space next to your own office, Archie can cover both.

Tactic

G2: 4.6 (554) | Pricing: quote-based, priced by resources

Tactic has the most G2 reviews of any tool here. It’s modular. Employees get desk and room booking, visitors, and office-day planning. Workplace teams get requests, move management, space management, and an AI assistant called Tessa. Its online estimator puts desk booking for 100 desks at 1 location at $3,600 to $4,800 a year. G2 reviewers praise the booking flow, and several mention slow loading and a cluttered interface.

How to choose the right space management software for you

The right tool depends on 2 things: which decisions you need to make, and which data you trust to make them. Below is a simple, yet efficient process, along with the metrics to track and the questions I’d ask in every demo.

Features to look for in each layer

Most mid-sized offices need layers 1 and 2 done well, plus the basics of layer 3. Full planning suites pay off when you manage many buildings or run moves every quarter.

LayerWhat it answersMust-havesWorth paying more for
Booking and rulesCan people get the space they need?Desks, rooms, and parking on a floor map. Booking from Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar, or Slack. Neighborhoods, booking windows, and approvalsTeam and recurring bookings, custom resources such as labs or lockers, room displays
Measuring useWas the booked space used?Check-in with auto-release, no-show and cancellation reports, attendance by teamWi-Fi or badge presence for automatic check-in. Sensors for rooms and open areas
PlanningHow much space do we need?Utilization by day, floor, and team. Peak-day views. At least a year of history. CSV or API exportScenario modeling, stack plans, and move management for large portfolios

Know what kind of data you’re buying

Every tool builds its utilization numbers from 1 or more of these sources:

Data sourceWhat it tells youWhat it missesCost
BookingsWho planned to come in and whereNo-shows, walk-ins, unbooked spaceIncluded
Check-ins with auto-releaseWhich booked desks and rooms were usedUnbooked space, and how long people stayedIncluded in most tools
Wi-Fi or badge presenceWho was in the building, without anyone tapping a buttonWhich desk or room they usedLow. Needs IT setup
Occupancy sensorsUse of every desk, room, and open area, booked or notWho used itHardware, installation, and maintenance

For desks with enforced check-in, check-in data is accurate enough to size an office. Sensors add the most for rooms and open areas.

Utilization metrics worth tracking

  • Typical-day desk utilization. Desks used on a normal working day, divided by total desks. Leave out holidays and closure days, or the average drifts down.
  • Peak-day utilization. How full your busiest days get, and how often you cross a threshold such as 80%. Capacity decisions belong here.
  • No-show rate. Bookings auto-canceled after a missed check-in. If it rises, your booking data is overstating demand.
  • Cancellation rate. Bookings released in advance. These are good, because desks go back to the pool. A very high rate on one day, often from recurring bookings people forget, means that day’s bookings overstate demand.
  • Day-of-week spread. The gap between your busiest and quietest day. It tells you whether to add desks or spread demand across the week.
  • Attendance against policy. Office days by team, compared with what your hybrid policy asks for. It shows which teams need better coordination and which need a different policy.
  • Room fit. People per meeting against room capacity. You need room sensors or people counters to measure it, and it often shows you have too few small rooms.

For outside benchmarks, sensor vendor XY Sense publishes the Workplace Utilization Index, built from 63,000+ sensor-tracked workspaces. It put average global utilization at 43% in 2025, still below pre-pandemic levels of about 60% to 65%. In Q1 2026:

  • Tuesday reached 52% and Friday 30%.
  • 25% of desks went unused on a given day.
  • Meetings with 1 or 2 people made up 68% of all sessions.

Sensor figures measure time in use. Booking-based figures count a desk as used once someone checks in, so they usually run higher. Compare your numbers with your own history first.

6 steps to choosing the right tool

#1 Name the decisions the data has to support

Different questions need different data:”Can we drop a floor?” needs peak-day data by floor.

  • “Is the 3-day policy working?” needs attendance by team.
  • “Why are rooms always full?” needs room occupancy.

Write these down with IT, HR, Facilities, and Finance before the first demo. The list tells you which layer to weight most, and it keeps each team’s must-haves visible from day one.

# 2 Put booking where people already work

Your data only means something if people use the tool. If most employees live in Teams, give 5 of them the same task in a native Teams app and in an Outlook add-in, then compare.

Also check that people can see who’s coming in and book near their team. People come to the office for colleagues.

#4 Set only the rules you’ll enforce.

Start with booking windows, check-in, and auto-release. Add neighborhoods, approvals, and quotas when a real conflict shows up. Every rule is one more thing to explain to employees.

#5 Measure use, then test the analytics against a real decision

Treat check-in with auto-release as a requirement. Without it, your utilization data counts ghost bookings as attendance.

Then ask each vendor to show peak days by floor for the last 12 months, and how much history each plan keeps.

In our own office, a typical day ran at 63% desk utilization over a full year, while Mondays averaged 73.3%. Our takeaway from that year of data was to plan capacity around the busiest day.

#5 Cover the rest of the office day

List every shared resource: parking, lockers, labs, visitor sign-in, room displays. Check whether each one is in the plan you’re quoted or sold as an add-on, and price it now.

#6 Check security, then run a pilot

  • Ask for a SOC 2 Type 2 or ISO 27001 report.
  • Confirm SSO and SCIM are on the plan you’ll buy.
  • Check that admin roles match how your offices are run.
  • In the EU, ask where data is hosted and review the GDPR terms.

Then pilot on one floor or site for 4 to 6 weeks with check-in switched on. Those weeks will teach you more about adoption and no-shows than any demo.

Demo checklist

Ask the vendor to...A good answer looks like
Book a desk for you from Teams or Slack, liveDone in under a minute, without opening another app
Show what happens when you skip check-inThe desk is released and appears in a no-show report
Show last quarter's peak days by floorA chart by day and floor, filterable by team
Export the raw booking and check-in dataCSV or API, including canceled and auto-released bookings
Show who's coming in this week and book next to themColleagues visible on the map before you pick a desk
Add a parking space or locker as a bookable resourceAn admin sets it up in minutes, with no support ticket
List what each plan includes for analyticsHistory length and report types, per plan
Quote the full first-year costSetup, floor plans, add-ons, and hardware itemized
Share security documentsA SOC 2 Type 2 or ISO 27001 report under NDA
Commit to a go-live dateA date, plus a reference customer of your size you can call

What empty desks cost, and when the software pays for itself

The hard truth is that every empty desk costs you rent, cleaning, and energy, whether anyone books it or not. A space management platform pays off when its data lets you stop paying for desks you don’t need. These 4 numbers tell you whether that will happen in your office, and how fast.

#1 The cost of a desk in use

Add up your annual office cost: rent, service charges, cleaning, and utilities. Divide it by the number of desks, then by your typical-day utilization.

Example: a 12,000 sq ft office with 80 desks. At the US average full-service listing rate of $33.20 per square foot (CommercialEdge, August 2026), it costs about $398,400 a year:

  • That’s $4,980 per desk.
  • At 50% typical-day utilization, each desk in use costs $9,960 a year.

Use your own lease figures. National averages hide big gaps between cities. And here’s a quick office space planning guide.

#2 The desks you need

Size to peak-day attendance plus a 10 to 15% margin. Our guide on how much office space you need explains the method.

Continuing the example: 12 months of data show the office never goes above 60 desks in use. With a 15% margin, you need 69 desks, and 11 are surplus.

Before you have booking data, use badge swipes, Wi-Fi logs, or a pilot. Our free office space calculator models peak-day attendance and desk sharing based on your team size and hybrid policy, then exports a PDF report you can share. In addition, you can check the ideal amount of office space per hybrid employee.

#3 What the surplus is worth

Surplus desks turn into savings in 3 ways:

  • At the next lease event, you give up space.
  • When you hire, new people take desks you already have.
  • On quiet days, you close a floor and save its cleaning and energy.

In the example, the 11 surplus desks take up about 1,650 sq ft at 150 sq ft per desk, including shared areas. That’s about $54,780 a year.

#4 The payback

Payback in months = first-year software cost ÷ (annual savings ÷ 12)

Use the full first-year quote: setup, floor plans, add-ons, and any hardware. With a $10,000 first-year quote, the example pays back in just over 2 months.

Lease savings arrive on a date: a renewal, a sublease, or an expansion you avoid. Write that date next to the payback figure, because it’s the first thing anyone approving the budget will ask.

So, here’s the summary in a table format:

NumberHow to get itExample
Cost per desk in useAnnual office cost ÷ desks ÷ typical-day utilization$9,960
Desks neededPeak-day attendance + 10 to 15%69 of 80
Annual value of the surplusSurplus sq ft × cost per sq ft$54,780
PaybackFirst-year software cost ÷ monthly savingsJust over 2 months
Savings startNext lease event, hire, or floor closureYour lease date

List softer gains separately, such as admin hours saved or better attendance on team days. The hard numbers carry more weight on their own.

Pricing compared at 3 office sizes

Like it or not, most pricing pages show a starting price. That number tells you little until you know what each tool charges for: desks, rooms, users, or plan tiers.

Below are the 4 pricing models on this list, then what 6 tools with public prices would cost for the same 3 offices.

The 4 pricing models:

ModelsCost followsTools on the listWatch for
Per bookable resourceDesks and roomsOfficeRnD Workplace, Skedda, Gable, Roomzilla, Eden, ArchiePlan minimums, and user caps on some plans
Per user or active userHeadcountWorkInSync, deskbird, KadenceUser minimums, and how "active" is defined
Flat tiersSize bands (users, places, or floor plans)YAROOMS, Elia, Floor Plan MapperPrice jumps when you cross a tier
Quote onlyWhatever the contract saysOfficeSpace, Robin, Eptura, Spaceti, TacticSetup and hardware hidden inside the quote

What 6 tools cost for the same offices

All 3 offices share desks at about 1.4 employees per desk:

  • Small: 50 employees, 35 desks, 4 meeting rooms
  • Mid-sized: 200 employees, 140 desks, 12 meeting rooms
  • Large: 800 employees, 560 desks, 40 meeting rooms

Prices are monthly list prices on annual billing, using the entry plan that fits each office, before volume discounts.

ToolHow it chargesSmallMid-sizedLarge
OfficeRnD Workplace$2 per resource + $8 per room (Start, $99 minimum, up to 150 users); $3 + $10 (Professional, $399 minimum, up to 1,000 users)$102$540$2,080
Gable Essentials$4 per bookable resource$156$608$2,400
Eden$2.25 per desk in sets of 25, + $15 per room$173$518$1,894
WorkInSync$2.25 per user, 250-user minimum$563$563$1,800
deskbird Business$3.75 per active user (all employees active)$188$750$3,000
Roomzilla Business$10 per desk + $17 per room$418$1,604$6,280

What the numbers show:

  • Small office: OfficeRnD Workplace costs the least. Minimums hurt small offices most. WorkInSync charges for 250 users even if you have 50.
  • Mid-sized office: Eden, OfficeRnD Workplace, and WorkInSync come within $45 of each other. At this size, choose on features.
  • Large office: per-user pricing with a low rate catches up. WorkInSync is the lowest at 800 people, with Eden and OfficeRnD Workplace close behind.
  • Active-user billing gets cheaper the fewer people book. If only 60% of deskbird users book in a month, the large-office cost drops to $1,800.
  • Desk-heavy offices on room-first tools pay the most. Roomzilla is priced for rooms, and 560 desks at $10 each add up.

The plans aren’t identical. In the mid-sized and large offices, OfficeRnD’s price is for Professional, which includes SSO, Wi-Fi check-in, and attendance policy analytics. Eden’s figure covers desks and rooms only.

Compare what each plan includes before comparing totals. For another per-user example, see our OfficeRnD Workplace vs desk.ly comparison.

Skedda isn’t in the table because its US per-space rate beyond the 35 included spaces isn’t published. Plus starts at $249 a month for 35 spaces.

Costs that don’t show in the starting price

  • Visitor management is usually priced per location. For example, Eden charges $89, Skedda $99, and Gable $199 a month. OfficeRnD’s Visitor Hub is also an add-on on every plan.
  • Floor plan setup: Kadence charges $250 per floor. Gable says it charges no setup fee.
  • Minimums: WorkInSync bills at least 250 users, Eden sells desks in sets of 25, and OfficeRnD’s plans have $99 and $399 monthly minimums.
  • User caps: OfficeRnD Start covers up to 150 users and Professional up to 1,000. YAROOMS tiers cap users, locations, and spaces.
  • Hardware: Elia sells desk sensors at $50 and room sensors at $500. Room displays and kiosks add more.
  • Monthly billing: OfficeRnD charges 25% less on annual billing, Eden $2.25 vs $3 per desk, and Roomzilla $10 vs $12 per resource.
  • Plan jumps: check which plan includes the features you listed in step 1 of the buyer guide. SSO, Wi-Fi check-in, parking, and API access often sit one tier up.

Try OfficeRnD Workplace to manage your office space

If you want one tool that handles bookings, check-ins, and the utilization data you’ll use to plan your office, OfficeRnD Workplace ticks all those boxes with a bang.

People book desks, rooms, and parking inside Teams, Slack, Outlook, or Google Calendar. Check-in rules release no-show desks automatically. The reports come from bookings people actually confirm, and that data was enough to size our own new office.

For most hybrid offices, start with OfficeRnD Workplace. Book a demo and see it running on your own floor plan.

Name: Flex operators know which integrations they need. Most haven’t connected them.
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: TL;DR
Post body:
TL;DR

  • We looked at connection data from 1,276 flex operator accounts. Exactly 1 has all 5 core categories connected: payments, accounting, door access, CRM, and network.
  • The average operator has 1.65 of 5 connected. 14% have none.
  • Operators know what they need. 57% call accounting integration a must-have; 40% have it switched on. For door access it’s 54% vs 30%.
  • 68% of operators name integration gaps as their top tech challenge, up from 61% in 2025.
  • AI use dropped from 26% to 18%. Two-thirds of AI users feed their tools by hand or pay for a custom build.
  • Fix: a one-hour audit of what’s connected vs. what you pay for. The full report has the other 5 moves.

We checked 1,276 flex operator accounts on the OfficeRnD platform for 5 core connections: payments, accounting, door access, CRM, and network.

The results: exactly 1 account has all 5.

The average is 1.65. 14% of accounts have none.

The survey answers next to that data make it even stranger. When we asked 334 operators which integrations they consider essential, they gave a clear, consistent list. Most of that list is still unconnected, and the work it would automate is being done by hand, every week, by the same small teams who named it as their biggest problem.

These numbers come from The 2026 Flex Space Tech Stack Report, which combines a survey of 334 operators with that platform data. We covered the headline findings in our launch post.

This article goes after one question: if operators know which connections they need, why haven’t they made them, and what is it costing them?

Operators already know which connections they need

We asked 334 operators to pick the 3 integrations that matter most to them. Accounting, payments, and door access came back within 3 points of each other, and 15 points clear of everything else. That’s the money coming in, the money being recorded, and the front door.

Then we compared those answers with what’s switched on.

Payments is the only category where connection runs ahead of demand. That’s no surprise. You can’t take a card payment without a gateway, so that connection gets made on day 1.

Every other connection is optional to set up, and each one is further behind. Door access has the widest gap at 24 points. More than half of operators call it a must-have, and fewer than 1 in 3 have it running.

The spread across accounts tells the same story:

Operators have the list. They haven’t done the setup. We’ve made the case for why open integrations matter in coworking before. This data shows the case has landed; the follow-through hasn’t.

Every missing connection has a person behind it

A gap between 2 systems gets filled by a person, a spreadsheet or a paid connector. Usually a person.

The survey shows where those hours go. We asked operators, in their own words, which part of their week is the most repetitive. The top answers:

Most of that list is re-keying. An invoice raised in one system and reconciled by hand in another. A signed quote typed into the platform. A key card still active 2 weeks after someone left.

One operator in the survey traced 44% of a full year’s member tickets to access cards. That’s what a 24-point gap in door access looks like at the front desk.

It also explains why 68% of operators name integration gaps as their biggest tech challenge (up from 61% in 2025), and 52% name implementation cost. The report calls these the same complaint, counted twice. Every unconnected system shows up later as payroll hours.

Larger companies have the same problem. MuleSoft’s 2025 Connectivity Benchmark Report found that enterprises connect only 29% of their applications. The difference is staffing. An enterprise has an integration team. A 2-site coworking space has a community manager who also runs the front desk.

The operators who close the gap feel it fast. Among multi-location operators, invoicing drops from the #1 time sink to #8, because payments and accounting are talking to each other. iQ Offices grew from 2 to 5 locations in Canada and runs a QuickBooks connection for each site from a single OfficeRnD account.

CEO Kane Willmott put it plainly:

the platform is “taking a huge administrative burden out of our location level.

The full report breaks down the time-sink ranking by portfolio size. It flips almost completely as you grow, and it tells you which problem is coming next. For the billing side specifically, here’s how automated billing works across multiple locations.

Why AI stalled in flex this year

In 2025, 26% of operators told us they were using AI tools and only 14% ruled them out. In 2026, active use is 18% and 30% have no plans.

Part of that drop is method. This year we asked about specific business functions, which produces more careful answers, and the sample is larger. The direction is still clear: a year of trying AI moved a real share of operators from curious to uninterested.

The likely reason sits in one small question. We asked the operators using AI how their tools connect to their space management platform. Only 18 had a setup to describe, so treat this as a signal:

Two-thirds are copy-pasting or paying a developer. Smaller operators are about twice as likely to be the ones copy-pasting, and they’re the group with the least spare time to do it.

An AI tool that can’t read your members, bookings, invoices and occupancy has nothing to work with. Someone has to feed it, and that usually stops by week 3.

This matches what’s happening outside flex. Gartner predicts that through 2026, organisations will abandon 60% of AI projects that aren’t supported by AI-ready data. In MuleSoft’s research, 80% of IT leaders named data integration as a major obstacle to AI adoption.

For a flex operator, “AI-ready” has a simple meaning. The tool can see live member and booking data without anyone exporting a CSV. An operator with 1.65 of 5 systems connected has very little for AI to read.

If you’re still weighing where AI fits, our guide to practical AI for coworking covers small, measurable starting points. The first question to ask any vendor: can it read my platform data directly, or does it need an export?

The one-hour audit

Most operators who run this check find at least one integration they already pay for and never switched on. It costs nothing, and it’s the quickest way to find out which side of the 1.65 average you’re on.

  1. List the 5 categories. Payments, accounting, door access, CRM, network. Next to each, write the vendor you pay today.
  2. Check your platform settings. Mark which ones are live. Check the settings page itself; memory tends to overcount.
  3. Match what’s unconnected against your platform’s integration list. On OfficeRnD Flex, that’s the integrations page. Anything on your list and theirs is a quick win.
  4. For each live connection, write down what still needs a person. Does door access switch off automatically when a membership ends? Do credit notes reach the ledger? A connection that syncs half the data still leaves the other half to your team.
  5. Fix in this order. Payments to accounting first, since billing is the market’s #1 time sink. Door access second, because it has the widest gap and generates the most tickets.

For what each connection should do once it’s live, see our breakdown of the 8 integrations every coworking tech stack needs.
