Name: AI Hub Webinar Recap: What Happened When a 2-site Operator Let AI Answer Its Hot Desk Enquiries
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: TL;DR:
Post body:
TL;DR:

  • OfficeRnD’s AI Sales Agent answers form, email, and web chat enquiries 24/7. It qualifies leads, offers alternative locations, books on behalf of prospects, and hands off to your team based on rules you set.
  • Will Ballantyne of MyWorkSpot estimates about 65% of their conversations are now handled all the way through by the agent. A lot of their hot desk enquiries no longer need a human.
  • MyWorkSpot tested the agent privately before going live. They chose which products it answers for and kept private office enquiries with the team.
  • OfficeRnD demoed a member concierge agent live. It answers plan questions and books meeting rooms from a chat in the member app. A beta is starting now, and an analytics agent is coming soon.
  • The on-demand recording has the full demo, the guardrails discussion, and a Q&A on pricing, CRM connections, and opting out.

It’s 11 pm, and you’re hosting a webinar tomorrow. Your internet has just died, and you need a desk somewhere by morning.

That happened to Crispin Piney 3 weeks into his job at OfficeRnD. He found MyWorkSpot, the nearest coworking space, but nobody there would see his problem until the next day. He got lucky: Will Ballantyne, MyWorkSpot’s co-founder, got into the office early.

Crispin told that story while hosting our latest webinar, Sales, Support & Beyond: What’s Next for OfficeRnD AI Hub. If MyWorkSpot’s AI agent had been running that night, he said, it would have been a lot easier.

That’s the problem the session was about. Enquiries arrive in the evening, on weekends, and during a busy afternoon when the team is with members. The operators who answer first get the booking.

Crispin, Managing Director, UK & I at OfficeRnD, hosted on his birthday and admitted he came to AI with some skepticism. Joining him were Momchil Blaskov, Principal Product Manager at OfficeRnD, who leads AI Hub, and Will, whose 2-site operation in Maidenhead, just west of London, has been open for about 7 years.

Where AI Hub is going

Momchil described OfficeRnD Flex today as a system of record. Your team goes in, creates a member, issues an invoice, and the software stores what happened.

The plan is a set of agents that act inside the platform across the member journey: bookings, memberships, renewals. They’ll run day and night, and you’ll approve what they do. Momchil said the transition has started and will speed up in Q4 and early next year.

The first agent is already live.

What the AI Sales Agent does today

The AI Sales Agent picks up form, email, and web chat enquiries around the clock. It answers from your own inventory, plans, locations, and FAQs. It asks about budget and team size, then points the prospect to a tour or a direct purchase, such as a day pass or virtual office.

Recent releases let it suggest another location when one is full and make bookings for prospects. Tour booking is coming.

Setup got faster too. A new pre-fill step populates tone, style, guidance and your product list, so you can start testing sooner. The recording shows it in a short video.

MyWorkSpot: a small team and a lot of tyre kickers

Before the agent, every enquiry was a manual pickup. Front of house handled hot desks. A senior team member took larger enquiries, including those from property agents. Everyone wore several hats, so time spent on a low-intent lead was time taken from existing members.

Web chat was the weak spot. A chat would pop up, someone got a notification, and by the time they reached it the visitor had often left. Will said it got bad enough that they questioned keeping chat on the website at all.

MyWorkSpot had already built its own agent with a general AI tool. That work helped, because they already had the data OfficeRnD asked for during onboarding. Momchil noted their homemade attempt didn’t work smoothly with their system. With the agent inside OfficeRnD, it sends prospects straight to MyWorkSpot’s own booking links.

That pattern shows up in wider research too. MIT’s 2025 study, reported by Fortune, found that AI tools bought from specialized vendors succeed about 67% of the time, while internal builds succeed only a third as often. Our breakdown of building versus buying coworking software runs the numbers for flex.

Testing before anything went live

Will’s biggest worry was handing customer conversations to something whose answers he couldn’t predict. MyWorkSpot prides itself on knowing the people in its space.

2 features settled it. He could test the agent in the background before putting it live. And he could choose which products it answers for, such as hot desking, while private office queries still go to the team.

When testing showed the agent elaborating on a topic, they added a rule telling it to hand those questions over.

The results

Will estimates about 65% of their conversations are now handled all the way through by the agent, across web chat and forms. He doesn’t track conversion separately, but he sees a good share of those enquiries convert without the team stepping in.

A lot of hot desk enquiries are now no-touch. People turn up knowing what they’ve signed up for, without having spoken to anyone.

The agent also covers the evenings. Someone at home decides they need a desk tomorrow, gets an answer straight away, and is sent to book. Before, that email sat unread until morning, and Will thinks they may have lost some of those people.

It follows up with prospects who go quiet, too. His team used to note those down and chase them by hand.

Did it make the business feel less personal? When the first agent-handled customer arrived, Will went to talk to them in person. They had no idea they hadn’t been talking to someone from his team. How MyWorkSpot decided whether to tell prospects they’re talking to AI, and the name they gave the agent, is one of the best moments in the recording.

The member concierge agent, demoed live

Momchil demoed the next agent live. The concierge will sit in the member portal and mobile app, and it already knows who’s asking.

In a few messages, he checked whether he could bring a guest, confirmed printing was included in his plan, and booked a meeting room for 8 people next Monday at 10 am. No calendar, no filters. He opened the calendar, and the booking was there.

Momchil said it will expand to credit allowances, invoices, and possibly contracts. The goal is for answers to match member type, so a drop-in and a monthly member see different information. The beta is starting now.

He also previewed an analytics agent, coming soon, that lets you ask questions about your revenue, occupancy, invoicing, and pricing data in plain language. He left space on the roadmap slide for more agents and asked operators which time-consuming jobs they’d want handed over next.

Guardrails

Every Sales Agent conversation is logged in its own tab. The agents are designed to follow your existing roles and permissions: if an admin can’t make a booking, an agent acting for them won’t be able to either. Momchil said future agent actions will appear in the audit log along with who approved them.

The gap between AI promises and results in flex is wide. OfficeRnD’s 2026 survey of 334 operators found AI use fell from 26% to 18% in a year, and the report links that drop to how poorly connected most operators’ tools are.

The ceiling is high for the operators who get it right. Gartner predicts that by 2029, agentic AI will autonomously resolve 80% of common customer service issues without human help, cutting operational costs by 30%. For where to start, read our guide to practical AI for coworking and the 2026 flex space tech stack report.

What the Q&A covered

Attendees asked how long setup takes. Some operators went live in 2 weeks, and the longest so far was a 15-location operator at about 2 months.

They also asked about pricing and free trials, whether the agent works with CRMs like HubSpot, Microsoft Dynamics and monday.com, whether enquiries from property agents can go to the team, and whether you can opt out.

The answers are in the recording.

Watch the full session on-demand

Name: What a Year of Our Own Hybrid Work Data Actually Showed Us
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: This is our story – what 13,024 bookings, 365 days, and one office move look like in real life.
Post body:
This is our story – what 13,024 bookings, 365 days, and one office move look like in real life. 

Most hybrid work research asks people what they do. We wanted to know what our team actually did, which is a different question and often a different answer. Here’s what we found.

Our Average Was the Least Useful Number We Found

On a typical working day, our office runs at 63% desk utilization. That sounds like a manageable, well-sized office with room to spare. But in fact, it isn’t, and the daily numbers explain why. Our busiest day runs at roughly double our quietest one. Nearly one working day in five pushes past 80%, and the busiest days of the year hit capacity exactly. The average sits in a gap that almost none of our actual days occupy – the full weekday breakdown is in the report.

If our office was sized for 63% attendance, it would be under real pressure at the start of every week and half-empty every Friday. If your desk ratio comes from an average, you might face issues when utilizing it. We actually worked on a calculator that can help you size your new office if you plan a move. Check it out here.

Nobody Asked for the Attendance We Got

Our hybrid work policy asks for eight office days a month. Against a typical 21 working days, that’s a floor of roughly 40%.

Most of the week runs well clear of that floor. Friday sits almost exactly on it.

That gap is the finding we didn’t expect. If people treated the mandate as a box to tick, they’d spread their required days evenly and thinly – minimum disruption, maximum compliance. Instead, we noticed that people pile onto the days their colleagues will be there and skip the days they won’t. How far above the floor they go, and which days carry it, is in the report.

One Setting Reclaimed About 8% of Our Capacity

Every desk booking in our office requires a check-in. Miss it, and the booking cancels itself, putting the desk back in the pool.

Across the year, nearly one booking in ten was auto-cancelled at check-in time. Every one of those would have been a ghost booking — a desk reserved, never used, and blocked all day — and instead our policy setting put it straight back in the pool.

In practical terms, that’s several desks recovered every single working day, on top of a much larger number released by people cancelling ahead of time – which mostly happens because they expect the system to hold them accountable. Without any of it, our reported utilization would have been inflated by phantom occupancy, and anyone hunting for a desk on a busy Tuesday would have been staring at a floor map full of empty “occupied” desks.

Our Monday Doesn’t Behave Like Everyone Else’s

This is the comparison we found most interesting. Almost everywhere else, Monday is a quiet day – global occupancy data has long treated Monday and Friday as the light ends of a “barbell” week.

Ours doesn’t do that at all. It’s the busiest day of our year. Only Friday sits where the rest of the world’s bookends do.

What this means, along with data from major research, you’ll find in the full report.

What We Couldn’t Prove

We moved offices in May 2026 and added roughly 11% more desks. Utilization didn’t fall to absorb them (a typical day got busier rather than quieter), and almost all of that movement landed on one single weekday, while Friday didn’t change its attendance.

But that’s 13 weeks of data, landing squarely in summer, when our headcount also grew. We can’t separate the move from the season or the hiring, so we’ve written it up as a signal to watch rather than a finding. The report says so explicitly, along with the claims we had to throw out entirely.

What’s in the Full Case Study

The report is the version with the numbers in it:

  • Every weekday, before and after the move, in one table
  • The Friday paradox — our most habitual day is also our least reliable one, and we can show why
  • The full booking-status breakdown behind the 8% capacity we got back
  • How our week compares against Gallup, Stanford, Kastle and XY Sense — and why the regional detail matters more than the global average
  • What the office move did to our peak days, and the findings we had to throw out
  • The full methodology, including what we excluded and why

Read the full case study, including the day-by-day breakdown, the office move analysis, the Friday paradox, and more on how you can put your data against the global findings.

Name: OfficeRnD Flex vs Nexudus: Full Comparison
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Your coworking platform is something you feel every day, in every invoice, booking, and member question. If you run on Nexudus and wonder whether there is an easier way, or you are comparing the two before you commit, this guide shows where they differ and where they are similar. We cover ease of use, billing, reporting, growth tools, support and pricing, and, if you decide to move, what switching actually looks like.
Post body:
Your coworking platform is something you feel every day, in every invoice, booking, and member question. If you run on Nexudus and wonder whether there is an easier way, or you are comparing the two before you commit, this guide shows where they differ and where they are similar. We cover ease of use, billing, reporting, growth tools, support and pricing, and, if you decide to move, what switching actually looks like.

Winner for most flex operators: OfficeRnD Flex. It rates higher on G2 (4.6 vs 4.2), it is easier to run day-to-day; it keeps billing, accounting, e-commerce, and reporting in one connected platform whether you run a single or multiple locations. Nexudus is still a good fit for a space that wants a built-in CRM.

OfficeRnD Flex vs Nexudus: At-a-Glance Comparison

Understanding What Each One Is

OfficeRnD Flex is a flex and coworking space platform used by 3,500+ spaces worldwide. It is organized into hubs, so you switch on what you need: Operations for members, Bookings and Billing, Growth Hub for e-commerce, Data Hub for reporting, Experience Hub for branded apps, Visitor Hub, and AI Hub.

Nexudus is a London-based coworking software company founded in 2012. It says it runs in 3,000+ locations across 90+ countries, and it describes itself as bootstrapped. 

On paper, the two cover the same ground: memberships, bookings, invoicing, community, inventory. The difference is where each one puts the weight. OfficeRnD Flex is built to work well from day one, and it goes further: it’s designed to grow your revenue, not just manage your space. Nexudus gives you more dials to configure yourself, which means more setup and more upkeep. 

Ease of Use: Your Team and Your Members

A coworking platform gets used by two groups: the staff who run the space, and the members who book, pay, and check in. If either group finds it awkward, the work ends up back on your desk.

G2 reviewers score OfficeRnD Flex higher on the three ease measures. Ease of use is 8.6 vs 7.8, ease of setup is 8.2 vs 7.7, and ease of admin is 8.6 vs 7.7. A third-party review of Nexudus also points to a steep learning curve and an older admin interface, and says some operators bring in a consultant to set it up.

In evaluations, operators tell us the same thing. Nexudus takes time to learn, registration flows can be heavy for simple tasks like booking an event, and the member portal looks almost the same to every location. With OfficeRnD Flex, new staff get comfortable faster, and each location can carry its own branding.

The practical test is simple. Ask how long it takes a new community manager to run a normal day without help. Then check how much time your employees spend on fixing settings. Then the clear winner will be OfficeRnD Flex.

Billing, Accounting and Reporting

Billing is where a platform earns its keep, because every error lands in a member’s inbox.

OfficeRnD Flex automates invoicing and payments, and it syncs both ways with QuickBooks and Xero. Nexudus also connects to QuickBooks and Xero, and it partners with Spreedly.

The gap shows up in how much manual work is left. The gap often shows up in how much manual work your team still has to do. Nexudus trails on G2’s ease-of-admin score (7.7 vs. 8.6 for OfficeRnD Flex), and third-party reviews point to a steeper learning curve for day-to-day billing and admin tasks. If your finance lead is spending real time each month on manual reconciliation or invoice fixes, it is worth asking any vendor you evaluate how much of that work their platform actually automates.

Reporting is the other half. Data Hub gives you live reports you can build, export, and schedule, with the option to self-host your data. Nexudus ships standard reports, but it doesn’t have deeper analytics options. Pro plan gives you access to a third-party tool.

Growth: E-commerce and AI

Both platforms let you sell desks, rooms, and memberships online. Nexudus offers an embeddable storefront with dynamic pricing, guest checkout, an AI page builder, and a follow-up automation for enquiries. 

OfficeRnD Flex builds its growth tools around conversion. Growth Hub adds dynamic pricing, cart abandonment recovery, and a buying journey that stays connected to billing and bookings. At x+why, the team reported that Growth Hub lifted their conversion rate from 6% to 27%, with a 149% increase in average booking value.

We also provide an AI Sales Agent that goes after the enquiry itself. It answers inbound questions, qualifies the lead, and uses real-time availability and pricing to move that person toward a booking. You can read how it works in Introducing AI Sales Agent for Web Chat.

The question to ask any vendor is whether their AI generates revenue or only answers questions. 4&Co’s story proves that Officernd’s AI Sales Agent is more than a chat widget. Today, their chatbot, named Oliver, handles the critical first touch for every inbound lead. Some people even thought that Oliver was just a teammate without realizing it’s AI. Oliver has held multi-email conversations with prospects, answered detailed questions, and seamlessly included tour booking links when the lead shows interest. Hear more about it in the next video:

Integrations and CRM

Nexudus lists 60+, covering payments, door access, networking, printing, and accounting. OfficeRnD Flex lists 50+, with a different focus: fewer connections built to run deep and stay reliable, rather than a headline count.

The number hides a difference in depth. Some Nexudus integrations are written against its API rather than built as native connections. Operators also report that door access and accounting integrations, such as Salto KS, Gallagher, and Xero, sometimes fail and force manual entry. When a problem sits between Nexudus and a partner, each side can point at the other.

OfficeRnD Flex focuses on fewer, deeper connections. The clearest example is HubSpot. Contract details fill in automatically, and contracts can be signed through Dropbox Sign, so the path from enquiry to signed member runs without retyping.

CRM is the other place where the two differ. Nexudus includes a built-in CRM. Once you run two or more locations, sales teams tend to move to an outside tool and import contacts only when a deal closes, which splits the sales process from the platform. That split is why we lean on HubSpot.

Running More Than One Location

Most operators start with one space and add more. That is where platforms show their design.

OfficeRnD Flex was built not only for single-location operators but for multi-location as well. You can create contracts that span locations, keep member data in one place, and set up each site with its own branding. 

With Nexudus, operators share that for more than 2 locations, the setup gets restrictive. Some end up with separate accounts per site or copy settings by hand between locations, and the member journey looks nearly identical everywhere. Nexudus offers role-based access for multi-location teams, so this is a matter of how much manual upkeep you are willing to do.

Support

Both companies score well on support in G2 reviews: 9.3 for OfficeRnD Flex and 9.0 for Nexudus. So this is not a case of one good and one bad. The difference is in how support is structured.

Nexudus runs support from three regions during business hours: London (08:00 to 18:30), Sydney (09:00 to 17:30) and Chicago (09:00 to 17:30), in English, Spanish, and French. Requests go through a support portal.

In Officernd, the Support team is one of the things we are best known for and proud of. Officernd Flex includes standard support in every plan. Ultimate Support is available as an add-on and comes with Scale, where you also get a dedicated Customer Success Manager. Migrating customers also get guided onboarding.

If you run a space that is open early, late, or on weekends, check the hours against your own. This matters most when you get a question at 7 pm on a Friday.

Security and Company Backing

OfficeRnD holds ISO 27001, SOC 2 and GDPR certifications, and publishes them in its Trust Center. Nexudus also has SOC 2 certification and is GDPR complient.

On backing, OfficeRnD has invested more than $60M in the platform, has two or more times the product and engineering capacity of Nexudus, and is backed by Blue Star Innovation Partners. 

What matters to you is delivery. Look at how often each vendor ships, how it handles feedback, and whether the roadmap is clear enough to plan around.

Pricing

The two platforms price on different things, so the sticker numbers do not line up.

Nexudus charges by active members per location. A third-party pricing comparison from May 2026 lists it from $150 a month for 1 to 75 (some articles state 80) active members at one location. Nexudus’s pricing page does not show the figures for the number of members, only the starting package at $150, so treat these as a guide and ask for a quote.

OfficeRnD Flex is a good fit for single-location operators as well as bigger businesses. Start is $165 a month on annual billing for 100 members and one location. Grow is $259 a month for 200 members and two locations. Scale is custom for larger, multi-location operators.

The real comparison is total cost, not entry price. Add up the branded app, training, any custom reporting, and the hours your team spends on manual invoicing and fixes. Operators who have moved from Nexudus tell us it can feel expensive for what it delivers, especially once you factor in reporting and admin time.

If you want a direct number, book a demo, and we will price your space against your current Nexudus invoice.

What Reviewers Say

On G2, OfficeRnD Flex holds 4.6 out of 5 from 91 reviews, and Nexudus holds 4.2 out of 5 from 47 reviews.

Nexudus edges ahead on one line: meets requirements. That fits what its users say. It offers a lot of configuration, which appeals mainly to operators willing to spend the time setting it up and keeping it that way. OfficeRnD Flex leads on everything that describes daily use, which is where operators spend their time.

So, Who Should Pick Which?

Pick OfficeRnD Flex if:

  • You want a platform that will serve as a revenue growth instrument
  • You are a single or multi-location operator
  • Your team spends too much time on invoices, reconciliation, and manual fixes
  • You want reporting you can build and schedule yourself
  • You want to grow revenue through online sales and a faster response to enquiries using AI
  • You use HubSpot, or another CRM, for sales
  • Security certifications are part of your buying process

Pick Nexudus if:

  • You want a CRM built into the platform
  • You want configuration, including HTML and CSS control over your portal
  • You need a niche integration that Nexudus supports, and we do not

If you are on Nexudus today and none of the second list describes you, it is worth a look at what a move would involve.

Switching From Nexudus to OfficeRnD Flex

Switching sounds harder than it is. We have helped hundreds of coworking operators move their core system, from single spaces to global operators, and the process is well worn. Moving from Nexudus comes down to three things: exporting your data cleanly, importing it without mismatches, and ending Nexudus billing before your next cycle so members are not charged twice. Plan around your billing cycle from the start, because that is where most migrations go wrong.

Here is the path, in order:

  1. Prepare. Check your Nexudus contract terms and cancellation window, name one person to own the migration, and pick a go-live date in a quiet period, away from month-end.
  2. Export. An admin exports your resources, plans, memberships, companies, members, and bookings from Nexudus.
  3. Format. Match your files to OfficeRnD’s import templates. Names of plans and rooms must match exactly.
  4. Import. Use bulk upload for most spaces, or enter data manually for a small one.
  5. End Nexudus memberships. Set end dates one to two weeks before your next invoice cycle, and tell members that the next invoice comes from OfficeRnD Flex.
  6. Set up your account. Follow the onboarding guide for billing, services, floor plans, integrations, and member tools.
  7. Review and go live. Check operations, billing, and space settings, and work through the troubleshooting guides. You can also request a branded mobile app.

You do not do this alone. Guided onboarding, data migration, training, and go-live support are available on request, and multi-location accounts get a dedicated Customer Success Manager. If you want to see what your own move would look like, we will map it with you before you commit.

For the full walkthrough, read Migrate from Nexudus in our Help Center. To see it done, read the SpaceMade case study. 

Final Verdict

For most flex and coworking operators, OfficeRnD Flex is the stronger platform whether you’re a single-location operator or not. It rates higher on G2, it is easier for staff and members, and it keeps billing, accounting, reporting, and online sales in one connected system rather than a set of separate jobs.

Want to see what your move would look like? Book a demo, and we will walk through your data, your billing cycle, and a plan for going live.

OfficeRnD Workplace Vs Robin: At-a-Glance Comparison

Understanding What Each One Is

Both products manage desks, rooms, and office days. They were built for very different audiences, and it shows within five minutes of a demo.

At OfficeRnD, we have built workplace software since 2015 (starting with the coworking segment) with employee experience as the design center: easy booking, day coordination, and getting people to visit the office regularly. OfficeRnD Workplace also enables booking of any kind of resource your company has, like a parking spot or EV charger, and supports workplace analytics. It holds 4.6 on G2 from 158 reviews, with Leader badges in Desk Booking, Meeting Room Booking, Space Management, and Hybrid Enablement.

Robin started in room scheduling and grew into a broad enterprise platform: resource booking for desks, rooms, parking, and lockers, visitor management, meeting services workflows, space management with CAD import, workplace analytics, wayfinding, and employee experience tools. It has a slightly lower rating on G2: 4.4 from 211 reviews.

The difference is in who each one expects to be in charge. Robin’s own pricing page describes its fit as organizations with more than 150 hybrid employees using an office, generally 500+ overall, with at least a third of them coming in regularly. That is a deliberate, honest bit of qualification, and it tells you a lot.

The short version: OfficeRnD Workplace optimizes for the employee opening the app on a regular Tuesday morning. Robin optimizes for the workplace team running a large estate. The rest of this comparison is where that split plays out. Let’s get into more detail.

There are Two Ways to Think About the Office

A workplace platform reflects what its makers think the office is for, and that shapes how it feels to use every day.

Robin treats the office as an estate to operate. CAD imports, change validation before you publish a floor plan, badge and sensor data feeding occupancy, catering and AV workflows attached to meetings. For a company with several buildings and a team whose full-time job is running them, that depth is exactly right.

OfficeRnD Workplace starts from the employee moment instead. The bet is that most empty desks come from a clumsy booking experience, not from too much space. When booking takes seconds, and the office is worth the trip, people come in on their own, and utilization follows.

Both views are valid. Which one fits depends on whether you are operating a large estate or trying to earn attendance in one to a handful of offices. Most hybrid companies in 2026 are doing the second thing, and the rest of this comparison is written with that reader in mind.

So, Who Should Pick Which?

Pick Robin if you run a large multi-building estate, you need meeting services workflows for catering, room setup, and AV, you want floor plans imported straight from CAD, or you need occupancy stitched together from badge readers and sensors rather than bookings alone.

Robin is an enterprise product with ISO 27001 and SOC 2, a mature analytics layer, and the operational depth a dedicated workplace team can put to work. If that is your setup, shortlist it properly.

And Pick OfficeRnD Workplace if your company runs on Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, you want a tool people adopt without training, and you want to know the cost before you book a call. It also holds ISO 27001 and SOC 2 and is GDPR compliant. OfficeRnD Workplace adds CCPA, which matters if you have US operations.

Most hybrid offices fall into the second group. Here’s why.

Getting People to Actually Use It

Sometimes that’s tricky.

A booking tool only pays off when employees open it. When the office is optional, the easiest tool wins.

OfficeRnD Workplace sits inside Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar, and Slack. Someone books a desk from the chat thread they already have open with no extra apps or training.

Robin integrates with the same tools, and its floor plans genuinely are among the best-looking in the category. The friction shows up elsewhere. The recurring complaint from Robin reviewers is administrative: floor plan edits often need help from the Robin team, availability does not always refresh instantly, and the interface gets crowded at peak booking times. Reviewers also flag gaps when connecting to Outlook and the wider Microsoft ecosystem.

For a facilities or IT lead who needs to move a bank of desks on a Friday afternoon, “raise a ticket with the vendor” feels very different from doing it yourself in the admin panel.

There’s a timing difference too. OfficeRnD Workplace can be live in a couple of hours for a smaller organization, because there’s nothing to scope – you connect Teams or Google, import your floor plan, and open it to staff. Robin runs an implementation project, with a few weeks the commonly cited figure. For a two-site company that wants desks bookable before the quarter turns, that gap is the difference between a rollout and a roadmap item.

Müller: 22 Locations, 31,700 People, Booked from Teams

Robin’s pitch is that enterprise scale needs an enterprise platform. Müller Group is a useful test of that, because it is exactly the company Robin describes: a €7 billion food and logistics business with around 31,700 employees and 22 offices across Central Europe and the UK.

Müller went fully remote during 2020, then came back to a three-day office week and found itself coordinating desks and rooms across 22 locations on manual spreadsheets, while opening new German sites and refurbishing UK ones at the same time. That is an estate-management problem by any definition, and precisely the scenario Robin makes its case.

Müller chose OfficeRnD Workplace, and the reason its IT project manager gives is worth reading twice:

The reasons we went with OfficeRnD were the MS Teams integration, fast implementation without issues, great collaboration with OfficeRnD, everything worked as expected.

The numbers show it stuck. 86% of desks are now booked directly through Teams, and 98% of meeting rooms through Outlook or Teams. So for all 31,700 people booking desks happens through the app that they’ve already opened.

At the end, the enterprise argument cuts both ways. Robin is built for companies the size of Müller. Müller looked at that category and bought the product its people would actually use with ease. Read the full case study here.

Coordinating Office Days That Are Worth It

Hybrid work breaks down when everyone shows up on different days, and the office stays half full with people working alone. Visibility into who is coming in is the first fix, and both products handle it.

Robin shows who is on site through maps and wayfinding, and its booking flow offers AI-assisted resource recommendations. OfficeRnD Workplace shows the same picture of who is in and where they sit.

The edge is what OfficeRnD Workplace does on top of that. Instead of leaving you to read a map and work it out, it suggests thebest days for you to come in.

Those Suggested Days are calculated from the colleagues you mark as Favorites, the onsite meetings you have been invited to, and the level of occupancy of the office. Suggested Days  arrive as a weekly nudge from the Teams chatbot and are also marked in the Chrome extension and in the app itself.

You can follow up to 15 people, see which desk a teammate booked and grab one nearby, but also send an invite to pull a remote colleague in for a specific day. 

Both products tell you who is in. OfficeRnD Workplace tells you which day is worth the commute, then helps you sit next to the people you came in for. That is the step that turns visibility into actual collaboration.

Reading the Numbers

Empty desks usually mean the booking experience is annoying, not that you have too much space. Good analytics tell you which one you are dealing with. For more info about that, read our guide on the top-rated space management tools this year.

Robin is strong here, and it deserves the credit. Real-time occupancy, utilization tracking, capacity forecasting, customizable reporting, and the ability to blend booking data with badge-in and sensor data for a fuller picture. An AI analytics assistant and custom reports are available as an add-on. If you have the estate and the team to act on all that, it is a genuine strength.

OfficeRnD Workplace tracks desk and room utilization, parking spot usage, attendance patterns, and presence through check-ins, tying the numbers to real attendance rather than assumed bookings.

Where OfficeRnD Workplace turns analytics into value is the chain it sits in.

Easier booking drives higher adoption, the suggestions pull people in on the same days, and the utilization data then shows facilities and finance which desks, rooms, and floors are actually earning their keep. The numbers are only as good as the behavior feeding them, and that is the loop OfficeRnD Workplace is built to close.

To show you real numbers, we wrote our own report on using OfficeRnD Workplace – we gathered a year’s worth of data and presented it in our hybrid work story. You can check the full report here.

Visitors

Robin includes visitor management in the platform: pre-registration, check-in workflows, compliance handling, and badge printing. OfficeRnD Workplace offers it as the Visitor Hub add-on across plans, covering guest check-in, host notifications, badge printing, document signing, and delivery management.

On paper Robin wins this row, and for a single-quote enterprise deal it often does. The caveat is that the platform it comes bundled into is the expensive part. Reviewers also note Robin’s visitor app is iPad-only and light on extras like WiFi guest access.

Integrations

This is close to a tie. OfficeRnD Workplace connects natively to Microsoft 365, Teams, Outlook, Google Workspace, Google Calendar, Chrome, Slack, Okta for SSO, Brivo for access control, and Zapier.

Robin covers the same essentials: Outlook, Teams, Google Calendar, Slack, Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, SAML and SSO, plus deeper badge and sensor integrations for occupancy data.

Robin has the edge on access control and sensor hardware. OfficeRnD Workplace has the edge on how the calendar and chat integrations feel in daily use, which is where reviewers on both sides keep landing.

What Reviewers Say

OfficeRnD Workplace users consistently call out how easy it is for both employees and admins, and the way it works inside Teams and Outlook. The standing requests are tighter Outlook out-of-office sync and more granular admin permissions – fair gaps, worth weighing.

Support is a consistent strength rather than an upsell: OfficeRnD Workplace holds a 9.5 quality-of-support score on G2, with hands-on onboarding at every tier rather than only at the top one.

Robin users praise the floor plan visualization, the polished employee experience, and responsive support. The recurring criticism is specific rather than broad: floor plan edits that need vendor help, a crowded interface at busy times, availability that lags, and Microsoft integration friction. Several reviewers describe a learning curve that comes with the product’s breadth.

Pricing

Entry tierStarts at $99 / month annual, up to 150 users. Roughly $2.70 a desk, $11 a roomNo published entry tier. Sized for 500+ employee organizations

OfficeRnD Workplace publishes its full price list. Robin does not, and that is the single biggest practical difference between them.

Here is the scenario that settles it. Picture 100 people in one office sharing 60 desks.

With OfficeRnD Workplace, those 100 sit inside the Start tier, and you pay for the 60 desks and the rooms you manage. Not the headcount, the space. You can work the total out yourself in about a minute.

With Robin, you cannot. You book a call, get scoped, and receive a number. Third-party procurement data suggests average annual contracts around $10,500, with ranges commonly quoted from $10,000 to $30,000 for smaller companies and higher from there. Treat those as indicative rather than official, because Robin does not confirm them, which is the point.

The bigger difference is what scales your bill. OfficeRnD Workplace scales with desks and rooms, so a company with far more employees than desks pays for the fewer. Robin scales with the scope of the deal you negotiate, and it is explicitly built for organizations large enough to make that worthwhile.

Before comparing totals, map your own desk-to-headcount ratio, count your sites, and be honest about whether you are the size of company Robin says it serves.

How It Lands for Each Stakeholder

A workplace platform has to satisfy several people at once, and they do not all want the same thing. Here is how the two compare for the four who usually sit in the room.

Final Verdict

Robin is a capable enterprise platform and the right pick if you run a large multi-building estate with a dedicated workplace team, and you need meeting services workflows, CAD imports, or sensor-fed occupancy data. Give it a serious look in those cases.

For everyone else, OfficeRnD Workplace is the stronger workplace management choice in 2026. Post body:
Imagine the following scenario for a bit: a meeting room display stops working on a Tuesday morning. Four teams had that room booked. One standup moves to the kitchen, one call gets taken from a phone booth, and by 11am three people have mentioned the problem to the office manager in passing. Nobody writes it down. The display gets fixed on Thursday, or the following week, or after the fifth person complains.

We’ve shipped desk booking, room booking, parking and visitor management for years, and workplace requests kept arriving the same way they always have: Slack DMs, hallway conversations, a shared inbox nobody owns.

So we built Helpdesk. It’s live in OfficeRnD Workplace now, in the same web portal and mobile app your team already uses to book a desk.

Here’s the thinking behind it.

The hybrid week concentrates more than people

We ran 12 months of our own office data through OfficeRnD Workplace and looked at what a week actually does. Monday averaged 73.3% desk utilization. Friday averaged 36.2% – roughly double, every week, for a year.

That gap changes the job of a facilities team. Coffee, cleaning cycles, meeting room hardware, phone booths, printers and parking get consumed on 3 days instead of 5. The same faulty display costs twice as much on a Tuesday as it does on a Friday, measured in people who can’t do the thing they came in for.

The midweek shape isn’t specific to us. WFH Research has tracked working-from-home days across dozens of countries since 2020, and the pattern of a compressed in-office core holds broadly.

Gallup finds hybrid is now the standing arrangement for most remote-capable employees, so this is the load profile workplace teams will be managing for years, not for a quarter.

The tickets you never receive

Most workplace problems are reported verbally, and verbal reports don’t accumulate.

Three people tell you the chair in the quiet zone is broken. You fix it. Six weeks later someone tells you again, and you have no way of knowing whether it’s the same chair, the same fault, or the third repair on the same unit. The office manager carries the entire maintenance history in their head, and it leaves with them when they go on holiday.

The second cost shows up at budget time. A workplace lead asking for 12,000 EUR of new meeting room hardware brings observations. Finance brings a spreadsheet. Without a record of how often rooms failed, which ones, and how many bookings were affected, the request looks like a preference rather than a repair schedule.

And employees stop reporting. Not because they’ve stopped caring, but because the last four things they mentioned produced no visible response. Silence trains people out of the habit, and then the workplace team loses the only sensor it had.

Problems have addresses

One finding from our own year of data sits directly under this.

We never assigned team neighborhoods in our Sofia office. Nobody gave Marketing a corner or Engineering a bank of desks. Teams formed neighborhoods anyway, in the old office, and then again in the new one after we moved. People don’t book desks as individuals. They move as a unit.

Which means wear concentrates. The zones that fill up on Tuesday are the zones where monitor arms loosen, cables disappear and chairs give out. A request with a location attached turns “the chairs are getting old” into “7 tickets from the same desk bank since March.” That’s a purchase order.

You can see which areas run hottest in space management. Helpdesk tells you what breaks there.

What we built

Helpdesk runs inside OfficeRnD Workplace, alongside desks, rooms, parking and visitors. No separate tool, no second login, no new app for employees to forget about.

Here’s what it offers:

  • Reporting in seconds. Employees report broken equipment, maintenance problems, IT issues or general feedback from the Workplace web portal or mobile app, in the same place they booked their desk that morning. Ticket status stays visible from their profile.
  • Custom categories and automatic routing. You define the categories that match your office and name the responders for each one. A facilities request goes to facilities, an IT request goes to IT, without anyone forwarding an email. Routing rules are set per location, so a request in one office never lands in another office’s queue.
  • Two-way conversation inside the ticket. Questions, photos, details and updates stay attached to the request, from first report to resolution. The employee can see what’s happening, which is the single thing that keeps people reporting.
  • Two priority scales. Employees set severity based on how much the issue blocks their work. Admins set internal priority based on urgency, cost and available resources. These are different questions, and one field can’t answer both.
  • Exportable ticket history. CSV export and reporting, so recurring problems, high-maintenance locations and underinvested areas show up as counts and dates. That’s what turns a maintenance complaint into a budget line.
  • Multi-location support. Each office gets its own categories, its own responders and its own notifications, so employees only see what’s relevant to the building they’re in.

We’ve done this once already

There’s a precedent in our own numbers for what happens when you start recording something you used to ignore.

Every desk booking in our office requires a check-in. Miss it and the booking auto-cancels, returning the desk to the pool. Over the year, 9.1% of bookings were caught that way. That’s about 4.5 desks recovered every working day, roughly 8% of the office’s capacity, from one policy setting applied to behavior that used to be invisible.

Workplace requests sit in the same category. Right now, most of them exist only as a memory, and you can’t schedule, budget or plan against a memory.

Give them a form field and a timestamp, and within a month you have a picture of your office that no walkthrough will give you. Workplace analytics does the rest.

See Helpdesk working

Helpdesk is available now to OfficeRnD Workplace customers. If you want to see how it fits with desk booking, rooms, parking and visitor management, and what your first month of ticket data would tell you, the fastest route is a 30-minute call with our team.

A typical hybrid office day: you book a desk in Teams (or Slack), the floor plan fills up with faces, and never once wonder how the software works. That’s exactly what both products are designed for.
The harder question is what month six looks like after adopting a new hybrid work tool. That’s when the office lead wants a report showing whether people are actually following the attendance policy, IT wants automated provisioning, finance wants parking on the same invoice, and tech people start asking if there’s an API. On deskbird, most of those answers are “that’s the Professional tier” or “that’s an add-on” and none of those have a published price on their website.
OfficeRnD Workplace starts from the same employee moment, but it was built for the sixth month as much as the first. Desks, rooms, parking, ticketing, visitors, policy reporting, and multi-location admin all sit in one product, and you can see what it costs up to the mid-tier.
This article walks you through where each product earns its place, uses public G2 reviews and both vendors’ published pricing to back up the claims that need it, and plainly says which one is the best buy for a particular use case.

Let’s begin with a quick comparison.

deskbird vs OfficeRnD Workplace: Quick Comparison

Do Teams Really Use It Every Day?

You have to agree that a booking tool is worth nothing the moment people stop using it. When the office is optional, the tool with the least friction wins, and this is the one round where the two products are genuinely close.

Both products live inside Microsoft Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar, and Slack. Both have iOS and Android apps. Both let someone book a desk from the chat window they already had open. Reviewers of both call them easy, and both vendors have earned that.

Where OfficeRnD Workplace pulls ahead is on the numbers underneath the headline rating: 9.4 for ease of use, 9.2 for ease of setup, and 9.5 for quality of support on G2. That last one matters more than it looks, because the first three weeks of a rollout are when it either sticks or quietly dies.

One practical gap for global teams: OfficeRnD Workplace ships its employee apps in 26+ languages; deskbird in only 9. If your rollout includes offices in Poland, Japan or Brazil, that is not a detail. Take, for example, the Müller case study.

Müller: 22 Offices, Shared Desks, And a Spreadsheet Retired

The family-owned food and logistics group has around 31,700 employees and 22 office locations across Central Europe and the UK. It went from a fully in-office model to fully remote and back to a hybrid policy of roughly three office days a week, and it tried to coordinate all of that on an Excel spreadsheet.

Two things made the replacement stick. The first is where the booking happens: 86% of desks are now booked directly through Microsoft Teams and 98% of meeting rooms through Outlook or Teams, so nobody had to be persuaded to adopt a new app. The second is that Müller wanted to keep a shared-desk model while opening a new German office and refurbishing a UK one, which means running 22 sites with fewer desks than people and needing location-by-location analytics to see which resources could be cut.

That combination is exactly where the two products differentiate. deskbird gives you unlimited locations on its entry plan, which is genuinely generous, but the analytics you would need to compare 22 of them sit in the custom-priced Professional tier, and per-user billing means every desk you remove saves you rent and nothing else. Imagine if your team expands, but you want to keep the same amount of office space/desks. This automatically means you’ll be paying more for deskbird’s service. On OfficeRnD Workplace, cutting desks cuts the software bill too, and team neighbourhoods keep groups together across sites even when people belong to more than one team.
Read the full Müller case study.

The reasons we went with OfficeRnD were the MS Teams integration, fast implementation without issues, great collaboration with OfficeRnD, everything worked as expected, and no concerns that the solution will cause issues in the future. It was also super easy to get started. 
Thomas Sluka, IT Project Manager

Coordinating Days That Are Worth The Commute

The hybrid work setting falls apart when everyone picks different days, and the office sits half empty, full of people working alone. Seeing who is coming in is the first fix, and both tools handle it well: colleague search, floor plans showing where people sit, weekly schedules, and team filters.

deskbird adds smart booking recommendations and workplace events, so people can see what is happening in the office before deciding whether to come in. It is a nice touch, and reviewers mention it. 

OfficeRnD Workplace goes a step further and recommends the specific days you should be in. Those Suggested Days are calculated from the colleagues you mark as favourites and the onsite meetings in your calendar, and they arrive as a weekly nudge from the Teams chatbot. You can follow up to 15 people, see which desk a teammate booked and grab one nearby, send an invite to pull a remote colleague in for a specific day, and keep a group together with team neighbourhoods instead of scattering them across the whole office.

Both tools tell you who is in. One of them tells you which day is worth the drive, then seats you next to the people you came for. This was one of the criteria we used to evaluate the best desk booking software of 2026 and the best hybrid work solutions.

What Happens When You Outgrow The Simple Plan

This is the part of the comparison that decides most shortlists, and it is the part demos skip.

Almost every hybrid work setup grows the same way. Booking works, so the office lead asks whether anyone is actually meeting the two-days-a-week expectation. IT asks for automated provisioning so leavers drop out of the system. Facilities want parking on the same booking flow. Someone wants tickets raised when a monitor dies. Finance wants one invoice, not four.

On OfficeRnD Workplace, those are named line items on a published plan. Internal ticketing, parking as a custom bookable resource, policy compliance and adoption reports, SCIM provisioning, digital signage, Outlook out-of-office sync and multi-location management all arrive at Professional, from €399 a month. Door access through Brivo, API and webhooks, an admin audit trail and per-location admin roles sit at Enterprise.

On deskbird, the same list is split across a custom-priced tier and three add-ons. Workplace ticketing, advanced analytics, public API access, access control integrations, the AI floor plan designer and compliance management are all Professional, which is quote-only. SAML authentication, SCIM provisioning and HRIS sync are the User & Data Management Plus add-on. Meeting room kiosks and catering requests are available in Rooms Plus. Visitor management is included in the Visitor Plus paid plan. None of the add-ons carry a public price so we can’t honestly compare them in that sense.

Analytics deserve a specific mention, because it’s where reviewers themselves flag the gap. deskbird includes office and workforce analytics on their Business Plan, but custom exports and advanced analytics are Professional, and one G2 reviewer describes struggling to work out average weekly office attendance because of how bookings and presence are counted.

OfficeRnD Workplace reports resource utilisation, room utilisation, workplace presence, and employee space usage trends from the Start plan, and ties them to real attendance through check-ins.

Workplace Analytics helped us a lot when we decided to move our office to a different location, but we talk about it further down in this article.

Fair is fair, though. deskbird is the more generous of the two at the entry level in three specific ways: unlimited locations on Business where OfficeRnD needs Professional for multi-location management, parking booking included where OfficeRnD treats it as a custom bookable resource at Professional, and a much longer list of HRIS connectors – BambooHR, Personio, Workday, HiBob, Factorial and  more. If syncing leave data from your HR system is the thing that makes or breaks the rollout, deskbird has done more work there.

What a Year of Our Own Data Actually Looked Like

We run our own office on OfficeRnD Workplace, and we published the results rather than describing them. A year of hybrid work data from our own office covers 13,024 desk bookings and one office move.

The numbers that changed how we work:

  • 63% desk utilisation on a typical working day, and a Monday that runs at 73% against a Friday at 36%. Two to one, every week.
  • A policy asking for 40% attendance, against 73% actual attendance on Mondays and Tuesdays. People were already coming in more than we required, which is a very different problem from the one we thought we had.
  • 34.7% of booked desk-days were released back to the pool before they were wasted, and 9.1% of bookings were caught as would-be ghost bookings.
  • 76.2% of attendance was booked one week at a time rather than on a recurring schedule, which tells you people are planning around meetings and colleagues, not habit.

Those findings did two jobs. They shaped our own hybrid policy – there was no point mandating days people were already choosing, and every point of the Friday gap was a real question about what the office is for. And they made the team more productive in a practical way: the release and ghost-booking mechanics mean a desk that someone booked and then skipped goes back on the map the same morning, so the person who did make the trip finds a seat.

Now price that exercise on the other model. To get recurrence rates, release rates, ghost-booking counts, weekday splits, and custom exports out of deskbird, you need advanced analytics and custom exports, which are Professional, which is quote-only – and its own reviewers say the standard attendance reporting is hard to read, with one describing being unable to work out average weekly attendance at all.

Then there is the bill underneath it. Our data says the office runs at 63% on a normal (average) day and 36% on a Friday. A per-user model charges you for 100% of your headcount to run that office, every month, and keeps charging the same amount as you act on the findings. A per-resource model charges you for the desks, so the moment the data tells you to shed ten of them, the software gets cheaper too. The analytics and the pricing model pull in the same direction, which is the whole point of measuring anything. Read the full report below.

How About Pricing?

The starting numbers look close. The models underneath are not, and it matters far more than the sticker.

Here is the scenario that settles it. Picture 100 people in one office sharing 60 desks and 6 meeting rooms.

On OfficeRnD Workplace, those 100 people sit inside the Start tier, and you pay for the space: 60 desks at €2 and 6 rooms at €8 comes to €168 a month on an annual contract. On deskbird, 100 active users at €2.75 comes to €275 a month. Same office, same desks, but you get roughly 64% more on price.

Now grow to 150 people without adding a desk, which is exactly what a desk-sharing setup is for. OfficeRnD Workplace stays at €168, because you did not add any resources. deskbird goes to €412.50.

The reverse case is real too, and worth saying out loud. A 30-person company with 20 desks and 2 rooms would pay €56 of resource value on OfficeRnD Workplace, but the €99 monthly minimum applies, so the bill is €99. The same team on deskbird pays about €82.50. Below roughly 35 people, deskbird is the cheaper option, and the smaller you are, the more suitable that gets.

So do the maths on two things before you trust any quote: your desk-to-headcount ratio, and how many of the Professional-tier features and add-ons you will actually switch on. OfficeRnD Workplace scales with desks and rooms. deskbird scales with people, then again with every add-on.

What People Say Once It Is Running

Strip out the marketing and read the reviews.

OfficeRnD Workplace users point to how easy it is for staff and admins alike, the visual map showing who is in the office, and how naturally it works in Teams and Outlook. Support scores 9.5. The two standing requests: tighter Outlook out-of-office sync and finer-grained admin permissions. Fair gaps, worth weighing.

deskbird users are positive too, and there are more of them: 311 reviews, 4.5 overall, with ease of use as the single most-mentioned strength. The criticisms are specific rather than broad, and they cluster. The app is slow to load, sometimes failing outright – one reviewer describes fighting for a desk at 9am while it spins.

Outlook sync draws the sharpest complaint: one admin reports calendar entries sent for the wrong date, and imports a third meeting room, breaking calendar sync for all of them, with a fix outstanding for two months. Reporting comes up repeatedly, with reviewers unable to work out average weekly attendance or to choose what goes into an export. And HRIS sync, deskbird’s own headline strength, draws requests for cleaner syncing from people who otherwise rate it five stars.

Read both sets, and the pattern is consistent with the products. deskbird gets praised hardest for the first week. OfficeRnD Workplace gets praised hardest for support and administration, which is what the tenth month feels like.

Security and Compliance

This one is close to a draw, and both vendors have done the work. Both carry ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type 2 and are GDPR compliant. OfficeRnD Workplace adds CCPA, which matters if you have US operations.

deskbird’s edge is data residency: built in Switzerland, hosted in Germany, processed exclusively in the EU. If your security review has a hard EU-only requirement, that is a genuine advantage, and you should weigh it.

OfficeRnD Workplace’s edge is administrative control at the top end: customisable admin roles and permissions per location, an admin audit trail, employee custom location permissions and advanced privacy settings, all at Enterprise. The nuance to watch on both sides is that single sign-on is an add-on on OfficeRnD’s Start plan and included from Professional, while on deskbird, Entra ID and Google Workspace SSO come with Business but SAML and SCIM are a paid add-on on every tier.

The Four People Who Have to Say Yes

A workplace product has to please several people at once, and they rarely want the same thing.

IT runs close between them, and deskbird takes it outright if EU-only hosting is non-negotiable. OfficeRnD Workplace takes the other three rows for most hybrid offices, because adoption, coordination and usage you can point to are what those stakeholders get measured on.

So, Which One You Should Pick?

deskbird is a good product and the right pick in a few clear cases: you are under about 35 people, your headcount and desk count are close to the same number, you need several locations on the cheapest possible plan, EU-only hosting is a hard requirement, or HRIS sync is the feature the whole rollout hangs on. In those situations, shortlist it and mean it.

For most hybrid teams, OfficeRnD Workplace is the better workplace management choice in 2026. It rates higher on G2, it puts the coordination features that make hybrid work on the entry plan instead of behind a quote, and it prices by the desks and rooms you manage rather than the people you hire, so the bill stops climbing every time you make an offer.

Better experience feeds higher utilisation, and higher utilisation is what finally justifies the lease. Dewhirst held a 23% desk-to-employee ratio by starting exactly there.

Name: New report reveals where coworking operators lose their week
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: For most of the past decade, the hard question in flex software was which product to buy. Operators compared platforms, argued about feature lists, and worried about picking wrong.
Post body:
For most of the past decade, the hard question in flex software was which product to buy. Operators compared platforms, argued about feature lists, and worried about picking wrong.

That question is close to answered. Our 2026 survey of 334 operators, from single-site independents to 30-plus-location portfolios, shows category leadership that barely moved in a year.

Stripe is now used by 85% of operators, up 8 points. HubSpot holds 54% of CRM. Salto leads door access. A shortlist drawn up in 2025 is still the right shortlist in 2026.

So this year we asked a different question, and checked the answers against anonymised connection data from 1,276 accounts on our platform. Once you own good software, why is the job still manual?

Download the newest Flex Space Tech Stack Report 2026 for free here. 

The average operator has connected 1.65 of 5 systems

Five categories run a flex space: payments, accounting, door access, CRM and network. Across 1,276 accounts, the average operator has 1.65 of them actively connected.

14% have connected nothing. A third have exactly 1, and it is nearly always payments, because payments is the connection you cannot avoid making. Out of 1,276 accounts, exactly 1 has all 5.

Set that against what the same operators say they want. 57% call accounting a must-have integration. 40% have connected it. Every other category shows the same shape, and 3 of them are wider.

The market can name the connections that would help. Most have not switched them on, and several are already paying for the one they never turned on.

Connection depth is a margin question, not an IT question

This is where the report gets uncomfortable, and where it gets useful.

If you and the operator down the road run the same platform, the same payment gateway and the same door access system, your software is not what separates you.

What separates you is how many of those systems hand data to each other without a person in between. That difference shows up in payroll, in month-end close, and in how many hours your community manager spends on data entry instead of members.

68% of operators named integration gaps as their biggest technology challenge this year, ahead of cost, training and AI. That number went up, not down. Every gap between 2 systems gets filled by a person, a spreadsheet, or a paid connector, which is why the cost complaint and the integration complaint are usually the same complaint counted twice.

Flex is not unusual in this. Salesforce’s 2025 Connectivity Benchmark Report found 90% of IT leaders say data silos are creating business problems. What flex has that most industries don’t is a short, stable vendor list, which makes the connection work tractable. A 12-person operator can close this gap in a quarter. That is a genuine opening.

One example of the cost. An operator in this survey traced 44% of their annual member support tickets to access cards. Gather, 7 sites and 2,800 members in Virginia, runs door access so it follows the membership automatically, and that ticket category mostly stops existing.

Manual work doesn’t disappear as you grow. It relocates

We asked one open question with no answer options: what is the most repetitive, time-consuming process in your day? 142 operators answered in their own words, and billing came first for the market overall.

Run the same analysis on multi-location operators only and the ranking turns over almost completely. Billing falls from 1st place to 8th. A different process takes the top spot.

That reordering is the most strategically useful finding in the report, because it tells you what your week looks like at 7 sites while you are still running 2. Most operators solve the bottleneck they have today and get ambushed by the next one. The chart is in the report, and it is worth planning against.

One number from the same section, since it holds at every size: 36% of operators still write contracts and quotes by hand in Word, PDF or email. Only 7% pay for software that does it.

If billing is your current version of this, our guide to automated coworking billing across locations covers what changes when payments and accounting talk to each other.

AI inherits whatever your stack already is

Last year, 26% of operators told us they were using AI tools. This year it’s 18%, and the share ruling AI out more than doubled.

Part of that is a stricter question. The direction is still real, and the explanation sits in how those tools were connected, which the report shows in one chart. MIT’s NANDA study found 95% of enterprise AI pilots delivered no measurable return, with integration into existing workflows as the dividing line.

The practical version for operators: an AI tool that cannot read your live member, booking and invoice data will produce confident answers about nothing in particular. Connection depth is the prerequisite for the entire AI conversation, which is why we put the AI section after the integration data rather than before it. Our view on where to start is in practical AI for coworking.

Operators have already told the industry what they want

Asked whether they would rather their space management platform absorb more functionality so they can drop vendors, or connect better to the tools they already keep, 66% chose connection. 34% chose consolidation. That split held across every cut of the data, by portfolio size and by region, across 2 years of surveys.

It should change what gets asked in a demo. Not how many features the platform has, but which of your named vendors have native integrations, what those integrations actually sync, and what still needs a person. We made the longer argument in why open integration ecosystems win and in 8 must-have coworking software integrations.

Why read the full thing

This post gives you just the argument. The report gives you the numbers to act on it.

Inside: category leaders for all 5 systems with regional breakdowns, including why the global accounting chart misleads anyone operating outside North America.

The complete say-versus-connected table across 1,276 accounts. The time-sink ranking cut by portfolio size, so you can see your next bottleneck before it arrives. AI spend, use cases and connection methods. And 6 moves for your 2026 roadmap, ordered, where the first costs nothing and takes an hour.

If you are budgeting for next year, or deciding whether to buy another tool or connect the ones you have, this is the peer benchmark to do it against.
