Name: Best States for Hybrid and Remote Work
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Hybrid work has settled from a temporary measure to a fixed way of how people work – but where you do it from makes the real difference. Home office days can mean a comfortable dedicated room and gigabit fibre in one state, or a cramped corner and a connection that drops mid-call in another.
Post body:
Hybrid work has settled from a temporary measure to a fixed way of how people work – but where you do it from makes the real difference. Home office days can mean a comfortable dedicated room and gigabit fibre in one state, or a cramped corner and a connection that drops mid-call in another.

To find out where hybrid and remote workers get the best deal, we scored every US state across 12 factors covering the things that actually shape your day-to-day hybrid work routine. Some of the indicators we took into account include: the share of local job listings for remote/hybrid jobs, rent prices and trends, electricity rates and everyday living costs, and more (you can review all of the criteria below).

And because where you live also decides how much of your salary you keep, we have paired the rankings with the two things a map cannot show: the states and cities that will pay you to move there, and the tax rules that can quietly cost a remote worker more than a cheaper rent saves.

Click through our interactive map below to see where your state ranks.

Top 10 Best States for Hybrid and Remote Workers

Delaware

Delaware is the number one state for hybrid workers, scoring 64.18/100. Out of all jobs available on Glassdoor, 2.25% of those in Delaware have remote and hybrid-remote opportunities, the fifth highest percentage in the country and 111% higher than the national average of 1.06%. On top of this, 97.77% of units in the state have access to at least 100 Mbps download and 20 Mbps upload speeds.

Why it wins: Delaware pulls off the rarest combination in the dataset – a genuinely deep remote job market attached to East Coast infrastructure, without East Coast prices. At 2.25%, its share of remote and hybrid listings is more than double the national average, yet average rent is $1,524 rather than the $2,229 to $3,044 of the states it sits between. Being inside the Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington corridor means a hybrid worker can still reach three major employment centres for the occasional office day. Its fatal crash rate of 28.7 per 100k registered vehicles is the highest in the index and, under our methodology, a signal of exactly the car-dependent commuting that remote work removes.

Best for: East Coast hybrid workers who still need to be within driving distance of a city office once or twice a week, and anyone hoping to find a remote/hybrid role locally rather than bring one with them.

Utah

Utah places second, scoring 61.77/100. The average cost of electricity in Utah is $0.13 per kWh, the fourth lowest in the country. In the state, 35.72% of people work from home at least one day per week, the 4th-highest percentage in the US, while 74.9% of the population lives within half a mile of a park, the third-highest percentage in the country.

Why it wins: Utah wins because of the average home size. A median home of 2,800 sq ft is the largest in the country and roughly 500 sq ft more than second-placed Wyoming – the practical difference between a dedicated office with a door and a laptop at the kitchen table. Pair that with the fourth-cheapest electricity in the US and the running cost of a proper home setup is unusually low. With 35.72% of Utahns already working from home at least one day a week, the Wasatch Front has built its coworking supply, childcare, and daytime economy around hybrid schedules rather than treating them as an exception.

Best for: Families who need square footage and a spare room to work in, and outdoor-oriented workers – 74.9% of the population lives within half a mile of a park, the third-highest figure in the index.

North Dakota

With an index score of 61.46/100, North Dakota comes third. The average electricity price in the state is $0.12 per kWh, the cheapest in the US, and the average rent is $981, the third-lowest overall. North Dakota also has the fastest median upload speed in the country, at 194.04 Mbps.

Why it wins: North Dakota wins on running costs and raw connection quality rather than lifestyle. It has the cheapest electricity in America at $0.12 per kWh, the third-cheapest rent at $981, and the fastest median upload speed in the country at 194.04 Mbps – close to triple the national median. Upload speed is the measure that decides whether a video call holds up and how long a large file takes to send, and it is the one most cost-of-living rankings ignore entirely.

Best for: Bandwidth-heavy workers – video editors, engineers pushing large builds, anyone on camera for most of the day – and, of course, people who’d like to save more in their bank account (who doesn’t!). Less suited to those who want to spend more time in nature, with park access at 37.7%.

Nevada

Nevada is fourth, with an index score of 58.20/100. In the state, 64.6% of the population lives within half a mile of a park, the 8th-highest percentage in the US. Additionally, 97.77% of units have access to at least 100 Mbps download and 20 Mbps upload speeds.

Why it wins: Nevada has no personal income tax, which is why a lot of remote workers choose it instead of California. Broadband coverage of 97.77% and park access of 64.6% give it big-state infrastructure at mid-market prices, and rent of $1,346 is around 40% below its western neighbor. Las Vegas and Reno also put a major airport within reach, which matters more than people expect once quarterly team travel replaces the daily commute.

Best for: Higher earners relocating from California, where the state income tax savings alone can run to thousands of dollars a year, and people who need to fly frequently on business trips.

Nebraska

Scoring 57.05/100, Nebraska is next. The average cost of electricity in Nebraska is $0.13 per kWh, the third lowest in the country. It also has a median upload speed of 110.18 Mbps, the eighth fastest in the US and 52% higher than America’s average.

Why it wins: Nebraska is the quiet all-rounder. It leads no single category outright, but almost nothing sits below average either: electricity is the third-cheapest in the country, median upload speed of 110.18 Mbps (52% above the national average), and rent stays under $1,150. One caveat the index doesn’t capture: Nebraska is one of a small group of states that applies a convenience-of-the-employer rule, which matters if you work for a Nebraska employer from another state.

Best for: Mid-career workers optimizing for cost and reliability rather than scenery, and hybrid employees who want a short drive into Omaha or Lincoln for occasional in-person days.

On the other hand, the worst state for hybrid-remote workers is Massachusetts, with a score of just 34.78/100. Closely following are New York and California, with scores of 36.45/100 and 38.63/100, respectively.

Why the biggest states rank lowest

The bottom of the chart is not a list of bad places to live. It is a list of places where living well as a remote or hybrid worker costs the most. Massachusetts, New York and California combine the highest rents in the index with electricity at $0.29 to $0.33 per kWh and the smallest homes: the median New York home is 1,490 sq ft, barely half of Utah’s 2,800. They also post the thinnest remote job markets in the country – 0.42% of New York listings and 0.47% of Californian ones, against a 1.06% national average – because employers in the densest labor markets have been the quickest to call people back to the office.

Two states fall for less obvious reasons. Hawaii and Alaska score well on remote job availability, at 1.68% and 2.22% of listings, and on lifestyle measures – 82.9% of Hawaiians live within half a mile of a park, the highest figure in the index – but both are dragged down by the two most expensive electricity supplies in the country. That is a cost you pay every hour you are at your home office. Maine and New Hampshire, meanwhile, have the least park access of any state, at 17.4% and 17.2%, despite their outdoor reputation – a reminder that the measure captures walkable everyday green space, not wilderness.

Who should still choose them: Anyone whose industry cluster, family or partner’s career is anchored in a coastal metro. The index measures the cost and practicality of working from home, not career ceiling: Massachusetts and California still concentrate biotech, finance and technology employers, and a remote role paying a Boston or Bay Area salary can comfortably outweigh a lower index score. Within the bottom half, Wisconsin, Michigan and Pennsylvania are the value picks – rents of $1,157 to $1,553 are below the national average, and they rank low mainly on remote job availability rather than affordability.

Ivan Guberkov, Chief Product Officer at OfficeRnD, said the following:

More and more companies are embracing flexible work models not just for economic reasons but to reach more talent as people are drawn to the freedom that hybrid-remote work offers.

Through analyzing a mix of economic and technological factors, this data shows where in the US hybrid-remote work is most viable and serves as a guide for those who value their work set up above other factors such as wages or office perks. This can help employers and employees make more informed decisions about where to live and operate based on their preferred work style.

The factor the map does not show: state income tax

Our index measures the cost and practicality of working from home. It does not measure what your state takes from your salary before you spend any of it – and for remote workers, who can in principle live anywhere, that is often the single largest financial variable in the decision.

Nine states levy no personal income tax at all: Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington and Wyoming. New Hampshire is the newest member, having fully repealed its tax on interest and dividends from January 2025. Three of the nine appear in the top eleven of our index, so the tax advantage does not have to be bought at the cost of a poor working environment.

No income tax does not mean no tax, though. New Hampshire carries the highest property tax rate of the nine, Washington taxes capital gains, and Texas and Wyoming lean heavily on property and sales taxes to make up the difference. The saving is real, but it is smaller than the headline implies once a mortgage is involved.

Alaska is the contrarian pick. It ranks 47th on our index, held back by $0.27 electricity and distance, but it is the only state that pays its residents to live there, through the annual Permanent Fund Dividend.

Get paid to move: remote work relocation incentives

A growing number of states, cities and regions now pay remote workers cash to relocate. The logic is straightforward: someone who arrives with an out-of-state salary spends locally without competing for a local job, so remote and hybrid workers are precisely the target market. Several of the largest programs sit in states that score well on our index – which means the incentive and the working conditions can be stacked rather than traded off.

These schemes open and close with local budgets. Northwest Arkansas’s Life Works Here program, one of the best known, at $10,000 plus a bicycle, has closed to new applicants, and others pause intake between cohorts. So make sure you check the program’s own site and see what the criteria are.

The Bottom Line

No state wins on every measure, and the right answer depends on which aspects you feel strongly about. Also, hybrid work has moved from a policy to the normal way of working, especially in some parts of the country. This index is also interesting because it shows the locations that would be most appealing to some employees, and companies that want access to talent could consider them as next office locations.

Where OfficeRnD Workplace Fits in

OfficeRnD Workplace handles desk and meeting room booking, shows teams who is coming in on which days so a trip to the office is never wasted. It also has the “Suggested day” functionality, which prompts people to book desks on the days that fellow teammates are in too. If a company is opening a new office in a hybrid/remote friendly state, Workplace provides attendance data to size and shape their space around how it is actually used.

Its customer list reads like a stock index, and the sales pitch points squarely at regulated, multi-site enterprises in pharma, manufacturing, defense, healthcare, and government.

Boil it down, and you get this. OfficeRnD Workplace is tuned for the person opening the app to plan their week. Envoy is tuned for the security and facilities team standing up a governed, audited building. Everything below is that one difference playing out in the details.

Does anyone actually open it?

A booking tool is worthless the moment people stop using it. When the office is optional, the tool with the least friction wins, every time.

Otherwise, the rollout is doomed to fail.

OfficeRnD Workplace sits inside Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar, and Slack. Someone books a desk from the chat thread they already have open. No second app, no extra password, no training session on the calendar. Desk, room, or parking spot, it’s a few taps in a place people already live.

Envoy leans on its mobile app and lobby iPads. That’s a real advantage at the entrance and a drag for daily desk booking.

Envoy Workplace reviewers on G2 keep landing on the same complaint: the app is slow to wake up, and the check-in button sometimes swallows a tap or two before it registers.

If you’re the IT or facilities lead whose success is measured by whether people adopt the thing, that first-week feel is the whole difference between a tool people use and one they quietly abandon.

To be fair, plenty of Envoy reviewers find it clean and easy, especially for checking in and spotting who’s around. The question was never whether both have a Teams integration. It’s whether the daily flow feels effortless once it’s switched on.

PlentyONE: 91.6% opened it, no mandate

PlentyONE, the German e-commerce software company (you might know it as plentymarkets), runs a fully hybrid setup across Germany and Romania where people come in whenever they like.

It also runs an aggressive 16% desk-to-employee ratio: one desk for every four staff. Go that lean and you court the worst version of return-to-office, where someone makes the commute only to find the floor empty and their team on Slack from home.

OfficeRnD Workplace, plugged into the tools PlentyONE already ran on (Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar), gave employees a live read on who was coming in and when, through office maps and schedules. No app to adopt, no policy to enforce.

The payoff: 91.6% of the team books desks and rooms through it, without a mandate telling them to. That’s what genuine adoption looks like, and it’s what lets PlentyONE keep hiring without paying for more office than it needs.

Check out the full PlentyOne case study to learn more.

Turning a shared calendar into an actual plan

Hybrid falls apart when everyone picks different days, and the office sits half empty, full of people working alone. Seeing who’s coming in is the first fix, and both tools handle it. Envoy shows a live map and a running view of who’s on site. OfficeRnD Workplace shows the same.

The gap opens up in what OfficeRnD does next. Rather than leaving you to squint at a map and figure it out, it recommends your best days to come in. Those picks are drawn from the colleagues you flag as favorites and the onsite meetings already on your calendar, and they land as a weekly nudge in the Teams chatbot.

You can follow up to 15 people, see which desk a teammate grabbed and book one beside them, and pull a remote colleague in for a specific day with an invite. Team neighborhoods keep a group together instead of sprinkled across three floors.

Both tools can tell you who’s in. Only one tells you which day is worth the drive and then sits you next to the people you came for. That second step is where showing up turns into working together.

This was one of the criteria we used to evaluate the best desk booking software of 2026 and the top hybrid work solutions too.

How about pricing?

Both vendors publish their prices, which already puts them ahead of most of this category. The models underneath are where they split, and the model matters far more than the headline number.

Here’s the scenario that settles it. Picture 100 people in one office sharing 60 desks.

With OfficeRnD Workplace, those 100 sit inside the Start tier, and you pay for the 60 desks and the rooms you manage. Not the headcount, the space. Your cost follows what you actually run.

With Envoy, you pay the platform fee, then bolt on Reservations at $5 a desk, then add Visitors from around $362 a location if you want the lobby covered, then any other module you need, each one billed above the platform.

That $5 desk rate already runs ahead of OfficeRnD’s $2 to $3, and every extra module and site stacks on top.

So do the math on two things before you trust any quote: your desk-to-headcount ratio, and how many modules and locations you’ll really switch on. OfficeRnD Workplace scales with desks and rooms. Envoy scales with the platform fee, the modules, the users, and the sites.

What people say once it’s running

Strip out the marketing and read the reviews, because that’s where the truth lives.

OfficeRnD Workplace users point to how easy it is for staff and admins alike, and how naturally it works in Teams and Outlook. Their two standing requests: tighter Outlook out-of-office sync and finer-grained admin permissions. Fair gaps, worth weighing.

Envoy Workplace users praise the visitor experience, the integrations, and the polished interface. Their repeated gripes: app speed, the odd check-in bug, and price. More than one says the product only feels worth it on the Premium tier, and that capabilities like emergency alerts sit behind extra charges.

On analytics the two are close. Both report utilization, occupancy, and traffic. OfficeRnD Workplace ties its numbers to real attendance through check-ins, while Envoy brings stronger visitor and security reporting.

Envoy is a serious platform and the right pick when visitor security, compliance, and emergency readiness sit at the front of the decision. On regulated or high-security sites, shortlist it and mean it.

Name: OfficeRnD Workplace vs desk.ly: Which Hybrid Work Tool is Right for You?
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: OfficeRnD Workplace and desk.ly are both desk and meeting room booking software that let hybrid teams reserve desks, see who is coming into the office, and track how space gets used.
Post body:
OfficeRnD Workplace and desk.ly are both desk and meeting room booking software that let hybrid teams reserve desks, see who is coming into the office, and track how space gets used.

Both platforms solve the same starting problem. They let people book a desk, see who else is coming in, and give facilities a read on how the office actually gets used.

And I know, this makes choosing the right one for you even more difficult. But let’s dive deeper to see the differences.

desk.ly comes out of Basecom, a German software company. It’s built around a simple booking flow, GDPR compliance by design, and a free tier that covers real companies, not just a trial. It’s a strong fit for European teams that want to get desk sharing running without a procurement process.

OfficeRnD Workplace is from OfficeRnD, which has built workplace and coworking software since 2015. It’s built around getting people to choose to come in. It holds coordination features, meeting rooms, and visitor management in the core product, not as a separate purchase. It also supports booking a parking spot and other custom workplace resources (like company cars, meeting pods, and more).

The rest of this comparison works through where each one wins, using public G2 data and each vendor’s own pricing pages.

OfficeRnD Workplace vs desk.ly: at a glance

Who should pick desk.ly, and who should pick OfficeRnD Workplace?

Pick desk.ly if you have fewer than 15 people and want the free tier’s full feature set, your company is based in the EU, and GDPR-by-design matters to procurement, or you mainly need desk booking without meeting rooms, parking, or visitor management. Desk.ly is also included in our best desk booking software comparison as well as in our best hybrid work software for 2026 list. 

Pick OfficeRnD Workplace if you want the system to suggest which days are worth coming in, enforce employee hybrid work policies, you need meeting rooms and visitor management alongside desk booking, you run more than one office or your team is bigger than 50 people, and your buyer needs SOC 2 and CCPA on top of GDPR.

Getting people to actually use it

A booking tool only pays off if people open it. Both platforms integrate with Microsoft Teams and Outlook, and both have web and mobile apps. OfficeRnD also integrates with Slack to provide a seamless booking experience.

desk.ly reviewers on G2 consistently point to the interface as easy to use, and the floor-plan view is the most-praised feature at this price point. The recurring complaint is the mobile app: several reviewers describe it as slow to load or less stable than the web version, and some call the overall design dated.

OfficeRnD Workplace holds a 4.6 rating from 158 reviews, spanning small businesses up to enterprise accounts. Reviewers describe it as easy for both employees and admins to pick up, with the Microsoft Teams and Outlook integration named most often as the reason. The recurring request is better Outlook status sync and more granular admin permissions.

Coordinating office days that are worth it

Visibility into who’s in is the baseline. desk.ly shows colleague presence status on the floor plan, so you can see who’s booked in and filter by team. That’s useful for finding a desk near people you work with.

OfficeRnD Workplace does the same, then adds a layer on top: it recommends your best days to come in, calculated from the colleagues you mark as favorites and the onsite meetings on your calendar. You can follow colleagues, see where a teammate booked, and grab a desk nearby. You can also invite colleagues to come to the office to ensure better collaboration. desk.ly doesn’t have an equivalent feature; its presence view tells you who’s in, not which day you should join them. OfficeRnD Workplace is also able to support hybrid work policies – there’s a dedicated space for that in the product and it helps employees to monitor and follow a particular office policy (like office days mandate).

Where AI actually shows up in each product

desk.ly has a genuine AI feature: it studies your past booking behavior and recommends a desk, aiming to get a booking down to two clicks. It also learns which equipment or location you tend to prefer.

OfficeRnD Workplace’s suggested-days feature solves a related but different problem. It’s a rules-based recommendation drawn from your favorite colleagues and calendar, not marketed as AI, and it answers which day to come in rather than which desk to book. However, their product team has announced a new feature roadmap where AI will be included in the product.

Meeting rooms, parking, and visitors

This is where the two platforms diverge most in scope. On desk.ly, meeting rooms and parking are Enterprise-tier features, bundled with a catering add-on, starting around €2.75 per user per month. Below that tier, desk.ly is desk booking only. desk.ly also offers guest booking, which lets an employee book a desk on behalf of a visitor, but there’s no dedicated reception or visitor-log system.

OfficeRnD Workplace includes meeting room booking from its entry Start plan, priced per meeting room alongside bookable desks. Visitor management is a separate paid add-on, called Visitor Hub, but it’s a full system: guest check-in, host notifications, badge printing, and delivery management, available across all three plans.

For a team that only needs desks, desk.ly’s entry pricing is hard to beat. For a team that also wants to manage meeting rooms and guests without adding a second vendor, OfficeRnD Workplace’s structure gets there without an Enterprise-level commitment.

Reading the numbers

Both platforms report on how space gets used. desk.ly’s workplace analytics dashboard covers occupancy trends and booking behavior, and it sits behind the paid Corporate and Enterprise tiers. One recurring theme in desk.ly’s G2 reviews is a request for deeper reporting to support long-term space planning.

OfficeRnD Workplace’s analytics cover bookable-resource utilization, meeting room utilization, workplace presence, and policy compliance, with exports to CSV, PDF, and image, available from the entry plan. If your case for desk booking software depends on proving utilization to finance or real estate, OfficeRnD Workplace’s reporting goes further out of the box.

Integrations

desk.ly connects natively to Microsoft Teams, Outlook, and Google Workspace, plus Personio for HR data, and lists an API for custom connections. Other sources describe additional HR-system integrations, including BambooHR and SAP SuccessFactors, though desk.ly’s own G2 listing names Google Workspace, Microsoft Teams, and Personio as its core integrations.

OfficeRnD Workplace connects to Microsoft 365, Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar, Slack, Okta for single sign-on, Brivo for door access, and offers API and webhook access at the Enterprise tier. Slack is the clearer gap on desk.ly’s side: it doesn’t appear in desk.ly’s listed integrations, while it’s a native option in OfficeRnD Workplace from the entry plan.

What reviewers say

desk.ly users like: the floor-plan view, how fast booking is, and customer support response times. Several reviews mention the admin side has more settings than the simple branding suggests. They cover booking rules, permission groups, and check-in controls.

desk.ly users dislike: the mobile app, which multiple reviewers describe as unstable or slow, and a design that feels older than newer competitors. A few also ask for more advanced reporting.

OfficeRnD Workplace users like: the ease of setup for both admins and employees, and how well it works inside Teams, Outlook and Slack.

OfficeRnD Workplace users dislike: limited customization in some areas and a wish for better calendar synchronization, according to G2’s review summary.

Pricing

Prices are in different currencies: desk.ly in euros, OfficeRnD Workplace in US dollars. Convert both to your own currency before comparing totals.

The two pricing models push costs in different directions. desk.ly bills per active user. This means that a 10-person team pays nothing and a 50-person team pays for 50 people even if only 20 desks exist. OfficeRnD Workplace bills per bookable resource. A 50-person team sharing 25 desks pays for 25 resources, regardless of headcount. The Start plan carries a real minimum: roughly $99 a month even for a very small team.

A practical way to compare: take your own headcount, your desk count, and whether you need meeting rooms and visitor management. Then price both against those numbers rather than the headline figures above.

How it lands for each stakeholder

desk.ly is a strong pick for small teams, especially in Europe, that want free or low-cost desk booking without much else attached. Its floor-plan view and booking flow earn real praise, and the price is difficult to beat under 15 users.

For teams that have outgrown basic booking, OfficeRnD Workplace is the stronger platform in 2026. It bundles meeting rooms, coordination features, and a path to visitor management into one system. It holds a review base five times the size of desk.ly’s across a wider range of company sizes.

Want to see it against your own floor plans? Book a live demo of OfficeRnD Workplace and walk through desks, rooms, parking, and coordination with your own office in mind.

Name: 11 Essential Hybrid Work Trends To Watch In 2026 (And Beyond)
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Hybrid is the answer now, not the question. For most knowledge teams, it has settled into the default, and the data has stopped moving.
Post body:
Hybrid is the answer now, not the question. For most knowledge teams, it has settled into the default, and the data has stopped moving.

Stanford economist Nick Bloom tracks remote work three ways at once: worker surveys, building badge swipes, and phone location data. All three land near the same number.

About a quarter of U.S. paid workdays happen at home, and that figure has barely changed since early 2023 (Gable, 2026).

By 2026, most leaders have stopped debating whether hybrid works. The harder questions are operational. Which days do people actually show up? How much office should you keep? What do you do about the Wednesday desk shortage? Where does AI fit?

Here are 11 trends shaping that work in 2026, with the data behind each one and what it means if you run facilities, IT, or HR. One of them comes straight from our own booking data.

11 Hybrid Work Trends for 2026

1. Hybrid settled into the default, and the numbers stopped moving

Among remote-capable U.S. employees, Gallup’s panel data puts 53% in a hybrid arrangement, 27% fully remote, and 20% fully on-site. Eight in ten knowledge workers now have some location flexibility.

Globally, the pattern holds at a lower volume. Across 35 countries, the Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes finds workers average about 1.4 work-from-home days a week, rising to 1.7 in English-speaking countries.

Workers value the arrangement at roughly 8% of their salary. They would accept about 8% less pay to keep two or three home days. That makes flexibility one of the cheapest retention levers HR has.

The stability is the story. Bloom’s survey of more than 1,000 executives found 85% would not change their work-from-home policy even if unemployment doubled, and planned return-to-office mandates would cut the work-from-home share of paid days by just 0.4 percentage points. The balance between remote and in-office work is fixed for now. The work is in running it well.

We recently prepared a report listing the best states in America for hybrid work. Go check it out.

2. The midweek crunch is now the main planning problem

This trend comes from our own data, and it is the one most workplace teams underestimate.

Across OfficeRnD Workplace bookings and check-ins, Tuesday to Thursday now drives near-full occupancy while Monday and Friday run light.

Peak days sit roughly 35% above the weekly average (OfficeRnD office space planning). Size your office to the weekly average, and you are short on desks midweek. Size it to full headcount, and you pay rent on a half-empty floor every Friday.

Two more patterns show up in the booking data, and both reshape how you buy space:

  • About 80% of meetings happen in rooms built for 6 people or fewer, while boardrooms of 17 seats and up sit near 12% use (OfficeRnD, 2026). Most companies built the opposite: a few big rooms, not enough small ones.
  • About 40% of booked rooms end as no-shows. Ghost bookings hide real capacity. A room that reads “fully booked” on the calendar can sit empty half the day.

So, what do you do with these numbers?

For facilities: plan around peak-day attendance divided by your desk-sharing ratio, not headcount. A team of 120 on a 3-day policy might bring 97 people on a busy Wednesday and need about 70 desks at a 1.4x sharing ratio.

For IT and HR: turn on check-in confirmation and auto-release for no-shows, so a booked-but-unused desk or room goes back into the pool. That single setting recovers a large slice of the capacity you think you are missing.

And if you need to optimize your office space better or plan a new one, check out this office calculator.

3. RTO mandates keep running into the building itself

The loudest workplace story of the past year is also the most instructive. Amazon moved more than 350,000 corporate staff to five days in the office from January 2025 and built badge dashboards that flag “low-time badgers” and “zero badgers”

Then the buildings pushed back. Amazon needed roughly 30% more desks than it had in cities including Atlanta, Houston, Nashville, and New York, which forced delayed timelines and dented the policy’s credibility with staff.

The talent math is worse than the desk math. About 80% of employers reported losing people after RTO mandates, and a quarter still planned to add in-office days anyway (HR Dive, 2026).

Gartner found full-time mandates produce no measurable productivity gain and can lower morale and trust. University of Pittsburgh research found the same: strict mandates hurt satisfaction without improving financial performance, and senior, tenured staff are the most likely to walk (Speakwise, 2026).

The lesson for 2026 is narrow. Tie in-office days to work that genuinely needs the room, like planning, onboarding, and cross-team projects. A blanket five-day rule pays the cost of a mandate without buying the collaboration it promises.

4. Structured beats optional: anchor days win

Flexibility without coordination creates a coordination tax. People drive in and find their team scattered or absent.

Gallup’s data is direct on the fix. Teams with a written hybrid collaboration plan are 2.2x more likely to say their policy has an extremely positive effect on collaboration, 66% more likely to be engaged, and 29% less likely to be burned out (FlexOS, 2026). Clear hybrid work policies turn that plan into a routine people can follow.

The market is moving the same way. JLL’s 2026 benchmark found fixed in-office days are now required by 62% of organizations, and the share of employees in three to four days a week jumped from 36% to 55% in a single year.

Set anchor days by team rather than by company. Teams need a shared rhythm, and the point of the office day is intentional collaboration: planning, onboarding, and cross-team work that goes better in person. The know-how is everywhere now, from business schools to hybrid work influencers sharing playbooks online.

5. Offices get sized to attendance, not headcount

The fixed desk per person is over for hybrid teams. Most hybrid offices run about 43% daily utilization, so more than half the floor sits empty on an average day while you pay rent on all of it (XY Sense, 2025, via OfficeRnD). Done well, hybrid cuts real estate costs by Up to 40%.

Buildings are busier than they were, just not full. Global utilization climbed to 53% in 2026, up from 38% in 2024. In 2025, CBRE still found that 66% of American organizations were operating at below 60% utilization on average (Luxafor, 2026).

LinkedIn shows what right-sizing looks like in practice. Instead of building its pre-pandemic plan of 1,080 desks for about 1,500 employees, the team used attendance modeling to land on 569 workstations, a cut of nearly 50%, and redirected the space to collaboration zones (OfficeRnD, 2026)..

The working ratio in 2026 sits at 3 to 7 desks per 10 employees, depending on how often people come in. With attendance rising, plan toward the higher end and base it on midweek peaks, not the weekly mean.

6. The workplace tech stack collapses into one platform

The early hybrid years left companies with a drawer full of point tools: one app for desks, another for rooms, a third for visitors, a spreadsheet for analytics. That stack is consolidating.

Workplace teams now want one system that handles desk booking, room booking, visitor management, and analytics, and that works inside the tools people already live in: Microsoft Teams, Slack, Outlook, and Google Calendar. The maturity of the category is visible in software listings, where “hybrid enablement” became its own product class.

The reason is practical, not fashionable. Every separate tool is a separate login, a separate dataset, and a separate vendor for IT to secure. One platform gives facilities, IT, and HR the same numbers to argue from, which matters more as those three teams start making space and budget decisions together.

7. Occupancy data becomes the shared language of FM, IT, and HR

Workplace decisions in 2026 rest on measured use, not policy assumptions. The gap is in data quality. JLL found 90% of organizations track utilization, but only 7% rate their data quality as excellent (OfficeRnD, 2026).

Three sources combine to close that gap. Badge data counts who entered the building. Booking logs with check-in confirmation record which desks and rooms were actually used. Occupancy sensors detect presence at the desk or room level, with no cameras and no identity data.

Each team reads the same data for a different decision. Facilities uses peak-day occupancy to consolidate floors or exit a lease. IT provisions AV, bandwidth, and signage by zone, since those cost the same whether the space is full or empty.

HR reads day-of-week variance as a policy signal: if Tuesday through Thursday run at 85% and Monday and Friday are ghost floors, the anchor-day structure is doing its job, or it isn’t (OfficeRnD office utilization, 2026).

The shift for 2026 is organizational. The companies that plan space well are the ones where FM, IT, and HR stop guessing separately and read one shared dashboard.

And workplace analytics is one of the key features to consider when choosing the best hybrid work platform for your needs.

8. AI agents move from the chat window into the workflow

The AI conversation changed in 2026. It went from chat assistants that answer questions to agents that complete multi-step tasks on your behalf.

The adoption numbers are large and uneven. IDC forecasts that 40% of Global 2000 job roles will interact directly with AI systems by 2026, and expects AI copilots embedded in roughly 80% of enterprise workplace apps.

Microsoft’s 2026 Work Trend Index analyzed trillions of Microsoft 365 signals and surveyed 20,000 AI users across 10 countries, and found that when managers actively model AI use, employee trust in agentic AI rises by 30 points (Microsoft WorkLab, 2026).

For workplace operations specifically, agents start handling the busywork: suggesting a desk near your team, forecasting next week’s occupancy, flagging rooms that book but never get used.

The risk lands on IT. Okta’s 2026 survey found 67% of U.S. workers use unapproved AI tools, and only 43% of knowledge workers say their company’s AI policies are clear, against 65% of executives who think they are.

Write a plain AI usage policy, decide what data agents can touch, and give IT ownership of agent access before shadow tools decide it for you.

9. Flexibility now sits on the compensation ledger

Employees price flexibility like pay, and they leave when it disappears. Roughly one in three workers say they would look for a new job if forced back to the office full-time, a figure that climbs in tech, finance, and professional services.

Pew found 46% of current work-from-home employees would be unlikely to stay if remote work ended. That shouldn’t come as a surprise.

Preference data points the same direction. Owl Labs’ 2025 State of Hybrid Work report found 83% of workers prefer a hybrid arrangement

For you HRs, the math is concrete. Flexibility is worth about 8% of salary to the average worker, costs nothing to offer, and competitors will use it to recruit your people the moment you take it away. Put it on the retention ledger next to comp and benefits, because that is where employees already keep it.

10. The office has to earn the commute

People will drive in for work they can’t do at home. They resent driving in to sit on video calls in a room they could have taken from their kitchen.

JLL’s Workforce Preference Barometer, which surveyed 8,700 workers across 31 countries, found negative feelings about office requirements come less from the policy and more from poor physical environments and a lack of in-office support.

The problem is widespread. By one count, 63% of workers returned to spaces that hadn’t been remodeled since the pandemic.

The office that works in 2026 does the things home can’t: in-person problem-solving, onboarding new hires, and the quick back-and-forth that real collaboration needs.

Spend on the reason people come in, which means open-space designs with more small rooms and focus booths, fewer fixed desks, and quiet zones for the calls people still take alone.

The goal is one of those hospitable workplaces people actually choose over their kitchen table. We first saw this shift up close at the CoreNet Global Summit Conference in Chicago.

11. The map splits by region and generation

Hybrid is global, but the dial sits in a different place depending on where and who you are.

The U.S. stays more attached to the office than most of the world, while parts of APAC lean further into remote. Singapore workers average about 2.8 work-from-home days a week, among the highest anywhere (FlexOS, 2026).

Culture, more than technology or industry mix, drives the difference: countries with similar economies and very different face-time norms land far apart. Teams spread across time zones also run more on asynch communication, where a message gets answered hours later instead of in real time.

Generation matters too. About 65% of remote-capable Gen Z employees prefer a hybrid setup, a higher share than millennials, Gen X, or boomers.

Younger workers also walk away from a job that brings them stress faster than older colleagues do, so the experience of the office matters most to the people you are trying to keep. For companies hiring across borders and age groups, one global policy will fit no one. Set a framework, then let regions and teams tune the days.

So, what this means for 2026

The debate about whether hybrid is real has ended. The work now is measurement and design: knowing who comes in and when, sizing space to the midweek peak, giving teams anchor days worth showing up for, and putting AI to work on the operational drag. For the wider set of numbers behind these shifts, see our hybrid work statistics.

The companies that get this right in 2026 share one habit. Facilities, IT, and HR work from the same occupancy data instead of three separate guesses. Sound hybrid work policies need a system to run on.

That is what OfficeRnD Workplace was built for. Employees book desks and rooms from web, mobile, Microsoft Teams, Slack, or Google Calendar, with check-in confirmation so only real usage counts. Every booking and check-in feeds utilization reports by day, floor, and zone, so facilities, IT, and HR finally read one set of numbers. Auto-release clears no-show bookings, and the analytics show your real peak instead of your policy on paper.

OfficeRnD Workplace leans toward the employee side: making the office easy and worth showing up for, so people choose to come in. In a voluntary hybrid office, that second instinct is the one that fills desks, because adoption is the whole game.

Understanding what each one is

The two come at the same problem from opposite starting points, and it still shows.

OfficeRnD has built workplace software since 2015, with employee experience as the design center: easy booking, coordination, and getting people to actually come in.

That focus shows in the reviews and the badges. It holds 4.6 on G2 from 158 reviews, with Leader badges in Desk Booking, Meeting Room Booking, Space Management, and Hybrid Enablement, and a feature set built around adoption rather than enforcement.

Yarooms began as a meeting room booking tool and grew outward into a broad enterprise platform: desk and room booking, hybrid scheduling, visitor management, digital signage, analytics, the Yarvis AI assistant, and a carbon dashboard.

That breadth, plus a deep compliance stack, is its calling card, and it sells hard into finance, healthcare, government, and education. It carries 4.3 on G2 from 95 reviews and 4.6 on Capterra.

The short version: OfficeRnD Workplace optimizes for the employee opening the app on Tuesday morning, Yarooms for the facility and security team standing up a governed platform across many sites. The rest of this comparison is where that split plays out.

Two ways to think about the office

A workplace platform reflects what its makers think the office is for, and that shapes how it feels to use every day.

Yarooms is strong on the facility side of the problem. Its credential stack, role-based controls, and reporting are built to manage space as a governed asset and to prove policies were followed. For a regulated buyer, that is exactly the right priority, and Yarooms does it well. That’s why it earned a place in our best space management software list this year.

OfficeRnD Workplace starts from the employee moment instead. The bet is that most empty desks stem from a clumsy booking experience: when booking takes seconds and the office is worth the trip, people come in on their own, and utilization follows.

Both views are valid. Which one fits depends on whether your main job is enforcing a mandate or earning attendance. Most hybrid offices in 2026 are trying to earn it, and the rest of this comparison is written with that reader in mind.

So, who should pick which?

Pick Yarooms if you need a built-in carbon dashboard for ESG reporting, you require on-premise or regional data hosting, or compliance is the main thing driving the purchase.

We included Yarooms in our list of the most popular hybrid work tools of 2026.

Pick OfficeRnD Workplace if your company runs on Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace and you want the tool reviewers consistently find easier to use, so people adopt it without training, or you want the system to actively suggest the best days to come in.

A shared status calendar tells you who is in; OfficeRnD goes further and recommends your day. Most hybrid offices fall into the second group. Here is why.

Getting people to actually use it

A booking tool only pays off when employees open it. When the office is optional, the easiest tool wins.

Both platforms let people book from inside Microsoft Teams, both add as a tab or personal app, and both have mobile apps, so on the surface they look similar. Yarooms markets it the same way OfficeRnD does: book from Teams, no new tools, no learning curve. The honest difference is not whether a Teams integration exists, it is how usable the day-to-day experience turns out to be once it is live.

Employees booked desks from the chat window they already had open every day, with no separate app, no second login, and no training rollout.

The result was a 23% desk-to-employee ratio that actually held up, because the booking flow lived where people already worked.

The review scores back this up. On G2, OfficeRnD Workplace holds 4.6 overall from 158 reviews against Yarooms’ 4.3 from 95, with a 9.5 quality-of-support score and reviewers who consistently describe it as simple and easy to use.

Yarooms reviewers are positive overall, but the recurring criticism is specific: the mobile app can be harder to navigate once floor plans are involved. For an IT or facilities lead measured on rollout success, that day-one usability gap is the difference between a tool people adopt and one they avoid.

Coordinating office days that are worth it

Hybrid work breaks down when everyone shows up on different days, and the office stays half full of people working alone. Visibility into who is coming in is the first fix, and both platforms handle it.

Yarooms gives a shared calendar where everyone sets a weekly status, and reviewers genuinely like it for planning their week around colleagues. OfficeRnD Workplace shows the same picture of who is in and where they sit.

The edge is what OfficeRnD Workplace does on top of that. Instead of leaving you to read the calendar and work it out, it suggests your best days to come in.

Those Highlight Days are calculated from the colleagues you mark as Favorites and the onsite meetings you have been invited to, and they arrive as a weekly nudge from the Teams chatbot.

You can follow up to 15 people, see which desk a teammate booked and grab one nearby, and send an invite to pull a remote colleague in for a specific day.

So the honest line is this: both tools tell you who is in. OfficeRnD Workplace tells you which day is worth the commute, then helps you sit next to the people you came in for. That is the part that turns visibility into actual collaboration.

Reading the numbers

Empty desks usually mean the booking experience is annoying, not that you have too much space. Good analytics tell you which one you are dealing with, and both platforms deliver here. OfficeRnD Workplace tracks desk and room utilization, attendance patterns, and presence through check-ins.

Yarooms reports occupancy, booking patterns, hybrid attendance, and visitor traffic, and its real-time availability gets specific praise from reviewers who say it helps them see what is open and book faster. Call this one a draw on the core reporting.

Yarooms adds a carbon dashboard for sustainability tracking, which OfficeRnD Workplace does not match. If ESG reporting is on your roadmap, that is a real point in Yarooms’ favor.

Where OfficeRnD Workplace turns analytics into value is the chain it sits in.

Easier booking drives higher adoption, the suggestions pull people in on the same days, and the utilization data then shows facilities and finance which desks, rooms, and floors are actually earning their keep. The numbers are only as useful as the behavior feeding them, and that is the loop OfficeRnD Workplace is built to close.

Visitors

Yarooms covers the same essentials: Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar, Slack, Azure AD, Okta, and a REST API at the Enterprise tier. Both connect to the identity and calendar tools a typical IT team expects.

Both also book from inside Teams as a tab or personal app, so the integration breadth is genuinely even. The difference shows up in usability and the coordination features, not in the connector list.

OfficeRnD Workplace users consistently call out how easy it is for both employees and admins, and the way it works inside Teams and Outlook. The common request is better Outlook status sync and more granular admin permissions. Worth knowing, and a fair limitation to weigh.

Yarooms users like the real-time availability and how fast desk booking is, and they praise the support team during onboarding and rollout.

Name: Building Your Coworking Software vs Buying It: The Real Math
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: AI coding tools got good fast. Like, really fast. Post body:
AI coding tools got good fast. Like, really fast. You can sit down on a Friday night, type “build me a member portal with billing and door access” into one of them, and watch something real appear by Saturday morning. It logs members in. It takes a payment. It looks like the thing you’ve been paying for every month.

The appeal writes itself. No $500 monthly fee. Full control over every feature. Software built for your one space instead of 10,000 others. For an operator tired of tools that almost fit, that’s a tempting weekend.

I get the pull. The honest question is whether that weekend build survives contact with live members and real money, month after month, at volume. Mostly it doesn’t, and the reasons are specific enough to walk through.

Let’s dive in.

What vibe coding gets right

Some of this works well. A quick prototype to test an idea. A custom occupancy report your current tool won’t give you. A small Slack bot that posts today’s desk bookings. For throwaway tools and one-off internal scripts, building it yourself is often the right call.

The real trouble starts when the same approach runs your billing and your front door.

What the software actually has to do

A booking calendar is easy. Here’s the part operators underestimate.

Start with billing. It has to prorate when someone upgrades mid-month, handle credits and refunds, and apply the right tax across plans and locations.

When a card fails, it retries the charge and sends the reminder. It tracks contracts and renewals, and books meeting rooms against each member’s credit allowance.

Access control has to grant a fob on day 1 and pull it the day a membership ends. And it all has to sync both ways with Xero or QuickBooks so your bookkeeper trusts the numbers, then report cleanly enough for an owner to act on.

Billing 200 members on a dozen plan types, with mid-month changes and a clean accounting export: that’s the hard 80%, and it’s the part nobody shows in a demo. We covered the operational version of this in how automated billing handles multi-location coworking.

Where the custom-built version breaks

Billing bugs cost real money, and they hide. A proration error undercharges 30 members for 3 months before anyone notices. Now you’re choosing between eating the loss or sending 30 awkward correction invoices. The code looked fine in testing. Edge cases only show up at volume.

Member and payment data become a liability you own. You’re holding names, emails, and card details, plus a record of who can open which door. AI-generated code is rough here.

Veracode’s 2025 study of more than 100 models found that 45% of the code they produced introduced a known security vulnerability. A separate 2025 analysis put the share carrying design flaws or known vulnerabilities at 62%. A PCI or GDPR problem in software you wrote yourself is your problem to explain.

Maintenance has no off switch. The door integration breaks on a Saturday night. There’s no vendor to call, no on-call engineer, no SLA. You fix it, or your members stand outside. The same goes every time Stripe or your accounting tool changes an API ,and your export quietly stops matching.

The knowledge leaves when the builder does. If you wrote it, every change runs through you. If you hired a freelancer, the system rots the day they move on, and nobody else can read the code.

The cost that doesn’t show on the invoice

The build is cheap. Running it for a year is not. Every hour you spend debugging billing is an hour you’re not filling desks, renewing members, or running events. That’s the expensive part, and it never appears on a receipt.

Put a number on it. Say upkeep eats 5 hours a week. That’s roughly 250 hours a year of an operator’s time spent on software a vendor would maintain for a monthly fee. We made the longer argument in our guide to coworking space automation.

Build vs buy: the trade-offs

Here’s the trade-off in one view.

Vibe coding your own

Pros:

  • Cheap to start, with no monthly fee.
  • A working first version in a weekend.
  • Built for your one space, with no features you’ll never touch.
  • Full control over how it looks and behaves.

Cons:

  • Billing edge cases (proration, tax, retries) break quietly once you’re at volume.
  • You own the security and compliance risk, including PCI and GDPR.
  • No support line, no SLA, no one to call when it fails at 11pm on a Saturday.
  • Upkeep takes your time every week, and the knowledge walks out the door when the builder leaves.

Using an established coworking space vendor

Pros:

  • Billing logic already tested across thousands of operators and millions of invoices.
  • Payment, accounting, and access integrations maintained for you when APIs change.
  • Security and compliance handled at the platform level, with SOC 2 in place.
  • Support, onboarding, and product updates you don’t have to write.
  • You stop being the single point of failure.

Cons:

  • A monthly fee.
  • Some features you won’t use.
  • Setup and configuration time up front.
  • Less control over the product roadmap.

For a live space handling real money, the vendor’s downsides are mostly cost and control. The build’s downsides land on you as billing errors, security exposure, and lost hours.

What an established vendor gives you

Here’s the gist of it:

  • Billing logic already tested across thousands of operators and millions of invoices, including the edge cases you haven’t hit yet.
  • Payment and accounting integrations someone else maintains when the APIs change. Access control partnerships with Kisi and SALTO, for example.
  • Security and compliance handled at the platform level.
  • Support with response times.
  • Product updates you don’t have to write.

The wider picture is in the coworking integrations that actually matter.

You also stop being the single point of failure. When billing breaks, you file a ticket instead of opening a code editor.

One operator ran this experiment in real life. Common Desk, a 22-location operator across Texas and North Carolina, built a custom system to run billing, room bookings, and operations, then hit the exact problems above: invoicing errors, messy Stripe and Xero syncing, and no in-house developers to call when something broke. They moved to OfficeRnD Flex and got a connected billing process their community managers could run without leaning on senior staff. As one of their community managers put it, the team no longer dreads billing each month. You can read the Common Desk story here.

Where OfficeRnD Flex fits

OfficeRnD Flex is the coworking management platform operators land on after they’ve tried to build their own and counted the hours.

It runs automated billing across locations and currencies, syncs two ways with Xero and QuickBooks, handles bookings and credits, and connects to more than 50 native integrations, including Kisi and SALTO for door access.

It’s also built to grow operator revenue by closing the gaps where money leaks out: slow lead response, manual billing errors, and underbooked rooms. Members get a white-label app for booking, payments, and invoices, and owners get reporting they can act on.

Security matters here too. OfficeRnD Flex is SOC 2 compliant, so member and payment data sits inside audited controls instead of code you’re maintaining alone.

Post body:
Wellbeing now shapes how flex spaces compete. Air quality, acoustics, lighting, biophilia, and programming all change how long members stay and what they’re willing to pay, and the 2025 research finally ties each of these factors to specific operator metrics rather than general “office productivity” claims.

Churn in coworking is mostly drift. Members don’t write a complaint about CO2 levels or afternoon noise; they just stop showing up, and the renewal email goes unanswered. Wellbeing investments are how you reduce that drift.

The operators winning on retention in 2026 are doing 4 things at once: measuring the space, programming it, pricing for it, and showing members the data. This piece is the operator’s view on how to do each.

What wellbeing means to a flex operator

A February 2025 study in Ergonomics tracked remote workers using the Experience Sampling Method and found that working from a coworking space produced higher wellbeing, productivity, and work engagement than working from home.

That’s the macro case for coworking. The harder question for operators is what specifically inside your space changes how long members stay and what they’re willing to pay.

The honest answer: air, sound, light, plants, and programming. Each one has 2025 evidence behind it. Each one is a budget line you can defend with research.

UK operator x+why is the worked example. A certified B Corp, x+why designs every site to blend sustainability, high-quality design, and wellness, and has scaled from 1 to 13 locations across London, Birmingham, Manchester, Milton Keynes, and Leeds in 6 years. Wellbeing is not an amenity here. It's the product.

Wellbeing is a P&L item

Run the maths. A 5% retention lift on a 200-member site at $400 average revenue per member adds roughly $48,000 to annual revenue.

A 10-point NPS improvement typically correlates with double the referral rate, which lowers your blended CAC. Wellbeing investments are one of the few categories that touch retention, referrals, and pricing power at the same time.

Members rank wellness in their top 3 desired amenities across every recent industry survey. Corporate buyers paying for hybrid member access now screen spaces on environmental quality.

Ventilation rates, noise control, biophilic design, and wellness programming show up in RFPs from finance, professional services, and tech tenants.

Premium tiers depend on the room feeling premium. You can’t sell a $700 dedicated-desk membership in a space where the air is stale, the lighting is fluorescent, and the only “wellness” feature is a plant in reception.

For the upsell mechanics that turn wellbeing investments into revenue, see our guide to coworking upselling.

The 7 things to fix first

Each item below is a specific intervention with 2025 evidence behind it. Cost bands are rough US/UK estimates for a 10,000 sq ft, 150-member space.

1. Indoor air quality and ventilation

The British Safety Council’s 2026 review concluded that CO2 levels within normal office ranges still measurably slow cognition.

A separate body of WGBC ventilation research found that offices ventilated at 24 L/s/person recorded around 35% fewer short-term sick days than spaces ventilated at 12 L/s/person.

Operator action: install CO2 sensors in every room above 8-person capacity. Alert at 1,000 ppm. Publish your air quality readings inside the member app. Members notice when you treat IAQ as a feature.

Cost band: $400 to $1,200 in sensors, plus HVAC tuning.

2. Acoustics and phone-booth ratio

Noise is the most-complained-about factor in open-plan flex spaces. Acoustic treatments alone don’t solve it. The booth-to-seat ratio does most of the work.

Operator action: target 1 phone booth per 8 to 12 hot-desk seats. Add a second tier of quiet rooms for 1 to 4 person calls. Use felt and fabric on hard walls. Track booth utilisation in your booking system. If you’re consistently above 85% utilisation between 10am and 4pm, you don’t have enough.

Cost band: $5,000 to $12,000 per pre-fab booth, plus soft furnishings.

3. Lighting (circadian and task)

Daylight beats artificial light for mood and cognition; that finding has held across 30 years of studies. The 2025 update: tunable white LEDs in meeting rooms and adjustable task lighting at every dedicated desk now cost a fraction of what they did 5 years ago.

Operator action: put focus zones along windows. Specify 4000K to 5000K tunable fixtures in meeting rooms. Give every dedicated-desk member a task lamp. Avoid harsh overhead spotlights in lounge areas.

4. Biophilia and maintenance

Indoor plants reduce reported stress and improve reported productivity by around 15% according to recent reviews of biophilic design research. Dying plants produce the opposite effect and signal neglect.

Operator action: budget for a monthly plant maintenance contract, not a one-time install. Use a mix of small desk plants and larger statement greenery. Real plants outperform images and artificial “green walls” on every measure that matters.

5. Thermal control by zone

Members consistently rate thermal comfort below other amenity categories. The reason is that “the office is cold/hot” is a complaint with no clear fix in a multi-zone space without zone controls.

Operator action: install zone-level thermostats and add a 1-tap thermal feedback button in the member app. Aggregate the feedback weekly. Complaint volume drops sharply once people feel heard.

6. Spatial variety

Single-density floor plans fail because members do different work at different times of day. A focused 9am task needs a different room than a 3pm brainstorm or a 5pm informal chat.

Operator action: plan for at least 4 zone types. Focus (silent), collaboration (low chatter), lounge/social, and dedicated quiet rooms.

For the full layout discussion, see our coworking floor plan guide.

7. Programming, not just design

Wellness rooms deliver when staff run programming in them. A weekly 7:30am yoga class or a Tuesday lunch-and-learn earns its square footage. An empty meditation room doesn’t.

Operator action: publish a 4-week wellness calendar. Partner with 1 or 2 local fitness or mental health providers for recurring sessions. Track sign-ups and attendance per event.

For the broader community angle, see our coworking community guide.

For more amenity ideas across categories, our innovative amenities article covers 10 areas including wellness, F&B, and concierge.

What the recent research says

Three findings worth knowing:

  1. The Taylor & Francis (February 2025) study of remote workers using Experience Sampling Method showed coworking produced higher wellbeing, work engagement, and productivity than home-based work.
  2. Initial’s April 2025 IAQ report found that 60% of office workers said they would leave a job over indoor air quality concerns. The operator equivalent is member attrition.
  3. The British Safety Council’s 2026 guide reported that CO2 levels inside commonly accepted “safe” office ranges still produced slower response times and lower task throughput in a multinational study of 300+ office workers over 12 months.

The combined picture: members feel the difference between a well-ventilated, naturally lit, acoustically planned space and one that meets only the visual brief. They vote with their renewals.

How to measure wellbeing as an operator

Track 3 metrics quarterly:

  1. NPS with a wellbeing sub-question. Add one line: “How do you rate the physical environment of the space?” Score it 0 to 10 alongside your standard NPS. Watch the gap between the 2 numbers.
  2. CO2 ppm logs. A 30-day rolling average per zone. Anything over 1,000 ppm consistently is a ventilation problem.
  3. Quiet-room and booth utilisation. Pull this from your booking system. Above 85% utilisation in core hours means under-supplied. Below 40% means overspent.

OfficeRnD Flex’s Data Hub gives you the booking, occupancy, and member feedback data in one place. The IAQ sensors are a separate hardware spend.

The operator wellbeing checklist

Score yourself yes or no on each:

  • CO2 sensors installed in every meeting room and the largest open-plan zone
  • Ventilation rate hits 20 L/s/person or higher
  • 1 phone booth per 8 to 12 hot-desk seats
  • At least 1 quiet room per floor
  • Tunable white LED lighting in meeting rooms
  • Task lamp on every dedicated desk
  • Real plants in every member-facing zone, maintained monthly
  • Zone-level thermostats
  • 4-week rolling wellness programme published in the member app
  • Member feedback mechanism for thermal, acoustic, and air-quality issues
  • Wellbeing NPS sub-question tracked quarterly
  • At least 1 wellness-aligned local partner (gym, studio, mental health provider)

8 or more “yes” answers: you’re well ahead of most flex operators. 4 to 7: you have the basics and a clear list of upgrades. 3 or fewer: retention is probably suffering, and you don’t have the data to see it yet.

Where this fits in 2026

Wellbeing is one of the strongest differentiators left in a market where most operators offer the same core stack: WiFi, desks, meeting rooms, coffee.

Operators competing on environment, programming, and member experience are pulling ahead on retention and ARPU. For the wider trend picture, see our coworking and flex space trends for 2026: the operator playbook.

The connection is indirect: when operations run themselves, your community team has the hours to run programming, gather feedback, and read the utilisation data that tells you what's working.
