Name: How to Measure Space Utilization on a University Campus
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Most US and UK campuses run their academic buildings somewhere between 25 and 45% utilization, and many planners can’t tell you which buildings are pulling down the average. The data exists.
Post body:
Most US and UK campuses run their academic buildings somewhere between 25 and 45% utilization, and many planners can’t tell you which buildings are pulling down the average. The data exists.

It just lives in 4 places at once: timetabling software, building swipe systems, sensor dashboards, and the memory of the facilities team that walks the corridors at 2pm.

Facilities directors, space planners, and operations VPs need a real number on campus utilization before any big decisions about leases, renovations, or new construction. Here’s how to get one.

TL;DR: Campus space utilization is frequency multiplied by occupancy. Most universities only measure booked time, which overstates actual use by a wide margin. The 3 data sources (booking systems, sensors, manual audits) all have limits, so run a 4-week manual audit to set a baseline before buying any software. UK benchmarks treat 35%+ as good, 25 to 35% as fair, and below 25% as poor, but available-hours definitions change the comparison across countries.

Before you start:

  • Define available hours per room class
  • Pull existing booking data for the past 14 weeks
  • Pick 30 to 50 representative rooms across building types
  • Audit at 30-minute intervals for 2 weeks
  • Compare booked frequency to observed frequency
  • Use the gap to decide what to do next

What space utilization actually measures

Space utilization (check out this guide) is one number built from two others.

Frequency is the share of available hours a room is used. If a seminar room is open 40 hours a week and gets booked for 24, frequency is 60%.

Occupancy is the share of seats filled when the room is in use. If that seminar room seats 30 and the average session has 18 students in it, occupancy is 60%.

Utilization is frequency multiplied by occupancy. In this case, 60% x 60% = 36%.

That last number is the one that matters. A room booked every hour but half-empty during each session is doing the same work as a room booked half the time but packed when in use.

One caveat. “Available hours” is a definition your team owns. Some institutions count 9am to 5pm Monday to Friday (40 hours). Others count 8am to 9pm Monday to Friday plus Saturday morning (60+ hours).

The benchmark you compare against has to use the same window, or the comparison is meaningless. The SCUP and NACUBO joint resource on data-informed space utilization makes this point repeatedly: agree on definitions internally before you measure anything externally.

Space utilization and workplace analytics are among the must-have features to look for when choosing the best hybrid work solution for your organization.

Why your timetable lies

Guess what – a booking records who reserved a room, not who used it.

Consider a 200-seat lecture hall booked Tuesday at 10am for a survey course. The timetable says: 100% frequency for that hour, 100% occupancy assumed, 100% utilization. The reality on a typical Tuesday in week 7: 62 students physically present.

The same room books at 11am for a lab section that gets cancelled because the instructor is at a conference. No one updates the calendar. The room sits empty. Frequency in the data: 100%. Frequency on the floor: 0%.

Across a 14-week semester, those gaps compound. Booked use and actual use are two different measurements, and most campuses are still confusing the two.

The fix is straightforward: measure both, and treat the gap between them as one of the most useful numbers you have.

3 data sources and where each falls short

1. Booking and scheduling data

What it tells you: who reserved what, when, for how long, and which department owns the booking.

Where it falls short: it counts intent, not presence. A 200-seat hall booked for a 30-person seminar reads as fully booked. A “ghost booking” that no one cancels reads as use. Recurring weekly bookings that haven’t met since week 3 of the semester still register.

The fix: combine booking data with cancellation data, and require check-ins for any booking over a certain size. A room ignored for 15 minutes past the start time gets released. Most modern booking platforms do this automatically.

2. Sensors and people counting

What it tells you: how many people were actually in the room, and when.

Sensor types vary. Passive infrared (PIR) sensors detect motion but don’t count. Wi-Fi probe counting estimates crowd size from device signals. Computer vision cameras count heads. Thermal sensors count without identifying anyone, which matters for GDPR in Europe and student privacy in the US.

Where it falls short: cost, installation friction, and noise. Wi-Fi counting overcounts students who carry 2 devices. PIR misses still classes. Cameras raise privacy reviews that can take 6 months to get through governance. Sensor data also tells you nothing about who used the room or why.

The fix: pick one sensor type per space class. Lecture halls do well with thermal or vision counters. Study rooms and faculty offices do well with PIR plus desk reservation data. Don’t try to instrument every room. Instrument the 15 to 20% that drive the most decisions.

3. Manual audits

What it tells you: ground truth.

The classic method, used by UK and Australian universities for decades, is the room-by-room walk-through. An auditor visits each room at fixed intervals (every 30 or 60 minutes), records whether it’s in use, and counts heads.

Two weeks of audits across a typical week gets you a defensible utilization number for a fraction of the cost of sensors.

Where it falls short: labor. A campus of 800 timetabled rooms needs roughly 200 to 300 hours of auditor time per cycle. The data also goes stale fast. By the time the report is written, the semester has changed.

The fix: use manual audits to calibrate. Run a 4-week audit once, get a true baseline, then use booking and sensor data going forward, with annual audit re-checks for drift.

Benchmarks worth using

The most cited target in the field comes from the UK National Audit Office’s 1996 Good Practice Guide and the Space Management Group’s 2006 follow-up: utilization of 35% or above is good, 25 to 35% is fair, below 25% is poor. Most UK universities still use these bands.

In Australia, TEFMA’s target is higher: 75% frequency multiplied by 75% occupancy gives a 56% utilization goal. In Virginia, the State Council of Higher Education for Virginia targets 60% x 60%, or 36%.

The honest read: these targets are policy decisions about how hard a campus should work its rooms. A 35% target reflects the reality that timetables don’t fill evenly, that students don’t show up at 8am, and that pedagogy needs slack. Pushing the same campus to 56% will produce schedules that work on paper and break in practice.

Two practical rules:

  1. Don’t benchmark across countries without adjusting for available-hours definitions. A 35% UK number and a 40% US number may describe the same building.
  2. Benchmark against your own historical data first. A campus that moved from 22% to 31% in 3 years is doing better than one that has held flat at 38%.

The Education Advisory Board’s analysis of multiple consulting reports shows how much benchmark choice changes the story. Across reports, actual classroom utilization varied from 18.6 to 29.5 weekly room hours, while the targets used in those same reports ranged from 24 to 40. Some institutions with high actual numbers got told they had problems.

Some with lower numbers got told they were on target. The benchmark drove the conclusion.

A 4-week audit you can run before buying anything

If you’re building the business case for a booking platform or a renovation, run this audit first. It takes 4 weeks, costs roughly $8,000 to $15,000 in auditor time, depending on campus size, and gives you a defensible baseline.

Week 1: scope and definitions.

Pick 30 to 50 representative rooms across building types (lecture halls, seminar rooms, labs, study rooms, faculty offices). Agree on available hours per room class. Pull existing booking data for those rooms for the past 14 weeks. Get a privacy review started if you plan to use any sensor or video data.

Weeks 2 and 3: observation.

Run room-by-room audits at 30-minute intervals during operating hours, 5 days a week. For each visit, record: room ID, time, in-use yes/no, headcount, and apparent activity (class, study, meeting, idle). Two auditors with clipboards and a Google Form is enough. Pair this with whatever booking data your timetabling system already produces.

Week 4: analysis and reporting.

Compute frequency, occupancy, and utilization for each room and each room class. Compare booked frequency to observed frequency.

The gap between them is your no-show rate. Build a simple report with 4 charts: utilization by room class, utilization by time of day, the booked-versus-actual gap, and the 10 most underused rooms by square footage.

Expected findings, based on what most campuses see: peak demand will cluster between 10am and 2pm, off-peak hours will look almost empty, lecture halls will be oversized for the classes assigned to them, and at least 1 building will turn out to be a candidate for repurposing or release.

These findings give you the case for whatever comes next. If new software is part of that case, the questions to put to scheduling vendors get much more specific once you have a real baseline to compare against.

What to do with the data

Once you have a real utilization number, the conversation changes. You stop arguing about whether the campus is overbuilt and start deciding what to do about it.

Common actions, in rough order of how often they get taken:

  1. Right-size classroom assignments. Move the 30-person class out of the 200-seat hall. This is the highest-frequency win and the easiest sell to academic departments.
  2. Consolidate underused buildings during low-demand periods. Close one wing on Fridays. Run summer programs in 2 buildings instead of 5.
  3. Introduce booking and check-in workflows for shared rooms and for shared desk areas used by hybrid faculty and staff. Released no-show bookings recover 8 to 15% of frequency in most studies.
  4. Make the case for repurposing or release. A building below 20% utilization for 2 consecutive years is a capital planning conversation.
  5. Inform new construction decisions. If existing space sits at 30% utilization, a new building should require either a 50%+ utilization commitment or a documented activity that current space can’t support.

Measuring before deciding matters more than which platform you pick. Universities that ran a clean baseline first tend to choose simpler tools and get more out of them. The right university booking software handles the booking, check-in, and reporting side once the baseline is in place. The audit comes first.

The single most useful exercise for any campus space team in the next academic year is the 4-week audit described above.

The number it produces will be defensible across the provost’s office, the CFO, the deans, and the facilities team. Once that number exists, decisions about renovations, leases, hybrid policies, and new buildings get faster and quieter.

Resources

  • SCUP and NACUBO. Data-Informed Space Utilization: Cultivating Partnerships (2022). Definitions, governance, and the case for agreeing on space data before benchmarking. https://www.scup.org/resource/nacubo-data-informed-space-utilization-cultivating-partnerships/
  • Education Advisory Board. Why space utilization reports may not be actionable enough for higher ed leaders (2025). Analysis of how benchmark choice changes conclusions across consulting reports, with weekly room hour ranges. https://eab.com/resources/blog/strategy-blog/space-utilization-reports-not-actionable-enough-higher-ed-leaders/
  • Ye et al. An Empirical Study on Assessing Classroom Space Utilization Efficiency in Higher Education Institutions. MDPI Buildings (2025). Reference for the UK National Audit Office 1996 thresholds (35%+ good, 25 to 35% moderate, below 25% inefficient). https://www.mdpi.com/2075-5309/16/10/1929
  • Abdullah, Mohd. Ali, and Alias. Classroom Management: Measuring Space Usage (2012). Comparative reference for TEFMA’s 56.25% target, SCHEV’s 36% target for Virginia, and the SMG 2006 benchmark bands. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/239938981_Classroom_Management_Measuring_Space_Usage
  • Occuspace. Top Platforms for University Space Utilization Reports (2026). Source for the Fall 2025 average campus utilization figure of 45%, down from 53% the year before. https://www.occuspace.com/blog/top-platforms-for-university-space-utilization-reports

Name: Desk Booking for Universities: How to Support Faculty, Staff and Hybrid Academic Teams
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: University desks are harder to plan than they used to be.
Post body:
University desks are harder to plan than they used to be.

Faculty may teach on campus 2 days a week, hold office hours in different buildings, and split time between research, teaching and remote work. Administrative staff may follow hybrid schedules. Visiting researchers may need a temporary place to work. Departments may own rooms that other teams also need to use.

At OfficeRnD, we work with numerous universities, so we see the same pattern often: the issue is rarely just “not enough desks.” It is usually a mix of shared space, changing schedules, department rules, unclear availability, and limited visibility into how campus workspaces are used.

TL;DR: Desk booking helps universities manage shared workspaces for faculty, staff, adjuncts, visiting researchers and hybrid teams. It works best when universities define clear rules before rollout: who can book each area, how far in advance, whether recurring bookings are allowed and what happens when someone does not show up.
A good setup should include floor plans, role-based permissions, calendar connections, SSO, booking reminders and reporting by building, department and usage patterns. For small pilots, an Excel desk booking template can work. For multiple departments, campuses or user groups, dedicated desk booking software gives facilities, IT and workplace teams more control.

Desk booking gives universities a clearer way to manage shared workspaces across departments, buildings, and campuses. It lets faculty and staff reserve the right space before they arrive, gives facilities teams better usage data, and helps IT support hybrid work with fewer manual processes.

A fixed seating plan does not always match how higher education teams work today. Desk booking can make shared campus workspaces easier to find, easier to manage, and easier to report on.

What desk booking means in a university setting

Desk booking lets people reserve a desk, workstation or shared work area for a specific time.

In a university, that can include:

  • Faculty hot desks
  • Staff desks
  • Visiting researcher desks
  • Adjunct faculty workspaces
  • Administrative team areas
  • Shared department offices
  • Touchdown spaces between classes or meetings
  • Desks near labs, seminar rooms or student service areas

The goal is simple: people should know where they can work before they come to campus.

For facilities teams, desk booking also shows how shared workspaces are being used. Which buildings fill up on Tuesdays? Which desks are rarely booked? Which departments need more shared space? Which areas look busy in theory but sit empty most days?

That data can support better campus planning.

Where desk booking fits alongside room booking

Desk booking and room booking solve different day-to-day problems.

Room booking is usually for meetings, classes, interviews, group work or events. Desk booking is for individual work. A faculty member may book a desk in the morning, reserve a small meeting room for student office hours, and check in a guest lecturer later that day.

Universities often need both.

Desk booking becomes especially useful when:

  • Faculty no longer have assigned offices
  • Adjunct faculty need temporary workspace
  • Staff teams work hybrid schedules
  • Visiting researchers need short-term desks
  • Departments share work areas
  • Admin teams need predictable office days
  • Facilities teams need usage data before changing space plans

A basic shared calendar may handle a few rooms. It usually struggles when many people need to find desks by location, department, access rules and availability.

Here’s a guide on the best desk booking software for 2026, and another one on deciding on the right scheduling software for universities.

Common desk booking use cases in higher education

Faculty office days

Faculty schedules vary by semester, department, and teaching load. Some faculty members need a quiet place for grading and research. Others need space near students, labs or department staff.

Desk booking can help faculty reserve space around their campus days instead of depending on informal arrangements.

Useful features include:

  • Booking by building or floor
  • Filters for quiet areas
  • Visibility into nearby colleagues
  • Recurring bookings for office days
  • Easy cancellation when schedules change

Adjunct and part-time faculty

Adjunct faculty often move between campuses, classes, and institutions. They may need workspace for short blocks of time before or after teaching.

A desk booking system can give them access to shared faculty areas without assigning permanent offices that may sit unused. This can also reduce pressure on department coordinators who would otherwise manage requests manually.

Administrative teams

University admin teams often need some shared in-person time for planning, student services, finance, HR, operations or IT support.

Desk booking can help teams coordinate office days around the work that benefits from being on campus.

For example, a student services team may reserve nearby desks on peak advising days. An IT team may book workstations near service areas when new staff or faculty onboarding is scheduled.

Visiting researchers and fellows

Visiting researchers may need desks for a week, a semester or a short research project.

Desk booking helps departments provide access without changing long-term seating plans.

For this use case, permissions matter. A visiting researcher may need access to one building, one floor or one department area, with a defined start and end date.

Shared research or lab-adjacent spaces

Some work happens near labs, studios, clinics or research facilities. The desk itself may be ordinary, but the location matters.

Desk booking can help users find spaces near the rooms and resources they need.

This is useful when workspaces are tied to:

  • Research groups
  • Lab access
  • Specialist equipment
  • Recording rooms
  • Project teams
  • Department areas

Hybrid staff schedules

For hybrid staff, desk booking removes guesswork from campus days.

People can see where they can sit, who else plans to be in and whether a department area has enough capacity before they travel in.

This matters for employee experience, but it also matters for space planning. Booking data can show whether a hybrid policy matches how people use campus workspaces.

What good desk booking looks like for users

Adoption depends on the booking flow.

Faculty and staff should be able to book a desk in a few steps without knowing room codes, building abbreviations or internal facilities language.

A strong booking experience usually includes:

  • Search by building, floor or area
  • Interactive floor plans
  • Filters for space type or equipment
  • Real-time availability
  • Mobile and desktop access
  • Calendar visibility
  • Simple booking changes
  • Clear check-in instructions
  • Booking reminders

Floor plans are especially useful on large campuses. A desk name alone may mean little to a visiting lecturer or new staff member. A visual floor plan helps people understand where the desk is, what is nearby, and whether the location suits their day. This where Excel desk booking templates typically fail, for example.

Permissions are the hardest part

Desk booking for a small company can be simple. Desk booking for a university needs more control.

Different groups need different access. A shared admin area may be open to staff only. A faculty workspace may be available to one school or department. A visiting researcher may need temporary access. A student worker may need access during certain hours.

The system should support rules such as:

  • Department-based access
  • Role-based access
  • Building-level permissions
  • Faculty-only spaces
  • Staff-only spaces
  • Visiting researcher access
  • Booking windows
  • Booking duration limits
  • Recurring booking rules
  • Admin overrides

This is where universities should be careful. If permissions are too basic, the system may push teams back to spreadsheets, email approvals, and side agreements.

Desk booking data facilities teams can use

Desk booking gives facilities teams a clearer view of workspace demand.

Useful metrics include:

  • Desk bookings by building
  • Desk bookings by floor
  • Peak days and times
  • No-shows
  • Cancellation rates
  • Department-level usage
  • Low-use areas
  • High-demand areas
  • Recurring booking patterns
  • Average booking duration

Facilities teams need more than a booking count. They need data that explains where demand is concentrated, which areas are underused and which rules may need to change.

EAB’s 2025 analysis of higher education space utilization reports found that colleges and universities often collect room-by-room usage data, building inventories, floor plans, staffing data, and enrollment data.

It also found common patterns such as offices being used less than half the time, classrooms peaking from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., and labs being underused in some departments while constrained in others. That variation is why desk booking data should be reviewed by building, department, space type, and day of week.

Desk booking data can answer practical questions.

Do faculty desks fill up on the same 2 days every week? Are some buildings busy while others are underused? Do admin teams need more shared space near student-facing services? Are desks booked often but not checked into?

The answers can guide small changes, such as opening another shared area on peak days, changing access rules or converting low-use desks into rooms that match stronger demand.

They can also support larger planning conversations around renovations, consolidation, and campus workplace strategy.

How desk booking supports IT

IT should be involved early because desk booking touches identity, calendars, and access.

Key questions include:

  • Does the system support single sign-on?
  • Can it connect to Azure AD, Okta or Google?
  • Does it work with Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace?
  • How are users added and removed?
  • Can permissions follow departments or user groups?
  • What data does the system store?
  • What admin controls are available?
  • How does the system handle multiple campuses?

If the tool doesn’t fit the university’s identity and calendar setup, adoption will be harder. IT may also end up managing exceptions manually.

How desk booking supports HR and workplace teams

Desk booking can help HR and workplace teams understand how hybrid work is playing out.

The useful questions are practical:

  • Are teams coming in on the days they planned?
  • Do people have enough desk options on peak days?
  • Are departments using shared spaces fairly?
  • Are people booking near colleagues when they need to collaborate?
  • Are some teams avoiding campus because they cannot find suitable space?

Flexible work is still a live issue in higher education. CUPA-HR’s 2025 Higher Education Employee Retention Survey found that 28% of higher ed employees currently work in a hybrid or remote arrangement, while 61% prefer hybrid or remote work.

For HR and workplace teams, desk booking can help make those policies easier to manage by showing whether people have enough workspace on the days they come to campus.

Desk booking data should be used with care. It is more useful for planning than monitoring individuals. The goal is to understand patterns, fix space problems, and make office days easier to plan.

Booking rules universities should define before launch

Desk booking works better when the rules are clear before rollout.

Start with these decisions.

Who can book each area?

Define access by department, role, campus or user group.

How far in advance can people book?

A long booking window may help faculty plan the semester. A shorter booking window may reduce unused reservations.

Can people book recurring desks?

Recurring bookings can help with office days, but they can also block shared space. Use them carefully.

What happens when someone does not show up?

Check-in rules can help facilities teams separate planned usage from real usage.

Can people book on behalf of others?

In a university setting, that’s important. Department coordinators may need this option for guest lecturers, visiting researchers or new staff.

Which desks need extra instructions?

Some desks may be near restricted spaces, shared equipment or department-specific resources.

Rollout tips for universities

A full campus rollout can get messy if every department has different expectations.

A focused rollout is easier to manage.

Start with one area where the need is clear. Good pilot areas include:

  • A shared faculty workspace
  • An administrative department with hybrid schedules
  • A building with several shared desk areas
  • A visiting researcher workspace
  • A department that already manages desks manually

During the pilot, track:

  • How many users activate accounts
  • How many bookings are created
  • Which spaces are most booked
  • Which rules cause confusion
  • How many no-shows happen
  • Which support questions come up
  • Whether users can find the spaces they need

After 30 to 60 days, adjust the rules before expanding.

Common mistakes when rolling out desk booking in universities

Treating desk booking as a facilities-only project

Facilities may own the space, but IT, HR and departments all affect rollout. Bring them in early.

Ignoring department rules

Universities rarely have one simple access model. Department rules should be part of setup.

Using desk booking data without context

A low-use area may be in the wrong location, restricted to the wrong group or poorly explained in the system. Data should start the conversation.

Letting recurring bookings take over shared space

Recurring bookings can be useful for office days. They can also recreate assigned seating by accident.

Skipping communication

Users need to know which spaces are bookable, who can book them, and what to do when plans change.

Desk booking checklist for universities

Use this checklist before rollout:

  • List every desk area that should be bookable
  • Define access by department, role, and campus
  • Decide which users can make recurring bookings
  • Set booking windows and duration limits
  • Connect calendars where needed
  • Set up single sign-on
  • Add floor plans or clear location details
  • Write short booking instructions
  • Define no-show or check-in rules
  • Train department admins
  • Review usage after the first 30 to 60 days

How to connect desk booking with the wider campus scheduling strategy

Desk booking works best when it is treated as part of a wider campus space plan.

A university may start with shared desks for faculty or staff, then expand into related use cases:

  • Reserving small rooms for office hours
  • Managing visitor check-ins for guest lecturers or contractors
  • Tracking desk and room demand by building
  • Coordinating hybrid office days for departments
  • Giving facilities teams clearer space usage data

This helps teams avoid managing desks in one system, rooms in another, and visitors through a separate manual process.

Before choosing a desk booking tool, check how it would fit with the other scheduling workflows your university already manages.

The most useful setup is usually the one that gives people a simple way to find and book space while giving facilities, IT, and workplace teams enough control behind the scenes.

Name: How to Choose University Scheduling Software: A Practical Guide for Higher Education Teams
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Choosing university scheduling software gets complicated fast because universities schedule more than classes.
Post body:
Choosing university scheduling software gets complicated fast because universities schedule more than classes.

A campus may need to manage faculty offices, shared desks, meeting rooms, study rooms, labs, guest lecturers, visiting researchers, contractors, department-owned spaces, and hybrid staff schedules. Each group has different needs. Each space has different rules.

The buying process should start with a simple question: Which scheduling problem are you trying to solve?

University scheduling software can mean academic timetabling, room booking, event scheduling or campus workplace scheduling. This guide focuses on software for managing physical campus spaces, shared resources, visitors, and hybrid faculty or staff schedules.

That scope matters. Higher education teams are under pressure to make better use of existing space. Gordian’s 2025 State of Facilities in Higher Education report says conversations about space utilization continue across campuses and notes that hybrid or remote office practices are still affecting office occupancy patterns.

Quick summary: University scheduling software can mean several things, so start by defining the use case. Some tools manage academic timetables and exams. Others manage rooms, desks, visitors, shared resources and hybrid staff schedules. For campus workplace scheduling, look for software that supports:
  • Room booking for meeting rooms, seminar rooms, study spaces and department spaces
  • Desk booking for faculty, staff, visiting researchers and admin teams
  • Permissions by department, role, building or space type
  • Calendar connections with Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace
  • SSO through systems like Azure AD, Okta or Google
  • Visitor management for guest lecturers, contractors and external guests
  • Reporting on room usage, desk usage, no-shows, peak demand and department activity
The best choice depends on who needs to book space, which spaces need rules or approvals and what data facilities, IT, HR and campus leadership need after rollout.

At the same time, budgets are tight. NACUBO’s 2025 State of Higher Education research lists unreliable funding, workforce pressure and rising operating costs among the top business issues facing higher education business officers.

Scheduling software will not fix those issues by itself. It can give facilities, IT, HR and campus operations teams better control over how spaces are booked, used, and reported.

What exactly is university scheduling software?

University scheduling software lets higher education teams manage bookings, availability, access rules, and usage across campus spaces or resources.

Depending on the system, it may cover:

  • Rooms
  • Desks
  • Study spaces
  • Labs
  • Shared equipment
  • Parking
  • Visitors
  • Department spaces
  • Faculty and staff office days

The phrase has mixed search intent. Some people use it to mean course timetabling. Others use it to mean room scheduling, desk booking or space management.

That difference matters when you compare vendors.

The four main types of university scheduling software

Academic timetabling software

Academic timetabling software is used for course schedules, exams, instructors and classroom assignments.

It is usually owned by registrar teams, academic operations or scheduling offices.

Room booking software

Room booking software is used for meeting rooms, seminar rooms, conference rooms, study rooms and department-owned spaces.

It is usually used by facilities teams, faculty, staff, students, and administrative departments.

Event scheduling software

Event scheduling software is used for guest lectures, student events, ceremonies, conferences and large room requests. It often includes request forms, approvals, event services, and coordination across multiple teams.

Workplace scheduling software for universities

Workplace scheduling software is used for desk booking, hybrid staff schedules, shared workspaces, room reservations, visitor management and campus space usage.

It is usually relevant for facilities, HR, IT, workplace teams, and administrative departments.

Start by narrowing the category

A university may need more than one scheduling system. Academic timetabling, event scheduling and workplace scheduling often overlap in conversation, but they solve different problems.

Before comparing vendors, define the job the software needs to handle.

If you need to...Look for...
Build semester timetablesAcademic timetabling software
Schedule exams and instructorsAcademic timetabling software
Book meeting rooms, seminar rooms or study roomsRoom booking software
Manage shared desks for faculty and staffWorkplace scheduling software
Coordinate hybrid office daysWorkplace scheduling software
Manage guest lecturers, contractors or visiting researchersVisitor management software
Track how campus spaces are usedWorkplace or space management software
Manage large campus eventsEvent scheduling software

Many universities will need several of these capabilities. The key is to avoid choosing a system built for course scheduling when the real need is space booking, visitor check-in or hybrid staff coordination.

Start with the problems your university needs to solve

Before reviewing vendors, list the problems your current process creates.

Common examples include:

  • Rooms appear available in one calendar and booked in another
  • Faculty request space through email threads
  • Staff arrive on campus without knowing where to sit
  • Departments manage rooms in separate spreadsheets
  • Labs or specialist rooms need approval before booking
  • Visiting lecturers and contractors need manual check-in
  • Facilities teams lack clear space usage data
  • IT supports several disconnected booking tools
  • Students, staff and faculty need different access rules

These problems should shape your requirements. A generic booking tool may work for a small department. A university-wide system needs more control.

Ask these questions first:

  • Who needs to book space?
  • Which spaces need reservations?
  • Which spaces need approval?
  • Which spaces should be restricted by department or role?
  • Do users need mobile booking?
  • Do users need floor plans?
  • Should bookings sync with Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace?
  • Do users need single sign-on?
  • Do visitors need digital check-in?
  • Do facilities teams need usage reports?
  • Do departments need control over their own spaces?

Define the spaces and resources the software must support

University scheduling gets messy when teams only document the obvious rooms.

A better requirements list includes every space and resource people need to reserve.

Rooms

Include:

  • Meeting rooms
  • Seminar rooms
  • Lecture rooms
  • Study rooms
  • Interview rooms
  • Conference rooms
  • Department rooms

For each room, the software should show availability, capacity, location, equipment, booking rules and approval requirements.

Desks and shared workspaces

Desk booking matters when faculty, staff and visiting researchers split time across campus, home and other university locations.

Common use cases include:

  • Faculty hot desks
  • Staff desks
  • Visiting researcher desks
  • Administrative workspaces
  • Hybrid department areas
  • Shared offices across buildings

The system should make it easy to find a suitable desk, see where colleagues plan to work and book near a department or team when needed.

Labs and special-purpose spaces

Labs and specialist rooms often need stricter rules than normal meeting rooms.

Check whether the software can support:

  • Restricted access
  • Approval flows
  • Booking limits
  • Space-specific instructions
  • Department ownership
  • Visibility for central admins

This is especially relevant for research pods, recording rooms, specialist teaching spaces and equipment rooms.

Shared resources

Universities often need to book a space and a resource together.

Examples include:

  • AV equipment
  • Projectors
  • Whiteboards
  • Lockers
  • Parking spaces
  • Research equipment
  • Recording equipment

Check whether resources can be tied to specific rooms, buildings or user groups.

Visitors

Visitor workflows should be part of the review when bookings involve people from outside the institution.

Common visitor types include:

  • Guest lecturers
  • Contractors
  • Visiting researchers
  • Parents
  • External partners
  • Interview candidates
  • Donors

A room booking may need a visitor record, host notification and check-in process. If those steps happen outside the scheduling system, reception and security teams may still rely on manual work.

Check whether the software can handle university-level permissions

Permissions are one of the biggest differences between simple booking tools and university-ready scheduling software.

A space may be visible to one group, bookable by another and restricted for students during certain hours. A lab may need approval from a department owner. A shared meeting room may need rules for booking length, recurring use or access by external guests.

Look for support for:

  • Department-based access
  • Role-based access
  • Faculty-only spaces
  • Student-accessible spaces
  • Staff-only areas
  • Visitor access
  • Location-based rules
  • Booking windows
  • Maximum booking duration
  • Recurring booking rules
  • Approval requirements
  • Admin overrides

Good vendor questions include:

  • Can departments manage their own spaces?
  • Can central admins see all bookings?
  • Can some spaces require approval?
  • Can rules vary by role, department, space type or campus?
  • Can admins set booking limits?
  • Can the system prevent double bookings?
  • Can it handle multiple buildings or campuses?
  • Can permissions change when someone changes role?

Review the booking experience

The system may satisfy every admin requirement and still fail if people avoid using it. We write about adoption more extensively in our best desk booking platforms for 2026 guide.

The booking flow should let users:

  • Search by building or floor
  • Filter by room type
  • Filter by capacity
  • Filter by equipment
  • See real-time availability
  • Book from desktop or mobile
  • Edit or cancel bookings
  • Find spaces near colleagues or departments

Floor plans are useful across large campuses because room names are often unclear to new staff, visiting faculty or external guests. A floor plan lets people choose a space based on building, floor and location rather than guessing from a room code.

For hybrid teams, visibility also matters. Faculty and staff may need to see who plans to be on campus, book near colleagues or coordinate department days. This can support office hours, mentorship, admin meetings and team planning.

Check calendar, identity and communication connections

University scheduling software should fit into tools people already use.

Calendar connections

Review support for:

  • Microsoft 365
  • Google Workspace
  • Outlook Calendar
  • Google Calendar

Ask:

  • Do room bookings sync with user calendars?
  • Does availability update in real time?
  • Can users book in the scheduling tool and still see the event in their calendar?
  • Are cancellations reflected across systems?
  • Can recurring bookings sync correctly?

Single sign-on

IT should review identity requirements early.

Check for support for:

  • Azure AD
  • Okta
  • Google SSO

Single sign-on reduces separate accounts and gives IT more control over access. It also makes offboarding easier when access follows existing identity rules.

Notifications

Booking reminders and alerts can reduce confusion.

Look for:

  • Email reminders
  • Slack notifications
  • Microsoft Teams notifications
  • Host alerts for visitors
  • Booking confirmations
  • Cancellation updates

Evaluate reporting and campus space usage data

Reporting is where scheduling software becomes useful beyond day-to-day bookings.

Facilities teams may need to understand which rooms are overbooked, which desks sit unused, which buildings see peak demand and where space rules need to change.

Useful reports may include:

  • Bookings by room type
  • Desk bookings by building
  • Peak days and times
  • No-shows
  • Cancellations
  • Low-use spaces
  • High-demand spaces
  • Department-level demand
  • Visitor volume
  • Room size mismatch
  • Recurring booking patterns

Different teams will use this data differently.

Facilities teams can see which rooms, desks, and buildings are used most often. IT can review adoption, support needs, and integration issues.

HR can compare hybrid work policies with actual office patterns. Academic operations can understand how department spaces are used outside formal timetables.

Leadership can use space usage data when reviewing renovations, campus workplace plans, and real estate costs.

Ask vendors:

  • Can we report by building, floor, room type, and department?
  • Can we see no-shows?
  • Can we track desk and room usage separately?
  • Can we export reports?
  • Can department admins view their own data?
  • Can leaders see summary views?

Include visitor management in the review

Many campus bookings involve external guests.

A guest lecturer may need access to a seminar room. A contractor may need to check in at reception before reaching a building. A visiting researcher may need temporary access to a desk, lab or department area.

Visitor management features to check include:

  • Pre-registration
  • Digital check-in
  • Host notifications
  • Visitor logs
  • Badge printing, if needed
  • Building-level visitor records
  • Contractor tracking
  • Multi-location support

This is especially relevant when reception, security, facilities and academic departments all touch the visitor process.

Plan for rollout and administration

A university scheduling system needs careful setup.

Typical setup includes:

  • Buildings
  • Floors
  • Spaces
  • Departments
  • User groups
  • Booking rules
  • Calendar connections
  • SSO
  • Admin roles
  • Visitor flows
  • Reporting views

Decide who owns the system before launch. Ownership may sit with a central facilities team, IT, a workplace team or a shared group across facilities, HR and IT.

A focused rollout is usually easier to manage. Start with one campus, building or department. Define the spaces and rules. Set up calendar and identity connections. Train admins first. Share simple booking instructions with users. Review adoption after 30 to 60 days before expanding.

Ask vendors:

  • How long does implementation usually take?
  • Who creates and edits spaces?
  • Can departments manage their own spaces?
  • Can central admins override rules?
  • What training is included?
  • What support is available after launch?
  • Can the system expand across multiple campuses?

Use this checklist when comparing vendors

Evaluation areaWhat to check
Space typesRooms, desks, labs, study spaces, parking and shared resources
User groupsFaculty, staff, students, visitors and contractors
PermissionsDepartment rules, approvals, role-based access and admin overrides
Booking experienceDesktop, mobile, floor plans, filters and real-time availability
Calendar connectionsMicrosoft 365, Google Workspace, Outlook and Google Calendar
IdentitySSO through Azure AD, Okta or Google
NotificationsEmail, Slack, Microsoft Teams and host alerts
Visitor managementPre-registration, check-in, visitor logs and host notifications
ReportingUtilization, no-shows, peak demand and department usage
AdministrationMulti-campus setup, delegated admins and booking policies
SupportOnboarding, training, documentation and admin support

Five mistakes to avoid

#1 Choosing software before defining the use case

A registrar team, facilities team and HR team may all say “scheduling” and mean different things. Define the job first.

#2 Underestimating permissions

Basic booking tools often struggle with department rules, role-based access, approval flows, and multi-campus controls.

#3 Splitting desk booking, room booking, and visitors too early

Separate systems can increase admin work and make reporting harder. Review whether one system can cover the main campus workplace use cases.

#4 Leaving IT out of the buying process

IT should review SSO, calendar connections, data handling, user provisioning, and security requirements.

#5 Skipping reporting requirements

Without usage data, teams may still rely on anecdotal feedback when making space decisions.

When OfficeRnD Workplace is worth reviewing

OfficeRnD Workplace is worth reviewing if your university needs to manage desks, rooms, shared resources, visitors and hybrid staff schedules across campus spaces.

It supports desk booking, room reservations, interactive floor plans, visitor management, Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace calendar connections, SSO and booking reminders through Slack or Microsoft Teams.

Final checklist for choosing university scheduling software

Before choosing a vendor, confirm that you can:

  • Define the scheduling use case
  • List every space and resource that needs booking
  • Map user groups, departments and access rules
  • Check room, desk, lab and visitor use cases
  • Review Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace calendar connections
  • Confirm SSO options
  • Test the booking flow on desktop and mobile
  • Review floor plan support
  • Ask for reporting by building, space type and department
  • Include IT, facilities, HR and academic operations in the review
  • Start with a focused rollout before expanding across campus

Name: Lead Decay in Coworking: How to Measure it, What Causes it, and How to Stop it
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: There’s a number most coworking operators have never calculated, and would probably rather not look at if they did.
Post body:
There’s a number most coworking operators have never calculated, and would probably rather not look at if they did.

It’s the rate at which inbound leads lose interest while waiting for a response. Someone fills out a form on Sunday evening, hears nothing until Tuesday afternoon, and by then has already decided, without ever telling you, that they’re going somewhere else.

There’s a term for it: lead decay. It’s the gap between when a prospect’s intent peaks and when your team can actually respond, and it’s the specific problem the OfficeRnD AI Sales Agent, part of OfficeRnD Flex, is built to reduce.

What lead decay actually is

Lead decay is the rate at which a prospect’s likelihood of converting drops the longer your reply takes to arrive.

The drop is steepest in the first hour. It drops again after the first business day. By 72 hours, most leads are still technically open in your inbox but practically dead.

The pattern is well documented in lead-response research. A study published in Harvard Business Review found that firms contacting a web lead within 1 hour were 7 times more likely to have a meaningful sales conversation than those waiting just 60 minutes longer, and 60 times more likely than firms responding after 24 hours.

The study is from 2011. The numbers haven’t moved.

Coworking is exposed to this for structural reasons.

Inbound volume varies week to week. Inboxes are usually shared. Ownership is diffuse. Front-of-house staff are running tours, fixing printers, handling billing, and answering sales inquiries in the same hour.

By Saturday night, when a prospect is browsing flex spaces in your city, the people who could respond aren’t reading email.

Lead decay is the gap between when a prospect’s intent peaks (the moment they hit submit) and when your team can actually respond.

How to measure your decay rate, realistically

Most coworking operators don’t have the CRM tracking to calculate decay with statistical precision. Pretending otherwise wastes time.

The goal here is direction. You’re answering one question: am I losing leads to time, and how badly? In other words, how bad exactly is my revenue leak caused by slow response time?

There are 2 ways to do this, depending on what your data looks like.

Tier 1: the inbox audit

Anyone with email can run this. You need access to your inbound contact-form submissions and your sales inbox.

Pick a 30-day window. Pull every inbound inquiry that came through web forms, info@ aliases, or any channel where prospects reach out. For each one, find the timestamp of the first substantive human reply. Autoresponders don’t count. A “thanks, we’ll be in touch” template doesn’t count.

Sort what you find into time buckets:

  • Under 1 hour
  • 1 to 5 hours
  • 5 to 24 hours
  • 24 to 72 hours
  • 72+ hours, or no human response

Count how many inquiries fall in each.

You’ll learn 3 things from this. Your median first response time. Your no-response rate, which is almost always higher than operators expect and is the most damaging metric in the analysis. The distribution of where your inquiries actually sit, time-wise.

If most inquiries fall in the 5+ hour buckets, you’re operating in decayed territory. Lead-response research is consistent: the steepest conversion drop happens inside the first hour, with another step-down after the first business day.

Tier 2: the conversion map

If your inquiries flow into a CRM (HubSpot, Pipedrive, OfficeRnD Flex’s CRM, etc.) and you’ve been tagging outcomes back to lead records, you can extend the audit. Same buckets. Now compute the actual lead-to-tour conversion rate per bucket and plot the curve.

The under-1-hour bucket sits noticeably above the 5 to 24 hour bucket. The 24 to 72 hour bucket usually shows a steep drop. Exact shape varies by operator. Direction is consistent.

Caveats worth being honest about

Below 30 inquiries a month, the bucket-level conversion rates are statistically noisy. Read direction, not precision. A hiring decision based on 12 leads is a bad decision.

At higher volumes, treat the per-bucket rates as directional. Pull a quarter of data rather than a single month if you can. Month-to-month variance in coworking inbound is genuinely high.

A pragmatic benchmark

Coworking doesn’t have a public industry standard for “good” decay. What’s reasonable, based on cross-industry response data:

  • Median first response under 30 minutes
  • No-response rate at or near zero
  • 70%+ of inquiries getting a real reply within the first hour

Falling short of those numbers is the default state of inbound coworking sales without automation.

Most operators who run this audit for the first time find the same picture: response times that look fine on average, with a long tail of inquiries that quietly went unanswered. The point of measuring is to see where that tail starts.

The 4 causes of lead decay in flex spaces

Each cause leaves a different signature in your data and has a different fix.

#1 The coverage gap

Inquiries arrive when no one is there to answer. Evenings, weekends, public holidays, the hour your team is on a tour.

The signature in your audit data: long-response buckets correlated with predictable time windows. If you sort no-response leads by submission time and they cluster on Saturdays and after 6pm, this is your dominant cause.

#2 The triage problem

High-intent prospects sit in a shared inbox alongside spam, billing complaints, vendor outreach, and member requests. There’s no priority system and no clear ownership. Some leads get a reply in 15 minutes. Others sit for 2 days. The signature is variance in response times, and the variance itself is the diagnostic.

#3 The follow-up drop

This is the cause most operators don’t see. The first reply goes out fast. The prospect writes back with a question. A tour runs long. A member crisis pulls the manager away.

The thread sits for 36 hours. By the time someone replies, the prospect is gone. The signature: strong first-response times alongside threads that go cold after the second or third exchange. Mid-funnel leads stall here more than anywhere else.

#4 The qualification bottleneck

Even when leads get answered fast, qualification gets compressed or skipped because the person handling inquiries is also handling everything else.

Sales reps in flex spaces typically spend close to 40% of their time on repetitive qualification work, the kind of “are you a freelancer or a team of 8, do you need a private office or hot desk” exchanges that consume hours that should be going to tours and closes.

The signature: a high inquiry-to-tour ratio paired with a low tour-to-membership ratio. Reps end up doing discovery during the tour itself, which is too late.

Where most operators are losing the most leads

Based on our experience, most operators have 1 or 2 dominant causes, not 4 equally. Knowing which one you have changes what you should do about it.

Operator profileMost likely cause(s)Highest-risk window
Single-site / boutique (under 30 leads/mo)Coverage gap + follow-up dropEvenings, weekends, on-site busy hours
Multi-site, team at capacity (30 to 80 leads/mo)Triage + qualification bottleneckBusiness-hours volume spikes, staff absences
High-volume, high-growth (80+ leads/mo)All 4, capacity-drivenWhenever inbound exceeds team capacity

Take the bucket data from your inbox audit and overlay it on this. The dominant cause usually becomes obvious once the data is in front of you.

For boutique and owner-operator spaces, the cost of decay shows up most in brand perception. A slow reply makes a small operation look amateur next to global chains, and that judgment usually forms in the first message exchange, before anyone walks through the door for a tour.

How AI changes the shape of the decay curve

Standard process improvements (templated replies, response SLAs, weekend rotations, an extra hire) reduce the curve’s slope. They don’t change its shape, because they don’t remove the cause: a human being available, awake, and not currently doing something else.

An AI Sales Agent removes that dependency from the first response.

Against the 4 causes:

  • The coverage gap goes away. First response goes out in seconds regardless of time, day, or what the team is doing. The sharp early drop in the decay curve flattens for the entire after-hours window, which is when a meaningful share of inbound arrives in most operations.
  • The triage problem stops mattering at the inbox level. Inbound is sorted automatically. Routine questions get answered. High-intent leads are qualified and flagged. The shared inbox stops being a single queue with mixed priorities.
  • The follow-up drop goes away because the agent stays in the thread asynchronously. An 11pm question gets an 11pm answer. The thread doesn’t go cold because someone got busy.
  • The qualification bottleneck clears because team size, timeline, location preference, and intent are captured before a human picks up. Reps start with full context and recover most of the 40% of their time previously spent on repetitive qualification.

Salesforce’s State of Sales research has consistently found that high-performing sales teams use AI for lead qualification and routing at much higher rates than their average peers, because it absorbs the work that reps shouldn’t have been doing in the first place.

OfficeRnD Flex’s AI Hub benchmarks point in the same direction for coworking specifically: roughly 60% of inquiries handled end-to-end without a human touch, and a lift of up to 20% in lead-to-tour conversion.

The “up to” matters. Actual results depend on the starting decay rate, lead quality, and how the agent is configured.

What “fixed” actually looks like

Take a representative mid-market operator. 60 inquiries a month. Median first response time of 6 hours. Around 40% of inquiries arriving outside business hours. A no-response rate of around 15%. Lead-to-tour conversion sitting around 25%.

That’s a reasonably well-run operation. Pretty close to the average for the segment.

After putting an AI Sales Agent on the front of that pipeline:

  • Median first response drops to under 1 minute
  • After-hours coverage goes to 100%
  • The no-response rate falls to near zero
  • Roughly 60% of inquiries are handled to completion without a human ever touching them
  • Lead-to-tour conversion trends toward 30%+

Treat those numbers as directional benchmarks. Actual lift depends on where you started.

What the OfficeRnD AI Sales Agent does

It answers inbound inquiries instantly, 24/7. It qualifies each one in real time, capturing team size, timeline, location preference, and intent. Qualified leads get handed to your team with full context attached.

See how the OfficeRnD AI Sales Agent handles inbound from first response to booked tour. 

In practice, around 60% of inquiries get handled end-to-end without a human touch. Lead-to-tour conversion improves by up to 20%.

After-hours inquiries get the same response speed as midweek mornings. Every lead your team picks up arrives pre-qualified, so reps spend their time on tours and closes.

How to Choose the Right Desk Booking Software

Picking the right desk booking software sounds like it should be simple. You need desks. People need to book them. How hard can it be?

Check out this guide to learn more about why you really need a desk booking system for your office.

In practice, the decision is more nuanced than it looks, because the tool you choose doesn’t just affect reservations.

It shapes how people experience the office, how smoothly IT and Facilities can manage it, and whether hybrid days actually feel productive or just… mandatory.

JLL’s 2025 Occupancy Planning Benchmark Report found that 58% of organizations now invest in reservation systems as a core part of their hybrid workplace strategy, and 73% of corporate real estate leaders say portfolio optimization has overtaken cost-cutting as their top priority.

The implication is clear: desk booking software is no longer a nice-to-have utility. It’s part of how companies plan, operate, and optimize their workplaces.

But the gap between tools in this category is wider than most buyers expect. Some products are lightweight booking layers with minimal desk booking features.

Others are full workplace platforms. And the right choice depends less on which product has the longest feature list and more on what problem you are actually trying to solve.

Here is how to think through the decision before you start comparing screenshots and pricing pages.

What to evaluate at a glance:

AreaKey Questions to Ask
The problem you're solvingDo you need just desks, or desks plus rooms, parking, and visitors? Are you optimizing space, improving collaboration, or both?
Employee adoptionCan someone book a desk in under 10 seconds? Does it work inside the tools your team already uses (Teams, Slack, Outlook, Google Calendar)?
CollaborationCan employees see who else is coming in? Can teams book near each other and coordinate office days?
Admin controlsCan you set booking rules, permissions, and check-in policies without workarounds? Does it support both hot desking and dedicated seating?
Integrations and IT fitDoes it support SSO, SCIM, and your HRIS? How deep are the calendar and chat integrations — surface-level sync or native experience?
AnalyticsDoes it show utilization trends and attendance patterns, or just booking counts? Can you export data and connect it to BI tools?
Pricing modelIs it per user, per desk, or platform plus modules? What features are gated behind higher tiers or add-ons?
Rollout and supportIs onboarding included? How long does setup typically take? Does support quality hold up in independent reviews?

Start with the problem, not the features

Before you look at any product, get clear on what you are actually trying to fix. A surprising number of teams skip this step and end up either overbuying a platform they barely use or underbuying a tool they outgrow in six months.

Ask yourself: Do you only need desk booking, or do you also need meeting rooms, parking, lockers, or visitor management? Are you trying to improve collaboration across hybrid teams, reduce admin overhead, optimize underused space, or all three?

Do you need a lightweight booking layer that sits inside Slack, or a broader workplace platform that gives Facilities and IT real operational control?

A 30-person startup that just wants people to grab a desk is solving a fundamentally different problem than a 2,000-person enterprise managing five offices across three countries.

Prioritize employee adoption above everything else

This is the single most important factor in whether your investment pays off. A desk booking tool can have the most powerful admin controls, the deepest analytics, and the broadest integrations on the market, and none of it matters if employees don’t use it.

JLL’s 2025 Workforce Preference Barometer found that employee acceptance of office policies is directly tied to the quality of the experience, with 84% of employees who are satisfied with their workplace also viewing attendance policies positively.

The same logic applies to the tools you ask people to use when they come in. If booking a desk feels like filing a support ticket, adoption will be a constant battle.

Look for an intuitive booking flow that requires no training, interactive office maps, recurring bookings, and favorite desks for regulars, mobile and web access, and native integrations with the tools your team already lives in: Microsoft Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar, Slack.

The fewer clicks between “I want to come in tomorrow” and “done,” the higher your adoption rate will be.

The best desk booking software is the one people don’t think twice about using. If it fits naturally into their existing workflow, their calendar, their chat app, their morning routine, adoption takes care of itself. The moment you force people into a separate system that feels disconnected from how they already work, you’ve already lost half the battle— Ivan Guberkov, Chief Product Officer, OfficeRnD

Look beyond booking: does it support real collaboration?

This is where the category splits. Simple reservation tools answer one question: “Which desk is free?”

The better products answer a more useful one: “Who else is coming in, and how do I make this office day worthwhile?”

If your organization cares about making hybrid days more purposeful, look for coworker visibility, the ability to book near teammates, team neighborhoods, bulk or team booking, schedule coordination, and suggested office days, and visibility that helps people plan without feeling intrusive.

JLL’s research confirms that employees who view office attendance positively tend to work in environments where collaboration, culture, and learning opportunities are prioritized alongside the logistics.

The desk booking platform you choose can either help create that environment or just manage the inventory.

Check how flexible the admin controls really are

This matters most to Facilities managers, workplace operations leads, and IT teams: the people who have to configure, maintain, and enforce the system after launch day fades.

Evaluate:

  • Booking rules and policies (who can book what, when, and for how long)
  • Permissions by user, team, location, or resource type
  • Delegated booking or booking on behalf of others
  • Check-in requirements and auto-release for no-shows
  • Booking windows and approval flows for sensitive spaces
  • The ability to support both dedicated desks and flexible seating in the same system

That last point is especially important.

Many organizations run a mix of assigned desks and hot desking. If your tool only supports one model, you will end up managing exceptions manually.

Make sure it fits your existing tech stack

Desk booking software works best when it disappears into the tools employees and IT already use. At a minimum, evaluate:

  • Microsoft 365 and Teams integration
  • Outlook and Google Calendar sync
  • Slack integration
  • SSO and SCIM or automated user provisioning
  • HRIS integrations for keeping employee data current
  • API access or webhooks for custom workflows

The depth of these integrations matters. There is a big difference between a product that syncs calendar events and one that lets employees book directly from a Teams tab without ever leaving their workflow.

Don’t overlook analytics and space optimization

A lot of tools can tell you how many desks were booked last Tuesday. Fewer can help you understand what is actually happening in your workplace over time and make smarter decisions because of it.

Look for:

  • Occupancy and utilization analytics
  • Attendance patterns and peak-day visibility
  • Breakdowns by team, location, floor, or resource type
  • Policy compliance reporting
  • Data exports and BI tool integrations
  • Insights that connect back to real decisions about space planning, layout changes, or lease negotiations

If the analytics only tell you what already happened but never help you decide what to do next, they are not pulling their weight.

Averages hide the peaks. In our own office over the past year, desk use averaged 63% on a typical day, but Tuesday ran at 71.5% and Friday at 37.2%. About one working day in five went above 80%, and the busiest days hit full capacity. An office sized for the 63% average is under pressure every Tuesday and half empty every Friday. This is why peak-day and day-of-week analytics matter more than a single number when you set a hot-desking ratio.

Think about rollout, onboarding, and support

A product that takes five minutes to demo can still take five weeks to roll out properly, especially if you need to configure policies, upload floor plans, set up integrations, and train admins across multiple offices.

Evaluate:

  • How easy the initial setup looks and whether onboarding support is included
  • What support channels are available (chat, email, phone, dedicated CSM)
  • Whether the product feels self-serve or sales-led
  • Whether support quality shows up consistently in customer reviews

A smoother rollout directly affects how quickly employees adopt the tool, which circles back to the most important factor on this list.

Decide how much product you really need

One of the most common mistakes in this category is overbuying or underbuying. Both cost you: one in budget, the other in capability. If you mainly need straightforward desk reservations for a single office, a lightweight tool like Officely, Dibsido, or desk.ly will serve you well.

If coordination, employee experience, and making hybrid days more purposeful matter as much as the reservation itself, a collaboration-focused platform like OfficeRnD Workplace is a better fit.

If your needs extend into visitor management, compliance, security, and broader operations across multiple large offices, look at Robin, Envoy, or YAROOMS.

Matching the product to your actual complexity level is one of the best ways to avoid buyer’s remorse.

Red flags to watch for

A few warning signs that a product may not be the right fit, no matter how good the demo looks:

  • The booking flow feels clunky, confusing, or requires multiple steps for a simple reservation.
  • Pricing looks straightforward until add-ons, higher tiers, or platform fees appear.
  • Key integrations are weak, missing, or locked behind enterprise plans.
  • Analytics are too shallow to guide any real workplace decisions.
  • The product is broader than what you need, and you are paying for capabilities you will never use.
  • Or the product is too lightweight, and you already know you will outgrow it within a year.

No single tool gets everything right for every organization. But if you are clear about the problem you are solving, honest about how much complexity you actually need, and disciplined about testing adoption before you commit, you will end up with a product that genuinely makes hybrid work easier, not just another login for employees to forget.

How Desk Booking Software Pricing Works

Pricing in this category is not as straightforward as it looks. Two products can both say “starts at €2 per user per month” and end up costing very different amounts once you factor in tiers, add-ons, platform fees, and what is actually included at each level.

Before you compare prices, it helps to understand the models you will run into, and which ones make the most sense for how your organization is structured.

Per-user pricing

The most common model in the category. You pay a fixed monthly or annual fee for every employee who can access the system. deskbird, Officely, Dibsido, and desk.ly all use some version of this.

The upside is simplicity: headcount times price. The downside is that costs scale directly with your workforce, regardless of how many desks you actually have or how often people book. If you have 500 employees but only 200 desks, you are still paying for 500 users.

Per-desk or per-space pricing

Some products charge based on the number of bookable resources: desks, rooms, parking spots. Skedda is the clearest example, with pricing tied to spaces rather than people.

This model works better for organizations where the workforce is significantly larger than the physical footprint.

If you have 1,000 employees sharing 300 desks, paying per space is usually cheaper. The trade-off is that costs climb as you add locations or resources.

Tiered plans

Most products use some form of tiered pricing: a base plan for core features and higher tiers for deeper capabilities. OfficeRnD Workplace, YAROOMS, deskbird, and desk.ly all follow this pattern.

What matters is not the tier names but what sits behind the gates. Common features pushed into higher tiers include SSO and SCIM provisioning, advanced analytics and heatmaps, meeting room and parking booking, visitor management, API access, and dedicated support.

Always map your requirements against the tier that includes them, not against the entry price.

Platform fee plus modules

Some products charge a base platform fee and then add modular pricing on top. Envoy is the clearest example. Its Workplace platform has its own tier structure, Reservations is billed per bookable resource on top, and Visitors is a separate product entirely.

This can make sense for larger organizations standardizing on one vendor. But the commercial picture gets complex as you layer modules together. Ask for a fully loaded quote that reflects everything you plan to use.

Quote-only enterprise pricing

A few products don’t publish pricing at all. Robin is the most prominent example. YAROOMS and deskbird also move to custom pricing at their enterprise tiers.

Quote-based pricing gives vendors flexibility for complex deployments and often includes volume discounts. But it adds friction, makes comparisons harder, and can leave smaller teams feeling like the product isn’t built for them.

Ask early about minimum contract size, implementation fees, and what a typical deal looks like for your size.

Add-ons and hidden cost traps

This is where most pricing surprises come from. Common add-ons across the products in this roundup include:

  • Visitor management: YAROOMS charges per location, OfficeRnD Workplace offers it as a Visitor Hub add-on, and Envoy prices it as a separate product entirely.
  • SSO and identity management: desk.ly gates SCIM and HRIS integrations to Enterprise Plus, and deskbird sells User & Data Management Plus as an add-on.
  • Room displays and digital signage
  • Advanced analytics or custom reporting
  • Onboarding or setup services

Build your requirements list first, then ask each vendor for a quote that covers everything on it. If a vendor can’t give you a clear all-in number, that is worth noting.

Which model fits which type of company

Per-user pricing works best for smaller and mid-sized teams where headcount and desk count are relatively close, and predictable budgeting matters most.

Per-space pricing is usually more cost-effective when the workforce is much larger than the physical footprint, for example, 800 employees sharing 200 desks across two offices.

Tiered plans make sense for most mid-market buyers as long as you map requirements carefully to the right tier.

Platform-plus-modules and quote-based enterprise pricing suit larger organizations with complex, multi-location deployments that need booking, visitor management, analytics, and workplace operations under one roof.

Whatever model you are comparing, the question that matters most is not “What does it cost per user?” but “What will we actually pay for everything we need, and how will that number change as we grow?”
