Post body:
Walk into any coworking conference or operator community and you’ll hear the same conversations. Occupancy. Pricing. Member churn. RevPOD, RevPAD. These are the numbers that keep operators up at night, the metrics that get tracked, reported, and argued over.

And for good reason. They matter.

But there’s another number that almost nobody tracks, and it’s quietly costing flex spaces real revenue every single month. It doesn’t show up on any dashboard. It doesn’t trigger an alert. Most operators don’t even know it exists.

It’s the cost of slow, manual lead response.

Everyone’s Watching the Wrong Metrics

The numbers coworking operators focus on are, almost without exception, lagging indicators. By the time occupancy dips or churn spikes, the problem has already been happening for a while. You’re reading the aftermath, not the cause.

Lead response sits upstream of all of it. A prospect who doesn’t hear back in time doesn’t become a member. A non-member doesn’t show up in your churn data. They just quietly disappear, and you never knew they were there.

That’s what makes this particular leak so hard to spot. The absence of a conversion doesn’t look like a problem. It just looks like a normal day.

Most operators are running a reasonably tight ship on the metrics they can see, while leaving money on the table in a place they’re not looking. In other words, they don’t notice the so-called lead decay.

What’s Actually Happening When a Lead Comes In

Here’s a scenario that will feel familiar.

A prospect finds your space, either through Google, a listing site, or a referral from a friend. They’re interested.

They fill out the contact form or send an email. Maybe it’s a Tuesday afternoon, and your community manager is giving a tour. Maybe it’s Friday at 4pm. Maybe it’s Sunday evening, and nobody’s around.

The inquiry sits.

Your team gets to it the next morning, or later that day, and fires off a friendly reply. From your side, that feels like a reasonable turnaround.

But from the prospect’s side, a few things have happened in that window. They’ve probably reached out to one or two other spaces.

One of those spaces may have already responded. They may have already booked a tour somewhere else. In some cases, they’ve already made a decision.

The research on this is pretty unambiguous. A Harvard Business Review study analyzing 2.24 million sales leads found that companies responding to inquiries within an hour were nearly seven times as likely to qualify that lead.

The same study found that companies waiting 24 hours or more were 60 times less likely to qualify the lead compared to those who responded in the first hour.

And the industry average? Just 27% of leads ever get contacted at all, with the average response time sitting at 47 hours across businesses.

In a world where people can book a hotel, a flight, or a restaurant in thirty seconds, being asked to wait until tomorrow for a coworking inquiry feels like friction. And friction kills intent.

The uncomfortable reality is that a lot of operators assume their response time is fine, because they’re trying their best and nobody has complained. But lack of complaint is not the same as lack of problem.

The prospects who didn’t hear back just moved on. They didn’t write a bad review. They didn’t send a follow-up asking where you were. They vanished.

The Problem With “We Respond Pretty Quickly”

Ask most coworking operators about their lead response time, and they’ll say something like “we’re pretty quick” or “we try to get back to people same day.” Almost no one can give you an actual number.

And that’s the real issue. If you can’t measure it, you can’t manage it, and you definitely can’t improve it.

“Pretty quick” is not a strategy. It’s a feeling. And in a competitive market where other spaces in your city are actively working on this, feelings don’t close memberships.

Research from InsideSales found that 78% of buyers choose the first company that responds to them, regardless of price or brand. Not the best space. Not the cheapest. The first one. That single stat reframes the whole conversation: lead response isn’t a customer service nicety, it’s a competitive advantage that most operators are giving away for free.

The other problem is that response time isn’t the only variable. It’s not just about how fast you get back to someone. It’s about the quality of that first interaction, whether the right questions get asked, whether the follow-up actually happens.

Manual processes are inconsistent by nature. A great community manager on a calm Tuesday handles leads very differently from that same manager on a Friday when two members need help and someone’s billing is broken.

Inconsistency is invisible from the inside. From the outside, it looks like some leads convert and some don’t, and you never quite know why.

Putting a Number on It

Here’s where things get more specific.

Most operators have a reasonable sense of how many inquiries come in each month. What almost none of them have calculated is how much of their team’s time and salary is being absorbed by handling those leads manually.

That's exactly what this calculator is built to help you do. Enter your team's yearly on-target earnings and your monthly lead volume, and it calculates how much of that salary is being spent on manual inquiry handling, based on the industry average of 30 minutes per lead. It puts a real annual dollar figure on the hidden cost of having skilled people doing repetitive admin instead of building relationships and closing memberships. For most operators, that number is a wake-up call.

It’s not about making you feel bad about how you’re currently operating. It’s about making the invisible visible.

Every inquiry your team manually processes is 30 minutes they’re not spending on a tour, a member event, or a renewal conversation. That tradeoff has a price, and most operators have simply never added it up before.

Where This Is Heading

It’s worth being honest about the direction the industry is moving on this, because it’s going to reshape how flex spaces handle leads within the next couple of years.

AI-powered lead handling is starting to make its way into coworking operations, and the pitch is straightforward: every inquiry gets an instant, intelligent response, at any hour, any day of the week, without adding headcount. Leads get qualified automatically. Follow-ups happen on schedule. Nothing falls through the cracks on a Friday afternoon.

This isn’t science fiction, and it’s not just for large operators with big tech budgets. The tools are becoming more accessible, and the operators who start thinking about this now will have a real head start on the ones who wait until it becomes standard practice.

The goal isn’t to replace the human relationships that make coworking great. It’s to make sure those relationships have the chance to start.

A prospect who gets an instant, helpful response at 9pm on a Sunday is far more likely to show up for a tour on Monday. That tour is where your community manager does what they do best.

AI handles the first mile. Your team handles what matters.

Stop Guessing. Start Calculating.

The coworking operators who build strong businesses over the next few years won’t just have the best-designed spaces or the sharpest pricing. They’ll have tight systems that work even when nobody’s in the building.

Curious what manual lead handling is actually costing your space? Use the free calculator to find out.

Lead response is one of the most high-leverage, low-visibility areas in the entire operator toolbox. The upside of getting it right is significant. The cost of ignoring it is steady and silent.

Most operators are one honest calculation away from understanding exactly what manual lead handling is costing them in real salary dollars every year. That calculation takes about two minutes.

Start there. Know your number. Then decide what to do with it.

Name: Turn Your Coworking Website Into Your Highest-Performing Revenue Channel [Webinar Recap]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Your coworking website has one job: turn curious visitors into paying customers. But for most operators, it’s quietly leaking revenue every single day – through confusing layouts, missing booking flows, and marketing spend that can’t be measured.
Post body:
Your coworking website has one job: turn curious visitors into paying customers. But for most operators, it’s quietly leaking revenue every single day – through confusing layouts, missing booking flows, and marketing spend that can’t be measured.

In our recent webinar, “Turn Your Coworking Website Into the Highest-Performing Revenue Channel”, three product and marketing experts from the team walked through exactly how to fix that. Here’s what they covered, and what you can start acting on today.

This recap includes only some of the highlights discussed in the webinar. To get all the insights, watch the on-demand version for free.

Design Your Website Like It Has a Job to Do

Assen Tzekin, OfficeRnD’s Principal Product Designer, opened with a point that resonates with anyone who’s poured time, money, and energy into building a great physical space: your digital presence deserves the same investment as your four walls.

Atmosphere by Design

Before a visitor ever books a tour or submits an inquiry, your website is already forming an impression. Assen’s advice: use color, imagery, and language to translate the feel of your physical space into the digital experience.

Think of it as creating a consistent “aha moment”, so when someone walks through your door for the first time, it feels exactly like they expected from browsing your site. As Assen put it:

Ask yourself, what are the specific visual clues I can include in my website that will prepare my visitors for that moment? So when they go through my door, they get the same feeling they got when they were browsing my digital space.

Language as Hospitality

One underrated element is language, not just tone, but literally which languages your site supports. If a meaningful portion of your community speaks something other than your default language, your website might be closing the door before they even knock.

Assen frames multilingual support as an act of hospitality: removing barriers before people arrive. To make the written experience even more accessible, tools like Lara Translate, for example, can help translate website copy, booking information, and member-facing documents before local review.

The CTA: Your Most Important Design Decision

Every page on your site should have one clear primary action and one secondary option. No more, no less. Assen calls this eliminating “analysis paralysis” – when visitors face too many options, they often choose none.

For a coworking space, the most common options are Book a Tour and Book Online, but which one takes the primary spot depends on your business model. Some operators lead with online booking, others prioritize tour requests first. You might even have a single action that makes the most sense for your setup. The point isn’t which one goes first. it’s that you make a deliberate choice and stick to it.

A few CTA best practices Assen shared:

  • Make buttons discoverable, don’t crowd them with competing elements
  • Color should reflect your brand and what you want the visitor to feel
  • Text should be anchored in what matters most to your users, not what sounds clever
See how OfficeRnD Flex compares to Nexudus.

Growth by Clarity

Every page should be a pathway, not a dead end. Assen outlined three principles for a website layout that actually converts:

  1. Eliminate guesswork – visitors should never have to hunt for the next step
  2. Verify value instantly – show real-time availability so they can act immediately
  3. Drive the decision – surface what matters most to pull them over the line

Performance Is Not a Technical Metric

A slow website doesn’t just frustrate visitors, it destroys the brand experience you’ve worked hard to build. Assen is direct about this: if your images load slowly, visitors don’t experience your brand, they experience frustration.

Beyond speed, he introduced the concept of “invisible precisions” – small technical details that seem minor until they’re missing.

Something as simple as a shareable link to a specific meeting room can meaningfully affect how people recommend and promote your space on social media or by email.

Mobile-First Is Non-Negotiable

With 30–40% or more of website traffic coming from mobile devices across OfficeRnD’s customer base, building for desktop first is no longer an option.

Assen frames this around the “flexible worker”, someone who makes decisions on the move and expects to convert a thought into a booking with a thumb tap.

If your website doesn’t meet them there, they’ll find one that does.

Bring the Right People to Your Website

Great design means nothing without traffic. Silvia Ivanova, OfficeRnD’s Demand Generation expert, walked through how to think about marketing in a way that actually maps to how customers buy.

The Three-Stage Customer Journey

Before someone books a desk or a tour, they typically go through three stages:

  1. Discovery – they first encounter your space
  2. Comparison – they weigh their options (location, price, availability)
  3. Decision – they take action (book a tour, purchase a membership)

The key insight: most operators only run campaigns targeting stage three. But if no one knows you exist and hasn’t already compared you favorably against alternatives, a conversion-focused ad campaign will underperform no matter how good the offer is.

Silvia’s recommendation is to run campaigns that support all three stages simultaneously:

  • Awareness campaigns – build visibility and reach new audiences
  • Lead generation campaigns – capture intent through contact forms and tour requests
  • Conversion campaigns – drive immediate action, like a “10% off unlimited membership in Barcelona” promotion

The Four Channels That Work Best for Coworking

Silvia focused specifically on channels that are measurable online:

Google Search (paid and organic) is best for capturing high-intent searches – people actively looking for “coworking space near me” or “coworking in [city].”

Silvia also gave a heads-up on AI-powered search tools like ChatGPT and Perplexity gaining ground, but her advice for now: don’t abandon Google, it still holds the majority of search market share.

Social Media (Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn) works best for visibility and community storytelling, showcasing the vibe of your space and the people who work there.

Email typically delivers the highest conversion rates of any channel, because you’re talking to people who already expressed interest. Use it to promote new availability, seasonal offers, and new locations.

Retargeting is a high-ROI channel that’s often underused. Running ads to people who visited your pricing page but didn’t book, or who added a product to their cart but left – these audiences are warm and often just need a small nudge.

Measuring What Actually Works: GA4 and UTMs

Here’s the honest truth about marketing: if you’re not tracking properly, you’re guessing. Silvia walked through the mechanics of using Google Analytics 4 (GA4) as your measurement hub, and why UTMs are the backbone of understanding which campaigns actually drive revenue.

UTMs are tracking labels appended to your campaign URLs that tell GA4 where a visitor came from, how they got there, and which campaign brought them. With UTMs set up across all your channels, GA4 can show you:

  • Which source drove the most bookings
  • Which channel generated the most revenue
  • Where visitors drop off in the funnel

Silvia shared a telling example from the webinar: if your Google paid spend is under $15,000–$20,000, it’s likely your best-performing channel. But if you’re spending more than that, a well-executed email campaign with zero ad spend might be generating more revenue (in her example, $30,000). Silvia said it very well:

You should be sure to drive all the traffic you generate to your website, and that’s where you start tracking key actions — tour bookings, contact form submissions, website purchases.

The key metric for conversion campaigns? ROAS – Return on Ad Spend. A healthy benchmark is 3–4x: for every dollar you put in, you get three to four dollars back.

For awareness campaigns, focus on reach combined with engagement rates (reach alone tells you nothing about whether you’re reaching the right people).

Convert Traffic Into Revenue with Growth Hub

Once you’ve got a well-designed website bringing in qualified traffic, the final piece is making it dead simple to turn visitors into paying customers – automatically, without staff involvement.

That’s what Radoslav (Rado) Enchev, Senior Product Manager for Growth Hub, covered in the final third of the webinar.

What Growth Hub Actually Does

Growth Hub is OfficeRnD Flex’s e-commerce layer – it sits between your website and the OfficeRnD backend, enabling visitors to discover, book, and pay online for the products you offer.

Crucially, it’s built with all the design and tracking principles covered earlier baked in: it’s embeddable in your existing website, customizable to match your brand, and natively integrated with GA4 for full e-commerce event tracking. As Radoslav said:

The best part of it is that it generates revenue for you 24/7, even when your team is not there.

Where to Start: The Product Matrix

Not everything needs to be automated. Rado was clear that products like private offices (long-term), event venues, and large enterprise deals benefit from human conversation, they involve negotiation, relationship, and complexity that doesn’t lend itself to self-serve.

But a significant portion of what most operators sell – day passes, meeting rooms, day offices, and coworking memberships are high-volume, low-complexity purchases. There’s no good reason to route these through an inquiry form or involve staff time.

Rado’s advice: start with the top-left quadrant of the product matrix – high volume, low purchase complexity, and work your way across. That’s where the effort-to-impact ratio is best and where you’ll see results fastest.

Some operators using Growth Hub are now completing 60–70% of their day pass sales entirely online, with zero staff involvement, directly improving profitability per transaction.

4 Ways to Maximize Revenue with Growth Hub

1. Get your full product catalog online

By the time someone lands on your website, they’ve often already decided they want to use your space.

They heard about it from a colleague, walked past it, or found it on Google Maps. At that point, every extra step between them and a booking is a risk of losing them. Getting your core products bookable online removes that friction.

2. Monetize vacant private offices as daily inventory

Private offices are typically your largest inventory category, and between tenants, they generate zero revenue while you’re still paying rent.

The concept of daily offices isn’t new, but historically it’s been operationally painful: manual availability checks, double-booking risks, and no easy way to distinguish between long-term and short-term inventory.

Growth Hub automates all of that. Set daily or hourly rates for the same offices you rent long-term, and the system automatically makes them available only during periods with no active contract.

No manual checking, no admin overhead. Roto’s research suggests the sweet spot for daily offices is 2–10 person spaces, primarily serving small remote teams who need to gather once or twice a month.

3. Use pricing rules to charge the right price at the right time

The data across OfficeRnD’s customer base confirms a pattern every operator already knows anecdotally: meeting rooms are nearly empty on Friday afternoons, slow on Monday mornings, and in high demand Tuesday–Thursday around midday.

Growth Hub now supports dynamic pricing rules based on these demand patterns. Increase prices by 10–15% during peak hours (when rooms will likely book anyway), and discount off-peak slots that would otherwise sit empty.

The platform provides heat map dashboards showing booking patterns by day, time, and revenue, so you can make these decisions based on real data, not gut feeling.

4. Recover abandoned checkouts automatically

This is a feature launching imminently at the time of the webinar: automated abandoned checkout recovery emails.

The scenario is common – someone goes all the way to the checkout, their phone rings, and they never come back. With this feature, Growth Hub automatically sends a recovery email to those high-intent visitors who didn’t complete their purchase.

Based on benchmarks from traditional e-commerce and the hotel industry, similar features recover between 5–15% of abandoned checkouts. Rado noted that while coworking has lower overall traffic volumes than traditional e-commerce, purchase intent tends to be significantly higher, which could mean strong recovery rates.

Q&A: Your Questions, Answered

During the webinar, attendees submitted a range of great questions. Here are the answers from the team:

Q: If you have a limited or no budget as a new small business, what are the best marketing channels and campaigns to use?

Start with a small Google retargeting campaign targeting people who visited your homepage, pricing page, or added items to their cart but didn’t check out.

Offer something special to that warm audience to reduce abandonment. If the budget is even tighter, activate local partnerships and community groups – incentivize them to refer people to your space. Word of mouth is free and genuinely effective for local businesses.

Q: How can I do the same event capture in Meta (custom purchase events) as in the Google Tag Manager container?

This one gets technical quickly. Please reach out directly at product@officernd.com, and the team will follow up with you on the specifics.

Q: I don’t have access to the landing pages section in OfficeRnD. How can my administrator allow these settings changes?

We need a bit more context to answer this one fully. Please share your email, and the support team will follow up with the right answer for your setup.

Q: Do you have any advice on how operators can track the lifetime value of products like memberships to see which ones bring the most ROI?

Lifetime value is one of the most important metrics for any coworking business. OfficeRnD Flex recently introduced a Churn and Retention report in Data Hub that shows lifetime value broken down by product type – private offices, meeting rooms, memberships, and more. Head to Data Hub in your OfficeRnD account to find it.

Q: Why doesn’t Growth Hub replace the existing shopping cart / members portal system? Why have two systems?

The goal is absolutely to have Growth Hub become the single place where all product sales happen, to both members and non-members.

But replacing everything at once would take a long time to deliver value. The iterative approach means operators get meaningful improvements faster. Over time, Growth Hub will consolidate all of this into one seamless experience.

Q: What strategies should a new coworking space use when operating in a highly competitive city?

Start with a great website (non-negotiable), then build your presence through word of mouth, local partnerships, community events, and networking. Once you have some confidence and content, launch social media campaigns — videos and event photos perform especially well.

Also, differentiation is everything in a crowded market. A template website that looks like everyone else’s won’t help you stand out. Focus on translating your unique identity and vision into your digital presence, the right clients will find themselves in it.

We have single-location operators using Growth Hub that outperform 10-location operators on online revenue, simply because they follow these principles. One clear “Book Online” button, in the right place, can generate revenue that many operators are currently leaving on the table.

Q: What promo code capabilities does Growth Hub support, and any tips on using them?

Growth Hub supports the full range: promo codes per product, usage limits per user, and membership discounts (e.g., first month free, or first three months discounted).

You can also use pricing rules to create time-based discounts (like 50% off Friday bookings) without needing a promo code at all.

A word of caution – be thoughtful about how often and how deeply you discount. Too many promo codes can erode the perceived value of your space and increase churn. Use them strategically, not habitually.

Q: How do operators track the impact of their promo codes in Growth Hub?

Every purchase in Growth Hub, whether made with a promo code, a pricing rule, or at full price, is captured in the reporting in Data Hub.

There’s a dedicated promo code report where you can see how many times each code was used, who used it, and when. You can even export the list to run follow-up campaigns – for example, emailing everyone who redeemed a free day pass to invite them back with a membership offer.

Q: How does retargeting on the marketing side complement the new abandoned checkout recovery feature?

They work at different layers but toward the same goal. With GA4, you can create audiences based on behavior (visited pricing page, added to cart, didn’t purchase) and run paid ad campaigns targeting those people on Google or Meta.

The abandoned checkout recovery email in Growth Hub is a direct, automated touchpoint — a one-two punch for recovering high-intent visitors through both ad channels and email simultaneously.

Q: If you have a coworking space in a rural area, what would you focus on for advertising and promotion?

Partnerships with local businesses and communities are your best bet. Offer your space as a venue for events, even ones unrelated to coworking, to get people through the door and introduce them to what you do.

Additionally, location is consistently the number one decision-making factor for coworking customers. In a rural or suburban area, your customers are likely local, so outdoor advertising – signage, local placements, can actually be a more cost-effective channel than Google or social media. In this context, a well-placed sign might outperform a digital campaign.

Name: Why Most Workplace Software Rollouts Fail [And How to Choose One That Won’t]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Most workplace management tools look identical on a features page. Desk booking. Room scheduling. Analytics dashboard. Visitor management.
Post body:
Most workplace management tools look identical on a features page. Desk booking. Room scheduling. Analytics dashboard. Visitor management.

Every vendor demo is polished. Every G2 rating is suspiciously high. And yet, six months after rollout, IT teams are fielding login complaints, calendar sync issues, and the same question from leadership: “Why isn’t anyone actually using this?”

The hard truth: most evaluations focus on the wrong things. Features are table stakes. According to CBRE’s 2025 Americas Office Occupier Sentiment Survey, 66% of organizations report office space is less than 60% utilized on average — not because people don’t want to collaborate, but because the experience of coming in isn’t worth it.

That’s the real problem. Empty desks aren’t a space problem. They’re a usability problem. The platform you choose either makes the office easy to use, or it doesn’t, and that single variable drives everything downstream: adoption, utilization, and whether the investment ever makes sense to leadership.

This scorecard covers the six dimensions that actually predict success. Use it across vendor conversations, in your procurement review, and share it with the HR, Facilities, and leadership stakeholders who’ll be living with this decision too.

TL;DR

  • Most workplace software evaluations focus on features. The dimensions that actually predict success are harder to see in a demo.
  • Empty desks are a usability problem, not a space problem. The platform you choose either makes the office easy to use — or it doesn’t.
  • This scorecard covers the 6 dimensions IT managers should evaluate: integration depth, security & compliance, deployment complexity, end-user adoption potential, admin configurability, and vendor support quality.
  • Each dimension is scored 1–3. A total below 12 is a red flag before procurement.
  • HR, Facilities, and leadership all have a stake in this decision. The right platform is one every stakeholder can say yes to.

The IT Manager’s Workplace Software Scorecard

Score each dimension from 1 to 3. A perfect score is 18. Anything below 12 warrants serious scrutiny before you advance a vendor to procurement.

Dimension 1: Integration Depth

This is where most platforms oversell and underdeliver. “Integrates with Microsoft Teams” can mean anything from a fully native Teams tab with end-to-end functionality to a link that opens a separate browser window and calls it an integration.

Questions to ask:

  • Does booking work natively inside Teams, Outlook, Google Calendar, and Slack, or does it redirect users to a separate interface?
  • Is calendar sync bidirectional and real-time, or batch-synced with noticeable lag?
  • Can an employee book a desk, check who’s coming in, and confirm a meeting room without ever leaving the tool they’re already working in?

What good looks like: A genuinely app-less experience where employees interact with the platform entirely inside Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace. No separate login, no new tab, no friction, and therefore, no reason to skip it.

What to watch for: Vendors who rely on Zapier-only connectors for core booking workflows, or who position a standalone mobile app as the primary user interface.

Score 1–3: 1 = redirects to separate app or web portal | 2 = partial native integration | 3 = fully embedded in existing tools, no additional app required

Already evaluating your options? OfficeRnD Workplace is built around a simple idea: when coming to the office is easy and familiar, people choose to come in. Engagement rises, collaboration happens, and utilization follows naturally. That means no forced mandates. No shelfware. Just a platform that embeds itself into the tools your employees already use -  Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Slack, and a team that stays involved long after go-live. Because making hybrid work actually work takes more than software. 

Dimension 2: Security & Compliance

IT owns this conversation, and the answers here should be readily available – not something a vendor needs three follow-up emails to provide.

Questions to ask:

  • Is the platform SOC 2 Type II certified, and is the documentation publicly accessible?
  • Where is data stored, and can you specify regional data residency if required?
  • How does the platform handle GDPR, particularly for visitor logs and presence tracking data?
  • Does it support SSO via Azure AD, Okta, or Google, out of the box, without custom development?
  • How granular are role-based permissions across admin, employee, and facility manager levels?

What good looks like: A vendor with a public-facing Trust Center, clear compliance certifications, and straightforward answers on data handling architecture. You shouldn’t need to chase this information.

A note for HR and Facilities stakeholders: Presence tracking and visitor data carry employee privacy implications that HR will want to weigh in on. Loop them in before this dimension is closed.

Score 1–3: 1 = unclear or incomplete compliance documentation | 2 = compliant but information requires chasing | 3 = proactive transparency, public Trust Center, robust role-based access controls.

That’s one of the most critical components that IT managers consider when choosing the best desk booking software or university scheduling software.

Dimension 3: Deployment Complexity & Ongoing IT Overhead

The best platform for employees is worthless if it takes six months to deploy and generates persistent maintenance overhead for a team that already has a full plate.

Questions to ask:

  • What does a realistic implementation timeline look like for an organization of your size and complexity?
  • What does IT need to own post-launch, and what does the vendor actively handle?
  • How are room displays and kiosk hardware configured, updated, and maintained?
  • What is the escalation path when an employee can’t access the system at 9am on a Monday?

What good looks like: Fast, structured onboarding with a dedicated implementation team, clear IT documentation, and hardware that’s genuinely plug-and-play. A vendor that remains actively involved after go-live, not one that hands you a knowledge base article and disappears.

This is a meaningful differentiator in the market. Self-serve tools shift all deployment risk and ongoing management to IT. A platform that operates as a true partner stays involved as your office evolves, your team grows, and your policies change.

Score 1–3: 1 = DIY setup, limited post-sales support | 2 = assisted onboarding, standard support SLA | 3 = dedicated onboarding team, responsive customer success, proactive account management

Dimension 4: End-User Adoption Potential

This is the dimension that determines whether your rollout succeeds or quietly dies, and it’s the one most IT evaluations underweight. Consider the broader stakes: according to Owl Labs’ 2025 State of Hybrid Work report, 40% of employees say they would start job hunting if flexible work were taken away.

Which means the workplace tools you roll out need to support hybrid, not fight it. A platform that creates friction around office attendance doesn’t just generate IT tickets – it chips away at the employee experience your HR team is working hard to protect, and the retention numbers your leadership watches closely.

In a hybrid world where office attendance is largely voluntary, a platform employees find clunky simply won’t get used. No policy enforcement will fix a bad user experience. HR knows this. Leadership is increasingly aware of it. IT is usually the one left holding the bag when adoption flatlines.

Adoption and onboarding are also key considerations when choosing the best hybrid work software for your company.

Questions to ask:

  • Can an employee book a desk, see which teammates are coming in, and confirm a meeting room in under 60 seconds, with zero training?
  • Does the platform help teams coordinate office days together, or does it only handle individual, transactional bookings?
  • How does it solve the “who else is coming in?” problem, which is the real reason most people choose to come to the office in the first place?

What good looks like: A system that drives adoption by making the office genuinely easier to navigate, not by mandating usage through policy enforcement.

Employees should be able to see teammate schedules, align office days around meaningful collaboration, and book the resources they need in the same motion.

For HR and leadership: This dimension directly determines whether the platform improves employee experience or becomes another tool people resent. Adoption isn’t an IT metric, it’s a company metric.

Score 1–3: 1 = booking-only, no team coordination or presence visibility | 2 = basic presence display with limited scheduling context | 3 = full team scheduling, presence coordination, and collaborative office planning built in

Dimension 5: Admin Configurability

Every organization has its own policies, floor layouts, resource types, and workflow quirks.

A platform that can’t flex to match yours will force your organization to adapt around it, and that creates friction at every level, from the IT admin managing it to the facility manager trying to update a floor plan after a renovation.

Questions to ask:

  • Can booking policies be configured by team, floor, or resource type without involving a developer or submitting a support ticket?
  • How flexible is the floor plan setup, and how long does it take to update when the office layout changes?
  • Can the platform manage parking spots, labs, studios, or other non-standard resources, or is it limited to desks and meeting rooms?
  • What level of reporting and analytics is available to admins, and how configurable is it?

What good looks like: A platform that’s simple enough for a non-technical Facilities manager to configure day-to-day, but powerful enough to handle complex multi-location, multi-policy environments as the company scales.

Facilities, HR, and IT should each be able to access the configuration they need without depending on each other for every change.

Score 1–3: 1 = rigid templates, requires vendor involvement for most changes | 2 = configurable with IT assistance | 3 = full self-service admin control across resource types, policies, and floor plans

Dimension 6: Vendor Longevity & Support Quality

Hybrid work isn’t static. Offices get redesigned. Headcounts shift. Return-to-office policies evolve. You need a vendor built to grow with you, not one that treats contract signature as the end of the relationship.

Questions to ask:

  • What does the customer success motion look like six months after go-live not just during onboarding?
  • How frequently is the product updated, and how does the vendor communicate changes to IT admins and end users?
  • What is the support SLA, and who handles escalations when standard channels aren’t resolving an issue?
  • Can they provide a reference customer of similar size, industry, or office complexity to speak with?

What to watch for: Vendors who rely entirely on self-serve documentation and community forums for post-sales support, or who can’t readily produce customer references. This matters especially to leadership and Finance stakeholders who are thinking about the three-to-five year relationship, not just the initial deployment.

Score 1–3: 1 = self-serve support only | 2 = standard support with periodic check-ins | 3 = dedicated customer success, proactive engagement, strong and reachable reference network

Reading Your Results

  • 15–18: Strong candidate. Proceed to security review and procurement with confidence.
  • 10–14: Viable, but dig into the low-scoring dimensions before advancing. A 2 on adoption potential is a bigger risk than a 2 on configurability.
  • Below 10: Significant risk of low adoption, high IT overhead, or post-launch regret. Reconsider before moving forward.

One important caveat: the scorecard is a starting point, not a verdict. A platform that scores 16 but fails on adoption will underperform one that scores 13 and fits naturally into how your employees actually work. Keep returning to the same underlying question throughout your evaluation: does this platform make it easier for people to come to the office with purpose — or does it create friction that IT will spend the next year managing?

The answer to that question matters to IT, HR, Facilities, and leadership alike. Which means the right platform isn’t just the one that passes your technical checklist. It’s the one every stakeholder can say yes to.

Author: asen-stoyanchev

Post body:
Picture this: your company is paying for a 25,000 square foot office in the middle of a major city. The lease comes up for renewal in six months. Leadership is split – half want to downsize, half want to keep the space “for when we need it.”

Nobody can agree because nobody actually knows how much of that space gets used on any given day.

So the real estate decision worth millions of dollars over the next lease term gets made the way most workplace decisions still get made: on gut feel, seniority, and whoever is loudest in the room.

This is not an edge case. The XY Sense Workplace Utilization Index Q2+Q3 2025, which aggregates anonymous sensor data from over 59,000 workspaces globally, puts average office utilization at just 43%.

Even on the busiest days of the week, most offices are running well below the capacity they’re designed and priced for. Companies are paying full price for space they’re half-using — and most don’t have the data to prove or disprove it either way.

The metric that changes this conversation is office utilization rate. Once you know yours, the guesswork ends. Lease negotiations, space redesigns, hybrid policy decisions, IT provisioning, they all become data-driven rather than opinion-driven.

This guide will tell you exactly what office utilization rate is, how to measure it properly, what benchmarks to aim for, and crucially, what most teams get wrong when they start tracking it.

TL;DR – Key Takeaways

What it is: Office utilization rate measures how much of your available space – desks, rooms, zones, is actually being used. Formula: (Actual Usage / Available Capacity) × 100.

Why it matters right now: The global average sits at just 43% (XY Sense, 2025). Most companies are paying full price for space they’re half-using, and making million-dollar real estate decisions without data to back them up.

How to measure it accurately: No single data source is enough. Combine booking data with at least one passive signal — badge swipes, sensors, or Wi-Fi detection. The critical detail: booking data alone overstates utilization by 15–25% because of ghost bookings. Check-in verification is what makes the number real.

What “good” looks like:

  • Full RTO → 70–85%
  • Structured hybrid (3 days/week) → 55–70%
  • Flexible hybrid → 40–60%
  • Chasing 100% is a design mistake — it kills collaboration space and drives people back home

The biggest mistakes teams make: Tracking bookings instead of actual usage. Measuring averages instead of peaks. Looking at the whole building instead of zones. Measuring once and moving on.

What to do with the data: Below 50% = real estate optimization opportunity. Above 80% on peak days = capacity and experience problem. High variance = your hybrid policy needs more structure.

See your office utilization clearly - without the spreadsheet gymnastics. OfficeRnD Workplace includes built-in Workplace Analytics that tracks desk and room utilization, monitors hybrid policy adoption, and delivers custom reports straight to your inbox, all in real time. Facility, HR, and IT teams finally working from the same data. Book a live demo here to see it in action.

What Is Office Utilization Rate?

Office utilization rate measures how much of your available office space or specific resources – desks, meeting rooms, collaboration zones, is actually being used over a given period of time.

The core formula is straightforward: Utilization Rate = (Actual Usage / Available Capacity) × 100

If you have 100 desks and an average of 62 are occupied across a full work week, your desk utilization rate is 62%. Simple enough, but in practice, most teams conflate three related concepts that tell very different stories:

Occupancy rate measures whether people are physically present in the building, usually derived from badge swipes or access control systems.

It tells you how many people came in, but nothing about what they did once they got there. Desk utilization rate measures whether specific bookable desks were actually used, and for how long.

A desk that was booked for eight hours but sat empty for five has very different implications than one that was used continuously.

Space utilization rate takes the widest view, measuring how efficiently your entire footprint across all resource types, floors, and zones is being used.

If you want a deeper grounding in space utilization as a broader discipline, including how it connects to space management strategy, this guide covers it in full.

Each metric tells a different story. A floor can show 90% occupancy while desk utilization sits at 50% if people are clustering near windows and the kitchen, while the far end of the floor sits empty.

Understanding which metric you’re looking at, and why, is where most utilization tracking initiatives go wrong before they even start.

How Related Metrics Change What Your Utilization Rate Is Telling You

Your headline utilization rate is the starting point, not the destination. These secondary metrics are what give it meaning, and they often flip the story the top-line number seems to be telling.

Availability by zone reveals where your utilization rate is lying to you. A building-wide rate of 58% can mask a floor where specific zones are pinned at 95% every Tuesday, while others never break 20%.

When you map availability at the zone level, the headline number stops being a verdict and starts being a prompt, which zones to redesign, consolidate, or repurpose entirely.

Cost per square foot overlaid against utilization converts a percentage into a financial argument. If you’re paying $40 per square foot and running at 45% utilization, you can calculate precisely how many dollars per month are funding empty space.

That calculation is what turns a facility manager’s recommendation into a CFO-approved decision.

Space cost per employee on peak days sharpens it further. A hybrid office that looks reasonably utilized on average can reveal an uncomfortable number when you divide real estate costs by the headcount actually present on a given day, not the total headcount on the org chart.

This is often the figure that finally prompts a right-sizing conversation at the executive level.

Employee density by zone is the utilization rate’s quality check. A zone can show strong utilization numbers but still feel unbearably crowded if density is too high, or eerily empty if it’s too low.

Density data tells you whether your utilization rate is producing a good experience or just filling a spreadsheet, which is ultimately the question that determines whether people keep coming back.

By the way, all that also applies to other industries. For example, higher education industries can manage space by using university scheduling software.

Why It Matters More Than Ever in Hybrid Work

Office utilization has always mattered, but hybrid work has made it urgent. When employees are no longer expected to be in five days a week, the old relationship between headcount and required space breaks down entirely.

The real estate math has to be rebuilt from scratch, and utilization rate is the foundation.

For facility managers, the stakes are direct and financial. Real estate is typically the second-largest operating expense after payroll, and in most hybrid organizations it is now systematically oversized.

Utilization data is the only defensible basis for right-sizing your footprint, negotiating a lease, subleasing excess floors, or justifying a redesign budget. Without it, you’re arguing from assumption.

For HR managers, utilization data is a proxy for whether your hybrid policy is actually working. If Tuesday through Thursday are running at 85% and Monday and Friday are ghost floors, that is a culture and policy signal, not just a space management problem.

It tells you which anchor day structures are driving attendance, which teams are coordinating and which aren’t, and where the friction in your hybrid model actually lives.

For IT teams, space utilization directly informs infrastructure decisions. AV systems, network bandwidth, printing hardware, digital signage – these are all provisioned by floor and zone, and they cost the same whether the space is full or empty.

JLL’s 2025 Workforce Preference Barometer, which surveyed 8,700 office workers across 31 countries, found that negative perceptions of office requirements are driven less by the policies themselves and more by the lack of in-office support and poor physical environments.

In other words, when the space doesn’t match how people actually work, frustration follows and most of that misalignment is invisible without utilization data.

The broader point is this:

Office utilization rate is one of the few metrics in a modern organization that is simultaneously a real estate metric, a culture metric, an HR metric, and a technology metric.

When it’s tracked well and shared across teams, it becomes a common language for decisions that used to happen in silos.

How Is Office Utilization Actually Measured?

There is no single perfect data source for office utilization – each method has a different accuracy profile, cost structure, and coverage area. Most organizations that track utilization well use at least two methods in combination.

Badge and access control data tells you who entered the building and when. It’s passive, requires no employee action, and most companies already have it.

The limitation is granularity – it tells you bodies in the building, not what those bodies did or where they went.

Wi-Fi and network presence detection tracks devices connected to your network infrastructure by zone or floor.

It’s passive and reasonably accurate as a proxy for human presence, but it picks up devices, not people – a laptop left in a conference room looks like a human being. Privacy considerations also vary significantly by region.

Desk and room booking software is the most intentional data source: employees declare in advance where they’ll be, and that booking creates a structured utilization record.

The catch is the gap between bookings and actual usage. Ghost bookings – desks and rooms reserved but never occupied are endemic in hybrid offices and can inflate your reported utilization by 15–25% compared to physical reality.

Check-in verification, whether via QR code, door readers, or sensor confirmation, is what closes this gap.

Stop ghost bookings from skewing your utilization data. OfficeRnD Workplace lets employees book desks and meeting rooms from anywhere - via web, mobile app, Microsoft Teams, Slack, or Google Calendar, with built-in check-in confirmation that ensures only real usage counts. Every booking and check-in feeds directly into your utilization reports, so the numbers you're making decisions on actually reflect what's happening on the floor. Learn more.

Occupancy sensors – passive infrared, CO₂, ultrasonic, or camera-based, provide the highest-fidelity real-time data on whether a specific desk or room is physically occupied at any given moment.

They are the gold standard for accuracy but carry higher upfront hardware cost and require installation and maintenance. These could also boost the office attendance rate when applied correctly.

Manual audits – periodic walkthroughs with a clicker or clipboard are low cost and zero infrastructure.

They’re useful for establishing a baseline or validating other data sources, but they aren’t continuous and don’t scale to daily decision-making. The honest conclusion: no single source gives you the full picture. Booking data tells you intent; sensor or badge data tells you reality.

When those two inputs are combined, patterns that would otherwise be invisible become obvious – which floors are perpetually underused, which meeting rooms are always booked but rarely occupied, which teams are coordinating their days well and which aren’t.

Having those data streams in one place rather than in separate spreadsheets managed by different teams is where most organizations unlock their first real utilization insight.

OfficeRnD Workplace's Workplace Analytics is built specifically around this problem, combining real-time occupancy data, desk and room booking records, and hybrid policy adoption metrics in a single platform so executive teams aren't spending hours reconciling exports before they can ask a single question.

What Does a “Good” Utilization Rate Look Like?

This is the question everyone Googles and almost nobody answers directly. So here it is.

Pre-pandemic, offices were typically designed for 100% occupancy but ran at 60–70% on average.

Hybrid work has pushed that number down significantly. The XY Sense Workplace Utilization Index puts the current global average at 43%, with wide variance by industry, day of week, and company policy.

Here’s a rough benchmark framework by context:

Work ModelTarget Utilization Rate
Full return-to-office (5 days/week mandate)70–85%
Structured hybrid (3 designated days/week)55–70%
Flexible hybrid (employee-chosen days)40–60%
Hot desking / no assigned seats60–75%

One thing that trips up almost every organization doing this exercise for the first time: chasing 100% utilization is a mistake.

A fully saturated office has no buffer for collaboration, focus work, or spontaneous interaction.

It feels crowded, limits flexibility, and creates exactly the experience that drives employees to prefer working from home. The goal is not maximum utilization — it’s right utilization.

What does “right” look like in practice? Enough density to feel energetic and justify the real estate cost. Enough breathing room to feel comfortable, collaborative, and worth the commute.

Day-of-week variance is the other variable most benchmarks ignore. The reality in most hybrid offices is that Tuesday through Thursday are dramatically busier than Monday and Friday sometimes by a factor of two or three.

If you’re designing your space around average utilization, you’ll be oversized Monday and Friday and overwhelmed mid-week. Planning around peak days with buffer is more useful than optimizing for the mean.

What This Looks Like in Practice

LinkedIn redesigned its flagship hybrid office not around headcount, but around actual projected usage.

Rather than building the original pre-pandemic plan of 1,080 desks for roughly 1,500 employees, the team used attendance modeling and utilization targets to land on just 569 workstations – a reduction of nearly 50%.

The office didn’t shrink in quality; it was redesigned around collaboration zones and flexible space, with far fewer fixed desks. The result was a space that felt full and purposeful rather than half-empty.

The lesson isn’t that every company should cut its desks in half. It’s that utilization data gave LinkedIn’s team a defensible number to build around, rather than a political argument about how many days people “should” be in the office.

That’s the shift utilization rate tracking makes possible – from opinion to evidence.

The Most Common Mistakes Teams Make When Tracking Utilization

Most organizations that start tracking utilization run into the same set of problems. Knowing them in advance saves months of frustration.

Tracking bookings instead of actual usage

This is the most common and most expensive mistake. Booking data without check-in verification will consistently overstate your utilization by anywhere from 15% to 30%, depending on your no-show rate.

If your workspace platform doesn’t distinguish between “booked” and “confirmed occupied,” your utilization numbers aren’t real.

Measuring the average and ignoring the peaks

A 55% weekly average looks like a healthy, underutilized office — until you drill down and see that Thursday is running at 92% and employees are struggling to find desks.

Averages mask the distribution. Peak-day capacity is where the real planning constraint lives.

Looking at the building instead of the zones

Top-level utilization across a floor or building hides enormous variance at the zone level.

The desks near natural light and the kitchen might run at 90% while the interior rows sit at 30%. Neighborhood- or zone-level data is what actually drives space redesign decisions.

Measuring once and moving on

A utilization audit is useful. Continuous utilization tracking is transformative.

Utilization shifts with seasons, policy changes, team growth, cultural norms, and external events. Organizations that treat it as a one-time exercise get stale data and make decisions on a snapshot that no longer reflects reality.

Keeping the data siloed

Facilities owns the sensor data. HR owns the attendance records. IT owns the badge system.

Nobody shares. The insights die in dashboards nobody reads. Utilization data compounds in value when it’s shared across the teams that can act on it, which means the reporting infrastructure matters as much as the data itself.

What to Do With Your Utilization Data

Good utilization data is only valuable if it triggers a decision. Here’s how to act on the three most common scenarios.

If your utilization is consistently below 50%, you have a real estate optimization opportunity.

Model your footprint at a 65% target, calculate the square footage delta, and multiply by your cost per square foot.

In most major metro markets, that number will be material enough to support a lease renegotiation, a sublease conversation, or a floor consolidation.

This is the analysis your CFO has been waiting for – and now you can actually run it.

If your utilization is above 80% on peak days, you have a capacity problem that’s likely showing up as employee experience friction – inability to find desks, overbooked meeting rooms, a crowded and loud environment that undermines the reason people came in.

The response here is usually structural: desk neighborhoods that give teams priority access on their anchor days, zoned booking, or an expansion into satellite office space to distribute demand.

If your utilization is highly variable – low average but significant mid-week peaks ,your hybrid policy probably needs more structure.

Anchor days, team-level coordination tools, or demand-responsive booking incentives can flatten the curve without mandating full RTO.

In every scenario, the data is only actionable if it reaches the right people at the right cadence.

A weekly utilization summary to Facility, HR, and IT leadership, with trend data and zone-level breakdowns, is what converts a dashboard into an institutional habit. OfficeRnD Workplace's Workplace Analytics handles exactly this - automated scheduled reports delivered to the right inboxes, with custom dashboards and advanced filters. Hence, each team sees the slice of data most relevant to their decisions.

Stop Estimating. Start Measuring

The companies making the best hybrid office decisions right now aren’t doing it on intuition or the intuition of their most senior voices. They’re doing it on utilization data – continuous, granular, and shared across the teams who can act on it.

Office utilization rate is ultimately a proxy for a single question: is your physical space working as hard as your people are? If you can’t answer that question with a number, you’re flying blind on one of your largest operating expenses.

The good news is that tracking it isn’t as complex as it sounds. The right combination of booking data and one passive signal – sensors, badge data, or Wi-Fi detection- gives you more than enough to start making better decisions.

The rest is about making sure those insights reach the people who need them, consistently and without manual effort.

Name: Coworking Statistics for 2026: The Numbers That Matter, Plus What to do with Them
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: There’s no shortage of coworking statistics online. The problem is that most of them tell you what’s “happening” in the market, but not what to do on Monday morning.
Post body:
There’s no shortage of coworking statistics online. The problem is that most of them tell you what’s “happening” in the market, but not what to do on Monday morning.

This roundup is built for 2026 planning, so it combines the most recently published global research (mostly 2024–2025) with forward-looking 2026 forecasts where reliable sources provide them.

To keep it grounded, we’ve added a light layer of operator benchmarks from the OfficeRnD FlexIndex Q4 2025 report, which is built on anonymized data from 3,500+ coworking and flex space locations worldwide.

If you only read one part, jump to the Operator Scoreboard. It’s a useful baseline to start 2026 with.

Key coworking statistics for 2026

Before we get into the details, here’s the short version – the coworking statistics worth having in your back pocket as you plan the year ahead.

  • The global flexible office market is valued at USD 56 billion in 2026, projected to reach USD 100 billion by 2030 (Research and Markets)
  • Global coworking occupancy averaged 68% at the start of 2025, with major cities well above 70% (Deskmag)
  • 54% of coworking businesses were profitable over the previous 12 months; 18% reported losses (Deskmag)
  • 55% of global occupiers now use flexible office solutions; 17% plan to increase their use (Cushman & Wakefield)
  • Meeting room bookings surged worldwide: +24.5% in APAC, +22% in the Americas, +17.4% in EMEA (Cushman & Wakefield)
  • 85% of operators globally expect to expand their offer in 2026 (Workthere Flexmark 5.0)
  • Average flex lease terms reached 16.5 months in 2025 — the longest on record (Workthere)
  • 53% of operator transactions used a management agreement structure by Q3 2025 (Savills)
  • Average allocation of flexible space in European corporate portfolios rose to 21% in 2025, expected to hit 29% within two years (CBRE)
  • Global Revenue Occupancy: 74.49% | RevPOD: $520.15 | Price per Hour of Booking: $44.38 (The OfficeRnD FlexIndex Q4 2025, 3,500+ locations)

That’s the short version. Now, let’s go through what each of these numbers actually means for how you run your space.

The uncomfortable truth behind “flex is growing”

Everyone who works in flex has had a version of this experience: you look around at a full building, walk past a packed lounge, squeeze past someone setting up in the last available meeting room, and still feel uneasy about the month-end numbers.

That tension is real, and it’s worth naming before we get into any coworking stats. Because “flex is growing” is true. And it is also, by itself, not particularly useful.

The more useful question is: who’s capturing the upside?

The answer, based on the latest operator benchmarks, is spaces that treat revenue efficiency as a daily discipline – not just an annual pricing review.

According to the latest OfficeRnD FlexIndex report for Q4 2025, occupancy moved only slightly across the quarter. What moved meaningfully was yield. Price per hour of booking jumped from $40.71 in Q3 to $44.38 in Q4. RevPOD climbed steadily through all four quarters of 2025: $498.02 → $501.30 → $507.04 → $520.15.

That’s not a coincidence. It’s a signal about where the wins are being made, and they’re not being made by spaces that suddenly got dramatically fuller.

That’s the tone for 2026 set by the statistics: less “how do we fill seats” and more “how do we get paid correctly for the demand we already have.”

The market context (the short version)

The flexible office market is valued at an estimated USD 56.04 billion in 2026, projected to reach USD 100.4 billion by 2030 at a 15.7% CAGR (Research and Markets, 2026).

A separate estimate puts the coworking market specifically at $30.12 billion in 2026, reaching $53.46 billion by 2030.

Useful to know.

But here’s the thing: flex still makes up only a small slice of total office inventory. In Europe, flex accounts for roughly 2.5% of total office stock.

In major APAC markets tracked by CBRE, it sits at around 4% of total office stock and 3.2% of Grade A stock. In the US, flex is about 2.1% of total office space (CoworkingCafe, Q3 2025).

That combination – fast growth projections, tiny current share, is actually good news for operators who execute well.

The runway is long. The market isn’t saturated. What it does mean is that execution separates the businesses that grow from the ones that just stay busy.

Who’s in the building – and why it matters

Coworking’s member profile has evolved significantly. The average coworking member is around 36 years old, Millennials make up roughly 61% of members, and women now account for close to half of all users – a share that has grown steadily over time.

About 80% hold a college degree, though that number is gradually declining as coworking broadens its appeal.

But the more meaningful shift is the reason people are in the building.

Deskmag’s 2025 global survey captures this clearly: meeting spaces remained especially popular, and about every second coworking business reported high or very high demand for team offices and single-person offices.

So, this isn’t the “lone freelancer needs WiFi” era anymore.

Workthere’s UK H2 2025 market update frames it from the deals side: flex is now treated as a core component of corporate real estate strategy, and workplace right-sizing was the dominant driver behind enquiries.

Corporate teams made up roughly 27-28% of coworking users in recent surveys, and that share keeps growing. About 41% of corporations now use coworking or flex space in some form.

The practical implication: if you’re still selling based purely on community and vibes without a clear product architecture underneath, you’re going to lose deals you should be winning.

People aren’t buying “coworking.” They’re buying outcomes – right-sized space, smoother collaboration, and the ability to adjust without a multi-year lease hanging over them.

Occupancy is rising. Profitability is still uneven.

Here’s a number worth sitting with: 54% of coworking businesses were profitable over the previous 12 months. 18% reported losses. (Deskmag, early 2025)

Global occupancy reached an average of 68% at the start of 2025, with major cities well above 70%. So the spaces that reported losses weren’t all empty. Some were busy. They just weren’t profitable.

Deskmag also highlights that desk density alone has little direct impact on profitability – layout and product mix matter more. You can’t solve a margin problem by cramming in more desks.

The pressure points are familiar: member acquisition remains the biggest challenge by far, and every third operator cited high real estate or rental costs as a major concern.

The context varies sharply by market: in cities over 1 million residents, close to two-thirds of operators reported being profitable. In towns under 20,000 people, about one in five did.

The takeaway isn’t “move to a big city.” It’s that market context, product mix, and pricing discipline are usually what separate “busy and stressed” from “busy and profitable.”

Deals are getting bigger and stickier

One of the quietest but most meaningful shifts in flex is what’s happening to deal structure.

Workthere’s UK H2 2025 market report shows the average number of desks per deal in 2025 was 24.1. The average lease term reached 16.5 months – the longest on record, up 27% year-on-year.

This is flex maturing. Buyers aren’t just dipping a toe in; they’re making real commitments. And when that happens, the operator relationship changes. Renewals become genuinely strategic. The “we’ll figure it out next month” approach stops working.

For 2026, this rewards operators who have a real renewal process – one that starts three or four months before term, not three days before.

It also rewards bundles that let teams expand without renegotiating every component from scratch. If your current renewal rate feels like a coin flip, this is probably why.

Pricing: the gap between tiers is widening

The market isn’t raising all prices evenly. It’s rewarding clarity and quality, and leaving the fuzzy middle exposed.

US benchmarks (CoworkingCafe, Q3 2025):

  • National median membership: $225/month
  • Day pass: $30
  • Meeting room: $45/hour
  • Virtual office: $159/month

UK benchmarks (Workthere, 2025):

  • UK average monthly desk cost: £570
  • London: £775
  • Rest of UK: £364
  • Average London desk rates specifically reached £841 by the end of H1 2025, alongside 86% occupancy (Savills)

Those UK numbers deserve a second look. £841 per desk and 86% occupancy in the same market, at the same time – that’s what “flight to quality” actually looks like in practice.

Premium inventory, clearly positioned, in the right location, commands both higher rates and fills faster.

The uncomfortable message for operators in the middle: if you’re not investing in the things that justify premium pricing, the market will still charge you premium costs. That’s where margin gets quietly destroyed.

The business model shift operators cannot ignore

Most coworking statistics roundups skip this entirely, but deal structure might be the most strategically important data point in this whole article.

Savills reports that 53% of operator transactions used a management agreement deal structure at the end of Q3 2025 – the highest proportion recorded over the last five years. Their 2026 trends piece suggests this is expected to rise above 70% as the year progresses.

David Walker, Ashley Proctor, Ivan Guberkov, James Panepinto, and Pauline Roussel - all seasoned coworking leaders, recently underwrote “5 Coworking & Flex Space Trends for 2026 [According to Industry Experts]. You don’t want to miss the insights. Download it for free here.

A management agreement means the landlord takes on the lease risk. The operator delivers the model – the operations, the experience, the revenue mechanics.

For operators, that’s a significant opportunity. It’s also a higher bar. You can’t wing a management agreement. Landlords want reporting, consistency, predictability, and a model that doesn’t fall apart when a team member leaves.

The expansion intent backs this up: Workthere’s Flexmark 5.0 survey found that 85% of operators globally expect to grow their offer in 2026.

When most of your competitors are expanding at the same time, what protects you isn’t being the newest – it’s being the most operationally solid.

Enterprise adoption is mainstream. The expectations come with it.

You don’t need to chase enterprise to feel the impact of enterprise becoming the dominant flex buyer.

Cushman & Wakefield’s 2025 Global Flexible Office Trends report: 55% of global occupiers now use flexible office solutions, with 17% planning to increase their use.

CBRE’s European Flex Market Update 2025 adds that the average corporate allocation of flexible space rose to 21% in 2025, expected to climb to 29% within two years.

Savills’ 2026 trends piece adds texture: 44% of flex occupiers in EMEA are now global or national corporates, with some local markets exceeding 50%.

For context on how that demand scales – Regus, the largest US flex operator, runs roughly 1,185 locations nationwide (CoworkingCafe).

Enterprise clients choose providers that make their operations predictable. That sets the baseline expectations for the whole market.

For operators at every scale, the practical implication is the same: accurate invoicing, predictable policies, clean access rules, reporting that doesn’t require manual heroics at month-end.

These are now table stakes, not differentiators.

Meeting rooms are the revenue battleground of 2026

If there’s one operational shift every operator should make in 2026, it’s treating meeting rooms like a revenue product, not an amenity.

Growth Hub is a powerful e-commerce engine that embeds directly into your coworking website, letting visitors book meeting rooms, desks, and subscriptions instantly and turning demand into revenue. Check it out.

The demand signal is hard to ignore. Cushman & Wakefield reports that meeting room bookings surged worldwide in 2025: +24.5% in APAC, +22.0% in the Americas, +17.4% in EMEA.

Now pair that with the OfficeRnD FlexIndex yield signal. In Q4 2025, the quarter’s most notable movement was hourly pricing, jumping from $40.71 in Q3 to $44.38 globally by Q4 (+8.9% vs Q1 2025).

The FlexIndex notes this is “one of the most actionable levers” operators can pull, specifically because it responds quickly to good rate governance.

The math is simple and painful: if your rooms are consistently busy but your hourly yield is flat, you are doing free upgrades. The fix usually isn’t a major pricing overhaul, it’s three or four policy decisions enforced consistently:

  • Peak and off-peak pricing tiers
  • Minimum booking durations for prime slots
  • Standardized buffers and cancellation windows
  • Stopping the same exception being made for the same person every week

None of it is glamorous. All of it compounds.

Regional coworking statistics: where different markets start 2026

Global averages hide a lot. Here’s how coworking statistics and performance look by region, combining market data with FlexIndex operator benchmarks.

Americas

The US had 8,420 coworking locations covering roughly 152 million square feet as of Q3 2025, yet coworking is still only 2.1% of total US office space (CoworkingCafe).

Large operators like Regus are gaining share while trimming weaker locations, a pattern that favors operators with strong fundamentals over those just occupying space.

The FlexIndex story for the Americas in Q4 2025 is “a two-speed year.” Revenue efficiency improved – RevPOD reached $524.26, RevPAD $373.67, hourly pricing jumped from $39.91 (Q3) to $43.07 (Q4).

But private office occupancy softened to 69.82%, which matters because offices typically anchor recurring revenue.

What to watch: Private office softness in a market where revenue efficiency is improving usually points to a conversion and retention problem, not a demand problem. Tighter bundling and earlier renewals are the lever.

EMEA & UKI

Europe’s flex workspace footprint grew by more than 348,000 square meters in 2024 – a 4.4% year-on-year increase, bringing the total to 8.3 million square meters across 46 EMEA markets (Colliers, 2025).

Yet flex still represents only around 2.5% of total European office stock. The demand pressure is real – CBRE’s European brokerage activity showed transactions up 14% and desk volumes up 22%, but supply growth has been cautious.

The UK is a useful leading indicator.

There are 4,315 coworking spaces across the UK and Ireland as of Q3 2025, with London’s 1,191 spaces making it the dominant hub (CoworkingCafe). Manchester (120 spaces), Glasgow (68), and Birmingham (67) are the leading regional markets.

The OfficeRnD FlexIndex picture for EMEA & UKI in Q4 2025: strong occupancy (revenue occupancy at 76.22% – highest of the three regions), but RevPOD and RevPAD softened year-on-year.

The report frames it bluntly: “demand was strong, but revenue per desk did not rise with it, which typically points to yield discipline issues.”

EMEA & UKI FlexIndex Q4 2025:

  • Revenue Occupancy 76.22%
  • Desk Occupancy 74.66%
  • Private Office Occupancy 73.11%
  • RevPOD $474.74

  • Price/Hour $41.25
What to watch: Being the region with the highest occupancy but the lowest RevPOD is the definition of "busy but underpaid." The 2026 opportunity here is getting paid correctly for already being full.

APAC

The Asia-Pacific flex market reached 89 million sq ft as of June 2025, representing roughly 4% of total office stock across 20 major markets (CBRE).

The region’s growth story has moderated from hyper-expansion (51% annualized 2015-2019) to a more sustainable pace (~4% recently), which is actually healthy maturation.

The FlexIndex story for APAC in Q4 2025: a “clear utilization win.” Private Office Occupancy rose from 68.92% (Q1) to 71.45% (Q4) – the strongest occupancy improvement of any region.

But RevPOD finished slightly below Q1, meaning the region got busier without fully converting that busyness into revenue.

  • Revenue Occupancy 71.47%
  • Desk Occupancy 71.61%
  • Private Office Occupancy 71.45%
  • RevPOD $649.53

  • Price/Hour $55.97
What to watch: APAC has the highest RevPOD and highest hourly rates of any region — the monetization ceiling is real. The upside in 2026 is tighter yield governance to close the gap between utilization gains and revenue capture.

Operator Scoreboard: the baseline entering 2026

Here’s the part worth screenshotting.

FlexIndex is built on anonymized data from 3,500+ coworking and flex space locations worldwide, tracking six KPIs that reflect how flex businesses actually run.

The methodology excludes canceled bookings, free bookings, zero-duration or 12h+ bookings, and zero-priced discounts, so what you see reflects real, paid usage.

The occupancy numbers barely moved. The revenue numbers moved meaningfully. That’s the 2025 story in one table, and the 2026 playbook.

Two ways to use this immediately:

Track RevPAD as your monthly profitability dashboard, by location and by product line. If occupancy is rising but RevPOD isn’t, the culprit is almost always pricing governance: inconsistent discounting, packaging exceptions, or billing leakage.

Three operator paths for 2026

Numbers only matter if they lead somewhere. Here’s how the data applies depending on what you’re running.

If you run a single-location, community-led space

Your competitive advantage is usually specificity – a clear audience, a clear culture, a clear reason to choose you over the generic option. Your profitability edge is yield, not volume.

For 2026: productize your meeting rooms with simple, consistent pricing rules. Build a “team starter” bundle that reduces negotiation friction. Find your “busy but underpaid” inventory and fix yield there first, that’s usually where the hidden margin lives.

If you run a multi-location operation

Two locations can look equally busy on the surface and deliver very different margins. The gap usually comes from discount inconsistency, packaging variance, or billing exceptions that compound across sites without anyone noticing.

For 2026: standardize bundle structures so pricing is defensible at every location.

How?

Use RevPOD and RevPAD by site to spot margin erosion early. Build a renewal rhythm that doesn’t depend on individual managers remembering to start the conversation.

If you grow through landlord partnerships or management agreements

The data makes clear this is becoming the default growth lane in mature markets. Savills’ 2026 trends data expects management agreements to represent over 70% of transactions this year. This model rewards operational predictability above everything else.

For 2026: keep your operational playbook simple enough to replicate without you in the room. Treat monthly reporting as a standard, not a request.

Lock in meeting room yield with rules that remove one-off pricing from daily operations — that’s what landlords see, and it’s what builds long-term trust.

If you operate primarily in one region, use your regional FlexIndex scorecard instead of the global benchmark.

What 2026 is really asking from operators

The coworking statistics, taken together, tell a coherent story, one that’s less about market size and more about operational maturity.

Demand is increasingly shaped by teams and collaboration needs. Deals are getting larger and longer, which rewards operators who package, renew, and report well.

Management agreements are reshaping how growth happens in mature markets. Enterprise expectations are now the market baseline, even for operators who never chase enterprise clients.

And a meaningful share of 2025’s performance improvement came not from a wave of new demand, but from tighter yield and better revenue capture.

The spaces that look back on 2026 as a good year probably won’t all be the biggest, newest, or best-located. They’ll be the ones that made “busy” actually mean something on the P&L.

The scoreboard is a starting point. Pick one number that’s below benchmark. Tighten one lever. Then do it again next month. That’s how busy becomes profitable, and how profitable becomes scalable.
