Name: OfficeRnD Flex: 2025 Product Year in Review
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: 2025 has been a significant year for OfficeRnD Flex. As flex space operators continued to expand, diversify, and refine their business models, we focused on delivering solutions that help them grow revenue, streamline operations, and provide a better experience for members and visitors.
Post body:
2025 has been a significant year for OfficeRnD Flex. As flex space operators continued to expand, diversify, and refine their business models, we focused on delivering solutions that help them grow revenue, streamline operations, and provide a better experience for members and visitors.

This year, we invested heavily in delivering exactly that.

OfficeRnD Flex now powers 3,500+ flex spaces, supports 500,000+ active community members, and is trusted in 90+ countries. As we marked our 10th anniversary, our focus remained clear: build a platform that helps operators run more efficient, profitable, and scalable businesses.

What makes OfficeRnD Flex unique is its modular Hub-based architecture. Each Hub focuses on solving a distinct operator and member challenge — from daily operations and billing, to member experience, to e-commerce, to analytics, to access control and finance integrations. This structure allows the platform to evolve deeply in each area, delivering more value, more clarity, and more customization for operators of all sizes.

Below is a look at how each Hub grew in 2025 — and how these advancements shaped a more modern, connected flex workspace experience.

Growth Hub: The new revenue engine for flex space operators

Growth Hub was the biggest evolution of our platform this year. Operators increasingly need to turn their websites into real revenue engines, and Growth Hub delivered that in a transformative way.

From its rapid adoption across 100+ organizations and 300+ locations, Growth Hub has become a powerful driver of self-serve bookings, conversion, and monetization. Operators saw more visitors booking on their own, more prospects purchasing subscriptions independently, and becoming members, and far fewer manual steps for front-desk teams.

Throughout the year, we expanded Growth Hub with capabilities that elevated both revenue generation and operational efficiency:

  • iFrame embedding enables operators to add Growth Hub as a seamless ecommerce storefront on their website, so customers can browse, book, and pay without leaving the page.
  • Dynamic pricing helps operators optimize revenue by adjusting prices to real demand — filling quiet periods and capturing additional revenue at peak times.
  • More powerful promo codes allow operators to run targeted marketing campaigns, including membership-specific offers and per-user redemption limits ideal for public or partner promotions.
  • Localization enabled Growth Hub to be fully adaptable to global audiences, allowing operators to deliver a native browsing, booking, and checkout experience in any language.
  • Smarter checkout flows — multiple payment methods we support ( Cards, Google Pay, Apple Pay, IDEAL, ACH), customizable billing detail forms, saved payment details, ACH support for recurring payments, and improvements to default calendar behavior. These enhancements make purchases smoother for customers while reducing manual work for teams.
  • High performance and fast load times create a responsive and reliable booking experience that reduces friction and drop-off compared to other solutions in the market.

Together, these improvements positioned Growth Hub as the go-to modern revenue engine for flex space operators, designed to drive more revenue, higher conversion, and less manual work across every stage of the customer journey.

Flex Operations Hub: Operational efficiency at scale

The Operations Hub remained the backbone of the platform — and this year, it became even more powerful, automated, and scalable.

We focused on helping teams simplify complex processes, reduce repetitive work, and gain more control over billing and pricing. Key improvements included:

  • Flexible capacity resources, a smarter way to manage shared spaces like hot desk zones, lounges, group bookings, and day-pass-friendly areas. Instead of juggling dozens of identical desks, operators can now manage a single resource with a set capacity — unlocking cleaner scheduling, better utilization, and clearer reporting.
  • Pricing automation through the new price adjustment rules, allowing consistent updates across memberships based on CPI, anniversaries, or monthly changes — with full previews and automated member notifications.
  • Enhanced billing workflows, including a redesigned billing settings page, faster and more reliable bill runs, and greater control through contract-level approval rules.
  • More transparent operations, supported by a revamped Activity Log with deeper detail, cleaner filtering, and longer retention.

The result is a stronger, more automated operational core — helping operators save time, maintain financial consistency, and scale with confidence.

Experience Hub: Stronger communication and deeper engagement

Experience Hub is all about helping operators communicate effectively and build vibrant communities. In 2025, we strengthened both communication and engagement across the ecosystem.

A key enhancement this year was the introduction of Email Announcements — built-in, on-brand, targeted communication directly from OfficeRnD Flex. Teams can now send beautifully styled updates to members without relying on external tools, with improvements like drafts, duplication, and tracking that make collaboration even easier.

To deepen engagement, we added likes and comments on posts and events across the Member Portal and mobile app, giving operators insight into what resonates and helping members engage with the community in a natural way.

We also introduced member privacy controls, ensuring profiles appear only after members set their preferences during onboarding — a meaningful step toward transparency and trust.

Experience Hub is now a more complete communication layer, connecting members with the space, the team, and each other.

Visitor Hub: Modernizing the front-of-house experience

This year, our customers saved more than 12,500 hours of administrative work—the equivalent of six full years—by using Visitor Hub to streamline over 300,000 visitor check-ins and 150,000 deliveries.

Our focus was clear: modernize the front-of-house experience while reducing repetitive work for onsite teams.

We introduced:

  • Badge printing, customizable success screens, and branded visitor emails that make every arrival more polished and consistent.
  • Customizable notifications across email, SMS, and push, ensuring hosts and recipients get the right information at the right time.
  • Delivery management, including photos, structured details, custom flows, and an organized delivery log — bringing oversight and transparency to one of the busiest parts of the reception desk.
  • Custom shortcut buttons and Growth Hub-connected flows that streamline day pass purchases and reduce friction for walk-ins.

Visitor Hub now delivers a modern, secure, and branded arrival journey that enhances first impressions and frees up valuable staff time.

Data Hub: Insights that drive action

Data Hub continued its evolution into a powerful insight engine that helps operators understand performance and take action faster.

This year, we shipped new dashboards that reveal patterns in member behavior, adoption, event engagement, and location activity. The member activity overview and events dashboards make it easier to spot gaps, celebrate strengths, and act on real-world behavior.

We also introduced benchmarking, enabling operators to compare key metrics — like revenue per desk, occupancy, and booking prices — against anonymized peers across regions. And with NIA insights, operators now have more meaningful spatial metrics like revenue per square meter.

To support better data governance, we added granular dashboard permissions and improved how filters persist across dashboards and shared links.

Data Hub now provides clearer visibility, more relevant insights, and the context operators need to grow strategically.

Integrations Hub: A stronger financial and digital ecosystem

2025 was a major year for strengthening the Integrations Hub — particularly in finance, payments, access, and infrastructure.

The highlight of the year was the launch of the Sage Intacct integration, bringing automated AR workflows, real-time invoice and payment sync, customizable mapping, and enterprise-grade financial precision to operators who rely on Intacct.

We also expanded our payments capabilities with Stripe Terminal, enabling in-person card charging and easy card capture for recurring billing — an impactful bridge between front-desk interactions and automated invoicing.

In addition, we introduced two new integrations with essensys:

  • essensys elumo, enabling a seamless booking-to-access experience for meeting rooms with mobile-first entry, automatic booking sync, and centralized control.
  • essensys Platform, bringing automated WiFi provisioning to members, real-time status updates, enterprise-grade authentication, and instant onboarding across locations.

Together, these integrations strengthen Flex as the operational core that connects payments, access, connectivity, and finance — enabling operators to deliver a consistent, premium experience across all locations.

Looking back at a transformative year

Name: Defining Coworking and Flex Space Trends for 2026 [Webinar Recap]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: The flex space industry has never been more dynamic – or more complex. In our recent webinar, Defining Coworking & Flex Space Trends for 2026 , we brought together five leaders who’ve shaped the industry from different angles and regions:
Post body:
The flex space industry has never been more dynamic – or more complex. In our recent webinar, Defining Coworking & Flex Space Trends for 2026, we brought together five leaders who’ve shaped the industry from different angles and regions:

  • James Panepinto – General Manager, Clockwise Offices, UK Chair, Future Leaders of Coworking
  • David Walker – Founder, CoworkingConsulting.com
  • Pauline Roussel – Co-Founder & CEO, Coworkies
  • Ashley Proctor – Founder, Creative Blueprint & Executive Director, Coworking Canada
  • Moderator: Ivan Guberkov – Chief Product Officer, OfficeRnD

Together, they unpacked what changed in 2025 and what will really matter in 2026 – from macroeconomics and member expectations to landlords, AI, and business models.

Below is a structured recap with key insights and operator-ready takeaways.

Note: This is a quick recap of all the insights discussed. Head here to watch the discussion on demand and capture all the knowledge bombs.

1. Flex is now mainstream – and the “lease cliff” is real

One of the strongest themes: flex is no longer niche.

David Walker put it bluntly:

Coworking has become mainstream. Businesses of all sizes are looking at flexible options and no one wants traditional leases anymore.”

He described what he calls the “pandemic lease cliff.” Around 2020, many companies renegotiated leases. Now, at the 5-year mark, a lot of those leases are coming up for renewal – and tenants are seriously questioning going back into long, static commitments.

That creates a huge moment of opportunity and competition:

  • Building owners are asking: “How do we keep these tenants?”
  • Operators are asking: “How do we win these members?”

The result? Flex is increasingly the default conversation, not the alternative.

2. Back to roots: community and “human infrastructure.”

At the same time, the panel emphasized a strong cultural swing back to coworking’s origins.

Ashley Proctor reminded everyone where it started:

Coworking began as a grassroots movement rooted in community and mutual aid.

With AI and automation everywhere, she sees people craving the human side more than ever – genuine connection, real conversations, and mutual support.

That’s particularly good news for independent operators and community-driven brands that actually live those values, not just market them.

David added that as more corporate users arrive, operators need to be intentional about culture:

Historically there were ‘corporate members’ and ‘real members’. Now it’s on the operator to unify that community in a meaningful way.

In other words: hybrid member bases will be the norm – but it’s up to operators to prevent cultural silos and keep community at the center.

3. Macro forces: inflation, slow growth, and decentralization

From a European perspective, Pauline highlighted inflation and slower economic growth as major drivers of flex demand in 2025 – and into 2026.

She noted that in much of Europe, inflation has cooled but still squeezed margins, while growth in countries like France, Italy and Germany has been muted. That pushed many businesses toward shorter commitments and flexible space instead of long leases.

In the UK, James sees another structural shift:

It’s no longer London-centric. It’s no longer London first and everyone else three years later.

Regional cities now have strong operators in their own right – not just satellite locations. And alongside that, there’s a clear move away from competing purely on price:

  • Less “cheapest space wins”
  • More “this is our product, these are our values – if price is the only driver, we might not be for you.”

That values-driven positioning will likely become a bigger differentiator in 2026.

4. How people are using flex space differently

From one-size-fits-all to “say yes” packaging

On the demand side, both individuals and companies are using coworking more fluidly than ever.

David argued that the old “one membership for everyone” approach is increasingly broken. A company may arrive with 50 people and no obvious fit in your standard plans – unless you can think flexibly:

  • A mix of private offices
  • A bundle of hot desk memberships
  • A package of meeting room credits
  • Access across multiple locations or days

“It’s incumbent upon operators to meet people where they are,” he said. Technology now makes this complexity manageable – but only if you embrace it.

Members as “multi-space” users

Ashley also described a big behavioral shift: people don’t necessarily commit to one space anymore.

I’m a member at multiple spaces now. I go one place when I want to really focus and be quiet, another when I want to be social, and another for the events.

Employers may fund the access, but employees choose when and where they work – often across different brands and locations.

Fractional offices and “near home” locations

Pauline highlighted rising interest in fractional offices (different companies using the same office on different days) and the growth of flex in residential and suburban areas. Many brands are deliberately going closer to where people live instead of betting everything on CBDs.

Coworking is also appearing inside other venues:

  • Climbing gyms
  • Hotels
  • Mixed-use community hubs
  • Even train carriages designed as proper workspaces

Her favorite line sums it up:

Coworking is the same dish everyone cooks differently.”

And increasingly, coworking is becoming a service layer that can be plugged into all kinds of places – not just a standalone space.

5. Landlords, “brandlords” and building-wide ecosystems

The group spent time on the evolving role of landlords – including the rise of “brandlords,” asset owners building their own flex brands.

David shared what he sees in his consulting work: many landlords first look to coworking as a way to plug vacancy, then realize they may need:

  • A third-party operator
  • Or a management partner
  • Or to develop their own operating brand

His prediction goes a step further:

“Coworking will become the operating ecosystem of the flexible office asset.”

In other words, the operator doesn’t just run a floor – they orchestrate the experience and services across the whole building, integrating tenants, amenities, and flex space into a single ecosystem.

Pauline pointed out that in more mature markets like Paris, this is already happening, including corporate owner-occupiers turning underused HQ space into branded coworking for partners and collaborators.

For operators, the implication is clear: partnership skills and asset-wide thinking will be increasingly valuable.

6. Technology, AI and dynamic pricing: opportunity with guardrails

AI as “central brain”, not silver bullet

Everyone agreed: AI is the “elephant in the room,” but we’re still early.

David joked,

Happy birthday to ChatGPT – it just turned three. It’s a baby.

His main advice: don’t just adopt random AI tools. Start by feeding all your data – financials, occupancy, member behavior, brand principles – into a centralized AI “brain” you can query for decisions:

  • “What’s the best way to structure this 300-person deal in my current space?”
  • “Which rooms should I discount on Fridays based on historic utilization?”

AI then becomes a strategic co-pilot, not a gimmick.

Pauline noted that most operators she saw at recent conferences still use AI mainly for content (emails, posts, etc.), but the real upside is automating operations so teams can spend more time with members.

James added the flip side: fully automated experiences are coming too – from self-check-in to spaces that “remember” your lighting or temperature preferences. The balance between high-touch hospitality and automation will be a key design choice.

Dynamic pricing: start simple, don’t abdicate control

Dynamic pricing came up as a hot topic. The consensus: it’s powerful but overhyped and very context-dependent.

Key points from the discussion:

  • It works best when you already have strong e-commerce, real traffic, and meaningful booking volume.
  • The biggest early win is often simple rule-based adjustments:
    • Cheaper prices on chronically quiet days (e.g. Mondays/Fridays)
    • Off-peak discounts for low-demand time slots
  • Over-automating pricing without monitoring can confuse members and hurt revenue before you notice.

Treat dynamic pricing as optimization on top of a healthy funnel, not a rescue lever for a struggling space.

7. What will separate thriving operators in 2026?

When asked what differentiates thriving operators from struggling ones, the panel kept coming back to three themes.

1. A solid financial model (not just a busy space)

David warned that a buzzing space doesn’t always mean a healthy P&L:

You can walk into a space that feels packed and exciting, and the owner is still stressed because the numbers don’t work.

Private offices, management agreements, events, multi-use models – all can work, but you need a clear path to sustainable margins.

2. Investing in your team, especially community

Pauline stressed the importance of teams in an increasingly “professionalized” industry. Community and experience teams are under huge pressure to be the face of the brand, handle operations, and deliver hospitality.

If you want to thrive, you need to:

  • Invest in training, peer networks and growth paths
  • Avoid unrealistic expectations for one person to “do it all”
  • Protect community managers from burnout so they can build real relationships

James added that community cannot be “tick-box Peroni and pizza nights” anymore. Operators don’t own the community; they facilitate it.

3. Ruthless attention to early warning signs

Asked for red flags, the panel called out:

  • Quiet churn – members leaving without clear reasons or feedback
  • Exit surveys shifting from “I moved city” to “culture/amenities/service issues”
  • High staff turnover, especially in community roles, before they’ve had time to embed in the member base
  • Loss of basic care: lights out, things broken, smells, messy common areas

As Pauline put it, the moment teams stop seeing what’s broken because they’re “there every day,” quality starts to slip – and members absolutely notice.

2026: bold predictions from the panel

To close, each speaker shared a bet for 2026 and beyond:

  • David Walker: Coworking becomes the operating ecosystem for entire office assets, with operators orchestrating value for all tenants, not just their own members.
  • Ashley Proctor: More cities and policymakers will treat coworking as essential community infrastructure, often embedded in multi-use hubs with childcare, culture, services and education.
  • James Panepinto: The winning operators will treat flex as a portfolio strategy, not just a single product, mapping every touchpoint like a hospitality journey and growing deliberately rather than “100 locations in 18 months.”
  • Pauline Roussel: Technology and AI will go much deeper into operations, but operators will need to educate themselves and connect their tools to actually unlock that value.
  • Ivan Guberkov: AI will increasingly “fill the systems itself” – reducing manual admin so teams spend more time with members – while landlords will feel more pressure to partner with experienced operators as vacancies persist and Gen Z expectations reshape workplace standards.

The common thread: more integration, more intelligence, more humanity.

Don’t forget to check out this blog post to get a more comprehensive view of the most anticipated coworking and flex space trends for 2026.

What this means for your space

If you’re operating a coworking or flex space today, the panel’s message for 2026 is both challenging and optimistic:

  • Flex is the default, not the fringe. Your competition is not just other spaces, but home, coffee shops, and entire neighborhoods.
  • Community and hospitality are your moat. AI and automation will level the operational playing field, but no one can copy your relationships and culture overnight.
  • Partnership thinking is non-negotiable. With landlords, cities, community organizations and even other operators.
  • Data + AI are becoming table stakes, but only if you feed them real information and keep humans in the loop.
  • Care – for your finances, your team, your members, and your space – is the ultimate early-warning system.
Watch the entire webinar on demand here and get all valuable insights.

Coworking just turned 20. As Pauline noted, it’s astonishing how far the industry has come in such a short time. If the panel is right, the next few years will be less about proving flex works – and more about deciding what kind of flex future you want to build.

Name: The Month-End Billing Runbook for Multi-Location Coworking Operators
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Month-end at a multi-location coworking brand often feels like déjà vu.
Post body:
Month-end at a multi-location coworking brand often feels like déjà vu.

Slack pings nonstop. Every location has its own spreadsheet. Finance is waiting on “latest numbers” while leadership is already asking, “So how did we do this month?”

Meanwhile, the industry is growing fast. Some reports project the global coworking market to roughly double in size by 2030, with operators investing heavily in tech to keep up.

If your billing is slow or inaccurate, you’re not just dealing with admin pain, you’re putting cash flow and growth at risk.

This article gives you a practical, repeatable month-end billing runbook designed for multi-location coworking operators. You can run it today and gradually automate it with tools like OfficeRnD Flex, Stripe, and your accounting system.

Why Month-End Explodes in Complexity When You Add Locations

Once you go beyond a single location, everything multiplies:

  • Multiple legal entities and bank accounts
  • Different tax rules across regions or countries
  • Different product mixes and prices per site

At the same time, your revenue blends recurring (offices, desks, virtual memberships) with variable (meeting rooms, passes, events). Each has its own billing rules, discounts, and edge cases.

Manual invoice processing is not built for this. Studies show manual invoice data entry error rates around 1–3%, and fixing each error can be surprisingly expensive in both time and money.

Scattered Workflows Across Teams and Tools

For many operators, data lives everywhere:

  • Community teams log changes in Slack or local sheets
  • Bookings sit in a separate calendar or booking tool
  • Invoices and accounting are in Xero or QuickBooks

Every handoff is a chance for data to be delayed or distorted. Research across industries links manual invoice workflows to higher error rates, slower processing, and worse visibility into cash flow.

See the most common mistakes coworking operators make that stop them from scaling properly. 

The “Hero Operator” Problem

Most multi-site brands have a “billing hero” at each region or flagship site—the person who just “knows how it works.”

That’s not a system.

If that person is off or leaves, billing slows down or breaks. You also can’t scale from 3 to 10+ locations if everything depends on individual knowledge instead of a documented, repeatable runbook.

Related read: From Chaos to Control: How Automated Billing Streamlines Multi-Location Coworking Operations

What a “Good” Month-End Close Looks Like

Before changing tools or processes, decide what success looks like.

Clear Targets for Time to Close and Accuracy

Set simple, measurable targets such as:

  • Time to close: “All invoices sent within 3 business days of month-end.”
  • Accuracy: “Less than 2–3% of invoices require correction.”

Invoice errors don’t just annoy members; they also delay payments and create extra work for finance.

Predictable Experience for Members and Teams

A good month-end close is predictable:

  • Members know when invoices arrive and what they’ll contain
  • Local teams follow a checklist instead of scrambling
  • Finance gets clean, consistent data into accounting

Clear Ownership: Who Does What, When

Define roles first, tools second:

  • Location managers: Keep member and contract data clean; review local drafts
  • Central ops: Own product catalog, billing rules, and playbooks
  • Finance: Own collections, accounting integrations, and reporting

When everyone understands their part of the runbook, fewer tasks fall through the cracks.

The Step-By-Step Month-End Billing Runbook

You can start by doing these steps manually, then progressively automate them.

Step 1 – Freeze Changes and Confirm Cut-Off Dates

Decide what belongs to this billing cycle vs. the next:

  • Set a recurring cut-off date for contract changes and plan switches
  • Communicate the cut-off clearly to each location
  • Reduce last-minute changes that force manual invoice edits

Even this alone can dramatically reduce exceptions.

Check out the most impactful coworking statistics for 2026 here.

Step 2 – Reconcile Memberships and Contracts Across Locations

Run the same standard reports for every site:

  • New members
  • Cancellations/churn
  • Upgrades and downgrades
  • Renewals and expiring contracts

Check for anomalies such as:

  • Active access, but no active plan
  • “Free” members who should be under a paying company
  • Offices marked as occupied but not tied to a billed contract
In a platform like OfficeRnD Flex, member and contract data is centralized, so you’re reconciling one system rather than five. 

Step 3 – Pull In Variable Revenue (Bookings, Passes, Add-Ons)

Variable revenue is where many operators leak money.

Make sure you capture all of this before invoices go out:

  • Meeting room and event bookings
  • Day passes and drop-ins
  • Add-ons like lockers, parking, printing, or mail handling

Ideally, bookings and one-off charges should live in the same system that creates invoices, so usage is automatically added as line items.

Common leak points:

  • “Free” meeting room hours that creep beyond policy
  • Credits not deducted properly
  • One-off discounts that quietly become permanent

Step 4 – Generate and Review Draft Invoices in Bulk

Next, generate draft invoices in bulk by entity, location, or segment.

Instead of inspecting every invoice, use a sampling + exceptions approach:

  • Spot-check a subset per location (new members, large accounts, complex deals)
  • Review exception reports: negative totals, zero-value invoices, unusual discount levels, missing tax

You keep strong control without turning month-end into a line-by-line audit.

Step 5 – Send Invoices and Trigger Collections

Send invoices on a consistent schedule using:

  • Branded email templates
  • Clear line items and tax breakdowns
  • A member portal where customers can see invoice history and pay online

Late payments are a real threat to SMEs. One recent study found 44% of invoices were paid late, tying up billions in working capital and hurting small business cash flow.

Encourage modern payment methods that speed up cash collection:

  • Card payments
  • Direct debit or ACH
  • Automated retries on failed payments
With the OfficeRnD + Stripe integration, you can automatically charge invoices for memberships, bookings, and services via credit cards, SEPA, ACH, and other methods. Successful charges are pushed back into OfficeRnD and, if connected, into your accounting system—keeping your collected vs. overdue revenue up to date.

Are you operating in Europe? Then learn more about VIDA and e-invoicing.

Step 6 – Sync to Accounting and Lock the Period

Finally, push your billing data into accounting:

  • Sync invoices, payments, and credits into Xero or QuickBooks Online
  • Reconcile payments and bank statements
  • Close the period in both your billing and accounting systems

OfficeRnD Flex automates much of this flow, sending invoices from Flex to tools like QuickBooks and Xero, and linking successful charges made via Stripe back to the right invoices in both systems.

Want these six steps to feel like a one-click bill run? Book a live demo with OfficeRnD Flex and see how multi-location operators do it.

Designing a Billing Architecture That Actually Scales

The runbook is easier to run when your billing architecture is solid.

Standardized Product Catalog with Location-Aware Pricing

Define your products centrally, then allow for local nuance:

  • Use consistent naming across locations (e.g., “Dedicated Desk,” “Private Office – Large”)
  • Apply location-specific pricing and tax rules where needed
  • Map each product to the right revenue account

This gives you comparable reporting across sites while still reflecting local market realities.

Handling Multiple Entities, Taxes, and Currencies

If you operate across countries or entities:

  • Assign each location to an entity and tax profile
  • Standardize how deposits, prepayments, and refunds are handled
  • Bake tax logic and account mappings into your system instead of someone’s memory

Contract Logic: Proration, Deposits, and Term Changes

Decide once and apply everywhere:

  • When do you prorate vs. bill full month?
  • How do you charge, hold, and refund deposits?
  • How do mid-month upgrades and downgrades show up on invoices?

Configured properly in your coworking management platform, contract changes flow automatically into billing and access control.

Governance, QA, and Controls: Protecting Revenue at Scale

Monthly Billing QA Checklist

Create a simple monthly checklist for finance or central ops:

  • Any members/companies with active access but no invoice?
  • Any invoices with negative or zero values?
  • Any unusually high discounts without notes?
  • Any locations where invoice volume or revenue looks “off”?

Saved views and exception reports can help you run this QA quickly.

Spotting and Plugging Revenue Leakage

Revenue leakage is often invisible until you look for it:

  • Complimentary meeting hours that keep stretching
  • Legacy discounts that never expire
  • Add-ons that are delivered but not billed

Studies on manual invoice processing show that even small error rates create meaningful financial leakage and extra admin work, especially at scale.

Documenting the Runbook So New Locations Can Plug In

Turn your month-end flow into a documented asset:

  • Convert the steps into a one-pager or internal wiki
  • Add screenshots from your billing platform
  • Include it in onboarding for new location managers and finance hires

Every new location should plug into the same runbook instead of reinventing billing from scratch.

Turning Billing Data into a Multi-Location Performance Dashboard

Core Billing KPIs by Location

Use billing data to track health at each site:

  • Monthly recurring vs. one-off revenue
  • Overdue balances and aging buckets
  • Average days to collect payment
  • Discounts and write-offs as a % of revenue

Late payments are one of the biggest drivers of SME cash flow problems, and in some markets nearly two-thirds of invoices are paid late. These KPIs help you see risk early.

Comparing Locations with a Standard Dashboard

If every site has its own reporting format, it’s hard to see patterns.

Instead, build one standard dashboard template and reuse it:

  • Same KPIs
  • Same filters
  • Same definitions

Then compare locations and ask better questions: Why does Location A consistently collect faster? Why does Location C give more discounts?

Using Billing Insights to Shape Strategy

Over time, billing data should guide big decisions:

  • Which products are most profitable across the network?
  • Where are you consistently underpricing or over-discounting?
  • Which locations are ready to expand—and which need a reset?

Billing stops being “admin” and becomes a strategic signal.

Rolling This Runbook Out Across Your Network

Start with 1–2 Pilot Locations

Don’t roll everything out at once.

  • Choose 1–2 locations that reflect your “typical” complexity
  • Run the new process for 2–3 cycles
  • Gather feedback and refine your checklists and templates

Once you’re confident, roll it out region by region.

Train Local Teams with Simple Playbooks

Support teams with:

  • Short video walk-throughs of each step
  • Month-end checklists per role
  • FAQs for the most common invoice questions

Make billing hygiene part of how you measure and coach local leaders.

Communicating Changes to Members

If the new process changes invoice dates, formats, or payment options:

  • Email members explaining what’s changing and why
  • Update billing FAQs in your member portal or app
  • Equip front-of-house teams with simple talking points

This reduces friction and billing-related support tickets when the new process goes live.

Where OfficeRnD Flex and Stripe Fit in Your Month-End Runbook

You can run this playbook with almost any toolset, but a dedicated coworking platform plus a modern payment gateway makes it much easier, especially at a multi-location scale.

OfficeRnD Flex is built for coworking and flex operators and helps you:

  • Centralize member, contract, and product data across locations
  • Standardize your catalog while allowing for location-specific pricing
  • Automate recurring invoices from memberships and bookings
  • Run bulk invoice batches and send branded invoices in a few clicks
  • Sync data to leading accounting tools like Xero and QuickBooks

The OfficeRnD + Stripe integration then takes care of collecting payments:

  • Automatically charge invoices for memberships, bookings, and services
  • Accept credit and debit cards, SEPA direct debit, ACH, and additional payment methods with Stripe 2.0
  • Reflect successful charges in OfficeRnD immediately and, if connected, in your accounting system
  • Support multi-location and multi-currency setups across your portfolio
  • Offer in-person card payments via Stripe Terminal in supported regions, tied directly to OfficeRnD invoices

Real-world operators are already seeing the impact. For example, Workbar used OfficeRnD + Stripe to automate invoicing and payment tracking, cutting manual work and reducing late payments across memberships, meeting rooms, and events.

When you combine a clear month-end runbook with tools like OfficeRnD Flex and Stripe, month-end can shift from a recurring fire drill to a predictable, repeatable process that supports rapid multi-location growth.

The Big Shift: Meeting Rooms as Ecommerce

Across industries, people expect to book everything – from yoga classes to medical appointments—online, without picking up the phone. Studies on online booking and ecommerce show that modern buyers now see self-service booking as the default, not a bonus.

In coworking and flex, the same shift is underway:

What These Stories Reveal About the Future of Flex

Name: Why Private Offices Are Making a Comeback [And What It Means for the Future of Coworking]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: For years, coworking spaces built their identity around openness. Shared desks, buzzing lounges, community kitchens, all symbols of a new kind of work life where collaboration trumped cubicles.
Post body:
For years, coworking spaces built their identity around openness. Shared desks, buzzing lounges, community kitchens, all symbols of a new kind of work life where collaboration trumped cubicles.

Then, as the world shifted through remote work waves, hybrid models, and economic uncertainty, something interesting started to happen: the private office – once seen as a relic of traditional work — began quietly regaining momentum.

According to the OfficeRnD FlexIndex, Private Office Occupancy climbed to 71.3% globally, its highest level in nearly two years. While open-desk usage stayed stable at 72.5%, the growth in private offices marks a turning point.

It’s not that coworking is going backwards; it’s evolving. Teams and companies are rediscovering the value of privacy, consistency, and control, but without giving up flexibility or community.

Here’s why private offices are back in demand, what’s driving the shift, and how operators can seize the moment to design products that truly fit the new world of work.

TL;DR:
  • The OfficeRnD FlexIndex Q2 2025 shows Private Office Occupancy rose to 71.3%, signaling renewed corporate and team demand.
  • Private offices are a major focus in coworking, with studies showing that approximately 80% of coworking space is now allocated to private offices.
  • Companies want privacy with flexibility - not long leases, but not full open plans either.
  • Operators can capitalize by offering short-term private suites, hybrid bundles, and scalable office memberships.
  • The future of coworking isn’t just open - it’s modular, blending privacy, flexibility, and connection under one roof.

Why Private Offices Fell Out of Favor (and Why They’re Back)

In the early coworking boom, private offices were often treated as a necessary evil, a way to subsidize open space. They were rented to larger teams but didn’t carry the same sense of innovation or culture as the hot-desk areas.

But as hybrid work matured, teams began craving a middle ground: a space they could personalize, meet privately, and use as a stable “home base”, but without being locked into long-term leases.

Now, those same operators who used to favor open seating are rethinking private space as a strategic advantage.

The FlexIndex confirms it: Private Office Occupancy climbed steadily throughout 2025, outpacing growth in desk occupancy and signaling a rebalancing of product demand across the industry.

It’s not nostalgia for the old office, it’s the realization that focus and belonging matter, especially in a hybrid world.

The New Drivers of Private Office Demand

Let’s unpack what’s fueling this resurgence, because it’s not just about preference. It’s about necessity.

Hybrid Work Fatigue

After years of remote work, many professionals are feeling the downsides – isolation, distractions, and blurred boundaries.

Combined with growing return-to-office mandates, this is driving demand for spaces that offer structure without rigidity. Private offices in coworking environments strike that balance perfectly.

Corporate Flex Strategies

Enterprises are adopting “core + flex” models – keeping small HQs while distributing satellite teams in flexible offices. Private offices let them maintain control over brand and privacy while still tapping into shared infrastructure.

Economic Caution

With uncertain economic signals globally, long leases are risky. Private offices provide cost control – short-term commitments, all-inclusive pricing, and flexibility to scale up or down.

Member Experience and Privacy

Even in community-driven environments, not everyone wants to take calls in open lounges. Offering private spaces for calls, deep work, and meetings makes the overall experience stronger, not less social.

In other words, this isn’t a retreat from coworking culture. It’s a refinement of it.

What the FlexIndex Data Really Tells Us

The OfficeRnD FlexIndex for Q2 2025 offers valuable clues for operators about how this trend fits into the bigger picture.

Globally, Desk Occupancy held at 72.5%, showing consistent demand for flexible, open seating. At the same time, Private Office Occupancy rose by nearly a full percentage point from the previous quarter and sits 0.6 points above the 2024 average.

That might sound small, but across 3,500+ tracked locations, it represents thousands of additional private suites being filled, and millions in extra recurring revenue.

Even more interesting: Revenue per Available Desk (RevPAD) and Revenue per Occupied Desk (RevPOD) also climbed, signaling that operators are successfully capturing higher yields through premium products like private offices.

In short: the market isn’t just getting fuller, it’s getting smarter about how to monetize space.

Want more important coworking and flex space statistics for 2026? Check out our latest article.

The “Hybrid Office” Opportunity

The companies driving this shift aren’t looking for big, branded floors. They’re looking for adaptable space that acts as an extension of their hybrid model.

Operators who understand this are blending private offices with coworking-style flexibility to create what many are calling the hybrid office.

Here’s what that can look like:

  • Flexible terms: 3–12 month agreements instead of multi-year leases.
  • Scalable configurations: Add or remove desks within the same suite as team size changes.
  • Shared amenities: Private offices still share kitchens, lounges, and event spaces — reducing overhead.
  • Brand customization: Simple branding options (like signage or decor) that give teams ownership without permanent buildouts.

These offerings combine the autonomy of a traditional office with the adaptability and community of coworking – a blend that’s proving especially popular with 10–50 person teams.

Practical Steps to Reposition Private Offices

If you’re a flex operator, this is the perfect time to revisit how you market, price, and design your private office offerings. Here’s how to make the most of the trend:

Market the Benefits, Not the Walls

Private offices aren’t just about privacy – they’re about productivity, focus, and team culture. Frame them as spaces for doing your best work, not as an escape from the open floor.

Introduce Tiered Private Office Packages

Offer variations like:

  • Essential Suites: Affordable, functional offices for startups.
  • Team Studios: Upgraded spaces with more room and dedicated meeting access.
  • Enterprise Pods: Customizable offices with brand add-ons and dedicated support.

Tiering lets you attract different buyer personas while maximizing yield per square meter.

Integrate with Flexible Memberships

Combine private offices with shared-area access or meeting credits. This hybrid approach encourages members to use your space more often and feel part of the larger community.

Rethink Lease Lengths

Shorter contracts don’t mean less stability, they mean higher agility. Many operators are thriving with 3–6 month renewals, which allow them to reprice or reconfigure as demand shifts.

Enhance the Experience

Private doesn’t have to mean isolated. Offer concierge-style support, event invitations, and community-building perks for office tenants. The goal is to deliver premium privacy and a sense of belonging.

What This Means for the Future of Coworking

The rise of private offices doesn’t spell the end of open coworking. It simply confirms that the industry is broadening its definition of flexibility.

Coworking is still rooted in community and hospitality, which hasn’t changed. What’s changing is how operators deliver those values through greater choice and flexibility.

Members should be able to move seamlessly between open desks, private offices, and meeting rooms, depending on their workday needs.

Operators who embrace this “modular mindset” – designing adaptable, multi-use spaces will not only capture more revenue but also retain members longer. When people can evolve within your ecosystem, they have no reason to leave it.

To learn more about the future of coworking, check out the 13 most expected coworking trends for 2026

The Balancing Act: Privacy and Belonging

One risk of the private office trend is that it can fragment community if not managed carefully. But the best operators are proving it doesn’t have to.

They’re doing things like:

  • Hosting cross-office events to connect teams who work in different suites.
  • Designing glass-front offices to keep energy and visibility high.
  • Offering shared amenities that encourage natural mingling.

The physical walls might be back, but the cultural walls don’t have to be.

A Smarter Mix for the Years Ahead

The coworking model is entering its next phase, less about open vs. private, and more about mix and match.

Operators that once leaned 80% open / 20% private may soon reverse that ratio as demand continues to shift. And that’s not a bad thing. Private offices offer higher margins, more predictable revenue, and broader appeal, from freelancers to global enterprises.

The key is to remain flexible. Your product mix should evolve with your members’ needs, not your past layout.

Name: From Square Meters to Revenue per Meter: The Metric That Will Define the Next Decade of Flex
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: For years, the flex space industry has been obsessed with occupancy. “How full is your space?” became the ultimate measure of success — the higher, the better.
Post body:
For years, the flex space industry has been obsessed with occupancy.
“How full is your space?” became the ultimate measure of success — the higher, the better.

But as the industry matures and stabilizes, that question is starting to miss the point. Occupancy tells you how much of your space is being used. It doesn’t tell you how well it’s performing.

A new metric is taking the spotlight – Revenue per Available Desk (RevPAD), and it’s quietly becoming one of the most important indicators of health and profitability for coworking and flexible workspace operators.

The latest OfficeRnD FlexIndex for Q2 2025 shows that, globally, RevPAD climbed to $363.14, up nearly $7 compared to last year. And that growth came even as overall occupancy stayed almost flat at 72.5%. In other words: smart operators are earning more from the same amount of space.

Let’s unpack what that means, and how you can start tracking and improving this powerful metric in your own workspace.

TL;DR:

  • The latest OfficeRnD FlexIndex Q2 2025 shows global RevPAD (Revenue per Available Desk) rose to $363.14, even as occupancy stayed flat at 72.5%.
  • Occupancy ≠ profitability. High fill rates don’t always mean higher revenue — RevPAD reveals how efficiently each desk generates income.
  • Focus on quality of revenue, not just quantity of members.
  • Improve RevPAD by refining pricing, bundling products, monetizing underused areas, and using data to balance demand.
  • The next decade of flex growth won’t come from more square meters — but from getting more value out of every one you already have.

Why “How Full You Are” Doesn’t Tell the Whole Story

Occupancy is easy to grasp, which is why it became the default industry benchmark. But it can be misleading.

Two spaces could both report 80% occupancy, yet one could be barely breaking even, while the other could be thriving.

Here’s why:

  • Occupancy measures volume. It shows how much space is filled.
  • Revenue per Available Desk (RevPAD) measures efficiency. It shows how much value you’re getting out of that space.

If you fill your desks with discounted memberships, your occupancy might look great, but your revenue per desk could actually drop.

Conversely, if you run a slightly smaller but higher-yielding member base through better pricing, premium services, or smarter packages, your RevPAD goes up even if your occupancy doesn’t change.

That’s why RevPAD is becoming the go-to metric for investors, lenders, and sophisticated operators. It focuses on quality of revenue, not just quantity of members.

The FlexIndex’s Quiet but Important Finding

The OfficeRnD FlexIndex Q2 2025 paints a global picture of a market that’s steady but smarter. Desk Occupancy sat at 72.5%, almost identical to the previous quarter. But Revenue per Available Desk continued to rise — up to $363.14, its highest point since 2023.

That small increase might sound modest, but it signals a much bigger shift: operators are no longer chasing growth through expansion alone. They’re growing through optimization — by squeezing more value out of the same square footage.

This trend runs parallel to what’s happened in industries like hospitality and aviation. Once hotels hit stable occupancy levels, they stopped trying to build more rooms and started improving how they priced and packaged them.

The result?

Higher revenue without adding capacity. The flex space world is now entering that same stage of maturity.

What Exactly Is RevPAD and How Do You Calculate It?

If you haven’t measured it before, RevPAD is simpler than it sounds:

Revenue per Available Desk (RevPAD) = Total Revenue / Total Available Desks

Let’s say your workspace has 100 desks.
Last month, you earned $40,000 in total revenue from memberships, private offices, meeting room bookings, and day passes.

Your RevPAD = $40,000 / 100 = $400.

That means each desk, on average, generated $400 in revenue — whether it was occupied or not.

This number becomes incredibly useful when you start comparing:

  • Across different locations – which site is truly performing better?
  • Across different product types – are private offices more profitable than hot desks?
  • Over time – are your yield and pricing strategies working?

Unlike occupancy, RevPAD factors in pricing, utilization, and sales performance all in one figure. It’s the closest thing to a “profitability pulse” your space can have.

Why RevPAD Matters More Than Ever

The coworking boom of the 2010s was all about filling space fast. But the 2020s are about refining and sustaining it.

As competition rises and member expectations evolve, revenue optimization has become the real differentiator. A few reasons why focusing on RevPAD makes sense now:

1. Growth Without Expansion

Opening new locations is what most operators want, but it isn’t always feasible or affordable, especially in high-rent markets. Improving your RevPAD lets you grow revenue without adding square meters.

2. Better Investor Conversations

Investors care about predictable, high-quality revenue. A steady or rising RevPAD shows strong demand and pricing discipline – a big confidence signal.

3. Clearer Operational Focus

Tracking RevPAD forces your team to look at both utilization and yield. It moves the focus from “how many members we have” to “how much value each desk delivers.”

4. Protection Against Price Wars

When you understand your revenue efficiency, you’re less likely to get dragged into unsustainable discounting. You’ll know when it’s better to hold your price than chase occupancy.

How to Start Improving Your RevPAD Today

Improving RevPAD doesn’t require fancy software or radical strategy shifts. It starts with simple, actionable tweaks that most operators can implement immediately.

Revisit Your Pricing Mix

Are your prices consistent with the value you deliver?

Many operators undervalue their meeting rooms, event spaces, and day passes compared to membership plans. Experiment with small price adjustments – even a 5–10% increase on your highest-demand assets can lift your RevPAD meaningfully.

Monetize Underused Areas

Unused corners can become revenue generators – think lockers, phone booths, podcast rooms, or bookable lounges.

Do you know that allowing website visitors to book resources directly on your website can increase your revenue? See how it’s done thanks to the Growth Hub.

The FlexIndex shows that Price per Hour of Booking globally remained strong at $40.90, proving people are still willing to pay for short-term, on-demand use. If you have idle space, make it bookable.

Bundle and Upsell

Members love simplicity. Package popular combinations — for instance, a “Hybrid Team Plan” that includes desk days, meeting hours, and mail handling. Bundles often command a higher total value while feeling like a deal to the customer.

Use Data to Optimize Utilization

Track which desks, rooms, and times of day are most and least used. If Tuesdays are always full but Fridays are quiet, test promotions or events that encourage more balanced use.

Many operators using tools like OfficeRnD Data Hub to track this are already leveraging this data to adjust pricing dynamically and fill capacity gaps faster.

Focus on Retention

Acquiring new members costs far more than retaining existing ones. A stable base of satisfied members keeps your revenue predictable, and predictability is the backbone of RevPAD growth.

Ask for feedback regularly (keep a close eye on your NPS score), reward loyalty, and don’t underestimate the power of genuine community engagement.

An Imaginary Example of Yield Thinking

Imagine two operators, both running 10,000-square-foot spaces:

  • Operator A: 90% occupied, average membership price $350/month.
  • Operator B: 75% occupied, average membership price $500/month.

At first glance, Operator A looks better – higher occupancy!
But Operator B’s RevPAD is 7% higher overall and with lower operational strain.

Operator B doesn’t need to sell more desks; they’re earning more from the same space. That’s the mindset shift RevPAD encourages.

The Next Decade: From Square Meters to Smart Meters

The OfficeRnD FlexIndex Q2 2025 shows us an industry that’s steadied after years of rapid growth and is now optimizing instead of expanding.

RevPAD, RevPOD, and other revenue metrics are the new frontier. They’ll separate the operators who merely fill space from those who build sustainable, scalable businesses.

The next era of coworking won’t be defined by who has the biggest footprint, but by who gets the most value out of every square meter.

Because in the end, it’s not about how full your space is, it’s about how well it performs.

To find out more about what’s next for the flex space industry, check out the most anticipated flex space trends for 2026.

Final Thoughts

If occupancy is the speedometer of your business, RevPAD is the fuel gauge. It tells you how efficiently you’re converting space into income, and how long you can keep going before you need to refuel or adjust.

Track it. Understand it. Improve it.

Because the flex operators who master RevPAD today will be the ones leading the industry tomorrow.

Name: How to Create a Strong Product Mix for Your Coworking Space
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Coworking and flex space markets have matured. What used to be a single open-space membership has evolved into a dynamic ecosystem of products – from private offices and day passes to digital memberships, event hosting, and premium add-ons.
Post body:
Coworking and flex space markets have matured. What used to be a single open-space membership has evolved into a dynamic ecosystem of products – from private offices and day passes to digital memberships, event hosting, and premium add-ons.

As competition grows and member expectations rise, your product mix becomes one of your most powerful levers for profitability, brand differentiation, and member satisfaction.

Whether you’re opening your first space or scaling across multiple locations, building a strong, balanced product mix is key to long-term success.

TL;DR: Building a Profitable Coworking Product Mix

  • Know your audience: Define member personas (freelancers, startups, corporates, etc.) and match offerings to their needs.

  • Layer your products: Build a mix of shared workspaces, private offices, meeting rooms, and high-margin add-ons.

  • Design for flexibility: Use modular spaces, tiered memberships, and dynamic pricing to optimize usage.

  • Go digital: Sell passes, bookings, and memberships online for 24/7 sales and streamlined operations.

  • Balance smartly: Target 50–70% revenue from private offices, 20–35% from flex offerings, and 5–20% from add-ons.

  • Test and adapt: Pilot new offerings, analyze utilization, and refine your mix with data.

  • Avoid common traps: Don’t overcomplicate, misprice, or ignore tech and segmentation.

  • Embrace trends: Hybrid work, self-service booking, experience-focused design, and automation are shaping the future.

Start With Who You’re Serving

Before deciding how to allocate your space or price your memberships, define your target audiences. Your mix should reflect who you serve and why they choose you over alternatives.

Here are a few common personas and what they value:

PersonaKey NeedsIdeal Offerings
Freelancers / CreatorsAffordability, social energy, flexibilityHot desks, day passes, community events, phone booths
Startups / Small TeamsScalability, 24/7 access, collaborationDedicated desks, small offices, meeting rooms
Remote Employees / Corporate MembersPrivacy, brand alignment, hybrid team setupPrivate offices, meeting credits, enterprise plans
Consultants / ProfessionalsClient-facing spaces, credibility, calmMeeting rooms, virtual offices, concierge services
Community Builders / Event HostsLarge gatherings, AV equipmentEvent halls, workshops, hybrid-ready setups

Your location, brand identity, and market density also influence the mix.

  • Suburban or near-home coworking spaces often benefit from affordable hot-desking and flexible day passes.
  • City-center operators can command higher rates for private offices and premium meeting facilities.

Tip: Revisit your personas every 6–12 months. Member profiles evolve faster than floor plans.

The Core Layers of a Strong Product Mix

Think of your product mix as a pyramid: a solid base of recurring revenue, supported by layers of flexible, high-margin, and experiential offerings.

A. Open / Shared Workspace

Your open workspace fuels energy, community, and accessibility – but it must balance density, comfort, and profitability.

Key strategies:

  • Offer tiered memberships (e.g., 10-day, 20-day, unlimited).
  • Add credits for meeting rooms or printing to drive cross-usage.
  • Use zoning: quiet zones, social zones, phone booths.
  • Consider dynamic pricing for desks based on usage peaks.

Metrics to watch: Desk utilization, revenue per available desk, revenue per occupied desk, churn rate.

Example: A 50-desk open area with 75% utilization can generate stable monthly cash flow — but introducing part-time or credit-based passes can push utilization closer to 90% without adding more space.

B. Private Offices

Private offices remain the anchor of financial stability for most coworking spaces. They offer predictable revenue and appeal to remote teams, startups, and SMEs seeking flexible leases.

Best practices:

  • Create modular offices that can be reconfigured as teams grow or shrink.
  • Offer “plug-and-play” packages with furniture, connectivity, cleaning, and branding.
  • Bundle meeting room credits and storage.
  • Use upgrade paths – move members from shared desks to private suites.

Pro tip: Track your occupancy rate alongside pipeline length for new space inquiries. An efficient product mix ensures minimal idle time between tenants.

C. Meeting & Event Spaces

Your meeting rooms and event areas are both revenue generators and lead magnets.

Monetization ideas:

  • Make meeting rooms bookable by non-members through your website (that’s where OfficeRnD Growth Hub shines).
  • Implement dynamic pricing for off-peak hours or weekend rentals.
  • Offer hybrid-ready spaces (cameras, mics, screens).
  • Convert underused space into rentable training or content rooms.

Tip: Promote meeting credits as part of membership upgrades – it boosts perceived value and engagement.

Example: Operators using online booking integrated into their site often see higher utilization of meeting rooms compared to those relying on manual bookings.

Read this blog if you want to dive deeper into some really valuable coworking stats for 2026 and learn more about the topic.

D. Value-Added Services & Amenities

Your amenities transform a space into an experience – and experience drives loyalty.

Three layers of value-added services:

  1. Core amenities: coffee, printing, cleaning, mail handling, community events.
  2. Premium paid add-ons: lockers, parking, storage, extra IT support, dedicated bandwidth. See this guide on unique amenities that set you apart.
  3. Partner services: local gyms, wellness sessions, childcare, catering, HR or legal consulting.

Innovative ideas:

  • Creator Studios: podcast or video rooms for rent.
  • Wellness Corners: yoga, meditation, or massage spaces.
  • Pop-up Retail: partner with local artisans or cafés.
  • Virtual Memberships: digital access to community and booking platform.

Each amenity can become a small but steady profit center.

Don’t Forget Digital Products and Ecommerce

In 2025 and beyond, your “product mix” doesn’t stop at your front door.

Forward-thinking operators monetize digital channels and online sales just like physical space.

Examples:

  • Sell day passes and meeting room bookings online – instantly, not via inquiry forms.
  • Offer memberships that include both virtual community access and physical usage credits.
  • Create a members-only portal for perks, partner discounts, and events.

If you’re using OfficeRnD Growth Hub, you can integrate this directly into your website, enabling real-time booking, checkout, and payments.

Your website becomes a 24/7 sales engine, no staff intervention needed. Check out the case study with UK-based coworking space “x+why”

Balancing Your Mix: The 3 Key Ratios

A balanced coworking product mix typically aligns around three strategic ratios. These aren’t strict rules but helpful benchmarks:

RatioNew / Growing OperatorsMature / Multi-location Operators
Revenue base (private offices)60–70%50–60%
Flexible offerings (hot desks, meeting rooms)20–30%25–35%
Add-ons & services5–10%10–20%

As your operation scales, recurring office revenue becomes your foundation – but differentiation comes from high-margin, experience-driven add-ons.

Experiment, Measure, and Iterate

A strong product mix isn’t set once; it evolves. The most successful operators constantly test, measure, and refine.

Practical ways to experiment:

  • Run 3–6 month pilots for new services (e.g., podcast studio, day-pass bundle).
  • Use NPS and occupancy metrics to evaluate success.
  • Track utilization trends, not just bookings.
  • Use attribution reports to understand which products bring new leads (meeting rooms often act as acquisition gateways).
  • Monitor pricing sensitivity: if you’re always at full capacity, you’re likely underpricing.

Tool tip: With the OfficeRnD Data Hub, you can visualize utilization, revenue mix, and booking patterns across all products and locations, helping you optimize your offering with data, not guesswork.

Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

Even experienced operators fall into traps when diversifying their mix.

Here’s how to steer clear:

PitfallConsequenceSolution
Trying too many new offerings at onceOperational complexity, brand dilutionAdd one new line at a time; pilot before rollout
Misaligned pricingLow margins, cannibalizationModel contribution margin per product
Ignoring member segmentationLow retentionMatch product tiers to customer personas
Underinvesting in technologyManual friction, low conversionAdopt a unified platform for bookings, billing, and CRM
Neglecting underused spaceLost revenueUse data to reconfigure or repurpose idle zones

7. Watch Emerging Trends Shaping the Product Mix

Looking ahead, several trends are reshaping how operators design and monetize their spaces:

  1. Hybrid work normalization: Demand for team suites and short-term project rooms is growing.
  2. Ecommerce and self-service: Members expect instant booking and checkout experiences.
  3. Community & experience-first spaces: Social and wellness amenities are becoming differentiators.
  4. AI and automation: From dynamic pricing to predictive analytics, smart systems optimize occupancy.
  5. Sustainability: Green design and energy-efficient layouts are influencing space allocation.

Name: Beyond the Plateau: How the Flex Space Industry Found Stability in 2025
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: By the end of this article, you’ll understand why the global flex market’s stability in 2025 isn’t a slowdown, it’s a sign of maturity, and how operators are turning steady demand into sustainable growth through smarter pricing, data insights, and stronger member experiences.
Post body:
By the end of this article, you’ll understand why the global flex market’s stability in 2025 isn’t a slowdown, it’s a sign of maturity, and how operators are turning steady demand into sustainable growth through smarter pricing, data insights, and stronger member experiences.

The flexible workspace industry has come a long way since the pandemic reset the way we think about offices. What started as an alternative model has now become a cornerstone of corporate real estate strategy. (see Cushman & Wakefield’s Global Flexible Office Trends 2025 for how adoption is rising among occupiers)

But as the global economy continues to shift, many operators are asking a familiar question: what’s next for flex?

The latest OfficeRnD FlexIndex Report for Q2 2025 offers a revealing snapshot. Despite headwinds like inflationary pressure, changing work patterns, and uneven regional recoveries, the global flex market remains remarkably stable.

Occupancy rates have plateaued, but not in a worrying way. They’re holding their ground, a sign that demand has matured and operators are learning to manage supply more efficiently.

The data tells a story of quiet resilience and strategic evolution rather than explosive growth. Let’s unpack what that means for operators worldwide.

TL;DR
  • Desk occupancy held steady globally at 72.5%, reflecting a mature and balanced market.
  • Revenue per Occupied Desk (RevPOD) climbed to $500.59 and Revenue per Available Desk (RevPAD) reached $363.14, signaling improved monetization strategies.
  • Private Office Occupancy rebounded to 71.3%, driven by renewed corporate confidence in Europe and the UK.
  • Hourly booking rates remained strong ($40–$42 globally), showing that professionals continue to value on-demand flexibility.
  • Regional trends vary: EMEA & UKI show strong momentum; the Americas are recalibrating amid competition;
  • APAC balances steady desk use with yield challenges.
  • The industry is shifting from growth to optimization - using data, dynamic pricing, and utilization analytics to fine-tune operations and strengthen profitability.

Desk Occupancy: A Symbol of Maturity

Globally, desk occupancy held firm at 72.5% in Q2 2025, nearly identical to both Q1 2025 and the 2024 annual average.

This steadiness might not make headlines, but it should. It signals that flexible work has found its footing as a permanent part of the office landscape.

To put this in perspective, back in 2021, many operators were still recovering from occupancy rates below 60%. The steady climb since then shows how demand for flexible options, especially hot-desking, has solidified into long-term habits.

In markets like North America and APAC, hot desks are now the backbone of flex portfolios, outpacing private office growth for the first time in several years.

Operators no longer need to chase growth through expansion alone. Instead, they’re focusing on optimizing utilization – fine-tuning how existing spaces are used throughout the week.

Monday and Friday occupancy gaps, for example, have inspired creative pricing, community-driven events, and hybrid membership models that keep energy flowing even on slow days.

The message from the data is clear: stability is not stagnation. It’s maturity.

The Subtle Dance Between Revenue and Occupancy

While occupancy rates stayed consistent, revenue-focused metrics continued to rise. Revenue per Occupied Desk (RevPOD) reached $500.59, and Revenue per Available Desk (RevPAD) climbed to $363.14, both representing steady quarter-over-quarter gains.

This divergence between occupancy and revenue is one of the most telling insights in the report. It means operators are becoming more sophisticated at monetizing their inventory. They’re not simply filling seats; they’re finding ways to make each seat more valuable.

Dynamic pricing, tiered memberships, and add-on services are playing a major role. Some operators have even introduced “micro-upgrades” – small, optional charges for premium views, privacy pods, or tech-enabled meeting tools.

Others are refining their approach to upselling, offering concierge services or flexible meeting credits that increase member stickiness.

The takeaway?

The most successful operators aren’t those with the fullest spaces, but those who understand where and how revenue is created within their footprint.

Curious how your workspace compares? Download the full FlexIndex Report for Q2 2025 to see global and regional benchmarks, deep-dive KPIs, and practical insights designed to help you plan your next move.

Private Offices: The Return of Commitment

After years of volatility, private office demand has rebounded. The global private office occupancy rate rose to 71.3%, up from Q1 and above 2024 levels.

According to JLL’s Future of Work Survey, 42 % of corporate occupiers intend to increase their use of flexible space in the next few years, and over half prefer to lease flex via third-party providers.

This momentum underpins demand in Europe & UKI, reinforcing your observation that private office occupancy is rebounding with hybrid commitment.

The recovery is particularly strong in Europe and the UK, where corporate renewals and longer-term leases have surged. This reflects a broader shift in corporate behavior. While many companies still embrace hybrid models, they’re also seeking predictability.

Private offices give them a controlled environment without the burden of long-term leases. It’s flexibility with structure – a combination increasingly valued by enterprise clients.

Interestingly, private office demand tends to mirror macroeconomic sentiment. When uncertainty rises, teams crave stability and privacy. When confidence grows, shared spaces see a boost. For now, we’re in the middle ground, steady confidence paired with pragmatic caution.

Operators who offer adaptable private office models, like flexible lease terms or hybrid suite memberships, are positioned to capture this trend.

The Pricing Sweet Spot

The average price per hour of booking globally hovered between $40 and $42, showing resilience despite economic fluctuations.

This stability underscores something important: even in a cost-conscious climate, customers still value on-demand access to professional space.

Members are willing to pay a premium for reliability, community, and design that supports productivity. In a world of coffee shops and home offices, a well-run coworking space offers something priceless – focus.

But the story behind the number is more nuanced. In the Americas, hourly rates rose to $41.80, while APAC outperformed its 2024 benchmark by AUD 1.32.

This shows how local economic conditions shape pricing elasticity. Operators who understand these micro-patterns, down to city-level variations, can price confidently without racing to the bottom.

There’s an emerging “psychology of pricing” in flex. Members don’t just evaluate cost, they assess value per experience. A well-priced space that feels alive and purposeful will always outperform a cheaper but soulless alternative.

Regional Contrasts: The Global Patchwork

One of the report’s strengths is how vividly it captures regional nuances.

EMEA & UKI stood out as the global growth engine. Revenue Occupancy climbed to 75.6%, and RevPOD jumped €18.92 year-over-year, indicating that European operators are not just recovering, they’re excelling. Corporate demand has reignited, and dynamic pricing is paying off.

In contrast, the Americas saw a modest cooling, with Revenue Occupancy dipping 2.2 percentage points.

But this wasn’t a collapse, it was a recalibration. Urban saturation and competition are pushing operators to innovate, whether through suburban expansion or hybrid memberships that balance dedicated and shared use.

Meanwhile, APAC tells a mixed story. Desk Occupancy held steady at 69.8%, but Private Office Occupancy slipped to 68.3%. Still, hourly booking rates remained strong at AUD 53.59, showing that the region’s appetite for on-demand work remains robust. This reinforces a global truth: flexibility thrives where adaptability leads.

The New Playbook: From Occupancy to Optimization

Across all these data points, one message stands out – the flex industry is entering its optimization era. Growth isn’t just about adding locations or seats anymore. It’s about refining what’s already there.

Operators are asking smarter questions:

  • Which resources generate the highest yield per square meter?
  • What time slots or membership types drive the most value?
  • How can pricing, design, and experience align to boost utilization?

The answers often lie in data – real, granular data like that captured in the FlexIndex. By tracking patterns across thousands of locations, operators can see when their spaces hum with activity, when they lag, and how to intervene before dips turn into trends.

Some are already experimenting with dynamic pricing systems that automatically adjust rates based on demand. Others use occupancy heatmaps to redesign layouts or introduce new amenities. The smartest players treat every data point as a feedback loop.

The goal isn’t just to fill space. It’s to orchestrate performance.

Why Stability Is a Strength

In a market known for volatility, stability can feel like a quiet victory. A global occupancy plateau around 72–74% is not a warning sign, it’s a foundation. It reflects that flex has moved beyond novelty into normalcy.

The challenge ahead is not proving that flexible work works—it’s proving that it can scale sustainably.

The OfficeRnD FlexIndex shows that operators who lean on data, pricing sophistication, and customer experience are already leading the way.

Let’s not forget: the very essence of flex lies in adaptation. From community managers reimagining events to enterprise teams rethinking workspace footprints, the industry’s strength has always been its ability to pivot.

And in 2025, that adaptability looks more grounded, more data-informed, and more human than ever before.

What This Means for Operators

If you’re running a coworking or flex space today, here are three key takeaways from the Q2 2025 FlexIndex:

  1. Lean into Pricing Intelligence
     You can’t control macro trends, but you can control how you respond. Invest in pricing analytics to understand where you can raise rates, or when you should hold steady. The operators capturing higher RevPOD and RevPAD aren’t guessing; they’re testing.
  2. Reimagine Occupancy as Engagement
     A full space doesn’t always mean a successful one. Focus on engagement metrics, how often members visit, how long they stay, what they use. The more they connect with your space, the higher your retention and upsell potential.
  3. Balance Flexibility with Structure
     The corporate rebound in private offices suggests a sweet spot between agility and commitment. Offering variable-term private suites or “team pods” can attract both startups and enterprises seeking predictability.

Looking Ahead: The Next Frontier

If 2024 was the year of recovery, 2025 is shaping up to be the year of refinement. The global flex market is no longer chasing growth at all costs. It’s learning to grow wisely.

Curious how your workspace compares? Download the full FlexIndex Report for Q2 2025 to see global and regional benchmarks, deep-dive KPIs, and practical insights designed to help you plan your next move.

Technology will play a pivotal role in that evolution. From data dashboards that monitor occupancy in real time to AI-driven dynamic pricing that predicts demand curves, the industry is quietly becoming more analytical and more human-centric at once.

Because ultimately, flex isn’t about square meters, it’s about people. The freelancers finding community, the teams discovering their rhythm, the enterprises rediscovering what flexibility truly means.

The global data tells a story of consistency, resilience, and readiness for the next chapter. And as 2025 unfolds, one truth remains: the operators who balance data with empathy, and insight with imagination, will define the future of flexible work.
