Name: EMEA and UKI Flex Space Industry 2025: Key Metrics and Analysis
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: The coworking and flex space industry in EMEA and UKI is evolving faster than ever. Once niche providers of shared offices, flex spaces have become integral to corporate real estate strategies and the future of work.
Post body:
The coworking and flex space industry in EMEA and UKI is evolving faster than ever. Once niche providers of shared offices, flex spaces have become integral to corporate real estate strategies and the future of work.

Operators are scaling up, enterprises are embracing hybrid work, and member expectations for service, sustainability, and community are higher than ever.

This article highlights the most important trends and forecasts for 2025 (and beyond) and provides strategic recommendations for flex space operators in the EMEA and UKI region.

We also integrate fresh insights from the OfficeRnD FlexIndex Q1 2025 Report – a benchmark of 2,000+ flex locations across the Americas, EMEA & UKI, and APAC, tracking six key KPIs. These data-driven benchmarks will help you see where you stand and how to plan your next moves.

Quick Summary

  • Hybrid work is now the baseline: 42% of European corporate occupiers plan to increase flex space usage over the next three years (JLL).
  • Enterprise demand soars: Large companies use flex as a “bridge to quality,” driving growth in private, managed suites.
  • Shorter leases preferred: 65% of French firms now favor shorter or coworking leases, converting fixed costs into variable ones.
  • Record supply expansion: UK flex office inventory jumped 32% YoY in Q1 2025, pushing total to 8.6 million sq ft.
  • Strong performance benchmarks:
    • 74.7% average desk occupancy in Q1 2025 (OfficeRnD FlexIndex)
    • Private offices often 90%+ occupied
    • RevPOD and RevPAD up, with London desk rates at ~£500/month (+2.2% YoY)
  • Hotelification, community, and ESG are now table stakes for member experience.
  • City highlights:
    • London: 39% YoY supply growth; hub-and-spoke models emerging
    • Berlin: 330,000 sqm of flex space; 75%+ occupancy in large centers
    • Amsterdam: 80%+ occupancy; pioneer in sustainable repurposed spaces
    • Paris: 750+ spaces; private offices 85–90% occupied; up to 25% cost savings vs. leases
    • Dubai: 92%+ traditional office occupancy; flex eases supply gap
  • Outlook: Flex could comprise 20–30% of corporate portfolios by 2030.

Whether you run a coworking hub in London or a flex office network across Europe, this guide will help you understand where the industry is heading and how to adapt to stay ahead. Let’s dive into the key trends shaping the flex space landscape in EMEA & UKI in 2025.

Hybrid Work Reshapes Demand – and Enterprise Adoption Surges

It’s clear that hybrid work has shifted from buzzword to baseline. Most organizations now blend remote and in-office work, which is fundamentally changing demand for flexible workspace.

Instead of long leases for fixed headcounts, companies large and small are turning to flex space to scale up or down as needed.

A recent JLL survey found that 42% of corporate occupiers in Europe plan to use more flexible space over the next three years. This represents a huge demand influx from the enterprise segment, historically not the primary user of coworking.

Now, larger companies are embracing flex as a strategic tool to navigate uncertainty in headcounts and office needs.

In fact, flex solutions are increasingly seen as a “bridge to quality,” allowing firms to secure high-end space on flexible terms while they reconfigure their long-term office strategies.

Several factors are driving this enterprise uptake.

  • Return-to-office policies remain in flux, and many firms are fine-tuning hybrid arrangements. Flex space provides a safety valve – teams can convene in professional offices on-demand without requiring everyone to be in a HQ five days a week.
  • Office attendance rates are stabilizing at moderate levels (over 60% of European firms report average attendance between 41–80% of pre-pandemic levels) as hybrid becomes the norm. With employees coming in part-time, companies don’t want to pay for half-empty fixed offices.
  • Flexible “third spaces” and part-time desk usage are up ~10% year-on-year in Europe as firms seek to provide employees choice of where to work. The net effect is more enterprise demand for flex: instead of renewing a whole office lease, a company might take a smaller core office plus memberships or managed suites in flex centers for overflow and hybrid teams.

At the same time, economic uncertainty and cost focus are pushing enterprises toward flex. Committing to a 10-year lease with heavy capex is less appealing when a recession or rapid growth could be around the corner. Flex offers agility.

For example, in France 65% of companies now prefer shorter leases or coworking models over traditional long commitments. This gives CFOs flexibility to adjust real estate costs in real-time with business needs – a “pay-as-you-go” approach to office space.

Moreover, many enterprises find that flex can reduce operating costs by 20–30% by converting fixed costs (rent, fit-out, utilities) into all-inclusive variable costs.

The recent analysis by Workways linked above also noted that in France, companies save up to 25% on office operation costs with flex solutions, especially in high-cost cities like Paris.

Hybrid work is also accelerating new flex space formats tailored to enterprise needs. The fastest-growing segment is managed offices – private, customizable suites provided by an operator on a flexible agreement.

Rather than coworking’s open desks, enterprises often want their own branded area but delivered turnkey.

In the UK, the supply of managed flex offices jumped 111% year-on-year in Q1 2025 as providers rushed to meet this demand.

These managed spaces give big companies the best of both worlds: privacy and control over their space, but none of the hassle of leases and facility management.

The appeal is evident in London, where large corporates now account for a significant share of flex uptake, and flex deals of 2–3 year terms are being used as interim solutions while companies reconfigure their main offices.

Importantly, landlords are also embracing hybrid and flex models, which further expands options for enterprises. Facing higher vacancies in some markets, traditional landlords are partnering with flex operators or launching their own flex offerings to capture tenants who demand more agility.

Many now offer “core and flex” arrangements, where a tenant leases a smaller traditional space (core) and can expand into flex suites in the same building as needed. In the UK, we see the rise of management agreements between landlords and operators – 93% of UK serviced office operators now use management contract models, up from just 9% in 2019.

This aligns incentives by sharing revenue and has enabled an explosion of flex locations in landlord portfolios without the operator carrying full lease liabilities.

The bottom line: hybrid work has firmly entrenched flex space in the corporate real estate toolkit. Larger companies are driving much of the current demand growth, seeking flexibility to navigate the post-pandemic work era.

For flex operators, this is a massive opportunity – but also means upping their game to meet enterprise expectations (for instance, on privacy, security, and service quality).

As we’ll explore, flex providers that cater to these evolving needs stand to thrive in 2025 and beyond.

Flex Space Adoption and Operator Expansion at Record Pace

Demand isn’t the only thing booming – supply of flex space is expanding rapidly across EMEA. After the pandemic pause, operators are back to growth mode, opening new locations and entering new markets.

In fact, flexible offices are now the fastest-growing segment of the office market. Recent forecasts project Europe’s flex office market will grow at around 10–11% CAGR through 2030, roughly doubling in size to over €30 billion by 2030.

Even near-term, growth is striking: in Q1 2025 alone, the UK saw a 32% year-on-year surge in flex office supply (by square footage).

This pushed total UK flex inventory past 8.6 million sq ft. Such expansion is far outpacing traditional office growth, underscoring that flex is where the momentum is.

What’s fueling this expansion?

Robust occupier demand and a shift in landlord strategy. As mentioned, enterprise interest is a big factor – operators are racing to add capacity for large customers seeking swing space or satellite offices.

Also, landlords are actively converting conventional space into flex. With many companies reducing their long-term footprint (due to hybrid work or cost-cutting), landlords have vacant floors in need of occupants.

Rather than wait for another 5–10 year lease (which may be slow to come by), landlords are increasingly choosing to offer those spaces as flex, often via partnerships with experienced operators.

This trend is evident in the UK: Property Week reports that facing weaker demand for traditional leases, many property owners are turning to managed flexible solutions to maintain occupancy and meet evolving tenant needs.

The result is a virtuous cycle – more flex supply brings more customers into the ecosystem, which further normalizes flex as a mainstream option.

Across Europe, major flex operators are in growth and consolidation mode. The big players (IWG/Regus, WeWork, local champions like Mindspace or Industrious in certain countries) are opening locations in secondary cities and suburban hubs, not just capitals.

Even amid challenges (e.g. WeWork’s widely publicized struggles), the sector overall is attracting investment. For example, CBRE’s acquisition of Industrious (a leading U.S. flex operator expanding internationally) shows traditional real estate firms doubling down on flex, effectively betting on its long-term success.

In Europe, M&A is picking up – in Germany, two regional operators (SleevesUp and WorkInn) merged in 2024 to form the country’s largest coworking network, aiming to achieve scale and operational efficiency.

JLL predicted years ago that with hundreds of operators in the market, consolidation was inevitable and the well-capitalized, innovative brands would flourish; we are now seeing that play out.

The flex segment’s resilience through recent turmoil has also emboldened expansion. Despite the pandemic and even recent headlines of specific operator woes, overall flex demand and occupancy have rebounded strongly.

Savills observes that flexible offices proved their strength with increased take-up and robust demand, even as traditional leasing faced headwinds.

Occupancy levels in many flex centers are back to or above pre-pandemic levels, thanks to the hybrid/workforce decentralization trend.

Our OfficeRnD FlexIndex data confirms that desk occupancy and revenue occupancy in EMEA & UKI have remained high through early 2025, with only minor fluctuations quarter-to-quarter.

For instance, revenue occupancy (which accounts for both occupancy and pricing) barely dipped by a fraction of a percent in recent months, indicating steadiness.

Likewise, private office occupancy is very strong – many centers report their private suites are near full, as teams gravitate to enclosed spaces for dedicated use.

In short, flex operators are generally achieving healthy utilization, encouraging them and their investors to expand capacity.

Let’s quantify some performance benchmarks.

According to the OiffceRnD FlexIndex Q1 2025 (EMEA & UKI region), average desk occupancy – the share of available desks that are occupied by members – is 74.7% in Q1 2025, which is roughly 0.2 percentage points higher than the Q4 2024 figure of 74.5%, and it slightly exceeds the 2024 average.

Private offices often run even higher, frequently 90 %+ occupied, reflecting the popularity of lockable team spaces.

Critically, revenue occupancy (a metric that factors in pricing, effectively measuring revenue yield vs. total capacity) has been robust – many operators are capturing a high percentage of potential revenue, thanks to improved pricing and ancillary income.

In the UK, for example, despite a 39% surge in available space in London, desk rates have held mostly steady (median price ~£500/month, up 2.2% year-on-year, even after a slight dip from Q4).

This suggests operators have avoided a “race to the bottom” on pricing even as supply expands. RevPOD (revenue per occupied desk) in many EMEA locations has actually edged up as higher quality space and amenities justify premium rates.

Meanwhile, RevPAD (revenue per available desk) – akin to the hotel industry’s RevPAR – has remained stable or grown, as strong occupancy offsets any small price discounts.

These figures collectively indicate a healthy market where operators are, on average, filling their space and getting good value for it.

Of course, expansion is not uniform everywhere. There are regional and city-level differences (we will highlight some in the city snapshots section).

Some markets are nearer to saturation, with intense competition among operators, while untapped demand still exists in others (secondary cities, emerging markets).

Smaller independent operators face challenges scaling up and staying profitable amidst the expansion wave.

As already reported by technologywithin, in markets like Germany, surveys show only ~20% of coworking spaces report being profitable, and smaller sites (<500 sqm) struggle with lower occupancy (often half the desks empty).

Rising operating costs (energy, rent) and thinner margins mean operational efficiency is key – one reason many smaller players either specialize in a niche or consider joining networks to survive.

Nonetheless, the overall trajectory is continued growth. Even in markets with temporary oversupply, demand is catching up as the flex value proposition appeals to a widening customer base (startups, freelancers, SMEs, and now enterprises).

For flex operators, this rapid adoption and expansion brings both opportunity and heightened competition. Standing out in a crowded market will require sharp positioning – whether by location, niche services, or superior execution.

In the next sections, we examine how customer expectations are evolving (hint: it’s more than just a cool space with coffee), and we take a quick tour of key city markets, before delving into strategies to succeed in 2025’s flex landscape.

So, keep reading!

Evolving Member Expectations: Service, Sustainability, and Wellness as Differentiators

With flex spaces becoming mainstream, member expectations have evolved far beyond a desk and Wi-Fi. Today’s tenants – from individual freelancers to large corporate teams – are looking for an experience and a workplace that supports their well-being and values.

Leading operators are responding by transforming their spaces with hospitality-level services, sustainable practices, and wellness amenities.

In 2025, these factors are not just “nice-to-haves” – they are essential to attracting and retaining customers in the flex market.

The Hotelification Is Happening

“Hotelification” of coworking is in full swing. The industry’s mantra has become amenity-rich, hospitality-infused workspaces.

In practical terms, this means flex centers now often feature perks you’d expect in a boutique hotel or a lifestyle club.

On-site barista cafes, artisanal snacks, fitness centers or yoga rooms, concierge-style reception, curated artwork and interior design, weekly social events – these are increasingly common.

According to the London Flex Space Brand Index, “amenity-rich reigns supreme” among top-rated flex spaces.

It’s a recognition that people come to coworking for an elevated experience they might not get at a home office or a traditional dull office. The goal is to make the workspace not just functional, but enjoyable and inspiring.

Underpinning this hospitality vibe is a renewed focus on service quality and community. Many operators are hiring community managers with backgrounds in hospitality (hotels, travel, events) who excel in creating a warm, welcoming atmosphere.

These staff members orchestrate everything from remembering members’ birthdays to organizing networking happy hours. The result is that members feel part of a community and well cared for – a strong incentive to stay.

Wellness and Well-Being – More Important Than Ever

Wellness and well-being have become top priorities in workspace design. The pandemic refocused everyone on health, and now employees expect offices to actively support their physical and mental well-being.

In coworking, this translates to features like improved air filtration, natural lighting, biophilic design (plants, access to nature), ergonomic furniture, quiet zones, and wellness programs (meditation sessions, healthy food options, etc.).

The International WELL Building Institute even piloted a WELL Health-Safety Rating specifically for coworking spaces, and forward-thinking operators are pursuing such certifications as a mark of quality.

Why?

Because it makes a difference: studies find that healthier workspace environments can lead to a 26% improvement in overall well-being and 10% boost in mental health for occupants.

Sustainability and ESG Practices as the New Norm

Closely tied to wellness is the emphasis on sustainability and ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) values.

Watch our highly rated "Attract More Members by Focusing on Workplace Sustainability" webinar on-demand here.

Flex space users, especially younger companies and freelancers, increasingly care about the environmental footprint and social impact of their workspace.

Millennials and Gen Z rank environmental issues as a top priority and prefer businesses (and workplaces) that align with those values.

In France, 72% of startups now prioritize ESG when choosing offices, often opting for eco-certified buildings.

Flex brands that demonstrate a commitment to sustainability (some even becoming B Corp certified) can gain a competitive edge in this values-driven market.

Key City Snapshots: London, Berlin, Amsterdam, Paris, Dubai

The flex workspace revolution is a global phenomenon, but it manifests uniquely in each city. Here we provide a brief snapshot of five key cities in the EMEA & UKI region – London, Berlin, Amsterdam, Paris, and Dubai – focusing on the local flex market’s status and trends.

These cities are all important hubs that illustrate broader regional dynamics.

London’s Flex Market is on the Rise

Europe’s largest flex office market continues to break records. London accounts for roughly three-quarters of all UK flexible office inventory, and it’s still growing fast.

As, Allwork.space reports, supply in London ballooned by 39% year-on-year as of Q1 2025 – an enormous expansion driven by both coworking providers and landlords adding space.

Despite this surge, demand has kept pace: occupancy levels are high in prime locations and desk prices in London have remained resilient, nudging up ~1% quarter-on-quarter in early 2025.

Corporate demand is especially strong in London’s West End and City submarkets, where many large firms are using flex space while upgrading their main offices.

JLL’s London team noted that tech and finance companies account for 68% of flex transactions by volume. London’s role as a global business hub ensures a steady pipeline of startups, scale-ups, and international firms needing project space or swing space.

Looking ahead, there’s little sign of slowdown – if anything, London is pioneering the “hub-and-spoke” model, where companies keep a London HQ hub but use flex space in outer zones or commuter towns as spokes.

Berlin: Germany’s Flex Space Capital

The startup capital of Germany, Berlin is a vibrant flex space market with strong growth. Berlin is hailed as Germany’s “flex office capital,” boasting about 330,000 sq m of existing and planned flexible workspace – the largest in the country by far.

Providers from local firms (e.g. Unicorn Workspaces) to international ones (WeWork, Mindspace) have a big presence.

Demand in Berlin is fueled by its booming tech and creative industries. The city consistently attracts entrepreneurs and remote-working creatives, many of whom prefer coworking environments.

Berlin’s flex growth is also supported by landlords: with office vacancy creeping up (projected to hit ~8%), many landlords are open to flex solutions or management agreements to fill space.

Recent high-profile moves include U.S.-based Industrious entering Berlin under a management agreement, and local pioneer betahaus expanding via a partnership with a major landlord. These signal a landlord embrace of flex models in Berlin, similar to London.

On the occupancy side, Berlin centers saw a dip during the pandemic but have largely rebounded; however, as in Germany generally, smaller coworking sites still face challenges achieving high occupancy (many under 500 sqm struggle below 60-70%).

The average large center, though, enjoys around 75% occupancy or higher. Pricing in Berlin is moderate relative to London or Paris, which, combined with its cultural cool factor, makes it attractive for flex.

The pipeline of ~78,000 sqm new flex space under development across Germany includes significant Berlin projects, so 2025 will bring more supply.

But given Berlin’s status as a magnet for innovation and remote workers, demand should keep rising.

Amsterdam still has High Occupancy Rates

A mature but growing flex market, Amsterdam is known for high occupancy and steady demand. As a major international business center (especially for creative industries, finance, and multinationals basing European HQs), Amsterdam has some of the highest office occupancy rates on the continent.

It was recently identified as one of the most “underpriced” major office markets in Europe, meaning there is value to be found, and it offers attractive opportunities for flex investment.

The city hosts hundreds of coworking spaces, from global brands (Spaces was founded here, WeWork has multiple sites) to local operators (e.g. Spaces (IWG), Tribes, and others).

By late 2024, Paris had about 750 coworking spaces, whereas Amsterdam’s count is a bit lower but significant given its smaller size, roughly in the few hundreds, with 15% growth in new spaces in 2024 according to industry data, shared by Workways. (the Netherlands overall saw a spike in flex supply).

Occupancy in Amsterdam flex space offices is generally strong (often 80%+), as the city’s popularity among startups and remote international workers means spaces fill up quickly.

Additionally, Amsterdam’s progressive business culture aligns well with coworking – many companies here adopted hybrid work early and are comfortable with employees using coworking memberships.

The city is also a pioneer in sustainability; some Amsterdam coworking hubs are in repurposed historic buildings with cutting-edge green design.

While new supply is coming (operators expanding into suburbs and secondary Dutch cities), demand remains solid enough to absorb it, aided by Amsterdam’s dynamic economy. The outlook here is stable growth, not explosive like London, but consistent.

One thing to watch is pricing: Amsterdam is cheaper than London/Paris, but not low-cost; prices have creeped up as quality and amenities improved.

Still, relative to traditional Dutch office leases, flex offers flexibility that many scale-ups and international branches prefer.

We expect Amsterdam to remain one of Europe’s most resilient flex markets, with high occupancy and a focus on hospitality and design to cater to its savvy clientele.

Paris’ Flex Space Growth Continues

The City of Light has wholeheartedly embraced coworking in recent years. Paris now counts over 750 coworking and flex workspaces, after growing about 15% in number in 2024 alone.

Initially driven by startup growth and a push for innovation spaces, Paris’s flex market is now also supported by traditional corporates.

French companies have historically favored long leases, but even they are shifting – as noted earlier, a majority now prefer shorter, flexible terms or coworking options.

Paris has seen heavy investment from big operators: WeWork’s largest European site is in Paris, while local champions like Wojo (backed by Accor and Bouygues) and Station F (for startups) have expanded.

Occupancy in top Paris flex locations is high, often above 85-90% for private offices, as demand is bolstered by both domestic firms and multinationals.

One interesting trend: many flex centers opened in Paris are amenity-rich “pro-working” spaces located in prime arrondissements, catering to professionals who want prestige addresses plus services.

This aligns with Paris being a center of business sophistication – flex offerings here tend to include concierge, high-end design, and even Michelin-star chefs (in one case!).

Pricing in Paris for coworking is on the higher side (average desk rates rank among the top in Europe, roughly similar to London’s outskirts, though slightly below London’s core).

Even so, the economics can favor flex: local studies show up to 25% cost savings using flex vs. traditional leasing in Paris.

Parisian operators are also leading on sustainability and wellness – for instance, many spaces feature eco-friendly designs and terraces or gardens for wellness (taking advantage of Paris’s beautiful architecture and courtyards).

In 2025 and beyond, Paris is expected to keep growing its flex footprint, including into its suburbs and secondary cities (e.g. Lyon, Marseille have burgeoning coworking scenes).

Given France’s strong push for “workplace innovation” at the policy and corporate level, flex space has government support too.

DUBAI – Still a Standout in the Middle East

A standout in the Middle East, Dubai’s flex space scene is thriving against the backdrop of a red-hot office market. Dubai’s overall office occupancy is one of the highest in the world – about 92% in early 2025, and forecast to exceed 94% by end of 2025.

This is driven by surging business activity and an influx of companies (and remote workers) drawn by Dubai’s open economy and visa incentives. With such tight traditional office supply – prime office rents jumped 22% in 2024 alone – many firms literally cannot find large office spaces easily.

This supply-demand gap has been a boon for flexible spaces, which act as an immediate solution for companies that need space quickly or for short terms.

International operators like Regus/Spaces and WeWork are present in Dubai, but the city also has homegrown brands (e.g. Astrolabs, Letswork, Hub71 in Abu Dhabi) and a strong serviced office sector.

The government, through free zones like Dubai Internet City and DIFC (Dubai International Financial Centre), has also integrated coworking-style hubs as part of their offerings to attract entrepreneurs.

Demand in Dubai’s flex spaces comes from diverse sources: startups (especially in tech, crypto, and media), foreign companies setting up regional offices, and a growing pool of digital nomads and freelancers taking advantage of Dubai’s remote work visa.

With office space scarce, even larger corporations are now taking interim space in flex centers while they await new developments. (Notably, DIFC is adding significant new supply, but much of it is pre-leased given the unrelenting demand.)

As a result, flex space occupancy in Dubai is very high; many centers operate at full capacity or close to it, and membership churn is low because new entrants quickly backfill any departures.

One challenge is that Dubai’s summers are extreme, so operators ensure their spaces are comfortable year-round and often located in accessible, central locations to minimize commutes in the heat.

Looking forward, Dubai’s flex market will likely expand along with the overall growth of the city as a global business hub. New coworking locations are opening not just in the traditional centers (Downtown, Marina) but also in emerging areas and even other Emirates (Abu Dhabi, Sharjah) for diversification.

As long as Dubai’s economy stays strong and its pro-business policies continue, flex providers will find a steady stream of customers.

These five cities each illustrate key aspects of the flex revolution.

Of course, many other cities in EMEA & UKI are experiencing their own coworking booms: Manchester and Birmingham in the UK (both seeing double-digit percent growth in flex supply and rising prices as noted, e.g. Birmingham desk costs up 23% YoY amidst shortage), Dublin and Warsaw (attracting U.S. tech firms into flex space), Madrid and Barcelona (with a strong post-pandemic recovery in flex demand), and more.

The common thread is that flexible working is transforming city real estate markets across the board, offering agility and convenience that align with modern work trends.

Outlook for 2025 and Beyond: Flex Becomes Even More Mainstream and Data-Driven in EMEA and UKI

As we look beyond Q1 2025 into the remainder of the year and the rest of the decade, the future of the coworking and flex space industry in EMEA & UKI appears bright, but not without challenges.

The consensus among industry experts and our own in-house data powered by the OfficeRnD FlexIndex is that flexible space is here to stay, and will claim an increasing share of the office market.

In fact, some forecasts suggest that flex space could comprise 20–30% of corporate real estate portfolios by 2030, a remarkable jump from low-single-digits a decade ago.

This “new normal” will see flexible options integrated into how virtually every company plans their workplace strategy.

What’s Next?

The coworking and flex space sector in EMEA & UKI is poised for sustained growth, driven by hybrid work, enterprise demand, and evolving member expectations.

Operators who harness technology, streamline operations, and deliver exceptional experiences will lead the pack.

What Is an “Open Integration Ecosystem”?

Name: AI-Powered Search and SEO: Impact on Coworking & Flex Space Visibility
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: The rise of AI-driven search engines – from Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) to LLMs like ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude and Bing Chat – is reshaping how members discover coworking and flex spaces online.
Post body:
The rise of AI-driven search engines – from Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) to LLMs like ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude and Bing Chat – is reshaping how members discover coworking and flex spaces online.

This article examines the global impact of AI-powered search on coworking space visibility, compares traditional SEO practices with emerging AI-focused SEO strategies, and provides real examples, risks, and actionable recommendations for coworking and flex space owners to stay competitive.

All insights are backed by recent research, in-house expertise, and case studies, ensuring relevance in 2025 and beyond.

Quick Summary:

  • AI-Powered Search Revolution: Generative AI (e.g., Google SGE, ChatGPT, Gemini) is transforming how users find coworking and flex spaces, favoring zero‑click answers and conversational queries over traditional blue‑link clicks.
  • Traditional SEO Alone Isn’t Enough: Ranking on page one no longer guarantees visibility; only ~4.5% of AI‑generated answers cite top organic results, so you must optimize for AI discovery (GEO/LLMO).
  • Critical AI‑SEO Tactics: Ensure consistent business listings (NAP, hours, photos), implement structured data (LocalBusiness, Review, FAQ schema), and craft conversational, intent‑focused content to be AI‑readable and reliable.
  • Leverage Reviews & Authority: Collect diverse, keyword‑rich reviews and secure mentions in high‑authority local directories and media lists to boost AI citations and credibility.
  • Case Study Insights: Examples like Expansive’s market‑specific landing pages and Industrious’s live review widgets drove +150% traffic lifts and higher conversions by aligning with AI search trends.
  • Risk of Inaction: Failing to adapt can lead to reduced organic traffic, missed leads due to zero‑click results, and potential misinformation harming your reputation.

How AI Search Is Changing Visibility for Coworking Spaces

Online search has long been critical for coworking businesses. In fact, Google remains the first stop for most people to find coworking spaces in their area.

Traditionally, a coworking space that ranked high for “coworking in [City]” or appeared in Google’s local map pack would attract substantial organic traffic.

Now, AI-powered search is disrupting this model in several key ways:

Direct Answers Over Clicks

AI search tools can answer user queries directly with generated summaries. For example, users are already asking conversational questions like “Affordable coworking spaces in Lisbon” and getting answers that list spaces without any click-through links. If a coworking brand isn’t referenced in that answer, it essentially becomes invisible in that interaction. This “zero-click” dynamic means fewer users may reach your website at all, unless your brand is part of the AI’s answer.

AI Answers Dominate the Screen

On Google, the new SGE AI-generated overview often occupies a large portion of the results page, pushing traditional listings far below the fold. Studies show that in SGE tests, the AI answer can push the #1 organic result down by over 1,500 pixels – more than an entire screen’s height.

Featured snippets and other rich results get similarly displaced (a 1478 px drop on average for snippets). For coworking operators, this means even if you have strong SEO and rank on page one, users might not see your link unless you’re also featured within the AI summary.

Learn insider tips and expert strategies to market your coworking space like pro in 2025. Check out the "Turn Traffic Into Bookings: Marketing Strategies for Flexible Workspaces" on-demand webinar.

Different Content Gets Pulled

AI search doesn’t always cite the top-ranked sites. Remarkably, only about 4.5% of the URLs that Google’s generative AI uses in answers are identical to the traditional top 10 organic results. In other words, the vast majority of sources used in AI answers come from beyond page one (often from deeper or alternative sources).

This leveling effect can be a double-edged sword: a less-SEO-optimized blog with highly relevant info might get cited by the AI, while a top-ranked homepage might be skipped. Traditional ranking alone no longer guarantees visibility if the AI finds a more contextually relevant snippet elsewhere.

Integration of Local Data

For local-intent queries (like “coworking space near me”), Google’s AI can incorporate Google Business Profile details, maps info, hours, photos, and review snippets directly into the answer.

This creates a hybrid result where the AI might say, for example, “Workspace Hub – open 24/7, located downtown, rated 4.8★ – is one option” pulling from your listings. Incomplete or inconsistent business listings now pose a bigger risk: an AI might present outdated info if your Google/Bing profile isn’t updated. It also means aspects like photos and review text are part of your first impression in AI results – not just your meta description.

Prevalence of AI in Search

AI-generated answers are quickly becoming common. Google’s SGE is appearing for an estimated 86.8% of all searches in testing, and roughly 68% of local business queries now trigger an AI overview on the results page. And in the last few weeks these numbers climbed even more.

By contrast, the traditional local pack (map + listings) appeared for only ~39% of those same searches. In general, the more conversational or specific the query, the more likely an AI answer will appear. Informational questions (e.g. “What’s the cheapest coworking option in Tokyo?”) trigger AI answers over 90% of the time, whereas a basic location search (“coworking space Tokyo”) might show a classic map pack more often.

Implication: You, as a coworking or flex space provider, must adapt to this new reality. Members are increasingly discovering spaces via AI-curated answers and conversational queries, not just the old list of 10 blue links. Your online visibility is no longer solely about your website’s Google rank, but about whether AI assistants recognize, understand, and mention your space when users ask for “the best coworking space nearby” or “flex space with meeting rooms in… .” In short, being the answer has become as important as being the top search result.

Traditional SEO vs. AI-Powered SEO: What’s the Difference?

The fundamentals of SEO (Search Engine Optimization) are evolving. Traditional SEO focused on making your website rank higher on search engine result pages.

AI-powered SEO (often dubbed Generative Engine Optimization or LLM Optimization) extends those principles to ensure your business is also visible to AI-driven search and recommendation engines.

The table below highlights the key differences:

AspectTraditional SEO (pre-AI)AI-Driven SEO
Primary GoalRank high on search engine results pages to drive clicks and traffic.Be featured or cited within AI-generated answers and summaries to maintain visibility. In an AI-first world, being part of the answer is the new top position.
Keyword StrategyTarget specific keywords and short phrases that users type into search bars. Optimize pages around those terms (e.g. “coworking space London”).Optimize content for natural-language queries and questions that users speak or ask AI assistants (e.g. “What are the top coworking spaces in London for networking?”). Focus on long-tail, conversational phrases that reflect user intent
Content OptimisationCreate relevant pages and blog posts with the right keywords, meta tags, and backlinks. Content is often formatted for desktop/mobile screens and Google’s crawlers.Provide comprehensive, trustworthy content that directly answers questions users ask. Use FAQ sections and conversational tone so that AI can easily digest and quote your content in its summaries. The emphasis is on factual clarity and context (since the AI might quote one sentence out of your page).
Structural DataProvide comprehensive, trustworthy content that directly answers questions users ask. Use FAQ sections and conversational tone so that AI can easily digest and quote your content in its summaries. The emphasis is on factual clarity and context (since the AI might quote one sentence out of your page).Heavy use of structured data to label your content for AI consumption. Mark up your site with schema for LocalBusiness (name, address, phone), Products/Offers (workspace plans), FAQs, Reviews, etc., so that AI models can accurately parse facts about your space.
Local VisibilityMaintain a robust Google My Business (Google Business Profile) listing and accumulate Google reviews to rank in the local pack. Target local keywords on your site (e.g. pages for each city/neighborhood).Be present on all platforms that AI trusts – not only Google, but also Bing Places, Yelp, TripAdvisor, Facebook, local business directories and niche forums. Generative AI pulls in data from across the web, so a strong multi-platform presence and consistent positive reviews (on all major review sites) improve your chances of being mentioned. Local SEO now means everywhere your business might be mentioned, not just Google Maps
Authority & MentionsBuild domain authority via backlinks from reputable sites, and establish your site as an authority (through content marketing, guest posts, etc.) to boost ranking.Cultivate a broad digital footprint and brand authority. AI models consider the overall prominence of your brand online. Being mentioned in news articles, “Top 10 coworking” listicles, local blogs, and forums can increase the AI’s confidence in your business. In practice, this means PR and content partnerships can directly influence whether an AI lists your space as a notable recommendation.

User InteractionThe user journey typically involves a click: users see your link in Google and click to visit your website for details and conversion (tour booking, contact, etc.).Users might get their answer without clicking to your site. For instance, an AI might tell them “Workspace Hub has open desks at $199/month and meeting rooms, located downtown” drawn from your online info, and the user might never visit your page. Ensuring the AI’s answer includes your name, key details, and a positive impression is critical since the traditional click-based funnel is shortened. Voice search via Alexa/Siri/ChatGPT will amplify this “answer, no click” behavior.

Success MetricsKey metrics include organic traffic volume from search, click-through rate (CTR) on search results, and your ranking positions for target keywordsNew metrics of success include frequency of being mentioned in AI responses, share of “voice” in conversational search results, and referral traffic from AI tools. Businesses are starting to monitor their presence in ChatGPT/SGE outputs. Also, success is measured by what isn’t happening – e.g. not being omitted or misrepresented by AI (since exclusion can make you invisible). In short, staying on the AI’s radar is itself a KPI now.
Takeaway: Traditional SEO tactics (good website UX, relevant content, keywords, backlinks) still matter – but they are no longer sufficient on their own. You must now optimize your content and online presence for AI-driven discovery. This emerging practice has been termed Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) or Large Language Model Optimization (LLMO), and it builds upon SEO by asking: “How can we ensure an AI assistant will find and recommend our business?”

Case Studies: Coworking Spaces Already Using AI Search Strategies

Forward-thinking flex-space businesses have begun adapting their digital strategies to align with AI-driven search trends.

In many cases, these organizations implemented effective approaches even before AI search became prominent, and those same strategies continue to deliver results today.

The Growth of Expansive

Background: Expansive (formelry known as Novel Coworking) is one of the largest independent flex-space providers in the U.S., with over 40 markets under management.

They faced stiff competition from national brands and needed a way to scale efficiently while maintaining strong local visibility in the early AI-search era.

How they did it?

  • Localized SEO Roll-out: For each new market launch, Novel implemented city- and neighborhood-specific landing pages, fully optimized with localized keywords, schema markup (LocalBusiness + Offer + FAQ), and regionally targeted meta tags.
  • Content & PR Integration: They ran PR campaigns to get featured in local business journals and blogs (e.g. Chicago Business, Denver Inno), then repurposed those mentions into “As featured in…” social proof on their site.
  • Advanced Tracking: They set up end-to-end attribution to measure organic, paid, and referral traffic down to the market level.

Results:

  • +156% Organic Traffic across all locations in the first year after the SEO overhaul
  • +152% Overall Traffic, driving not just more visits but higher-quality leads through better conversion tracking
  • Achieved market-leading share in key queries like “coworking space in Chicago” and “flexible office Denver” within three months of launch.
  • Big bump in AI Overview mentions

Expansive outperformed every other space in Chicago, setting the template for our nationwide expansion.
 — Bill Bennett, CEO, Expansive

Industrious – Integrating Google Reviews to Boost Conversions and AI Online Visibility

Background: Industrious is a U.S.–based coworking and flexible office provider with a growing footprint of locations nationwide. They wanted to leverage member testimonials more effectively to stand out in a crowded market.

Solution: Industrious partnered with EmbedSocial’s EmbedReviews platform to automatically collect and synchronize all Google Business Profile reviews and display them as dynamic widgets and badges directly on their website.

This gave potential members immediate, trustworthy “social proof” without manual updates.

Impact:

  • Conversion Rate Lift: Displaying live Google reviews and star-rating badges on key pages led to a measurable increase in both new tour inquiries and membership sign-ups.
  • Operational Ease: By automating review aggregation and display, Industrious reduced the time spent on manual updates, ensuring always-fresh testimonials.
  • Member Trust: Prospects arriving via AI-driven search or zero-click scenarios saw real member feedback up front, reinforcing credibility before visiting the site.

These examples underline a common theme:

Coworking brands that proactively adapt – by enriching content, cultivating reviews, and tracking their presence in AI outputs – are maintaining or even expanding their online visibility. In contrast, spaces that stick to “business as usual” SEO (or neglect it entirely) risk losing ground as search behavior shifts.

The Risk of Inaction: Why Standing Still Is Not an Option

Failing to respond to AI-driven search changes can have serious consequences for coworking and flex space businesses. Here are the key risks of inaction:

Declining Organic Traffic

As AI answers siphon off clicks, overall search engine traffic is expected to shrink. Gartner predicts that organic search volume will drop 25% by 2026 due to AI chatbots and virtual agents.

If you do nothing, you may see fewer visitors finding your website via traditional Google search, month after month. A 25% traffic decline could mean a similar drop in tour bookings and inquiries originating from search. In short, an unchanged SEO strategy will yield diminishing returns.

“Invisible” to AI Users

Every day, more consumers are using AI assistants instead of search engines for recommendations. If your space is not being picked up in AI-generated answers, those users simply won’t hear about you.

Your competitor down the street might be the one the AI mentions as the best option, effectively cutting you out of a growing segment of the market. Being absent from AI answers = being invisible to a portion of your audience.

Losing the “Zero-Click” Race

Even if you rank #1 on Google, an AI summary might appear above you and satisfy the user’s query without any clicks. If that summary doesn’t include your brand, you lost an opportunity without even knowing it.

This zero-click phenomenon makes it hard to track what you’re losing – you simply receive fewer leads and might not realize an AI tool answered the query. Competitors that find a way into that AI summary essentially steal the lead before it ever reaches search results.

Misinformation or Reputation Damage

AI models can sometimes give incorrect or outdated information about your business if you haven’t kept your data fresh. For example, if your hours or pricing changed and your site or listings weren’t updated, an AI might confidently tell a user wrong details (e.g. old prices or “closed now” when you’re open).

Similarly, AI might surface a negative review or misleading comment as representative of your space if positive content is sparse. Not taking control of your online information and narrative opens the door to an AI accidentally harming your reputation.

Competitive Disadvantage

The flex space market is getting more competitive globally. If a few pioneering coworking operators in each city optimize for AI and voice search, they will capture the majority of new-gen search queries – whether it’s “Which coworking space has free parking in Bangalore?” or “Alexa, find me a coworking space with private offices in downtown Chicago.”

Late adopters will be left fighting over a shrinking share of traditional search referrals. Essentially, ignoring AI trends now is like neglecting SEO 10 years ago – your space could fall behind peers in discoverability and brand awareness.

Missing Out on Global/Remote Opportunities

AI search doesn’t just affect local discovery. Digital nomads and remote teams often use AI tools to research options worldwide (“ChatGPT, what are some great coworking spaces in Seoul?”). If you have locations in multiple cities or appeal to international members, failing to optimize for AI means you may miss out on these global queries.

In contrast, spaces that provide rich information online (in English and other languages) can get picked up in worldwide AI-driven searches, tapping into a broader audience.

In summary, the risk of inaction is clear: fewer leads, a weaker online presence, and letting competitors (or misinformation) define your business in the new search landscape. If your business depends on local customers, you can’t afford to be invisible in AI-driven search. The cost of adapting is far outweighed by the cost of getting left behind.

Adapting and Thriving: 9 AI SEO Strategies for Coworking Spaces

Fortunately, there are concrete steps coworking and flex space operators can take to improve their visibility in AI-powered search results. By updating your website, content, and local SEO practices, you can future-proof your business against these changes.

Below are actionable recommendations to remain visible and competitive.

#1 Ensure Your Business Data Is Consistent Everywhere

Audit all online listings for your space – Google Business Profile, Bing Places, Yelp, Facebook, Apple Maps, coworking directories, etc. Unify your NAP (Name, Address, Phone) and other details across all platforms.

Inconsistent or outdated info (different addresses, old phone numbers, varying names) can confuse AI and lead to wrong details in answers.

Also, make sure your hours, amenities, and descriptions are up to date. Google’s SGE and other AI pull from these sources heavily, so this is step one to “feed” the AI correct data.

#2 Double Down on Reviews and Ratings

Reviews are effectively content about your business written by members – content that AI models love to digest. Encourage your members to leave reviews on Google, Facebook, Yelp, and relevant sites.

Aim for detailed reviews that mention specific amenities or use-cases (e.g. “great for startups”, “fast Wi-Fi, quiet environment”) as these keywords might get picked up in AI responses.

A high volume of positive reviews on multiple platforms not only boosts traditional local SEO, but increases the likelihood that an AI will cite your business as a “top-rated” example.

Don’t focus only on Google – SGE pulls reviews from Tripadvisor and niche sites too – so diversify where you collect reviews.

Monitor your ratings and respond to reviews as well; showing engagement and up-to-date customer feedback can only help your credibility with AI algorithms.

Like John Williams, put it at the GCUC UK conference last year,

Search algorithms are developing yet again, and it’s good news for coworking spaces with strong brand identities – operators should double down on brand.

#3 Implement Structured Data Markup

Adding schema markup to your website is crucial in the AI era. Use LocalBusiness schema (or the more specific subtype if available, e.g. Office, Organization, etc.) to mark up your name, address, phone, geo-coordinates, opening hours, price range, and more.

Implement Review schema for testimonials and ratings on your site, FAQ schema for common questions, and Offer schema for any memberships or day-pass products.

This extra metadata makes it easier for AI to identify key facts about your space. For instance, with proper markup, an AI answer about your space could confidently state “open 24/7” or “prices start at $20/day” because it found structured info.

Use Google’s Structured Data Testing Tool to validate your schema. This might require a one-time web developer effort, but it’s worth the investment – businesses using schema have an edge in being correctly cited by AI.

#4 Create “AI-Friendly” Content (Conversational and Intent-Focused)

Adjust your content strategy to cover the kind of questions people ask AI. Add an FAQ page or expand it with questions phrased exactly as users would speak them (“Does [Your Space] offer day passes?”, “What’s the parking situation at [Your Space]?”, “Is it pet-friendly?” etc.). Write blog posts targeting specific long-tail queries: for example, a post on “How to choose a coworking space for a fintech startup” or “5 ways freelancers can benefit from coworking in [City]”.

These are the sorts of queries an AI might get, and if your content directly answers them, the AI is more likely to pull from it. Remember to write in a natural, conversational tone – LLMs prefer content that reads like how people talk.

Tools like ChatGPT can even help brainstorm questions or draft answers (just be sure to fact-check and humanize any AI-generated text before publishing).

The goal is to speak the user’s language so the AI finds your content highly relevant to the query. This also prepares you for the growing impact of voice search, where queries tend to be full questions.

#5 Produce Localized, Useful Resources

In addition to promotional content, offer value-driven content that can position you as a local authority. For example, create a guide like “Best Lunch Spots Near [Your Coworking Space]” or “Hosting Meetups in [City]: Tips from [Your Space]”.

These localized pieces can get traction and backlinks, and an AI might treat your site as a knowledge source for local insights (possibly citing your recommendations in an answer about the local area).

Google’s AI overview favors “topical authority,” so writing in-depth about your city’s remote work scene, events, or tips for using coworking effectively can indirectly boost your prominence in AI results.

#6 Be Present on All Key Platforms (Not Just Your Site)

Make it a point that your business has a profile or listing on every major platform relevant to local search. This includes establishing or updating your presence on: Google and Bing (obviously), Yelp, TripAdvisor (especially if you target digital nomads or travelers), niche coworking directories (e.g. Coworker, Deskpass), local business chambers or forums, and even Wikipedia if your brand is notable enough.

The reason is simple: AI models scour all these sources. If, say, Bing’s index or a popular app has a blurb about your space that others lack, an AI might use that information.

The more cross-verified and widespread your information is, the more confidently an AI will include you. Conversely, if you’re missing from one of these data sources, you might be left out from answers that rely on them.

A quick win is to claim and fill out profiles on any site that lists “workspace” or “office space” in your category – many are free and can send you leads in their own right.

#7 Monitor Your AI Search Presence and Mentions

Start treating AI visibility like you treat Google rankings. Use tools or manual checks to see what answers AI platforms give for key queries related to your business.

For example, ask ChatGPT (with browsing enabled or via Bing Chat) something like “What are good coworking spaces in [Your City]?”. See if and where you’re mentioned.

If you notice inaccuracies (e.g. wrong pricing or amenities), address them by correcting your site or major listings – the AI likely picked the info up from some data source.

If you’re not mentioned at all, analyze what the AI does mention – is it citing a blog list you’re absent from, or highlighting a feature you haven’t publicized?

This can inform your marketing. Google’s Search Console and Business Profile insights can also reveal if your traffic or impressions dip, possibly indicating AI answers are taking over some queries.

Additionally, stay alert for new AI features (like Google’s “SGE follow-ups” or Bing’s chat plugins) that could affect how your information is presented. The local search landscape is evolving quickly, so continuous monitoring and agile adjustments will be key.

A useful tool for monitoring your AI search presence are Hubspot’s Free AI Search Grader Tool.

#8 Local “Best of” Lists & AI Visibility

Many coworking operators are finding that getting featured in authoritative third-party content is now as important as optimizing their own site.

For instance, a high-traffic article like “Top 10 Coworking Spaces in the USA” can directly feed AI answers. If ChatGPT or SGE is asked “What are the best coworking spaces in Singapore?”, it may draw from such curated rankings and mention those ten spaces by name.

Coworking brands that have secured spots on popular lists (e.g. in local magazines, blogs, or platforms like Coworker.com) have a head start – the AI is more likely to “know” about them.

Spaces are responding by ramping up PR and partnerships to get mentioned in these roundup articles and local press.

The effect is verifiable: ask an AI assistant for the best coworking in your city, and you’ll notice it often echoes the names seen in media lists and high-rated review sites.

#9 Stay Agile and Keep Experimenting

The introduction of generative AI in search is not a one-time change – it’s an ongoing evolution. Make sure someone on your team (or an external consultant) is staying educated on AI search developments. For instance, voice and multimodal search are rising, meaning users might search by asking Alexa or by uploading a photo of a location.

Plan to adapt your SEO for these scenarios too (ensure your space’s name and images are recognizable and tagged).

In practical terms, regularly update your content to answer new questions members ask, use analytics to spot changes in how people find you, and be willing to A/B test new approaches (like different content formats or Q&A sections).

Those who treat this as a dynamic part of marketing – and not a one-and-done project – will fare best.

And so, by implementing these steps, coworking space owners can significantly improve their odds of being visible in the AI-driven search landscape.

In fact, many of these actions (e.g. maintaining listings, getting reviews, producing quality content) are extensions of good digital marketing practices you may already know – now tuned specifically to how AI systems gather and prioritize information.

The overarching theme is to make your business “AI-readable” and trusted: provide clear, structured info, demonstrate credibility through reviews and mentions, and speak to the user intents that AI is trying to satisfy.

Conclusion: Embracing the AI Search Revolution in Coworking

The advent of AI-powered search is a paradigm shift for online discovery, and coworking and flex space operators around the globe must respond proactively.

Operators who invest in AI-focused SEO can capture highly qualified, intent-driven leads (e.g. someone who asks an AI for “24/7 access coworking with a podcast studio” is probably ready to convert if your space fits).

Author: asen-stoyanchev

Post body:
In early April 2025, J.P. Morgan Research raised the odds of a U.S. recession in 2025 to 60%, up from 40% just months earlier. Whether or not that downturn materializes, the signal is clear: economic uncertainty is in the air.

For coworking space owners and operators, this moment calls for foresight and flexibility. While recessions bring challenges – shrinking startup budgets, corporate cost-cutting, unpredictable occupancy- they can also reward agile businesses that know how to adapt. Coworking spaces, by design, are built on adaptability.

Now it’s time to sharpen that edge.

This guide offers practical, proven strategies to help your space stay profitable and relevant in a downturn.

Let’s dive in.

Diversify Your Revenue Streams

Relying solely on coworking desk rentals or full-time memberships makes your business vulnerable during economic slowdowns.

If your main clientele – startups, freelancers, or small businesses tighten their belts, your revenue can quickly shrink. Diversifying helps you stay afloat even if one segment takes a hit.

Here are key avenues to explore:

Private Offices

Larger teams and remote-first companies often look for flexible, enclosed spaces, especially in uncertain times when signing a traditional lease isn’t appealing. Private offices deliver higher revenue per square foot and longer-term commitments than hot desks.

Pro tip: Offer scalable office suites that teams can grow into or contract from month to month. This flexibility is a major selling point during volatility.

Virtual Office Memberships

Virtual memberships – offering business addresses, mail handling, call answering, and occasional access to meeting rooms are low overhead and cater to solopreneurs, consultants, and remote teams.

Bonus: They’re an excellent funnel to upsell future in-person memberships.

Event and Meeting Room Rentals

Even in a downturn, businesses need spaces to host workshops, training, and strategy sessions. Turn underutilized areas into rentable event space outside peak coworking hours. Partner with local organizations or offer package deals for regular bookings.

Education and Upskilling

We’ve seen many coworking spaces partnering with local educators and course providers to host skill-building sessions, especially as professionals look to retool during uncertain job markets. This can generate income while increasing foot traffic and visibility.

E-commerce: Turning Your Website into a Revenue Powerhouse

In today’s digital-first world, your coworking website can do more than just showcase your space, it can directly drive bookings and boost your bottom line.

How?

By integrating a sleek ecommerce storefront, you give prospective members the power to reserve desks, rent meeting rooms, and grab add-ons in just a few clicks.

We recently teamed up with Hector Kolonas of This Week in Coworking for an in-depth report, gathering real-world insights from operators who have embraced online storefronts.

Their stories reveal that, beyond the convenience factor, ecommerce setups have unlocked entirely new income channels, often turning slow periods into opportunities for extra revenue.

Here’s the takeaway: adding an ecommerce layer to your site is like opening a satellite location, except without the overhead. All you need is the right tech.

That’s where the OfficeRnD Growth Hub comes in. Plenty of savvy operators have already tapped into its features to turn casual browsers into paying customers and watch their revenues climb.

So, check it out!

Download the OfficeRnD Flexindex and benchmark your space against 2000+ flex space locations worldwide.

Adopt Flexible Pricing and Membership Tiers

When the economy shifts, so do customer priorities. Some members may need to downgrade plans. Others may seek temporary space while closing a leased office. The key is meeting members where they are, not locking them into rigid models.

Offer options like:

  • Day Passes & 5-Day Packs: For drop-in users or travelers
  • Part-Time or “Lite” Plans: Use of space 2 -3 days a week
  • After-Hours Memberships: For night owls or those who work around other obligations
  • Corporate Flex Accounts: One company, many users; they rotate as needed
  • Extended-Term Discounts: Commitments of 6-12 months at a reduced rate

Why it matters: In a recession, flexibility sells. If you can shift with member needs, without sacrificing profitability, you’ll earn loyalty that lasts beyond the downturn.

Build Strategic Partnerships That Strengthen Your Ecosystem

We’ve said this so many times: coworking isn’t just about space; it’s about community. That community can also be your strongest buffer in lean times.

Here’s how to leverage partnerships:

Corporate Teams

Despite what you might read, hybrid work is here to stay, and many larger firms are reducing their real estate footprints. Offer your space as a satellite office for distributed teams. Highlight productivity, proximity to public transport, and plug-and-play ease.

Local Business Collaborations

Partner with nearby cafés, gyms, or service providers to offer member perks or bundle services. You support the local economy and add value to your memberships. Check out our guide: Coworking Meets Retail: Exploring Synergies Between Retail Businesses and Flex Spaces.

Universities & Accelerators

Tap into academic institutions or startup programs that need project space or presentation venues. Many colleges are rethinking how to bridge campus life with the future of work.

Cross-Promotional Marketing

Team up with complementary businesses to co-host events or run targeted ads. For example, an HR tech company might sponsor a hiring bootcamp in your space.

Bottom line: Partnerships extend your reach, deepen your local roots, and help fill your calendar with programs that add value, without draining your internal resources.

Increase Operational Efficiency

Cutting costs shouldn’t mean cutting corners. A lean, tech-savvy operation can maintain (or improve) service while trimming overhead.

Here’s where to look.

Energy Efficiency

Install motion-activated lighting, smart thermostats, and energy-efficient appliances. These small shifts can yield substantial utility savings over time. Plus, it’s sustainable and members love green coworking spaces.

Wondering how your space stacks up against industry benchmarks? Download the OfficeRnD FlexIndex report and see the most important coworking metrics across multiple regions to see where you stand.  

Smart Technology

Use coworking management software such as OfficeRnD Flex to automate:

  • Desk and room bookings
  • Access control
  • Invoicing and payment collection
  • Communications and driving the best possible experience for your members
  • Visitor management

OfficeRnD Flex also integrates with all the common tools that a coworking space operator might need to reduce admin hours.

Optimize Staffing

Cross-train your team to handle front desk, tours, and light tech support. Use part-time or flex staff to manage events. Outsource where feasible – think marketing or accounting – to reduce payroll obligations.

Space Optimization

Review usage data. Are some desks or rooms underused? Could a dead corner become a podcast booth or call room? Maximize every square foot.

Use a tool such as the OfficeRnD Data Hub for that.

Learn from Spaces That Thrived During Downturns

Case Study 1: The Rise of WeWork (Post-2008)

Say what you will about WeWork, but its meteoric early rise followed the 2008 financial crisis. As companies ditched expensive leases, WeWork offered low-risk, flexible alternatives.

Their key strength wasn’t just their design, it was their ability to position themselves as a cost-effective solution in uncertain times.

Case Study 2: The Pandemic Pivot

During COVID-19, coworking spaces like Industrious and The Wing ( yes it’s closed now, but still…) quickly restructured. They launched virtual community platforms, converted lounges into private offices, and emphasized health and safety. Industrious even offered enterprise-level services to companies shedding corporate space.

These examples underline a crucial truth: survival isn’t about scale, it’s about responsiveness.

Sharpen Your Value Proposition

During a recession, customers (think members) scrutinize every dollar they spend. You need to communicate exactly why your space is worth it.

Ask yourself:

  • What problem does our space solve today?
  • What sets us apart?
  • Why should someone choose us over working from home or a coffee shop?
  • Are we highlighting the amenities, services, and community that make us indispensable?

Update your messaging, refine your sales funnels, and focus on pain points: isolation, productivity, professionalism, flexibility, and, you guessed it right – hospitality and community.

Bonus: Here’s a good guide on some proven marketing strategies for coworking spaces.

Final Thoughts: The Opportunity Inside Uncertainty

Recessions are hard, but they also act as filters. Businesses that are overleveraged or inflexible struggle, while those with clear value and adaptive models often emerge stronger.

Coworking spaces that treat this moment as a chance to retool, connect, and evolve will be in a prime position, not just to survive a downturn, but to become foundational to the new economy it helps usher in.

Imagine an arena where industry pioneers converge to unravel the next chapter of work – a place where bold ideas take shape and data meets daring.

Navigating Economic Turbulence: Challenges & Opportunities

Miro opened the session by reflecting on the past five years of unprecedented business upheaval. And, boy, it was tough.

From the pandemic-induced boom in liquidity to hyperinflation, rising interest rates, geopolitical conflicts, and AI disruptions, operators have faced a roller coaster of external shocks.

Despite these headwinds, he emphasized that economic adversity often spurs innovation: we shouldn’t forget that flexible workspaces in their modern form emerged during the 2008 financial crisis.

  • True North Focus: As Miro emphasized, “It’s always better to actually do less and focus on what really matters,” urging operators to cut distractions and double down on their core offerings.
  • Benchmarking as a Compass: “Benchmarking basically means to learn from the best to improve yourself,” Miro explained, highlighting the need to measure performance, compare against peers, pinpoint gaps, and take action. Operators should measure performance, compare against peers, identify gaps, and implement targeted improvements.
  • Seizing Opportunity in Uncertainty: Tough times create demand for cost optimization, remote and hybrid work solutions, premium high-quality spaces, and entrepreneurship – areas where flexible workspaces excel.

Introducing the OfficeRnD FlexIndex

Miro unveiled the revamped FlexIndex, a quarterly report tracking six key flex space metrics:

  • Desk Occupancy
  • Revenue Occupancy
  • Private Office Occupancy
  • Revenue per Occupied Desk (RevPOD
  • Revenue per Available Desk (RevPAD)
  • Price per Available Booking

…across four regions: Americas, EMEA, APAC, and Global, with the data coming from over 2000 flex space locations worldwide.

The latest data shows resilience with a slight dip at end-2023, followed by a robust recovery, with average global revenue occupancy stabilizing around 75% in Q1 2025.

The Power of Collaborative Data: Workspace Intelligence Network (WIN)

Andy Williams debuted the Workspace Intelligence Network (WIN), a collaborative data initiative spearheaded by Runway East and fellow operators.

With 250 locations contributing data, WIN aims to standardize metrics and create a trusted industry benchmark akin to STR in hospitality.

  • Addressing Data Gaps: “Our industry suffers from a real lack of credible data,” Andy admitted, underscoring WIN’s mission to deliver granular, reliable benchmarks on pricing, occupancy, and performance.
  • Operational and Investment Benefits: Operators gain actionable insights for underwrites, board reporting, and strategic decisions. A transparent data foundation also de-risks investments by improving market understanding.

Financial Consolidation and Revenue Optimization: Insights from John Murphy

John Murphy, Revenue Specialist at Serendipity Labs and a seasoned finance manager with over four years in the sector, provided practical guidance on scaling multi-location operations.

He also described the powerful integration of OfficeRnD with Sage Intacct and the benefits it brings for operators.

  • Proactive System Migration: “If you wait until you feel overwhelmed to make a move, making the move itself will be exponentially more difficult,” he warned, encouraging operators to adopt robust ERP tools before complexity spikes.

Growth Strategies for Uncertain Times

In a landscape defined by volatility, flexible workspace operators can turn challenges into catalysts for expansion. As Miro noted, “coworking spaces thrive in uncertainty,” and here’s how to harness that edge:

  • Embrace Cost Optimization Demand: With 9 out of 10 companies finding flex more cost-effective than traditional leases, highlight your transparent, variable pricing models to attract budget-conscious clients.
  • Leverage Hybrid Work Trends: Offer a mix of hot desks, day passes, and bookable meeting/event spaces, catering to the growing number of teams adopting remote and hybrid schedules.
  • Target Entrepreneurial Growth: Economic downturns spur freelancing and startups—the original audience for coworking. Position your community as incubators for innovation and networking.

  • Partner with Tech & AI Innovators: Collaborate with AI-driven companies and embed cutting-edge tools in your space to attract talent and enhance member experience.

Why Flexible Spaces Thrive Amid Uncertainty

Miro highlighted why flexible spaces thrive during uncertainty: companies avoid long-term leases, favor cost optimization (9/10 firms save on flex over traditional leases), and increasingly adopt hybrid models, driving demand for meeting rooms, day passes, and event spaces.

Despite market volatility, flexible spaces hold distinct advantages that fuel growth even in downturns:

  • Product Quality & Location: High standards in hospitality, convenient locations, diverse product mixes, and strong communities are key differentiators.
  • Diversified Client Base: Overreliance on large corporates can be risky; a balanced portfolio of freelancers, SMEs, and enterprise clients enhances resilience.

Long-Term Vision: AI-Driven Automation

When times are hard, focus on your core offering.

Check out the recap of Flexworld Series 2025 session 2: Adversity as a Catalyst: Transforming Challenges into Workspace Innovation 

Main Insights

  • Focus on Your North Star: Trim side ventures, double down on your core product, and sharpen operational excellence to weather uncertainty.
  • Benchmarking as Compass: “Benchmarking basically means to learn from the best to improve yourself,” Miro urged. OfficeRnD Product Roadmap Highlights

Miro previewed key enhancements to OfficeRnD Flex. As a reminder, we recently restructured our coworking platform into six distinct hubs – Visitor Hub, Growth Hub, Operations Hub, Experience Hub, Integrations Hub, and Data Hub – each with its own roadmap and product team, enabling focused and faster innovation.

Here’s a quick look at the upcoming innovations:

  • Experience Hub: A new member communication system is being launched with an advanced email composer that supports scheduling, segmentation, and personalized content delivery, improving engagement and experience.

From Manual to Autonomous

Mihail Kyosev, Head of Product at OfficeRnD, framed AI’s promise:

Smart technologies are reshaping coworking spaces – from how they’re managed to how members experience them every day

The rest of the panel outlined a roadmap for AI development and its implementation across the industry, covering areas such as sales automation and IoT-driven efficiency.

Main Insights

Why FlexWorld 2025 Mattered

  2. Leverage Shared Intelligence: Data collaboration sets reliable benchmarks.
