Name: How Creating Dog-Friendly Coworking Spaces Boosts Revenue
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Forty-four percent of US households own a dog. And nearly all who do view their pet as a family member.
Post body:
Forty-four percent of US households own a dog. And nearly all who do view their pet as a family member.

Current remote and hybrid work opportunities mean many dog owners are now able to spend more of their working hours with their beloved pets.

For people who like the benefits of a coworking space, a no-dog policy can mean choosing between being a part of a community and cuddling with their pets.

Owners of dog-friendly coworking spaces have a real chance to differentiate themselves from competitors and attract pet-loving members.

But being dog-friendly isn’t as simple as marketing your business as pet-friendly and putting out a couple of dog beds. You have to think about the impact on other members and what having dogs around will mean for your investment.

So what do you need to know about welcoming dogs? Let’s find out.

Quick Summary

  • Dog-friendly coworking spaces allow owners to differentiate themselves from the competition.
  • Some of the benefits include increased member retention, higher productivity, and greater well-being.
  • While the pros outweigh the cons, setting clear expectations for all pet owners is key to success.
  • Smart space management can support a dog-friendly approach, as can additional amenities such as designated outdoor space, trash cans, and water stations.

What Are the Benefits of Dog-Friendly Coworking Spaces?

The main benefit of providing a dog-friendly coworking space is differentiation from competitors. And you need that in an industry with an increasing competition. Other benefits may include a wider potential audience and greater well-being for members.

USP Against Competitors

As a coworking space owner or manager, letting members bring their dogs is a unique selling point (USP) that competitors may not be exploiting.

Implementing a dog-friendly policy and providing appropriate amenities keeps businesses one step ahead of the competition. This is an important consideration for owners and managers looking to grow their coworking space membership.

Increased Membership and Member Retention

Until recently, working dog owners had to leave their pets at home alone all day or pay for dog walking services during office hours.

Now, with nearly 80% of US workers working remotely at least part of the week, they don’t have to choose between their pet and their career.

By creating a dog-friendly coworking space, owners can tap into this market to help boost their membership numbers.

You can target both remote and hybrid-working individuals and also remote teams who might need conference space for ad-hoc in-person meetings, events, or team development sessions.

Members working from a dog-friendly coworking space are also likely to be more relaxed as they’re not worrying about their beloved pet being home alone and trying to cram in as much work as possible before rushing back to them.

And if they’re successful in a coworking environment, they’re less likely to end their membership.

Click here to try the best coworking CRM and see how it can transform your space.

Greater Levels of Well-Being

It’s well-reported that spending time with a pet can decrease stress. Allowing members to work alongside their dogs supports their well-being.

And it’s not just pet owners that can benefit. Other members who love animals but don’t own a pet may enjoy being around them, too.

Even better, having dogs at work can increase a sense of community within a coworking environment as people bond over their pets.

It can also encourage healthy breaks. Bringing a pet means members default to having adequate breaks in their day as they walk and play with their dogs. Taking time in the day to stretch and spend some time outside can significantly improve well-being.

What Are the Challenges of Dog-Friendly Coworking Spaces?

The main challenges of dog-friendly coworking spaces include noise disruption, allergies, and safety concerns.

Owners of coworking spaces will need to mitigate these concerns to maximize the potential benefits of allowing members to bring their pets.

Noise Disruption

Most well-trained dogs don’t spend all day barking. But, even intermittent barking can be a disruption to those trying to focus.

Plus, delightful though they are, dogs generally can be a distraction.

Whether it’s their owners talking to them or other pet lovers stopping for a chat or a tummy tickle, over time it might prove too challenging for those with deadlines to meet.

Allergies

Worldwide, the percentage of pet allergy sufferers is between 10 to 20%. Allergic reactions can vary in their severity and can be debilitating for those most significantly affected. Sneezing, itching, and rashes are the most common symptoms.

Coworking space owners considering a move to a dog-friendly environment may choose to segment the workspace into areas that are pet-friendly and those that aren’t. Ensuring the workspace has a good air purification system may also help alleviate concerns.

All this would make your space good in the eyes of both visitors and members.

Safety Concerns

Some people just aren’t dog lovers and may have had an experience that makes them fearful or anxious around dogs.

It’s crucial that behavioral expectations are clearly stated and that any dogs showing unhelpful or aggressive traits are removed from the space. Owners need to be responsible for their dog’s actions at all times. Leashes may be requested for shared areas.

How to Make Your Space Dog-Friendly

With careful planning, the benefits of introducing dog-friendly coworking spaces outweigh the challenges. So, if you want to take the step, what should you consider?

Optimize Space Layout and Design

To minimize concerns about safety and allergies, consider segmenting coworking spaces into dog-friendly and human-only zones.

You can designate some meeting rooms and shared spaces specifically for members with pets. While bathrooms and kitchen areas should probably be a no-go, adding a small, fenced play area near these amenities means owners don’t have to leave their pets alone while grabbing a coffee.

Make sure the comfort of all users, human and canine, is taken care of by having easily accessible waste stations, pet hydration stations, safe outdoor spaces, and dog-friendly furniture.

Set Clear Expectations for All Users

To ensure everyone feels comfortable in a dog-friendly coworking space, it’s important to set clear expectations for all members and communicate them widely. This could include policies around pet behavior, vaccinations, cleanliness, and personal liability coverage.

In addition, make sure all legal and local regulatory requirements are met and any additional business insurance policies are in place, as required. These measures help create a safe, hygienic, and pleasant environment for all users.

Coworking management software such as OfficeRnD Flex can help keep this information visible.

For example, you can send periodic reminders to dog-owning members and share the coworking space floor plan via the Members Mobile App so it’s clear which spaces are designated as dog-friendly and which aren’t.

Visitor management and access control features can also help identify members or visitors who are pet owners and manage dog registrations of members and guests.

Consider Additional Amenities

To maximize the appeal of a coworking space to pet owners, consider additional facilities that show the comfort and safety of their pets are front and center.

Designated play areas, dog treats at reception, and partnering with local services, such as dog walking and grooming providers, offer added value to members.

OfficeRnD Flex can help streamline this process. For example, the software can automatically add fees for dog-related amenities or integrate with local service provider booking systems via the marketplace feature.

Build Community

Coworking spaces provide an opportunity to build community between dog owners and non-dog owners alike. Along with the benefits being around pets can bring, a sense of belonging boosts emotional well-being.

Shared events can be planned within the space and members can be encouraged to share their experiences and positive reviews on social media. Tagging in the coworking space provides social proof to potential members and can support member recruitment efforts.

Coworking space management software, like OfficeRnD Flex, can be used to gather feedback from members, and those testimonials can be used in marketing materials to attract new customers.

5 Examples of Successful Dog-Friendly Coworking Spaces

Worried about the hassle or cost of starting a coworking space that’s dog-friendly? Looking for additional proof of companies who’ve successfully implemented dog-friendly policies? Here are 5 of the best.

Second Home (Los Angeles)

Building a strong community has helped this coworking space succeed. Dogs and their parents fill the two-acre space, and members can attend events, including yoga and a weekly happy hour.

Second Home is a Certified B-Corp, and its friendly staff offers a warm welcome (and doggy treats!) for members and their furry friends.

Parents juggling both kids and pets can also take advantage of the childcare options provided.

Work & Woof (Austin)

Work & Woof has a fantastic range of coworking space amenities that support pet owners while they work.

They provide a 4,000-square-foot play area for pets, with both indoor and outdoor seating. This doggy daycare option supports Work & Woof’s motto, “You Work, They Play.”

Human members don’t miss out either. They can enjoy fast internet and free coffee while their pets burn off some energy on the doggie treadmill or get creative with an arts and crafts session.

Co+Hoots (Phoenix)

Co+ Hoots is a female-founded, minority-owned coworking space. It’s purpose-driven and offers the Rapid Launch business boot camp for entrepreneurs and aspiring business owners.

It also allows well-behaved pups. Policies that set expectations for dog-friendly coworking spaces ensure everyone is clear on what’s needed to make the space comfortable and accessible to all.

Industrious (Global)

Industrious is a global coworking behemoth, with over 160 locations in more than 65 cities. They provide shared spaces, private offices, and meeting rooms perfect for remote teams needing some in-person time.

Not all locations allow dogs to accompany their owners. For those that do, the segmentation of the workspace helps facilitate good relations between those who value a dog-friendly environment and those who might be less interested in the canine companionship.

Green Spaces (Denver)

Green Spaces is a coworking place, event space, and small business hub combined.

It’s famous for its biophilic design, with hundreds of plants on location helping to purify the air. This provides a salve for anyone with allergy concerns.

Green Spaces is proud of its dog-friendly ethos and dogs are welcome at no extra charge.

Create a Dog-Friendy Coworking Space with OfficeRnD Flex

The opportunity for remote and hybrid working means pet owners are enjoying more time with their beloved pooches than ever before.

For those who want the benefits of a coworking space, restrictions on pets can stop them from taking advantage.

Creating a pet-friendly coworking space can have its challenges, but a customizable and powerful coworking software like OfficeRnD Flex can help you coordinate a coworking space that’s great for both humans and their canine companions.

Name: The Role of Space Utilization Metrics in Measuring Coworking Success
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: It’s 2024 – data-driven decision-making is no longer optional if you truly want to be successful in the thriving coworking market. Post body:
It’s 2024 – data-driven decision-making is no longer optional if you truly want to be successful in the thriving coworking market. With flex spaces popping up across cities worldwide, coworking space operators must navigate a complex landscape of member needs, competition, and operational efficiency.

One of the most powerful tools they have at their disposal: space utilization metrics. These metrics go beyond just knowing how many desks are filled; they provide a roadmap to optimize space, boost profitability, and ultimately, enhance the member experience.

They also allow coworking operators to be proactive and make informed choices that lead to better space management and long-term business success.

Let’s dive into the most critical space utilization metrics that coworking operators should track and how they can unlock the full potential of their spaces.

Quick Summary

  • The most important space utilization metrics include:
    • Desk Occupancy,
    • Meeting Room Occupancy,
    • And Revenue Occupancy
  • These metrics provide insight into what your members want and need and when they need it
  • Space utilization metrics can help make informed decisions about space allocation, membership pricing options, scaling up or down, and so much more

What Are Space Utilization Metrics?

First, let’s take a look at space utilization metrics and really understand what they are and why they are important.

Space utilization metrics are key performance indicators (KPIs) that measure how effectively the physical space within a coworking facility is used.

They are invaluable for operators because they help manage resources, optimize profitability, and help plan for future growth. For example, if you want to expand your space by adding space for childcare, you need the right metrics to make a more informed decision.

From identifying peak usage times to revealing underutilized areas, these metrics give coworking operators the power to make data-backed decisions that directly impact their bottom line.

Whether maximizing the usage of desks, meeting rooms, or common areas, space utilization metrics provide insights into how to make the most of every square foot.

Key Space Utilization Metrics to Measure Success in Coworking Spaces

The Occupancy Index is an industry-standard measurement where coworking spaces can compare their occupancy to that of their competitors.

This metric offers a clear snapshot of how well your space is performing and help you plan accordingly.

A high occupancy rate indicates that your space and amenities are in high demand and providing members with what they need, while a low rate could signal that it’s time to make some strategic adjustments.

However, there are many flavors to space utilization metrics and several ways to interpret them, so let’s break it down:

Calculating Occupancy Rates

Generally speaking, occupancy rates are calculated by dividing the number of occupied units (desks, rooms, spaces, etc.) by the total available units.

That means, to calculate your desk occupancy, simply divide the number of occupied desks by the total desks you have to offer.

To find other types of occupancy rates, follow the same formula and substitute your unit of choice.

For instance, to calculate meeting room occupancy, divide the total number of hours the room is booked for by the total available hours.

Meeting room occupancy metrics help operators determine if their meeting rooms are in demand or taking up too much unused space.

Similarly, to calculate revenue occupancy, divide your actual revenue by the total potential revenue if you were at full occupancy.

Revenue occupancy is a great metric to use when it comes time to scale your business. Compare what you are making to what you could be making in a best-case scenario.

Don’t forget to include all sources of revenue. This includes events, on-site food and beverage options, etc.

And to calculate space or facility occupancy, calculate the area of your facility dedicated to your workspace by the total area of the entire facility.

This number will help you determine if you are using your space wisely or if there is a better way to lay out your workstations.

How to Leverage Space Utilization Data for Decision Making

Collecting space utilization data is only the first step; the real value comes from using that data to drive decisions. Here’s how coworking space operators can leverage these metrics to optimize operations.

Space Planning and Optimization

Data on desk, office space, and meeting room usage can guide decisions about adding or removing resources, redesigning spaces, or even expanding into new areas. If meeting room occupancy is high, it may indicate the need for more conference-style space.

If meeting room occupancy is low but private desks are in demand, you may want to consider eliminating the meeting space and turning it into individual workspaces. The numbers tell a story and help you prioritize, plan, and optimize.

Pricing Strategies

By understanding metrics like occupancy rates, desk utilization, and meeting room bookings, you can identify peak usage times, underutilized spaces, and member trends that will help better inform pricing strategies.

With this data, they can implement dynamic pricing models, offering higher rates during peak hours and discounts or promotions during slower periods to maximize revenue.

Pricing metrics help operators assess the effectiveness of different membership tiers and packages, allowing them to refine offerings that match demand, improve customer satisfaction, and increase retention.

This data-driven approach ensures that pricing strategies are aligned with market trends, usage patterns, and member behavior, optimizing profitability and resource allocation. You can apply this if you run a coliving space too!

Membership Adjustments

With the help of occupancy data, you can adjust membership offerings, such as offering part-time or off-peak memberships, based on utilization patterns.

Adapting membership pricing according to occupancy helps to increase usage during slower times and incentivizes workers to come when the space is in less demand.

Providing premium rates for high-demand areas or times, while offering discounts or promotional packages for lower-demand periods helps balance occupancy rates throughout the day/week.

Furthermore, these metrics help operators identify when to introduce new membership tiers, such as dedicated desk plans, private office memberships, or even short-term passes, ensuring they meet the evolving needs of their members while maximizing space efficiency.

Scaling Up or Down

If data shows consistently high utilization, it may be time to expand the space. Conversely, underutilized spaces could be repurposed for other activities or offerings.

Occupancy metrics help identify what’s working, what isn’t working, and what the options are for your space.

The goal is always to maximize profitability, but don’t do it at the expense of your members. Take a look at your occupancy rates to determine what, if any, adjustments need to be made.

Post body:
There’s more to a successful coworking space than just a vibrant office environment or a strong, connected community.

While those two components are wildly important, financial performance ultimately determines your company’s success. Financial performance is key to long-term viability, growth, and scaling opportunities.

For coworking operators, setting and tracking financial benchmarks are essential for understanding the health of the business, optimizing operations, and making informed decisions.

These benchmarks provide the data needed to evaluate profitability, allocate resources efficiently, and adjust strategies to stay competitive in a dynamic market.

In this post, we’ll explore the essential financial metrics every coworking space must track to ensure a thriving business.

Quick Summary

The key financial metrics of a coworking space are:

  • Revenue per Available Square Foot (RevPAF)
  • Total Revenue
  • Revenue Forecast
  • Revenue Occupancy
  • Revenue per Available Desk (RevPAD)
  • Revenue per Occupied Desk (RevPOD)
  • RevPAD Index
  • Rent Roll Report
  • Average Revenue per Customer/Account (ARPC/ARPA)
  • Additional Revenue
  • Average Revenue per Member
  • Invoiced Revenue
  • On-demand (Bookings) Revenue
  • Churn Rate (Revenue Churn Rate)
  • Committed Revenue
  • Desk Revenue
  • Gross Margin
  • Gross Profit
  • Lifetime Value of a Customer
  • Membership Revenue (Monthly Recurring Revenue – MRR)
  • Revenue Occupancy Index (CROI)
  • Profit Margin
  • Target Revenue

Understanding Financial Benchmarks in Coworking Spaces

Financial benchmarks are key performance indicators (KPIs) that measure the financial health of a business. In the context of coworking spaces, these benchmarks serve as guiding metrics to assess profitability, scalability, and operational efficiency.

By consistently tracking these metrics, operators can make informed decisions on pricing, reduce unnecessary expenses, and strategically invest in areas that yield high returns. Financial benchmarks help operators monitor performance, plan for growth, and ensure that coworking spaces remain competitive and sustainable.

Try this coworking management platform and see why thousands of spaces worldwide are loving it!

Key Financial Benchmarks to Measure Success

Now that we understand what financial benchmarks are and why they are important, let’s dive into the essential financial metrics every coworking space should monitor to track performance and measure success.

Revenue per Available Square Foot (RevPAF)

RevPAF Defined: A metric that measures the financial efficiency and profitability of the space based on the revenue generated relative to the physical size of the space.

Revenue per Square Foot = Total Revenue/Total Square Footage

Tracking RevPAF helps operators assess how effectively the physical space is being utilized to generate income. It lends insights into the effectiveness of current space allocation and aids in making adjustments to occupy the space better.

Read more about revenue per available square foot here.

Revenue (Total Revenue)

Total Revenue Defined: The comprehensive sum of all income generated from various sources within the coworking operation over a specific period of time.

Total Revenue = Membership Revenue + On-Demand Revenue + Additional Revenue

Being able to assess the coworking business’s financial health, sustainability, and growth potential comes from knowing your total revenue.

As this is a comprehensive total that comes from all revenue streams, it is a strong indicator of your business’s overall performance and viability. It is also a good indicator of the value of your service offerings and amenities.

Read more about total revenue here.

Revenue Forecast (Projected Revenue)

Revenue Forecast (Projected Revenue) Defined: A predictive analysis that estimates the future revenue, or projected revenue, generated by the coworking or flex space.

Identify your recurring membership revenue and build assumptions for how this may change and how the on-demand revenue will fluctuate.

Based on that the formula would be:

Projected Revenue for next month = Membership Revenue for next month + On-demand Revenue assumption

Projected revenue aids in strategy planning and resource management, and can help inform decisions that will ultimately drive business growth.

It’s important to note this number is merely a prediction and though it can get you close to your target, it will never be a guaranteed number. That being said, it is an important marker that can help prepare you for what’s to come.

Factors that influence Revenue Forecast include:

  • Historical Data Analysis: Comprehend past financial data and identify trends and patterns that can influence future projections.
  • Market Research: Conduct surveys and a market analysis to understand your competitors and their offerings.
  • Membership and Occupancy Rates: Analyze current and projected occupancy rates for membership types and office rentals.
  • Scenario Planning: Brainstorm multiple revenue scenarios (optimistic, pessimistic, and realistic) to account for different market conditions.
  • Growth Projections: Estimate total revenue based on past revenue, marketing efforts, and market demand.

Read more about projected revenue.

Revenue Occupancy

Revenue Occupancy Defined: The portion of Actual Membership (or Desk) Revenue realized as a percentage of the Target (or Potential) Revenue.

Revenue Occupancy = (Membership Revenue/Target Revenue) x 100

The most widely adopted metric at this stage of the game, Revenue Occupancy is beneficial as it not only indicates occupied spaces, but also provides the price at which they are being “sold” for. If prices are low, sheer volume is not enough to make your space profitable.

Tacking on the revenue in addition to the amount of spaces used provides a clearer picture of your financial health.

Factors that influence Revenue Occupancy include:

  • Financial Health: Financial health helps depict the space’s financial performance and indicates how well the space is being monetized.
  • Operational Efficiency: Revenue occupancy helps operators to identify underutilized areas and optimize space allocation and pricing strategies.
  • Benchmarking: Use your Revenue Occupancy to measure yourself over different periods of time as well as against your competitors

Read more about revenue occupancy.

Revenue per Available Desk (RevPAD/TrevPAD)

Revenue per Available Desk (RevPAD/TrevPAD) Defined: A measurement of the average income that could be generated by each desk within a coworking facility.

Revenue per Available Desk = Revenue/Number of Available Desks

RevPAD lends insight into the coworking space’s profitability as it quantifies the revenue each available desk provides over time. Higher RevPAD indicates consistently favorable utilization of space. This metric is a key player in assessing pricing and marketing strategies.

Factors that influence RevPAD:

  • Desk Volume and Space Layout: The amount of desks within the space and the way they are dispersed will impact the total revenue generated by desks.
  • Space Optimization: Use RevPAD to determine if the current layout is best for revenue or if there are other ways to design the space.

Learn more about revenue per available desk.

Revenue per Occupied Desk (RevPOD/TrevPOD)

Revenue per Occupied Desk (RevPOD/TrevPOD) Defined: The average income generated by each occupied desk within a coworking space.

Revenue per Occupied Desk = Revenue/Number of Occupied Desks

RevPOD highlights the space’s profitability by quantifying revenue brought in from occupied desks over time. It is a KPI that lends insights into how pricing strategies and discounts affect revenue. RevPOD can also be a strong indicator of whether or not it’s time for the business to expand based on demand and how effectively the current space generates revenue.

Factors that influence RevPOD:

  • Desk Volume and Space Layout: The amount of desks within the space and the way they are dispersed will impact the total revenue generated by desks.
  • Space Optimization: Use RevPAD to determine if the current layout is best for revenue or if there are other ways to design the space.

Learn more about revenue per occupied desk here.

RevPAD Index

RevPAD Index Defined: An evaluation and comparison of the revenue-generating efficiency of coworking spaces.

Calculating RevPAD Index: First, calculate your own Space’s RevPAD (using the formula above) and benchmark it against other spaces. Calculate the average RevPAD across all spaces through research and industry reports to compare against your own number.

RevPOD = Revenue / Occupied Desks

A metric that aids operators in understanding their space’s performance regarding Revenue per Available Desk, RevPAD allows coworking space operators to benchmark their space against industry standards and competitors.

Being able to measure against the rest of the industry helps investors, landlords, managers, and other stakeholders better assess efficiency and viability of the coworking space.

A solid understanding of RevPAD Index will encourage performance evaluations, competitive analyses, and operational optimization, and will influence future investment decisions.

Factors that influence RevPAD Index:

  • Location of coworking space
  • Size of coworking space
  • Services offered in different coworking spaces
  • Membership base

Read more about RevPAD index.

Rent Roll Report

Rent Roll Report Defined: A detailed report that lists all members and their respective membership or license agreements.

Components of a Coworking Rent Roll Report:

  • Member Identifiers: This includes names and contact information of all current members
  • Membership Details: This entails specifics of each membership or license agreement, including the type of workspace(s) they are operating as well as contract start dates, end dates, and renewal options.
  • Rent Amounts: The monthly rent of membership fees each member is responsible for, including discounts, promotions, or special pricing agreements.
  • Payment Status: Insight into any outstanding invoices.
  • Additional Charges: Any additional fees or charges, such as for add-ons not built into membership packages.

Rent Roll Reports serve as a comprehensive overview of the financial performance of a coworking space related to the rental income generated.

They are crucial for tracking membership dues and occupancy levels, highlighting any financial discrepancies and helping operators understand space utilization.

This is a great tool to help predict future membership income and can serve as useful collateral for investors and stakeholders. Maintaining comprehensive and organized membership accounts will make retrieving Rent Roll Reports much easier.

Factors that influence Rent Roll Reports:

  • Membership packages and pricing
  • Additional services and amenities
  • Available rentable spaces

Learn more about Rent Roll report here.

Average Revenue per Customer/Account (ARPC or ARPA)

Average Revenue per Customer/Account Defined: A metric that represents the size and financial contribution of your members.

Average Revenue per Customer/Account = Revenue/Active Customers

A metric more closely aligned with coworking spaces who lease workspace to other companies, ARPA indicates the size of each customer. In order to grow your ARPA, customers need to be better monetized by either obtaining larger customers to occupy the space better or by upselling services to existing customers.

Learn more about average revenue per customer/account here.

Additional Revenue

Additional Revenue Defined: Referring to all other forms of revenue besides desk/membership revenue and on-demand revenue.

Components of Additional Revenue:

  • Food and Beverage Revenue: Derived from food and beverage sales from on-site cafes to catering options and more.
  • Event Revenue: Income from events hosted by the coworking space.
  • Other Revenue: All other revenue generated outside of memberships, rentable spaces, food and beverage, and events.

Additional Revenue helps in assessing the “extras.” This metric lends insights into the demand and quality of your space’s service offerings and amenities.

Factors that influence Additional Revenue:

  • On-Demand Revenue: Typically, the more members and bookings you have in the space, the more you can upsell with food, beverages, events, and other amenities.
  • Additional Services and Amenities: The more, and better, your service offerings, the more members you’ll likely attract, therefore increasing your chance at these additional sales.

Here’s more info on additional revenue.

Average Revenue Per Member (ARPM)

Average Revenue Per Member Defined: The average revenue generated by each individual member.

Average Revenue Per Member = Revenue/Active Members

A KPI that indicates how engaged your members are with the space, ARPM also lends insights into selling strategies.

This will help operators assess how well their salespeople are selling and upselling services and memberships. It will also help determine if the services being offered are in demand and attractive to your member-base.

Factors that influence ARPM:

  • Membership Structure: This metric will help you determine which membership options are the most popular to your member-base.
  • Upselling Abilities: ARPM will indicate if all members are being sold the standard membership package as opposed to better offerings that will in turn generate more revenue.
  • Service Offerings and Amenities: Use this metric to determine if the additional services and amenities you are offering are what your members are looking for in coworking space.

You can learn more about average revenue per member here.

Invoiced Revenue

Invoiced Revenue Defined: The total amount billed to members for services and memberships with a specific period of time, regardless of when the billable event was or if it has been paid.

Invoiced revenue includes all memberships, bookings, and additional services, but is different from Total Revenue in that it is representative of a particular billing cycle or pattern.

Typically this number is studied on a monthly basis and provides information that aids operators in tracking performance, managing cash flow, and making informed financial decisions.

Check out an example of calculating invoiced revenue here.

On-Demand Revenue (Bookings Revenue)

On-Demand Revenue Defined: The income generated from services and amenities that both members and non-members can access as needed without a membership.

Components of On-Demand Revenue:

  • Meeting Room Bookings: Rent out meeting spaces by the hour or by the day to appeal to both members and external clients who need private space for slightly larger groups.
  • Day Passes: Individuals are able to access the coworking space for a single day, offering flexibility for those who do not require permanent workspace. This is also great for a potential new member to try and experience your space.
  • Event Space Rentals: Coworking spaces generally have their own areas for events, seminars, workshops, and networking functions, so renting out these spaces when not in use can generate significant on-demand revenue at little to no cost.
  • Other Additional Services: Other services could include but are not limited to printing, scanning, mail handling, administrative support, parking, loyalty programs, etc.

On-Demand Revenue generates income on top of recurring membership and allows coworking spaces the opportunity to reach a wider audience with their services as users do not need an active membership.

It is not uncommon for a coworking space to generate upwards of 20-30% more revenue with these additional offerings. It is crucial to a coworking space as it can provide stability that balances out revenue fluctuations in other areas.

It also allows operators to maximize their space and offerings while reaching a much broader client base that could potentially turn into recurring memberships.

Check out some important details about on-demand revenue.

Churn Rate (Revenue Churn Rate)

Churn Rate Defined: The percentage of recurring revenue lost over a specific period.

Churn Rate = Churn Memberships Revenue/Memberships Revenue

Churn Rate helps coworking space operators identify revenue retention and loss from existing members. This could be from membership cancellations, non-renewals, or downgrades. A high revenue churn indicates the coworking space is losing a significant amount of recurring revenue and strategic adjustments need to be made.

There could be misalignment with pricing strategies and service offerings, but this could also suggest poor customer service and member satisfaction. Regardless, high Revenue Churn signals the need for immediate change.

It is important to note that this metric only indicates lost revenue and does not account for new memberships or membership upgrades during the same period.

Interested in learning more about this important coworking space metric. Here’s everything you need to know about churn rate.

Committed Revenue

Committed Revenue Defined: The guaranteed income from members who have signed long-term contracts or agreements for using the space.

Committed Revenue = Sum of all active contracts and agreements

Committed Revenue is generated by members with fixed-duration contracts ranging from several months to multiple years and ensures a steady stream of revenue. It is not limited to membership contracts though and can also encompass recurring space rentals and other on-demand offerings.

Committed Revenue is guaranteed money that can ensure revenue for the coworking space and be used as a helpful budgeting tool. Investors and stakeholders will be looking for this number to better understand the business’s financial health and long-term viability. Committed Revenue also plays a key role in company valuation.

Learn more about committed revenue.

Desk Revenue

Desk Revenue Defined: The revenue generated over a specific period of time from all rentable and on-demand desks, including dedicated desks, private offices, and hot desks.

Desk Revenue = The sum of all revenue generated from rentable workspaces

This metric provides the total amount of revenue brought in from individual work stations.

Check out more about desk revenue here.

Gross Margin

Gross Margin Defined: The percentage of revenue exceeding operational costs

Gross Margin = (Total Revenue - COGS)/Total Revenue x 100

Gross Margin indicates how effective a coworking space’s services are. Understanding the relationship between revenue and operating costs allows operators to better plan budgets and processes going forward.

This can help determine pricing strategies for the future and can serve as a benchmark for investors and stakeholders assessing the company.

Analyzing your Gross Margin will allow you to make more informed decisions about pricing, service offerings, and cost management strategies to enhance your profitability and competitive advantage.

Here’s more on gross margin.

Gross Profit

Gross Profit Defined: The revenue that exceeds the direct costs associated with operating the coworking space.

Gross Profit = Total Revenue - Cost of Services

Gross Profit provides the coworking space’s profitability without taking into account indirect expenses such as administrative costs, marketing, and sales efforts. Costs of services generally include rent and utilities, cleaning and maintenance expenses, supplies and materials, staff wages, and depreciation of office equipment and furniture. It is an important number to know and understand as it highlights the efficiency of the space’s core operations and the difference between revenue and expenditures.

This can be useful in setting and adjusting pricing strategies as well as identifying where costs can and should be reduced.

Factors that influence Gross Profit:

  • Occupancy Rates: High occupancy rates generally lead to increased revenue, while lower rates equate to decreased revenue
  • Cost Control: Managing direct costs effectively can enhance Gross Profit
  • Service Offering: Additional revenue can be made by diverse services and amenities
  • Market Conditions: Market landscape can make an impact on Gross Profit with influences from competitors, demand, and economic conditions
  • Operational Efficiency: Streamlining coworking space operations and optimizing the space can reduce revenue loss

Read more here.

Lifetime Value of a Customer (LTV)

Lifetime Value of a Customer Defined: The total revenue a coworking space can expect to generate from a single member over the duration of their membership

LTV = Gross Margin x Average Revenue per Account x Length of Stay (in months)

LTV is helpful in identifying a customer’s long-term financial value and emphasizes the importance of retaining members. It can also drive service enhancements and member experience efforts as a way to increase the customer lifespan.

Forecasting future revenue is much easier when you’re able to base it on your customer base and their retention rates. Long-term members ensure financial stability and recurring revenue, which is attractive to investors and stakeholders alike.

Additionally, understanding your LTV will help you identify high-value customers so you’re better equipped to target marketing and sales efforts toward them.

Factors that influence LTV:

  • Membership Plans: A variety of pricing tiers and service offerings will impact your ARPC, and in turn will impact your LTV.
  • Customer Satisfaction and Retention: Happy members lead to longer customer lifespans.
  • Service Diversity: A wide variety of services and amenities will increase your member-base, therefore increasing your ARPC.
  • Engaged Community: A strong, connected community provides networking opportunities and can aid in customer retention.
  • Location and Accessibility: Convenient and desirable locations can attract and retain more members, which in turn positively impacts LTV

Learn more about lifetime value of a customer in a coworking space here.

Membership Revenue (Monthly Recurring Revenue – MRR)

Monthly Revenue Defined: The income generated from members who subscribe to various coworking space services.

Monthly Revenue = The sum of total monthly member subscriptions

Monthly Membership Revenue is a summation of dollars spent towards membership subscriptions and provides guaranteed income. In a subscription-based business like a coworking space, recurring revenue is one of the best indicators used to project revenue which helps with budgeting and strategic planning.

Consistent growth in this area implies strong market positioning. Furthermore, recurring memberships prove member retention is where it needs to be.

Check out more about membership revenue here.

Revenue Occupancy Index (CROI)

Revenue Occupancy Index Defined: A standardized measure used in the coworking industry to evaluate and compare the revenue occupancy rates of coworking spaces.

Revenue Occupancy Index = Total Revenue/Target Revenue

CROI serves as a benchmark to gauge the efficiency and performance of your coworking space compared to the rest of the industry.

In order to build a proper revenue occupancy benchmark, you’ll need to collect data from other coworking spaces to compare to. It’s smart to compare yourself to your competitors that are similar in size and offerings, as well as ones that differ from you to get the full picture.

Knowing how you measure up against the rest of the industry is crucial for coworking space operators as it allows them to be more strategic in their own space.

Discover more about the revenue occupancy index here.

Profit Margin

Profit Margin Defined: The percentage of revenue that exceeds the total costs associated with running the coworking space.

Profit Margin = Total Revenue - Total Costs

Profit Margin ultimately shows how much profit is made on every dollar brought in. The majority of coworking businesses take a few years before they are profitable, as it takes time for them to build out their brand and membership.

Tracking this metric allows you to stay on top of profit and losses and can help operators make decisions about how to optimize income and expenses.

Understanding your Profit Margin will also help you determine and adjust your pricing strategy and can inform strategic decisions such as expansion.

A healthy profit margin for coworking spaces is between 10 and 30%.

Read more about profit margin here.

Target Revenue (Potential Revenue)

Target Revenue Defined: The maximum possible income the space could generate if all available workspaces and services were fully utilized and occupied at their optimal pricing.

Target Revenue = (Total Available Workspaces x Optimal Price) + (Total Available Services x Optimal Price)

Knowing the potential revenue you could bring in from your coworking space allows you to better assess your current offerings. Use this as a tool to maximize your space and services.

How to Achieve and Maintain Financial Health

Achieving and maintaining financial health is essential for the long-term success of any coworking space.

Operators must focus on a balanced approach that not only maximizes revenue but also keeps costs in check. Below are some basic actionable steps to ensure financial health and hit key benchmarks:

  • Set Competitive Pricing: Offer flexible, competitive plans but ensure profitability
  • Diversify Revenue Streams: Add rentable meeting rooms, host events, and sell add-on services
  • Manage Operational Costs: Monitor fixed and variable costs like rent, utilities, and staff expenses
  • Reduce Churn: Implement retention strategies through community engagement and regular feedback loops

Tools for Tracking Financial Benchmarks

Financial management tools can streamline the process of tracking financial benchmarks. Such platforms offer analytics on space utilization, member retention, and financial performance, providing actionable insights for optimization.

Conclusion

Financial benchmarks are incredibly important and every coworking space operator should be monitoring theirs to ensure financial health.

While all are crucial measurements, metrics like Revenue per Available Square Foot, Average Revenue per Member, Membership Churn Rate, and Profit Margin are essential in assessing the performance and profitability of your space.

Diversifying revenue streams, managing operational costs, and focusing on member retention are equally crucial in achieving sustainable growth.

For coworking operators, the road to financial sustainability lies in continuous improvement, vigilant tracking of key metrics, and flexibility in adapting to market changes. With a focus on these key principles, your coworking space will not only survive, but truly flourish.

Post body:
The idea of smart workplaces isn’t new. And, with a predicted market growth rate of 10.11% from 2023 to 2030, clearly more employers are adopting this way of working.

Using IoT-enabled devices and software to streamline workflows and boost the employee experience offers serious growth opportunities.

The big win though is data.

The data collected from smart technology can help your company make better decisions that can impact everything from overhead costs to employee productivity.

So, as we watch this workplace trend become mainstream, the question is: how smart is your workplace?

Does your company have the technology it needs to support your workforce and stay competitive? And how can you create this type of environment?

This article examines smart workplaces, their advantages, and the solutions you can implement to make your workplace “smart.”

Quick Summary

  • Smart workplaces heavily integrate technology and systems to streamline processes and team collaboration.
  • There are four main solutions for smart workplaces: security, booking, space usage, and environmental solutions.
  • Before investing in these solutions, consider scalability, integration, and employee training requirements.

What Is a Smart Workplace?

A smart workplace goes beyond having fancy gadgets and tech.

Instead, it’s about combining advanced technology, human-centric design, and data-driven insights to create a more flexible work environment that adapts to different work styles and needs.

In other words, it allows employees to be more productive, collaborate, and experience greater job satisfaction, regardless of whether they’re working in the office, remotely, or as part of a hybrid model.

Generally, a smart workplace consists of the following:

  • Internet of Things (IoT) devices: Includes smart thermostats, automatically adjustable lighting, intelligent office wayfinding tools, and occupancy sensors.
  • Artificial intelligence: Includes virtual assistants (such as Amazon Alexa), AI-powered chatbots, and booking systems.
  • Data analytics: Include tools for tracking workplace usage, analyzing HR data, and managing energy efficiency.

In short, a smart workplace evolves with its people—which is something that traditional offices can’t do.

Why Your Company Should Make Your Workplace Smarter

According to a report from Facts and Factors, the smart workplace market was valued at $37.42 billion in 2022 and is expected to grow to $81.48 billion by the end of 2030.

One of the main reasons companies continue to adopt these workplaces is that they help them stay competitive in areas such as employee engagement, productivity, and office costs.

This is because these advanced work environments offer:

  • Personalized experiences that enhance employee satisfaction
  • Optimized resource management to reduce operational costs
  • Data that can help managers make more strategic decisions

As companies are making their workplaces smarter, you should consider doing the same to avoid falling behind.

Now, let’s have a deeper look at the benefits these spaces provide.

Benefits of Smart Workplace Technology

Here are some benefits your company can gain by using smart technology in your workplace.

1. Enable Collaboration Regardless of the Location

Smart workspaces are especially helpful for companies that use a hybrid work model.

Employees in these companies have flexible schedules and often work in and out of the office.

Smart workplace technologies and solutions can streamline workflows and allow employees to collaborate no matter where everyone is located.

Video conferencing software lets teams meet face-to-face to brainstorm and problem-solve. Communication tools like Slack and Microsoft Teams offer instant messaging functions and file sharing.

By using a resource booking system such as OfficeRnD Workplace, employees can easily book desks and spaces based on their projects. This ensures they have all the necessary resources (including space, equipment, and access to team members).

Here are some ideas for improving your hybrid workplace so that there is enough space for each employee.

2. Increase Productivity

Smart workplaces can significantly increase productivity by offering solutions that make the office more comfortable.

For example, smart desks and chairs automatically adjust based on a person’s preferences. This reduces physical strain and discomfort, allowing the employee to focus.

Also, IoT-connected lighting and climate systems can adjust the temperature and lighting based on occupancy rates, time of day, and personal preferences—making it more comfortable for employees, while also reducing your utility bill.

Regarding smart apps, AI-powered tools, such as virtual assistants, can take over many administrative duties, such as scheduling meetings and sending reminders. This reduces the time employees take to complete low-level tasks and allows them to focus on big-picture projects instead.

3. Attract and Retain Top Talent

A smart workplace gives professionals the freedom and resources they require to maintain a healthy work-life balance. One study found that 50% of workers believe that new technologies improve their work-life balance by giving them more flexibility and helping them manage their time better. Technology also allows employees to be location-independent.

Aside from tech, workers are becoming increasingly health and safety conscious. IoT sensors can track air quality, and intelligent security systems monitor the office in real time to increase workplace safety.

4. Make Data-Driven Decisions

One of the more powerful benefits of smart workplaces is the ability to collect and analyze data from the work environment.

Smart technologies provide companies with insights into space usage and employee behavior so they can:

  • Optimize operations
  • Allocate resources better
  • Reduce overall operational costs

For example, workplace data tools, like OfficeRnD Workplace’s workplace analytics feature, can help companies optimize their footprint, thus saving money.

The 4 Key Solutions of Smart Workplaces

Here are four smart workplace solutions you should consider if you want to create a more secure, flexible, and productive environment for your employees.

1. Security Solutions

Security should be a top priority for any business, including technologies and systems to protect physical and digital assets. Here are some things you can implement:

  • Access control systems: Biometric authentication, keycard systems, or mobile app-based entry ensure that only authorized staff can enter certain areas.
  • Surveillance cameras integrated with AI and IoT: Surveillance cameras with AI and IoT abilities provide real-time monitoring and advanced analytics, including facial recognition and movement detection. These systems automatically alert you when there’s unusual activity.
  • Cybersecurity measures: Protecting sensitive digital information has become critical as more hackers steal valuable company information. Strong cybersecurity measures, like firewalls and regular vulnerability checks, can help protect your data from these attacks.

All this will also keep your workplace fully compliant.

2. Booking Solutions

Effective space management is essential for companies with employees who alternate between remote and on-site work. Smart space management software allows workers to book desks, meeting rooms, and other resources.

  • Desk bookings allow employees to reserve desks in advance, ensuring all staff members have a dedicated workspace when they come to the office.
  • Meeting room bookings allow employees to schedule meeting rooms with tools that integrate with their calendars to avoid conflicts and ensure meeting spaces are used efficiently.
  • Besides desks and meeting rooms, employees can also use tools to book other resources, such as parking spaces and equipment.

3. Space Usage Solutions

Optimizing space usage based on data-driven insights can help reduce operational costs.

Smart workplaces use occupancy sensors and booking systems to monitor how the space is used in real-time. This helps companies determine which spaces are overused and underused so they can make the necessary improvements.

With smart technology, companies can also use hot-desking, which allows staff to use workstations as needed. This reduces the need for permanent desks and enables companies to design their workplaces to be adaptable and collaborative.

4. Environmental Solutions

Environmental sustainability is becoming an increasingly important workplace factor for employees. This means companies must strive to implement more environmentally friendly practices to attract and retain talent. Some environmental solutions include:

  • Smart lighting: Automated lighting that adjusts based on occupancy and natural light levels, reducing energy consumption.
  • Climate control: Smart HVAC systems help keep the temperature comfortable by automatically adjusting it based on occupancy and external weather conditions.
  • Energy management: Energy management systems can help track and control energy usage across the workplace. This allows companies to identify inefficiencies and implement more sustainable practices to reduce their carbon footprint and save costs.

Considerations to Make Before Adopting Smart Technology

Here are some things companies need to consider before adopting smart solutions.

Scalability and Future-Proofing

Before choosing technology and systems, you need to consider whether they can handle future growth and changes in business needs. For example, if your company were to grow from 50 employees to 500 employees, would the booking system still work?

You also need to consider the provider. How likely are they to continue to provide updates? Will they support evolving requirements?

Integration With Existing Systems

Next, consider whether the systems and technology you plan on using are compatible with your company’s existing systems, such as Microsoft Teams, Google Workspace, and Slack.

A smart hybrid workplace management system such as OfficeRnD Workplace, for example, seamlessly integrates with your existing tech stack.

Also, determine whether the provider will help you fix problems with integration without affecting your current work.

Employee Training and Adoption

Forty-five percent of employees say they’ve had to learn new technology and tools for their work in the last year.

It’s important to provide your employees with the necessary training to use your new tools and systems.

When considering new technology, think about how easy it is to use and the training your employees require to get value out of the software or hardware.

Use OfficeRnD Workplace to Manage Your Smart Workplace

Smart workplaces are here to stay, and many employers appreciate this type of environment.

By using smart workplace technology, such as OfficeRnD Workplace to manage your workplace, you can make both work and people thrive.

These consultants can advise on everything in the coworking industry, from optimizing your office space to increasing your revenue and enhancing your presence in your community.

These consultants work with a wide variety of coworking business owners and community managers, so they know what works (and what doesn’t).

Consultants might also recommend a comprehensive system that covers most of your needs. Ultimately, this means you’ll spend less overall and your members can navigate through your customer-facing apps more easily.

#3 Efficient Space Management

Plus, they can provide insight into features that are currently trendy, which may help you attract new members.

They can also help you understand your occupancy rate and how to tailor activities and discounts in a way that encourages optimal space usage.

Even if you have the most efficient, attractive coworking space in the world, people have to know about it to come to it.

Test the Waters Before Diving In

Name: 5 Smart Space Solutions for a Better-Used Office [2026]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Smart space solutions are workplace tools, sensors, and software that use booking data, occupancy tracking, and analytics to match office space to how employees actually use it.
Post body:
Smart space solutions are workplace tools, sensors, and software that use booking data, occupancy tracking, and analytics to match office space to how employees actually use it.

With more return-to-office (RTO) mandates calling employees back to the office, there’s never been a better time for employers to reimagine their physical workspaces.

Going back to the office doesn’t have to mean rows of cubicles and returning to the status quo. Instead, it presents an opportunity for companies to improve their current processes and build better places for people to work and connect.

The pressure is real. CBRE found the share of companies enforcing office-attendance policies doubled to 37% in 2025, up from 17% a year earlier. Getting people in is only half the job; giving them space worth the trip is the other half.

This article will explain what smart space solutions are, explore their benefits, and shows how organizations are using them to get more from their office real estate and improve workplace experiences.

Quick Summary:

  • Smart space solutions help workplaces make the best use of their space and resources through technology.
  • The top five are desk booking, custom space booking (like meeting room booking), collaborative scheduling, smart hybrid scheduling, and data analytics.
  • These tools help teams get the space and resources they need to come together and collaborate in the office.
  • Desk booking, collaborative scheduling, smart hybrid scheduling, and analytics help companies improve the workplace experience and how well they use their offices.

What are Smart Space Solutions?

Smart space solutions use technology to make the most of physical office space. They help companies design more efficient workspaces that support in-office and remote collaboration.

Today’s tools can turn even a small floor into a productive workspace. Companies now use automation, sensors, and analytics to build smarter offices instead of packing people into fixed cubicles.

Aspects of Smart Space Solutions

Smart space solutions may involve one or more of the following:

  • Space planning. The analysis of trends, space usage, and the needs of employees.
  • Asset management. The storage and use of physical resources.
  • Occupancy tracking. The examination of who is using different resources.
  • Environmental control. Aspects like lighting, temperature, and acoustics.
  • Office wayfinding solutions such as digital signs and room displays

The rest of this article will discuss how technology can help address some of these aspects.

Benefits of Smart Space Solutions

Smart space solutions have many benefits, but they mainly focus on two things — using resources wisely and making work better for employees.

Let’s look at both of these aspects in greater detail.

Resource Optimization

Office space is one of the biggest costs a company carries, and much of it sits empty. CBRE put global office utilization at 53% in 2025, so companies still pay for roughly half a floor that goes unused on an average day.

With smart office automation and better space utilization, companies can make the most of what they have, even with a tight budget or limited resources.

Talent Retention

Most companies know how important it is to hire top talent who can catapult their business to success. This means attracting qualified new hires and retaining star employees.

Salary is one of many things employees weigh. The physical workplace shapes their day too, and the data backs it up. In Gensler’s 2026 Global Workplace Survey of more than 16,400 workers, people in high-performing workplaces were far more likely to say the office lets them do their best work and that they want to stay. Two-thirds said they “hack” their space to make up for what it lacks.

Showing up and not having the physical space or tools to do a job can be frustrating. With smart space solutions, companies can ensure all employees have easy access to everything they need.

Top 5 Smart Space Solutions

Here are five types of smart space solutions you can use to get more from your workplace.

Desk Booking

In a hybrid workplace where most employees don’t work in the office every day, many companies favor desk sharing.

This can be a way to use resources more efficiently and reduce wasted space. However, it can also lead to problems when more people show up to the office than there are desks.

Desk booking software allows employees to quickly check which rooms or desks are available so they can easily book a workspace. They don’t have to worry about coming into the office and not having a place to work.

Plus, with interactive office maps and desk booking tools, employees can see where their team members are working so they can reserve a spot nearby. Those needing a distraction-free work environment can check the map to find a quiet place to focus.

Other valuable features include:

  • Recurring bookings
  • Search filters
  • Dedicated desk assignments
  • Office “neighborhoods” for designated teams, projects, or functionsDesk sharing is now common. CBRE reports global office occupancy reached 111% in 2025, meaning companies book more shared desks than they physically assign one-to-one, which makes a booking system essential.

Custom Spaces Booking

Desks are a must in any office, but there are other spaces people need to use.

Other spaces that are often in demand include:

  • Conference and meeting rooms
  • Huddle rooms
  • Private spaces
  • Social spaces
  • Reception areas
  • Parking spaces

Fortunately, smart space technology can help with these, too.

With the right room booking system, organizations can better utilize all kinds of custom spaces to suit their needs.

Both managers and staff can pull up an interactive map showing a detailed office layout and who’s working where.

Reserving a desk for yourself is as easy as booking a conference room for a whole team or department. There’s also the option to add other services like catering requests or room setup for further convenience.

You can also add rules for specific spaces to ensure equal (or limited) access. For example, you might only want employees to be able to book one meeting room per week.

Collaborative Scheduling

Some hybrid workplaces have a big problem with not knowing who will be in the office on a given day. Most people want to use their office days effectively by coordinating with team members and colleagues, but this can be tricky.

For instance, one team may work together on Tuesdays and Thursdays, while another chooses to work on Mondays and Wednesdays. This way, everyone has access to the resources they need.

Collaborative scheduling solves this issue by giving everyone a breakdown of who will be in the office at any given time on any given day. It can also show which resources are available and who’s working in which parts of the office.

Teams can also use collaborative scheduling to save “favorite” team members so they can track their schedules and coordinate easily. It’s also helpful for managers who need to know when specific teams will be in the office.

Such software also provides an easy way to invite others into the office. Managers can even bulk-book desks to ensure everyone can work together.

Smart hybrid scheduling

The solutions outlined above rely on employees and managers to oversee workplace schedules to optimize office workspaces.

But if we want to be truly “smart,” we’d let technology play a helping hand in this process.

For example, Smart Hybrid Scheduling helps employees find the best days to come into the office based on their co-workers’ schedules and availability. This is huge for hybrid teams, making it much easier to plan where they’ll work (i.e., on-site vs remote) and coordinate with one another.

It’s also tailor-made for hybrid workplaces. Companies can use it to create and implement hybrid work policies, while employees can ensure their schedules comply with the rules.

When accessing the Hybrid Scheduler, everyone can see:

  • Shared days (invites received to work on a given day)
  • Required days (based on workplace policy)
  • Highlight days (based on favorite times to come into the office)

Advanced analytics

Any organization that genuinely cares about using its space well should hope to keep improving its approach over time. This requires using data to make decisions. Fortunately, smart space technology can do a great job of compiling that data.

Data-driven insights and advanced workplace analytics can help organizations on this front. It allows companies to track information such as whether team members adopt workplace policies, which resources are the most in demand, and the regularity of bookings.

Managers can use these insights to create custom dashboards to strategically plan and refine workplace policies over time.

How AI fits into smart space management

The tools above still lean on people to plan their week. AI changes that by reading patterns in your booking and occupancy data.

It can suggest the best day to come in based on when your team is already there, flag meeting rooms that get booked but sit empty, and turn months of attendance data into a plain-language read on what to change.

AI is already part of how people work. In Gensler’s 2026 survey, 30% of employees now count as “AI power users,” and they spend more time collaborating and learning than their peers, which puts more demand on the office as a place to meet.

The catch is data quality. CBRE found 55% of companies name it as their top challenge with AI, so clean booking and occupancy data is the starting point.

Best Practices for Smart Space Solutions

Taking an intelligent approach to the workplace is about more than just implementing specific technologies and sitting back. Here are some further best practices to keep in mind.

Set clear goals and a budget

There’s no one-size-fits-all approach to smart space solutions. Set your main objectives and budget to ensure you take the route that works for you.

For instance, is the main issue a lack of office space for all employees? Or is it a struggle with coordination within teams?

Once you know what you aim to achieve, choose technology that suits your current budget. You don’t need to implement everything, so determine the most effective way to achieve your goals.

Refine your approach as you go

When implementing smart space solutions, you may not get everything right on the first attempt. Instead of thinking this is a failure, accept that you will need to make changes along the way and involve your team in creating a better process.

Ask managers or employees from different departments to help you make decisions. Listen to their feedback once you start — you need to find out what works and what doesn’t. A pilot project with smart space solutions could be an excellent approach.

You may want to apply this to other hybrid workplace improvements, too.

Don’t overlook data security

Using smart solutions means putting a lot of potentially sensitive data on the cloud, so you must take extra measures to ensure everything is protected.

Suppose you don’t have anyone on your team to verify whether your processes are sound from a data security standpoint. In that case, it may be worth bringing in a cybersecurity consultant to assess potential vulnerabilities.

Make sure your processes and the tools you use take data security seriously. Look for:

  • SOC 2 compliant
  • Certified ISO 27001
  • GDPR compliant

Author: asen-stoyanchev

These shared workplaces provide opportunities for in-person connection and collaboration without the constraints of a traditional office.
Post body:
For remote workers feeling lonely at home and digital nomads struggling to find reliable WiFi in local coffee shops, coworking spaces are the answer. These shared workplaces provide opportunities for in-person connection and collaboration without the constraints of a traditional office.

As office attendance decreases in major cities, professionals are increasingly gravitating toward urban coworking spaces to stay productive without sacrificing the community feel of the office.

But while the flexible office market grows, so does the competition. So whether you’re considering opening an urban coworking space in 2024 or looking to optimize your existing location, we dive into the benefits, challenges, and strategies here.

Quick Summary

  • With U.S. office vacancies hitting record highs in recent years and office attendance still nowhere near its pre-pandemic average, it can be an advantageous time to open or grow an urban coworking space.
  • The challenges of running an urban coworking space in 2024 include high rent, increased competition, and difficulty building a consistent community.
  • Choosing a favorable location, prioritizing user experience, and marketing your space are among the best ways you can make your urban coworking space successful.

Why Urban Coworking Spaces Are on the Rise

Coworking spaces are booming in popularity. In 2018, only around 331,000 people in the U.S. used them, but by 2022, that number had increased to a whopping 1.08 million. And while 45% of coworking spaces in 2024 are in suburban areas, over half are in urban locations.

Who Uses Urban Coworking Spaces?

When establishing your coworking space in a city, it’s essential to understand what kind of crowd you’ll be catering to. These are the most common types of people who use urban coworking offices:

  • Freelancers
  • Remote employees
  • Hybrid employees
  • Digital nomads
  • Entrepreneurs
  • Traveling employees
  • Don’t forget dog owners

Here’s a more extensive list of the most common industries that use coworking spaces.

What Are the Advantages of Running an Urban Coworking Space in 2024?

If you know how to run an urban coworking space well, 2024 can be a great time to establish or expand one.

In an increasingly remote world, workers are looking for shared spaces to socialize and build a community. While over 30% of all workers in some urban areas (like San Francisco and Washington, D.C.) are remote, 23% of remote workers have cited loneliness from staying home to be a major challenge.

Plus, thanks to the pandemic, traditional office attendance is still low in big cities. Quarter four (Q4) of 2023 saw U.S. office vacancies hit a record high of 19.6%. Also, as of March 2024, office attendance in metro areas was only 62% of its pre-pandemic average, even on the busiest day of the week.

But just because people aren’t heading into their regular offices, doesn’t mean they don’t crave human connection and a well-run working space.

What Are the Challenges of Running a Coworking Space in the City?

While this can be a great time to run an urban coworking space, doing so can also come with a few challenges, including the following.

Higher Rent Than Suburban Areas

On average, office space is more expensive in urban areas than in suburban locations. In Q4 of 2023, the annual quoted rent in downtown offices was $53.30 per square foot on average, much higher than the $35 per square foot average in suburban areas.

When your rent is higher, it becomes even more important to maintain a high occupancy rate so you can turn a profit.

Increased Competition

There is plenty of opportunity in the urban coworking space niche — but also more competition. Amid major international brands like WeWork that people recognize and gravitate toward, it’s crucial to make your space stand out from the crowd.

Difficulty Building a Community

To keep your customers coming back to your space, you need to build a community.

When people could just work from home, a community is a major reason they’d go to a coworking space instead.

It can be difficult to build a community in urban areas where people tend to be more transient, and it’s harder to attract a consistent crowd. But if people don’t feel connected to your space, they may just work elsewhere, whether it’s from home or at a local coffee shop.

7 Tips for Running a Successful Urban Coworking Space

Now that you know the pros and cons of managing an urban coworking space, let’s look at the top ways you can make yours more successful.

Choose a Favorable Location

The location of your coworking space is hugely important, especially in an urban setting. The type of customers you’re looking to attract (such as freelancers and remote employees) will often choose a spot based on convenience.

So what makes for an ideal coworking space location?

Make sure the most commonly used methods of transportation are easily accessible from your building, whether it’s the subway, the bus, or a bike path. It’s also ideal to have a few coffee and lunch spots within walking distance.

If possible, choose a central area in the business district of your city, located near other office buildings. Not only will this help you attract more customers than if you set up shop in a quiet neighborhood, but it can give your space a more professional feel.

Understand Your Coworking Community’s Needs

Before you put your new ideas in motion, it’s important to gain an understanding of what your customers need (and want) out of their coworking spaces. Then, tailor yours to fit your specific community.

For example, if your building is in an artsy neighborhood, you may attract a lot of people in creative professions. What supplies do they need to keep them coming back? Do they look for an open environment where they can talk while they work, or do they want private rooms where they can get in the zone?

Or, if your space is close to an airport, your consistent customer base may include digital nomads and employees traveling for business. How can you make them feel at home for a few days in a foreign environment?

Considering these kinds of questions will help foster happy workers and a memorable experience.

Optimize Your Layout

As people increasingly gravitate toward coworking spaces, they’re looking for access to many of the same features that private offices provide.

Aside from just a desk and chair, they may need meeting rooms, lunch rooms, private rooms for taking calls, and areas set aside for quiet work.

Again, you’ll want to get a solid understanding of what your community needs before you establish your office layout. Then use this data to figure out how many private rooms and how much open space you’ll need. Also, determine how many people you’ll need to accommodate each day.

When done properly, you can avoid both wasted office space and overcrowding. By the way, check out these space utilization metrics that every operator must track.

Figuring out this information ahead of time can also help you avoid overspending on rent and understand where you’ll profit the most. For example, knowing that coworking operators make 61% of their revenue from renting desks, but 10% comes from meeting offices and 10% from event rooms, you can optimize your space for desk use.

Last but not least, make sure to improve your space’s accessibility.

Prioritize User Experience

The more straightforward your space is to navigate, the more likely you’ll be to entice repeat customers.

Since you’re dealing with a wide range of independent professionals, teams, and schedules, implement an easy-to-use desk and meeting room booking system. The right software can help eliminate confusion and double booking, along with other frustrating issues like passive occupancy and ghost booking.

Aside from optimizing your user experience, a coworking space management platform can provide useful insight into who your customers are and how they’re using your space.

With OfficeRnD Flex, for example, your users can easily access a real-time view of which areas are open to book, so they’ll never have to deal with double bookings.

Market Your Space

With so much competition in the coworking space market, it’s crucial to advertise your location well. The better your marketing strategy, the more customers you’ll attract, the more you’ll stand out, and the more well-known your business will become.

To help your space stand out, create a distinct brand that’s geared toward your community. A few marketing methods you can utilize include:

  • Social media
  • Online listings
  • Digital advertising
  • In-person networking with your community
  • Establishing relationships with local shops
  • Email marketing

Consider offering free trials to potential members.

Automate Your Billing Process

Spending too much time stuck in the weeds of administrative tasks can take away from the important ones, like marketing your space and interacting with your community. And yet, you need to get paid.

Instead of juggling a million different spreadsheets, systems, and email threads, streamline your billing and payment processes into one unified coworking management system.

For example, it can be helpful to purchase adjustable desk chairs, since people of different heights may be using them on a daily basis.

Plants, flowers, and plenty of natural light can turn a workday into a more pleasant experience, especially if your customers don’t have those things at home.
