Post body:
Designing a coworking space in a way that will not only attract more members but keep them coming back again and again can be difficult.

How do you know what layout and furniture will resonate with your members? What mix of private and collaborative spaces should you use? How flexible should you make your design?

And what can you do to make your coworking space feel right? What features can you use to build a space that will help people feel inspired, creative, and ready to tackle the world?

To help you design the perfect space, we’ve put together a list of 10 creative coworking spaces. We also provide you with some additional tips for making your space unique.

Quick Summary

  • Creative coworking spaces can take on many different designs based on the target market and your location.
  • You can improve your coworking design by adding open space, natural light, and plants.
  • Coworking spaces with unique design elements and colors are usually more memorable and attract people in creative roles.

10 Examples of Creative Coworking Spaces to Draw Inspiration From

Here are ten creative coworking spaces that you can use as inspiration for your business.

Have you heard of OfficeRnD Flex? It's a super easy-to-use coworking booking platform.

1. Dojo – Bali

Dojo is a coworking space located a one-minute walk from Echo Beach. It embraces the beach and tropical atmosphere with unique decor. It features a mixture of:

  • Rustic wooden furniture
  • Lush greenery
  • Open-air workspaces
  • Blackboards with sticky notes

Its use of natural materials and open layouts, combined with the outdoors (including a swimming pool), gives the space a laid-back vibe that fits perfectly with the island’s tropical environment.

(Image Source)

Why this design works:

Dojo’s design appeals to remote workers and digital nomads who seek a balance of productivity and relaxation, giving them the perfect work-life balance.

2. Luminary – New York

Luminary is a female-founded coworking space that mainly caters to women but is also open to men. It has an elegant design that creates a welcoming atmosphere, including:

  • Brick walls
  • Chic furniture
  • A warm color palette
  • Cushioned chairs and lounges

The space has a mix of private offices, open spaces, and comfortable lounges. It’s perfect for professionals who work alone or with a team.

(Image Source)

Why this design works:

Luminary focuses on providing a supportive and women-centric environment with high-end amenities (including beauty rooms and fitness areas)—attracting female entrepreneurs and professionals.

3. The Work Project – Hong Kong

The Work Project is known for its luxurious design, combining beauty and function. It has lots of natural light and different types of workspaces, including open desks, couches, and private rooms.

The space features:

  • Tall ceilings
  • High-quality furniture
  • Art-inspired interiors
  • A vertical garden

The goal of the space is to provide a luxurious and productive work environment, with the company’s website reading, “Customised to maximize.”

(Image Source)

Why this design works:

The space attracts professionals and businesses that value great design and comfort. It provides a premium experience that enhances productivity by allowing people to relax and focus.

4. Pathwork – Paris

Pathwork is designed for artists, designers, and creative entrepreneurs. So, it’s no wonder the space uses a mixture of comfortable chairs, communal areas, and vibrant colors to create an electric and artistic atmosphere.

The space features:

  • A vibrant design
  • Quirky furniture
  • Colorful art
  • Unique lighting
  • Lots of plants

(Image Source)

Why this design works:

Its homey design inspires creativity and appeals to artists and freelancers who want a space to work solo or collaboratively.

5. Neuehouse Coworking – New York

Neuehouse Coworking is a one-of-a-kind coworking space with a timeless design, giving the impression that you’re in a cultural museum. It has private offices, open desks, social spaces, a podcast studio, and comfortable lounge areas.

The space features:

  • Mid-century furniture
  • Cultural art
  • A sun terrace

(Image Source)

Why this design works:

Neuehouse Coworking is perfect for creative individuals looking to work in a space rich with history and cultural significance. It tends to attract a younger audience (including Millenials and Gen Z), but all ages are welcome.

6. Ministry of New – Mumbai

The Ministry of New is a bright and open space with light wood furniture, clean lines, and soft colors. It was designed to be a place to escape the busy city of Mumbai.

The space features:

  • Scandinavian-inspired furniture
  • Large windows for natural light
  • Colorful plants
  • White walls

(Image Source)

Why this design works:

The space is intentionally designed to create a calm and aesthetically appealing environment. It appeals to creative professionals and entrepreneurs looking for a peaceful workplace while still feeling connected to the vibrant city. By the way, check out this guide if you’re interested in learning what makes urban coworking spaces successful.

7. Crew Collective & Cafe – Montreal

Crew Collective & Cafe is a spectacular place to work, featuring a blend of historic and contemporary design. Housed in a former bank, the building is big and dates back to 1920.

Things that make this space unique include:

  • 50-foot vaulted ceilings
  • Hung chandeliers
  • Vintage furniture
  • Long communal tables
  • Marble floors

The architect created separate areas for coworking members, employees, meeting room renters, and cafe visitors.

(Image Source)

Why this design works:

The unique combination of historic architecture and modern amenities attracts creatives, professionals, and remote workers who want to work alone or as a team.

8. THRIVE – USA

THRIVE provides a professional atmosphere with modern workstations and a clean and functional design.

Catering primarily to businesses, it offers several workspace options. These include dedicated desks, private offices, meeting and event spaces, and other adaptable spaces.

The space has:

  • Ergonomic furniture
  • Quiet zones
  • Local culture design elements (including art, decor, and furniture)

(Image Source)

Why this design works:

The clean layout and various workstation options attract businesses and remote workers looking for a space to collaborate and be more productive.

9. Toong – Vietnam

Toong combines traditional Vietnamese design with modern coworking space furniture and amenities. It has a warm and inviting atmosphere and a strong sense of local culture.

The space features the following:

  • Vietnamese architecture and art
  • Hundreds of pieces of mica (to represent different cultures and reflect the international spirit)
  • Close-up fine art photography
  • Natural materials, including bamboo, wood, and stone

(Image Source)

Why this design works:

The space attracts a diverse crowd, including locals and expatriates who appreciate the culturally rich and beautiful workspace.

10. The Hive – Hong Kong

Besides a really cool name, The Hive offers a gorgeous, minimalist, and functional work environment for startups, freelancers, and small businesses. It’s an excellent space for community and creativity with a mix of hot desks, private offices, and event spaces.

The space includes the following:

  • Rooftop terraces
  • Cafes
  • Light-colored wood furniture
  • Clean design
  • Plenty of natural light

(Image Source)

Why this design works:

The Hive’s space design is ideal for a variety of working professionals, from freelancers to business owners, because it’s flexible and fun. It encourages people to work together and network.

Tips for Designing a Creative Coworking Space

With the coworking space market valued at over $13 billion in 2022 and projected to grow by 14.9% from 2023 to 2030, ensuring your space stands out from the competition is crucial.

Now that you’ve seen some other creative coworking spaces that are killing it, let’s look at some additional tips you can implement to make your space even better

Create an Open Workspace

Open workspaces promote collaboration and creativity. You can cater to different working styles depending on your target audience by providing different workstations and seating options.

For example, you can include communal tables for those who want to work in teams, cozy nooks for those who want to work alone, and semi-private open areas for people who prefer a bit more privacy without feeling completely isolated.

You can make your membership experience better by using a tool like OfficeRnd Flex to help manage bookings. This way, members can easily reserve desks or meeting rooms based on their needs.

Add Enclosed Offices and Meeting Rooms

Open physical spaces are great for working together, but some of your members may need more privacy. This is especially true if you’re serving remote workers and company teams.

In this case, including enclosed offices and meeting rooms in your coworking space layout is necessary. You can make these spaces more conducive and productive by including:

  • Soundproofing
  • Whiteboards
  • Video conferencing equipment

Incorporate Proper Branding Elements

You can differentiate your coworking space by giving it a specific color. According to the Digital School of Marketing, branding is pivotal in attracting clients. Branding includes the colors you use on your walls, your furniture, and the style of your website.

Choose colors that represent the feelings you want your audience to associate with your space and brand. For example, according to colorpsychology.org, red is associated with energy and power, while green is associated with growth and harmony.

Use Ergonomic and Comfortable Furniture

Comfort is non-negotiable in workspaces. Investing in ergonomic furniture will support your members’ health and boost their productivity by providing a comfortable working environment. Make sure you:

  • Incorporate quality seating that caters to different body types.
  • Create relaxation zones with comfortable sofas and lounge chairs that allow members to take a break and recharge.

Consider Technology and Connectivity

Make sure that your space has high-speed internet in all areas to minimize downtime or frustration for your members.

Also, provide your members with access to tech equipment, including printers, scanners, and video conferencing tools so that they can complete all their work in your space.

Lastly, ensure you have plenty of power outlets available so your members can easily charge their phones and laptops regardless of where they’re sitting.

Enrich the Space With Natural Light and Plants

Natural light and plants create a more welcoming environment for your members. Try placing workstations close to the windows and adding many plants to help improve air quality and provide a calming atmosphere.

Post body:
In a dynamic, shared workspace, the flow of visitors – whether potential members, business partners, or delivery personnel – is constant. Effectively managing these visitors is crucial for running a successful business. Handling guests efficiently ensures seamless check-ins and smooth operations and reflects the professionalism and culture of your office community.

When visitor management is done well, it creates a welcoming atmosphere, reinforces trust, and enhances the overall experience for employees and guests alike. Additionally, quality visitor management ensures safety for all who frequent your establishment.

In this article, we’ll explore the strategies and intricacies of how to handle visitors in the office.

Quick Summary

Here are five key strategies and tips for handling office visitors effectively:

  • Use a Robust Visitor Management System: Implement a digital visitor management system, like OfficeRnD Workplace’s Visitor Hub, to streamline check-ins, pre-register visitors, and send real-time notifications. This enhances the guest experience, improves security, and reduces administrative burden.
  • Establish Clear Visitor Policies: Develop comprehensive visitor policies, including sign-in/out procedures, identification requirements, visitor badges, access levels, and confidentiality agreements, ensuring security and professionalism while managing guest flow.
  • Create a Welcoming Environment: Design an inviting reception area with comfortable seating, refreshments, and personalized interactions. A clean, organized space signals professionalism and enhances first impressions.
  • Train Reception Staff: Equip reception staff with skills in greeting guests warmly, managing check-ins efficiently, and balancing security with a friendly atmosphere. Regular training on communication, conflict resolution, and office protocols is essential.
  • Manage Visitor Flow Proactively: Use appointment scheduling tools to plan visits, reduce bottlenecks, and ensure smooth operations. Clear communication with guests about arrival procedures, parking, and check-in protocols also minimizes confusion.

How to Handle Visitors in the Office: Preparation

Preparation is the first step in ensuring a smooth and professional guest experience. Being proactive in your preparation allows you to create a welcoming environment, make a great first impression, and set the tone for all interactions going forward.

A clear visitor management process ensures that guests feel acknowledged and respected, while also helping your team stay organized and informed.

Whether it’s establishing visitor sign-in protocols, setting up identification procedures, or obtaining access approval, being well-prepared to handle whatever is thrown your way will minimize disruptions and set you up for continued success.

Enhance your office experience with the OfficeRnD Visitor Management Hub, designed to streamline visitor check-ins, improve office security, and ensure a seamless, branded visitor journey. Transform your workplace – get started today with OfficeRnD Visitor Hub!

Establishing a Visitor Policy

A well-defined visitor policy serves as the foundation for maintaining security, professionalism, and a frictionless visitor experience in your workplace. The purpose of this policy is to set clear guidelines for managing visitors, ensuring that everyone entering the space is accounted for and understands the expectations.

Key components of a comprehensive visitor policy include:

  • Visitor Sign-In/Sign-Out Process: Require all visitors to sign in upon arrival, preferably through a digital system. Likewise, have visitors sign out as they leave to help keep track of who is in the building at any given time. This becomes particularly important if any type of crisis occurs (i.e. a fire alarm). Establish clear expectations for checking out visitors, returning badges, and logging their exit times.
  • Identification Requirements: Request valid identification from visitors to verify their identity. This adds an extra layer of security and ensures that only authorized individuals enter the workspace.
  • Visitor Badges or Passes: Provide badges or temporary passes that clearly identify visitors, distinguishing them from members and staff. This helps employees easily recognize guests and improves overall security.
  • Host Responsibilities: Clearly define the duties of the staff hosting visitors, such as ensuring guests are properly checked in, informed of relevant rules, and escorted during their stay. Confirm hosts understand their guest is their responsibility.
  • Visitor Access Levels: Specify which areas of the office visitors are allowed to access. Limit access to private offices, sensitive areas, or employee-only zones unless accompanied by a host.
  • Confidentiality and Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs): Include requirements for visitors to sign confidentiality agreements if they might be exposed to sensitive information. This is especially important if clients, contractors, or partners frequently visit.
  • Visitor Etiquette and Conduct: Outline behavioral expectations for visitors, such as maintaining noise levels, respecting shared spaces, and adhering to community guidelines.
  • Health and Safety Protocols: Address health and safety measures, such as emergency procedures, building access restrictions, and hygiene practices – this is particularly relevant in a post-pandemic context.
  • Data Protection and Privacy: Include policies on how visitor data is collected, stored, and used, ensuring compliance with data protection regulations like GDPR.

These components help create a structured and secure environment, ensuring that visitor management aligns with the values and operational needs of your workplace.

Are you using the right hybrid work management software?

Communicating Visitor Policies

Effectively communicating the policy is just as important as its content. Employees should be trained on the procedures and encouraged to enforce them consistently.

Consider incorporating the policy into onboarding materials and holding regular refreshers. For visitors, displaying the policy at the entrance, integrating it into the check-in process, and providing a brief overview upon arrival can help ensure understanding.

In being prepared and setting clear expectations, you’ll create a secure and welcoming environment for everyone. In effectively communicating your policies, you’ll ensure a safe and effective operation that will thrive for years to come.

Creating a Welcoming Environment

The reception area of a workplace is more than just a waiting room – it’s the gateway to your community. The moment visitors walk in, they begin forming opinions about your office.

A warm, inviting reception area isn’t just about looking good; it’s about setting the tone for the visitor experience, making guests feel at ease, and showcasing the culture of your workplace.

Part of being prepared is being ready to accept a guest, both in your appearance and demeanor, as well as having a clean, organized space for them to enter into.

Also, how’s your office wayfinding? Is it easy to navigate? These are some important questions to answer.

The Power of First Impressions

A clean and organized reception area signals professionalism and care. Cluttered surfaces, outdated materials, or scattered supplies can make a space feel chaotic and unwelcoming. Regularly tidying up and ensuring everything is in its place can transform this area into a beacon of calm and order.

A well-maintained area suggests that your workplace is runnning smoothly and that attention to detail matters.

Tips for Creating an Inviting Reception Area

  • Comfortable Seating for All: Invest in seating that is not only stylish but also comfortable. A mix of seating options, from cozy armchairs to sleek sofas, caters to different preferences. Whether someone is waiting for a meeting or just dropping by to check out the space, a comfy seat can make their wait enjoyable. Here’s a list of the best office furniture brands.
  • Offer Refreshments: Offering coffee, team, or infused water instantly elevates the experience. A thoughtfully arranged refreshment station with a few light snacks adds a touch of hospitality, showing guests their comfort matters.
  • Curated Reading Materials: Keep a well-curated selection of reading materials that reflect your community’s mission and interests. Quality magazines, industry publications, and even books authored by members can entertain guests while subtly highlighting the vibrant culture of your workplace.
  • Warm Lighting and Thoughtful Decor: The right lighting can make your reception area feel both cozy and energizing. Natural light is ideal, but warm, well-placed lamps and subtle decor, like plants and artwork, create a welcoming ambiance that feels alive and personable. It can be a nice gesture to display artwork created by your team for an added sense of community and support.
  • Personalized Interactions: Nothing beats a friendly smile and a genuine greeting. Train your front desk team to not only assist but to engage with visitors. A thoughtful chat, a sincere compliment, or a helpful recommendation can go a long way in leaving a lasting impression that a simple sign-in kiosk might miss.

When you invest in creating a welcoming reception area, you’re not just designing a space – you’re crafting an experience.

Every detail, from seating to signage, contributes to making visitors feel like they’re stepping into a community where they belong, even if it’s just for a brief moment.

Think about it, if you entered into a serene oasis that was friendly, welcoming, and highlighted the little details, wouldn’t you be more curious about the larger ones?

Training Reception Staff

Reception staff are the heart and soul of your workplace, setting the tone for every visitor’s experience.

A well-trained receptionist does more than just manage the front desk – they become ambassadors for your brand, creating an atmosphere of warmth, professionalism, and efficiency.

Investing in comprehensive training to support your staff ensures that your reception team is equipped with the skills and qualities needed to make every interaction memorable.

Skills and Qualities of an Effective Receptionist

The best receptionists are more than just polite – they’re empathetic, resourceful, and excellent communicators.

An effective receptionist combines a welcoming demeanor with quick problem-solving abilities, ensuring that visitors feel at ease while getting the assistance they need. They’re detail-oriented, able to juggle multiple tasks without losing focus and maintain a calm, professional presence even during busy times.

Strong interpersonal skills and a genuine passion for customer service make a receptionist not just the first point of contact, but a key contributor to the overall reception experience.

Training Topics for Reception Staff

Though you may hire the perfect candidate, ongoing training and support is necessary. Here are some topics that would be beneficial to your team to train on:

  • Greeting Visitors with Styles and Substance: The first impression is everything. Training should focus on how to greet visitors warmly, with a personalized touch that makes each guest feel valued. Role-playing different scenarios, from welcoming potential members to assisting delivery personnel, can help staff master the art of making everyone feel like a priority.
  • Handling Questions Like a Pro: Visitors often have a range of questions, from simple directions to detailed inquiries. Receptionists need to be well-versed in everything the your business has to offer so they can provide accurate, helpful information on the spot. Training should include deep dives into everything important about your business, coupled with practice sessions on clear, confident communication.
  • Intro to Sales: While front desk teams don’t necessarily have “sales” in their titles, some light selling skills can also be beneficial. You never know, the next person to walk through the door could be on the hunt for the product you sell, and a well-versed receptionist thoroughly explaining all of your offerings could just close the deal.
  • Maintaining Security with a Smile: Balancing a welcoming environment with strict security protocols is crucial in a welcoming environment. Receptionists need to be trained on the visitor sign-in process, identification checks, and how to handle access control without compromising the friendly atmosphere.

A well-trained receptionist does more than just manage the constant flow of people. By focusing on both technical skills and interpersonal qualities, your reception team will feel confident about how to handle visitors in the office.

Managing Visitor Flow

In busy, thriving offices, visitor flow can quickly become chaotic without a well-coordinated system in place. Managing visitor flow is all about striking the perfect balance between efficiency and hospitality, ensuring that guests move seamlessly from entry to exit without feeling rushed or overlooked.

Whether handling a morning rush of clients or guiding a steady stream of deliveries, there are core strategies that help optimize visitor flow while maintaining the welcoming vibe your workplace is known for.

Scheduling and Appointments

An efficient visitor flow starts long before a guest steps through the doors. It begins with smart scheduling and well-organized appointments.

When your office adopts a proactive approach to visitor management, you can avoid bottlenecks, reduce wait times, and create a stress-free experience for guests, and staff.

The Importance of Schedule Appointments

Scheduling appointments allows your team to anticipate visitor needs, prepare ahead of time, and allocate resources effectively.

By planning visits, you can prevent overcrowding at peak times and ensure that each guest receives the attention they deserve. Structured scheduling also helps reception staff manage multiple arrivals without scrambling, allowing them to be prepared and stay organized.

Tools and Software for Managing Visitor Appointments

  • Compliant, Safe, and Secure Workplace: Pre-register visitors, obtain access, and allow guests to sign legal documents prior to arrival.

Best Practices for Communicating Appointment Details

Clear and timely communication ensures that visitors arrive well-prepared and know exactly what to expect. Here are some strategies to elevate this process:

  • Provide a Personalized Experience: Personalize appointment confirmations and reminders with the visitor’s name and relevant details, such as who they’re meeting or the purpose of the visit. This shows attention to detail and creates a welcoming atmosphere from the start.
  • Include Clear Directions and Parking Information: Make it easy for visitors to find your office by including detailed directions and information about parking. Consider offering a map or a “directions” link to a navigation tool for added support. OfficeRnD Workplace is also an intuitive parking booking software that you can use to organize visitors’ parking spotts.
  • Share Check-In Procedures: Clearly outline what visitors need to do upon arrival. For example, provide instructions on where to sign in, any required documentation (i.e. an ID), and how they’ll be greeted by the host or reception team. This will also serve as a reminder to bring specific documentation should it be required.
  • Send Digital Calendar Invites: Send calendar invites that include all relevant details, such as the appointment time, location, and contact information. Integrating this with tools like Google Calendar, Outlook, or Microsoft Teams allows visitors to have easy access and set reminders.
  • Offer Virtual Assistance: If visitors have the option to attend virtually, include details about how to join, including any relevant links, dial-in numbers, or meeting passcodes. Offering hybrid options can be particularly useful for remote workers or those traveling from out of town.
  • Set Expectations for Arrival Time: Encourage visitors to arrive a few minutes early by clearly stating recommended arrival times. This ensures they have time to sign in and get settled without feeling rushed.
  • Provide Contact Information for Assistance: Include contact details for someone on your team who can help with any last-minute questions or directions. Having a direct line or email available reassures visitors that help is just a call away.
  • Follow Up with Reminders: Send a friendly reminder email or text message 24 – 48 hours before the appointment. This reminder can recap key details and reduce the chances of no-shows.
  • Make Your Communications Mobile-Friendly: Many visitors will access appointment details on their mobile devices, so ensure that emails, links, and documents are optimized for mobile viewing and easy navigation.
  • Use Clear, Simple Language: Avoid jargon and overly technical terms. Communicate the essentials in a straightforward manner, ensuring that visitors of all backgrounds can easily understand the information provided.

Visitor Check-In Process

The visitor check-in process is the cornerstone of effective visitor management. It’s where first impressions are solidified and the tone for a seamless visit is set.

A smooth check-in not only enhances the visitor experience but also helps maintain order and security in your office.

Whether you’re using a high-tech digital system or sticking with a traditional manual approach (such an Excel visitor log template), refining this process is key to managing visitor flow efficiently.

Steps for an Efficient Check-In Process

  • Pre-Registration and Appointment Confirmation: Encourage members to pre-register their guests before arrival. This speeds up check-in, as visitor details are already in the system. Sending a confirmation email with directions, check-in instructions, and any necessary visitor requirements can help prepare guests in advance.
  • Welcome and Identification: Greet visitors warmly and verify their identity. If using a digital check-in system, visitors can sign in using a tablet, laptop, or kiosk. For manual check-ins, provide a clear sign-in sheet where they can log their details. Efficient identification ensures that the right people gain access while maintaining a secure environment.
  • Host Notification: Once checked in, the system or receptionist should notify the host that their visitor has arrived. Automated notifications via SMS, email, or communication channels (i.e. Microsoft Teams) can quickly alert members, minimizing wait times and keeping the visitor flow steady.
  • Issuing Visitor Badges: Provide visitors with a temporary badge or pass, making it easy to identify them as guests. This step is essential for maintaining security.
  • Clear Instructions on Next Steps: Direct visitors on where to go next, whether it’s guiding them to a specific office, meeting room, or waiting area. Clear, friendly instructions help avoid confusion and maintain smooth movement throughout the space.

Digital Check-In vs. Manual Check-In Systems

In today’s tech-driven world, digital check-in systems offer a range of benefits, including speed, automation, and enhanced security.

Tools like OfficeRnD Visitor Hub streamline the process by allowing pre-registration, capturing visitor data, and sending real-time notifications. This greatly reduces time and effort and provides the guest with a top-notch experience.

However, many workplaces are still operating under manual check-in protocols. While this can be effective in smaller organizations, the chance of errors is significant and you run the risk of slowing down the process and extending wait times.

With a manual process, staying organized, communicating clearly, and keeping well-maintained records is a must.

Ensuring Visitor Privacy and Data Security

Regardless of how you manage check-ins, protecting visitor data is essential. For digital systems, make sure they comply with data protection regulations, such as GDPR or CCPA.

Use encrypted storage, limit access to authorized personnel, and set data retention policies that automatically delete visitor information after a specified period.

For manual systems, avoid leaving visitor logs in plain view and securely store records after each day. Privacy policies should be communicated clearly during the check-in process, so visitors know their data is handled with care.

Whether you choose a digital solution, stick with traditional methods, or blend them together, the goal is the same – to ensure every guest’s journey, from arrival to departure, is smooth and

secure. A well-structured check-in process does just that.

Escorting Visitors

A guest’s experience doesn’t stop at the reception desk, and escorting visitors around the office is more than just guiding them from point A to point B.

Taking the time to show people around and strike up a conversation is an opportunity to showcase the hospitality, professionalism, and vibrancy of your workplace.

Protocol for Escorting Visitors to Their Destinations

The journey from reception to a visitor’s destination should be smooth and well-coordinated. This is often overlooked when processes are created but is an essential part of the guest experience.

Once a visitor has checked in, a staff member should promptly greet them, confirm their destination, and accompany them directly to the relevant area – be it a private office, meeting room, or event space.

During the escort, a brief introduction to the office layout and/or most important areas can enhance the experience, offering a glimpse into the community’s atmosphere.

Escorting visitors also ensures they don’t accidentally wander into restricted areas, keeping both guests and members safe.

Assigning Staff Members to Escort Visitors

To maintain efficient visitor flow, it can be helpful to have designated staff members to escort guests around the office.

Receptionists are often the first choice as they are the first point of contact when a visitor arrives, but depending on the layout and the size of your office, having extra support from other team members during peak times is also beneficial.

Clearly defining roles and responsibilities, with staff rotating duties and assignments, prevents delays and ensures a visitor is never left waiting or unacknowledged.

In offices that have visitor management systems such as the Visitor Hub, for example, hosts can also receive notifications that their visitor has arrived.

This allows for a seamless handoff. The guest will see the capabilities of your technology while your team continues to manage multiple guests efficiently.

Handling Unexpected or Unscheduled Visitors

Part of knowing how to handle visitors in the office is knowing how to handle unexpected or unscheduled visitors.

Surprise visits are inevitable, but how you handle them makes all the difference. When an unscheduled visitor arrives, the first step is to assess their needs.

A friendly greeting followed by a professional “How may I assist you?” will help you determine next steps.

If they need to meet with someone who’s unavailable, front desk staff should offer to schedule a formal appointment or suggest alternative solutions.

For unexpected guests like delivery personnel or walk-ins curious about your office, providing clear, concise assistance keeps visitor flow intact without disrupting appointments that are scheduled.

In cases where an immediate escort isn’t possible, offering a comfortable waiting area with refreshments and reading materials shows that every visitor is valued, even during busy moments.

Ensuring Security and Confidentiality

Many offices are unique in that diverse businesses and workers share the same space. This does however require a more sophisticated security and confidentiality approach.

As new faces enter and exit throughout the day, guaranteeing that sensitive information remains protected and that your community feels secure requires strategic planning and clear protocols.

Visitor Identification

Visitor identification is the first line of defense in maintaining security and confidentiality within your workplace.

Striking the right balance between verifying identities and preserving a warm, community-oriented environment can be challenging, but it’s essential to protect both your employees and their sensitive information.

Why Visitor Identification Matters

Unfamiliar faces tend to blend in amid humming offices, making it vital to have a system that confirms who is entering and why.

Confirming identities helps prevent security breaches and ensures that only authorized people are granted access to specific areas.

This process is vital for maintaining a safe, productive environment where members can focus on their work without worrying about who might be wandering the halls.

Best Practices for Visitor Identification

There are several easy ways to effectively identify visitors, each offering varying levels of security while keeping things friendly and straightforward. Some include:

  • Pre-Registered Guests: Encouraging team members to pre-register their visitors can speed up the process and enhance security. With pre-registration, details like the visitor’s name, reason for visit, and expected arrival time are already in the system, allowing for a smooth check-in experience upon arrival.
  • Visitor Badges: Upon arrival, visitors should receive a badge or pass that identifies them as guests. This temporary identification makes it clear that they are authorized to be in specific areas while also serving as a subtle reminder to other colleagues that a guest is present. Badges can be color-coded, numbered, or even display the visitor’s name and host, making it easy for staff and members to recognize guests at a glance.
  • Digital Check-In and Photo Capture: Digital check-in systems are the easiest and safest way to sign guests into your space. They save time and cut down on manual spreadsheets that are outdated and not secure. Have every guest check-in through your portal for the most secure process.
  • Visitor Logbooks: For organizations using manual systems, maintaining a detailed visitor logbook helps track who enters and exits the space each day. While it may seem basic, this logbook serves as an important reference in the event of any security issues, offering quick access to visitor information.
  • Access Restrictions and Escort Protocols: Not every area in an office is open to visitors. Ensure that your identification system is tied to access permissions, allowing only certain individuals into restricted zones. Escorting guests from reception to their intended destination is another effective way to maintain confidentiality and ensure that visitors are only in approved spaces.

Balancing Security with a Friendly Atmosphere

While security is paramount, it’s equally as important to maintain the welcoming, community-driven vibe that great offices are known for.

This balance can be achieved through thoughtful communication and subtle integration of security practices.

Ensure that reception staff greets visitors warmly when verifying their identity. While you want to hold your security measures to a high standard, check-ins shouldn’t feel like an interrogation.

Hiring capable staff and training them to be friendly and engaging during this process will go a long way in making your guests feel comfortable and your members at ease.

Furthermore, designing visitor badges or passes that are visually appealing and align with your brand’s image makes the process feel less transactional.

Providing clear signage and easy-to-understand instructions at reception can also help guests feel more confident in your establishment. By blending secure identification practices with a personable approach, you ensure that both security and hospitality coexist, creating an office where everyone feels safe and welcome.

Confidentiality Measures

From protecting trade secrets to securing client information, offices must implement robust measures to ensure that sensitive data stays out of sight and away from unintended eyes.

Here’s how your workplace e can strike the right balance between transparency and confidentiality.

Keeping Sensitive Information Out of Sight

In open workspaces, where desks, screens, and documents are often visible to anyone walking by, it’s essential to create practices that protect confidential information. Encourage team members to use privacy screens for their laptops or position their workstations away from high-traffic areas.

Additionally, providing lockable storage units for files and personal items ensures that sensitive documents aren’t left exposed. Implementing a clean desk policy, where employees are encouraged to clear their workspaces at the end of the day, helps reduce the risk of accidental exposure.

Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs) for Visitors

For offices hosting clients, contractors, or service providers, having visitors sign a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) before entering the workspace is a smart precaution.

An NDA sets clear expectations, ensuring that any information seen or heard during their visit remains confidential.

While some visitors may be familiar with NDAs, it’s important to present the process in a friendly, straightforward manner, emphasizing that it’s a standard practice to protect everyone’s business interests.

Secure Areas and Restricted Access Policies

Not all areas of an office are created equal. While common areas are designed for open collaboration, private offices, meeting rooms, and certain storage facilities often house sensitive materials that require added protection.

Implementing restricted access policies, such as keycard systems, password-protected entry, or staff escorts, ensures that only authorized personnel can enter secure zones. Signage indicating restricted access areas is a subtle but effective way to prevent unintentional breaches.

Combining Security and Confidentiality with Community

Confidentiality measures should be seamlessly integrated into the day-to-day operations of your workplace.

By offering tools and guidelines that protect information, encouraging NDAs when necessary, and designating secure areas with controlled access, you can create a safe environment where businesses can grow.

When confidentiality is prioritized alongside security, members can confidently collaborate and engage, knowing their sensitive information is well-guarded.

Handling Special Situations

While most visitor interactions are straightforward, unexpected situations can arise that require quick thinking and flexibility.

Whether it’s an unplanned visit from a high-profile guest, an emergency, or a last-minute change in plans, handling special scenarios with grace and finesse is key to maintaining a smooth operation and keeping your office running like clockwork.

VIP and High-Profile Visitors

When hosting VIPs and high-profile visitors in your office, extra care and attention to detail are crucial. These guests often require a higher level of service and discretion, so it’s important to have protocols in place that balance their needs with maintaining smooth daily operations.

From preparing staff to ensuring that the visit runs seamlessly, handling these special situations with tact is key.

Special Considerations for VIPs

VIPs and high-profile visitors often expect a tailored experience that reflects their status. This might include offering private meeting spaces, scheduling their visit during quieter hours, or assigning a dedicated staff member to be their point-person and assist them throughout their stay.

Thoughtful touches, like providing refreshments or preparing personalized welcome materials, can also go a long way in making a positive impression.

Confidentiality is another critical consideration. VIPs may be discussing sensitive topics or handling business deals during their visit, so ensuring that their activities remain discreet is essential.

Brief your team on confidentiality protocols and make sure that all staff members understand the importance of discretion in these situations.

Protocols for Handling High-Profile Visitors

Establishing clear protocols for VIP visits ensures that everything runs smoothly and that your team knows exactly what to do.

These protocols can include pre-visit coordination, setting up dedicated check-in points to avoid crowding and alleviate wait times, and assigning a team member to guide the VIP through the space.

Be sure your team is briefed and their questions are answered so they are prepared to greet your VIP. Everyone should be aware of the visit and their role in managing it, from reception staff greeting the guest upon arrival to any team members involved in logistics.

Having a clear timeline and checklist helps keep the visit on track, ensuring that all expectations are met. A designated person to oversee protocols and logistics throughout the duration of the visit will also help your team stay on track.

Ensuring Minimal Disruption to Operations

While VIP visits can be exciting, it’s important to maintain business as usual for your other employees.

Scheduling visits during off-peak hours or using private entrances and meeting rooms can help minimize disruption for both the guest and your working members.

It’s also helpful to inform team members in advance if a high-profile visit might affect their day, whether it’s temporary adjustments to access certain areas or the use of shared resources.

Managing Difficult Visitors

Not all visitor interactions will be smooth sailing. Regardless of how well your staff is trained and how much they prepare, you will encounter difficult or disruptive visitors on occasion who test your team’s patience and professionalism.

Whether it’s someone causing a scene in the lobby or a visitor who refuses to follow the space’s guidelines, having strategies in place for managing these situations is essential for maintaining a positive environment.

Strategies for Dealing with Difficult or Disruptive Visitors

The first step in managing difficult visitors is to remain calm and composed. It’s easy to get flustered in tense situations, but keeping a cool head helps you approach the problem with clarity.

Listening actively and acknowledging the visitor’s concerns, even if they’re unreasonable, can help diffuse tension. Sometimes, people just want to feel heard. Use polite, neutral language to de-escalate situations, and if necessary, offer to take the conversation to a more private space away from other members.

Setting boundaries is crucial when dealing with disruptive behavior. Politely but firmly communicate the rules and explain the consequences of not adhering to them.

If a visitor continues to act inappropriately, be prepared, and know it’s okay, to ask them to leave the premises.

Conflict Resolution Techniques

Effective conflict-resolution techniques focus on communication, empathy, and problem-solving. Here are some key approaches:

  • Active Listening: Pay full attention to the other person, listen without interrupting, and acknowledge their concerns. Repeating back what they’ve said to confirm understanding helps validate their feelings and shows you’re taking them seriously.
  • Stay Calm and Composed: Keeping emotions in check is essential. Staying calm helps de-escalate tension and allows you to think clearly when addressing the issue. Also remember this is business and not to take their frustrations personally.
  • Empathy and Understanding: Try to see the situation from the other person’s perspective. Acknowledging their feelings or frustrations can help lower defenses and create a more cooperative atmosphere. Put yourself in their shoes – if this was happening to you, how would you want someone to handle the situation?
  • Use “I” Statements: Instead of placing blame with “you” statements, focus on your own perspective and what you can do for the guest. For example, saying, “I understand this situation is frustrating. Here’s what I can do,” rather than, “You’re making this difficult,” or “You’re not listening,” shows you are validating their concerns and want to resolve the issue.
  • Focus on Solutions: Rather than dwelling on the problem, shift the conversation toward finding a solution that works for both parties. Ask, “What can we do to resolve this?” to encourage collaboration or “Does that seem fair?” once you’ve provided a solution.
  • Stay Neutral and Professional: Avoid taking sides, being accusatory, or letting personal emotions affect the conversation. Neutral language helps keep the discussion constructive.
  • Clarify Misunderstandings: Often, conflicts arise from miscommunication. Clarifying details and ensuring both parties are on the same page can resolve many issues quickly.
  • Bring in a Mediator: When conflicts can’t be resolved directly, involving a neutral third party—such as a manager or mediator—can help facilitate a fair resolution.
  • Agree to Disagree: If a resolution isn’t possible, sometimes it’s best to respectfully acknowledge differences and move on without letting the disagreement escalate further. Sometimes you have to know which battles to fight for and when to cut your losses.
  • Know When to Walk Away: If the situation becomes unproductive or too heated, it’s okay to suggest taking a break and revisiting the conversation later when emotions have cooled.

These techniques can help transform conflicts into opportunities for understanding and cooperation, ultimately leading to a more positive outcome for everyone involved.

When and How to Involve Security Personnel

There are times when a situation may become too volatile to handle alone and you summon the help of security personnel as a last resort.

This should be reserved for situations that pose safety risks or when all other conflict resolution methods have failed. Here are some tips on when and how to effectively involve security.

When to involve security personnel:

  • Aggressive or Threatening Behavior: If a visitor becomes verbally abusive, physically aggressive, or makes threats toward staff or members, immediate security intervention is necessary.
  • Refusal to Comply: When a visitor refuses to follow the office rules, repeatedly ignores requests to leave, or insists on entering restricted areas, involving security ensures compliance without risking staff safety.
  • Suspicious or Unusual Activity: If a visitor is acting suspiciously – such as loitering in unauthorized areas, trying to access sensitive information, or tampering with property – security personnel should be notified.
  • Escalated Conflicts: When a disagreement turns heated and there’s a risk of it spiraling into a physical altercation, bringing in security can help de-escalate the situation.

And here’s the best way to involve security personnel:

  • Have Clear Protocols: Establish clear guidelines for when and how staff should contact security. Include step-by-step instructions in your visitor management policy so everyone knows what to do in case of a security threat.
  • Designate a Point of Contact: Assign specific team members who are responsible for initiating contact with security personnel. This ensures a quick and organized response.
  • Discreet Communication: Whenever possible, involve security discreetly to avoid alarming other visitors or members. Use private communication methods like text messages or radio calls, rather than making loud public announcements. You could also classify different scenarios with codes to make security personnel aware of what they’re walking into without announcing it for all to hear.
  • Coordinate with Security Staff: If your office has onsite security, maintain regular communication between your team and the security staff. Ensure they are briefed on the visitor management policy and know the layout of the space.
  • Document the Incident: After involving security, document the incident in detail. Record what led to the situation, how it was handled, and any follow-up actions taken. This is crucial for refining protocols and preventing future issues.
  • Train Your Team: Staff should be trained on when and how to escalate situations to security. Regular drills and scenario-based training can prepare them to handle emergencies calmly and efficiently.

Name: Free Visitor Log Template in Excel That Tracks Who’s On Site [2026]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Most visitor log templates are…basic. They’re just a table with headers on top. You type a name, you type a time, and the file gives you nothing back.
Post body:
Most visitor log templates are…basic.
They’re just a table with headers on top. You type a name, you type a time, and the file gives you nothing back.

This one calculates. Our free visitor log template in Excel shows who is still in the building right now, flags anyone who left without signing out, and tells you which records are old enough to delete. The same file works in Google Sheets.

Both versions are free, and there’s no sign-up.

Below: how to open it without losing your edits, what each tab does, what to record in a visitor log, and the point where a spreadsheet stops being the right tool.

How to open the template (read this first)

For Google Sheets, you need to be signed in to a Google account. A personal Gmail address works, so does a Google Workspace account from your company. Once you’re signed in, go to File → Make a copy.

That step matters. The file we share is view-only, so anything you type into it won’t save and won’t be visible to anyone else. Your copy lands in your own Drive, under your control, and you can share it with reception from there.

If you see “View only” in the top right and the cells won’t accept typing, you either aren’t signed in or you haven’t made the copy yet.

For Excel –  download the .xlsx file and open it. Excel usually opens files from the internet in Protected View, so click Enable Editing in the yellow bar at the top. The dropdowns and calculations stay switched off until you do.

There are no macros in either version, so nothing to trust or allow beyond that.

What’s inside the visitor log template in Excel

Five tabs you’ll use, plus one helper sheet you can ignore.

Setup. Your site name, your host list (up to 50 people), your visit types, and your floors or areas. Fill this in once. Everything you enter here becomes a dropdown on the log, so reception picks from a list instead of typing “J. Smith” one day and “Jane Smith” the next.

You also set 2 numbers here: how many hours counts as a long visit, and how many days you keep visitor records. Both feed the dashboard.

Visitor log. 300 rows. You fill in the visitor, the host, the badge number and the times. The template fills in the visit number, the length of the visit, and a status for every row:

  • Expected if they’re booked in but haven’t arrived
  • On site if they’ve signed in and not out
  • Signed out if the visit is closed
  • Not signed out in red if they signed in on an earlier date and never signed out

There’s also a check that catches dates typed as text. If someone writes 16/09/2026 in a way the sheet reads as words instead of a date, a warning appears at the top of the log and tells you how many rows are affected. Those rows would otherwise vanish from every count without anyone noticing.

Dashboard. Pick any date and the tab shows who was on site, who was expected, the average visit length, and how many people across the whole log never signed out. Underneath that is a list of everyone currently in the building, with their host, badge number, and time in. Print it, and you have a roll call.

Visitor badge. Type a visit number and the printable pass fills itself in from the log: name, company, host, floor, date, time in, badge number. No handwriting, no retyping.

Lists. The helper sheet the dashboard reads from. Leave it alone.

The file is free to use and share, and the 3 sample rows are dummy data you can type straight over.

What to record in a visitor log

The fields below cover a normal office. Add or cut columns to suit your building, but be careful about adding fields you don’t have a reason to hold (more on that further down).

FieldWhy it's there
DateAnchors every count and every search of the log
Visitor nameThe record itself
CompanyTells you whether this is a client, a supplier or a contractor at a glance
Email and phoneReaching someone after they've left, and pre-registration
Visit typeMeeting, interview, delivery, contractor, audit. Useful for spotting patterns in traffic
HostWho's responsible for the guest while they're in the building
Area or floorWhere to look during an evacuation
Badge numberLinks the physical pass to the record
Time in and time outThe two fields that make a log a log
NDA or safety briefingProof the paperwork was done before they got past the lobby
NotesAccess needs, escort requirements, anything unusual

Two fields do most of the work: time in and time out. Almost every problem with a paper or spreadsheet visitor sign-in sheet traces back to the second one.

3 things a visitor sign-in sheet usually gets wrong

1. Nobody signs out

Signing in has a prompt. Someone hands you a clipboard or points at a tablet. Signing out has nothing. The visitor is already thinking about their train.

People skip steps that happen at the door, and we have our own numbers on this. Over 12 months in our Sofia office, we recorded 13,024 desk bookings, and 9.1% of them were never checked into at all. The step was 1 tap on a phone. You can read the full year of data here.

Visitor check-out has no tap and no reminder, so the failure rate is worse. The result is a log that says 14 people are in your building when 3 actually are.

Our template can’t force anyone to sign out. What it does is make the gap visible: any row with a sign-in time, no sign-out time, and a date before today turns red and reads Not signed out. The dashboard counts them for you.

2. It can’t answer “who is in the building” during an evacuation

This is the question a visitor log exists to answer, and a flat spreadsheet answers it badly. You’d be scrolling and filtering while the alarm is going.

Under OSHA’s emergency action plan rule (29 CFR 1910.38), an employer’s written plan has to include procedures to account for everyone after an evacuation. The standard is written around employees, but any evacuation warden will tell you the people nobody can account for are usually the guests, because they’re the ones not on a team list.

The Dashboard tab handles this. Pick today’s date and you get a printed list of names, companies, hosts, badge numbers and sign-in times for everyone currently on site. Keep a copy at reception or print it at the start of each afternoon.

3. The file keeps personal data forever

A visitor log holds names, phone numbers, email addresses and a record of someone’s movements through your building. That’s personal data, and most spreadsheet logs sit in a shared drive with 4 years of it and no deletion date.

The UK ICO’s guidance on the storage limitation principle is direct about this: GDPR sets no fixed retention periods, so you have to set your own, document them, and actually delete when they expire. Data held past the point you need it is data you probably have no lawful basis to hold.

So the template has a retention setting. Enter how many days you keep records on the Setup tab, and the Dashboard tells you how many rows are past that date and the exact cut-off to delete up to. Most offices land somewhere between 30 and 90 days unless a regulator says otherwise.

While you’re there, cut the columns you don’t have a reason to fill. A car registration field you use twice a year is personal data you’re storing for no purpose.

When an Excel visitor log stops working

A spreadsheet is the right answer for a small office with a handful of guests a day. It costs nothing, everyone can already use it, and it works offline.

It stops being the right answer around the point any of these become true:

  • More than 1 entrance, or more than 1 site, sharing the same file
  • Visitors who need to sign an NDA or a safety briefing before they get past the lobby
  • Hosts who want to know their guest has arrived without someone walking over to tell them
  • Somebody at reception whose job is partly retyping what’s already on a clipboard
  • A client security review that asks how you control access to visitor records

The last one catches people out. Excel can password-protect a file. It can’t give you role-based access, an audit trail of who opened the log, or a record of what changed.

Visitor log template vs visitor management software

Excel or Google sheetsVisitor management software
CostFreePaid, usually offered as an add-on too
Setup timeMinutesHours, plus a tablet at reception
Works offlineYesUsually needs a connection
Check-inSomeone types itThe guest does it on a tablet or a QR code
Sign-outManual, and often skippedAutomatic or prompted
Host notificationSomeone walks overInstant, in Teams, Slack or email
Pre-registrationNoYes, with an invite email and directions
Document signingPrinted and filedSigned on screen before entry
Badge printingPrint the tabPrinted automatically at the desk
Who's on site nowThe Dashboard tab, if the log is currentLive, always
Access controlFile permissionsRole-based, with an audit trail
RetentionYou delete rows on scheduleAutomated deletion policy
Export for complianceCopy and pasteAny date range, on demand

The honest summary: the spreadsheet wins on cost and speed of setup. Software wins on everything that depends on someone remembering to do something. And of course, easier and error-free automation, plus security.

Visitor Hub is the visitor management side of OfficeRnD Workplace. Guests pre-register before they arrive, sign your NDA on the way in, and check themselves in at a tablet. The host is notified in Microsoft Teams, Slack or email the moment it happens. Deliveries work the same way.

Every visit is logged without anyone typing it, so the on-site list is accurate by default and you can export any date range for an audit or a fire drill.

On enforcement, we can point at our own office again. Desk bookings at OfficeRnD auto-cancel if nobody checks in, and over the year that single rule returned about 4.5 desks a day to the pool, roughly 8% of the office. Rules that run by themselves collect data that people forget to enter.

Name: How To Grow A Coworking Space [9 Winning Strategies]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: You might have turned your vision of the perfect coworking space into a reality, but your work isn’t finished yet. In fact, this just spells the beginning of the work!
Post body:
You might have turned your vision of the perfect coworking space into a reality, but your work isn’t finished yet. In fact, this just spells the beginning of the work!

If you want your business to last, it’s crucial to attract more members, keep current members happy, and foster a sense of community.

This article will walk you through how to grow a coworking space through nine marketing strategies. These range from using technology to your advantage to creating a hub for local events.

Quick Summary:

  • Coworking spaces are becoming more popular than ever.
  • Owners should work on their online presence, track data, fine-tune their tours, and offer referrals.
  • They can also maximize their existing members through onboarding, events, upselling, and listening to their feedback.

Making Growth Priority #1 for Your Coworking Space

The global coworking space market was estimated to be worth $10.53 billion in 2023, and it’s expected to grow by 14.5% between 2024 and 2032

You might think this growth shows the coworking industry is doing well, so you can be sure about the future of your own business. But it may not be so easy.

Forecasts suggest the number of coworking spaces across the world will go from 19,345 in 2021 to 41,975 in 2024. While this shows steady growth, it also means that owners of coworking spaces can’t get too comfortable.

The competition is high, and you need to make sure you stand out. Fortunately, the rest of this guide is focused on the best tips and strategies to help you achieve exactly that.

#1 Work on Your Digital Storefront

Most leads will find your website or social media before they know anything about you. Making a good impression here may be even more important than making sure your coworking space looks good in person.

Plus, common industries using coworking include the tech and creative sectors, which are full of highly tech-literate professionals. They may judge you more harshly on your website’s appearance than those from other industries.

Your digital presence should:

  • Include membership fees and rate structure
  • List available amenities
  • Have an easy-to-navigate layout
  • Highlights what makes your coworking space unique

Social media can also be a chance to connect with potential customers on a more personal level. You may want to go beyond typical branding choices and give people a “feel” of the coworking space instead.

Why not shine a light on current members’ entrepreneurial journeys to showcase the kind of coworking community customers can expect to find? Or film the facilities so customers can check them out from the comfort of their sofas?

#2 Track Leads Through Data

Good growth plans aren’t pulled out of thin air — they should be informed by tracking data. This informs you about crucial info, such as where your leads are coming from. You can then use this to nudge them toward becoming customers.

For example, you might find that most of your website visitors come from Instagram and decide to pay for an ad campaign on the platform.

When you figure out what works and what doesn’t, you can make data-driven decisions to inform future marketing choices. Continuing the example above, you may decide to stick to Instagram because it’s delivering the results you want. Or, you might discover that another advertising platform is more effective at bringing in leads.

With data reporting and visualization tools, you can also run reports on coworking KPIs such as occupancy rates and a number of new memberships sold. You can also gain insight into which spaces or amenities members are using the most, or which one of your membership tiers is the most profitable.

#3 Finetune Your Tours

As important as your digital storefront is, first impressions in person still matter. Most customers will want to see a coworking space for themselves before they sign up, and they may compare it to other sites.

Tours offer a chance to shine!

You can stand out before your prospects even get through the front door by making it easy for them to book a tour. Provide a simple form online using an automatic booking tool that syncs with your CRM.

Coworking management software such as OfficeRnD Flex allows you to create branded, embeddable tour booking forms. Watch the short video below for more info:

When visitors come, make sure there’s someone waiting to greet them straightaway to kickstart a positive experience. During the tour itself, show an interest in the prospect’s needs, expectations, and what they plan to use the site for.

To help highlight the best parts of your coworking space during a tour, why not ask your current members? You can then try to incorporate these elements into your tours.

For more on this, check out: How to Deliver Great Coworking Tours Every Time (In 5 Steps).

#4 Have a Smooth Onboarding Process

After a successful tour, you can still lose potential leads by having a cumbersome sign-up process. Do everyone a favor by automating it and not asking new customers to provide more details than necessary.

Once a customer has signed up to join your coworking space, it doesn’t mean that you can relax. Now, you need to make sure they stick around!

Provide a welcome pack to help them settle in. This could include:

  • The facilities in your coworking space
  • Other nearby amenities (e.g., top lunch spots)
  • How to find out about events
  • Who to contact if they need help or support
  • How to book hot desks, conference rooms, or other facilities

If you really want to go the extra mile, you could even hold a regular event for new members. This would offer an opportunity for them to make friends or business contacts and become part of the community.

Using coworking software to automate repetitive, manual tasks can help simplify and streamline the onboarding process for new members. Some platforms offer coworking rental contract templates you can customize to suit your space.

#5 Market to Those Passing Through

Depending on where your coworking space is, locals might not be your only target audience.

Many sites are in bigger cities that get a lot of visitors. This means tourists and digital nomads could also be potential customers.

Tourist accommodation doesn’t usually cater to remote workers, so these people may be looking for a coworking space they can use. Advertise at hotels, hostels, airports, and other hotspots to reach them.

Most tourists and digital nomads will only want to join a coworking space temporarily — maybe even for a single day. Consider offering flexible coworking memberships or day passes to appeal to this demographic.

Events are another way to make your coworking space seem exciting for those passing through, which we’ll get to now.

#6 Turn Your Coworking Space Into an Events Hub

Lots of people seek out a shared workspace for networking and community-building. Organizing coworking events is a great way to capitalize on these opportunities. If you sell tickets or charge for admission, events can also provide an additional revenue stream.

Events can be anything from an organized lunch and learn activity to an after-5 office happy hour. Regardless of what type or topic, events give members a chance to connect and be part of a community.

But the possibilities are endless, really — you can host cultural events, film screenings, or even late-night concerts.

Putting on events with other local businesses can help grow your potential customer base. To reach a wider audience, consider co-hosting or co-sponsoring different types of events in your coworking space. Get creative with your event ideas; you can host:

  • Networking events
  • Skills workshops
  • Hackathons
  • Speaker or lecture series

It may seem overwhelming to organize your first event and start leveraging community, but it’s worth it.

Here’s an actionable article with some original event ideas.

#7 Upsell to Existing Members

Growing your coworking space doesn’t necessarily mean getting more customers. You can also sell more to your current members.

This may mean selling a more expensive product to current customers (upselling) or selling more items to your current customers (“cross-selling”).

Cross-selling makes up 21% of revenue for the average company, so don’t underestimate the power of this approach.

Some ideas include:

  • Tiered membership levels
  • Subscription-based meal and beverage plans
  • Virtual office services
  • Premium spaces and amenities (VIP lounges, quiet zones, podcast studios, and outdoor spaces)
  • Members-only networking events
  • Personalized wellness plans and mental health support

You can also upsell for members that have dogs.

#8 Listen to Your Members

As we’ve said already, members are at the heart of every coworking space. Deciding how to grow your business shouldn’t be a top-down approach.

Find out which services your current members use the most and least. Then, use this to figure out what your target audience would like you to offer.

Is there a particular perk you could provide, such as daycare or workshops? Or maybe there’s a certain kind of food everyone wants. Or maybe a mobile app for members?

Send out surveys to your email list to find out, and make sure there’s a clear way for members to give feedback at any time. For instance, you could include a link to an anonymous feedback survey in every email newsletter you send. Also, don’t sleep on your net promoter score.

Alex Hillman, co-founder of Indy Hall did just that to scale his business succesfully. Learn more about that here.

#9 Take Advantage of Referrals

Referrals are an age-old marketing strategy for helping businesses grow.

Your current customers probably know more potential customers. Because these prospects already know current members, they have social proof of how great your coworking space is. This makes them more likely to join than a random person who has never heard of you before.

Of course, you need to make sure it’s worthwhile for people to recommend you. Give discounted membership or fees to those who make a successful referral.

You could also give members a chance to bring a non-member to the coworking space once or twice a month for free. This can gently introduce a potential member to the coworking space without making a hard sell.

If you have a referral offer, don’t forget to check how well it is working using data and analytics.

  • Make more informed decisions thanks to powerful analytics
  • Keep members happy and automate the rest
