Name: How to Organize Coworking Events Like A Pro [2025]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Have you ever been in this situation—investing tons of energy, resources and time to organize an event for your coworking community, and eventually, you end up with just a few people attending?
Post body:
Have you ever been in this situation—investing tons of energy, resources and time to organize an event for your coworking community, and eventually, you end up with just a few people attending?

Feeling stuck or confused about what you did wrong (or if you did something wrong at all) is normal.

First, it’s not that easy to constantly come up with creative ideas about super-cool events that would be interesting to everyone and would bond the community.

And second, organizing great events, is a complex matter which includes research, people management, logistics, marketing, coordination, often dealing with budgets and stakeholders, the list goes on…

The good news is that you can use some “hacks” that will help you organize events that your members will love and attend!

But before we move to the tips, let’s put this question on the table:

Why are people not coming to your coworking events in the first place?

Not being interested in this particular event is a possible reason, but there are plenty of other circumstances such as:

  • Your members didn’t hear about the event
  • They did hear and planned to come but forgot
  • They had another appointment during that time
  • They were so tired after work that the only thing they wished was to go home, grab a beer and watch Netflix

To help you find out why you end up with not enough visitors and what to change to attract more of them, we’ve listed a few tips below.

Read on!

The Importance of Community Building in Coworking Spaces

Community building is a foundational element of successful coworking spaces, playing a vital role in creating an environment where members feel connected, supported, and engaged. Unlike traditional office settings, coworking spaces thrive on the sense of community and collaboration that they foster.

Here’s why community building is crucial in coworking spaces:

Fostering a Sense of Belonging

Events and activities within coworking spaces help cultivate a sense of belonging among members. When individuals feel part of a community, they are more likely to be engaged, productive, and loyal. This sense of belonging is built through regular interactions, shared experiences, and mutual support, which are often facilitated by well-organized events.

Enhancing Collaboration and Networking

Coworking spaces are designed to bring together people from diverse industries and backgrounds. Community-building events such as networking sessions, workshops, and social gatherings provide members with opportunities to connect, collaborate, and share knowledge. These interactions can lead to new business partnerships, creative collaborations, and a more dynamic work environment. In other words, this is known as the network effect.

Improving Member Retention and Satisfaction

A strong community can significantly enhance member retention and satisfaction. When members feel connected and supported, they are more likely to remain in the coworking space long-term. Regular events that cater to members’ professional and personal interests help maintain high levels of engagement and satisfaction.

Creating a Supportive Work Environment

Community-building efforts contribute to creating a supportive work environment where members can seek advice, share challenges, and celebrate successes.

This supportive atmosphere can reduce feelings of isolation, especially for freelancers and remote workers who might otherwise miss the social interactions of a traditional office.

Promoting Personal and Professional Growth

Events focused on skill development, wellness, and personal growth can greatly benefit members. Workshops, training sessions, and wellness activities provide opportunities for continuous learning and development, contributing to the overall well-being and growth of members.

Strengthening the Coworking Brand

A vibrant and engaged community enhances the reputation of the coworking space.

Prospective members are more likely to choose a coworking space known for its strong community and active events calendar. This positive reputation can also attract media attention and partnerships, further boosting the coworking space’s visibility and appeal.

Encouraging Member-Led Initiatives

Encouraging members to lead their own events and initiatives fosters a sense of ownership and empowerment.

When members are actively involved in organizing and participating in events, they are more invested in the community’s success. Member-led initiatives can range from informal meetups to structured workshops, adding diversity and richness to the event calendar.

Types of Coworking Events

Networking Events

These events are designed to help members connect, share ideas, and explore potential collaborations. Speed networking, meet-and-greet sessions, and industry-specific mixers are popular formats.

Workshops and Training Sessions

Workshops and training sessions offer skill-building opportunities and professional development. Topics can range from technical skills, such as coding and graphic design, to soft skills, like public speaking and leadership.

Social and Recreational Events

Social events, such as happy hours, game nights, and holiday parties, help members relax and bond outside of work. Recreational activities like yoga classes or group outings also contribute to a fun and engaging community.

Panel Discussions and Guest Speakers

Inviting industry experts for panel discussions or guest lectures can provide valuable insights and inspiration. These events encourage knowledge sharing and stimulate thought-provoking conversations.

Member-Led Events

Encourage members to host their own events. This could include anything from book clubs and hobby groups to peer-to-peer learning sessions. Member-led events empower the community and foster a sense of ownership.

How to Choose the Right Event for Your Community

Surveying Members’ Interests

Conduct regular surveys to understand your members’ interests and preferences. This ensures that the events you organize are relevant and appealing to your community.

Analyzing Past Event Success

Review feedback and attendance data from past events to identify what worked well and what didn’t. Use these insights to refine your future event planning.

Considering the Space and Resources Available

Take into account the physical space and resources you have when planning events. Ensure that your venue can accommodate the expected number of attendees and that you have the necessary equipment.

Consider the work and lifestyle of your members

When talking about bonding your community, you might often end up thinking about your members’ professional role only. But sometimes, community bonding happens outside professional activities.

Your people might be doing marketing all day, 5 days a week and a marketing workshop might be the last thing they’d like to attend after work. But instead, they’d enjoy an inspiring wine degustation or a relaxing yoga workshop that would help them get their mind off of work.

Of course, this doesn’t mean to stop hosting professional events, but to mix them with something different and see if this will work.

Consider not only the interests of your members but their lifestyle too. Do they have kids? Do they do sports after work? Are they often on work trips? Do they live far away from your coworking space?

If you’re a parent and you have to take your kids from school, help them with their homework, do the laundry, make dinner, and find time to rest in between all this…staying at a Beer Friday event after work is just not much appealing.

Such members might be a lot pickier about events and would prefer to plan much in advance so they can find out who to look after their kids while they’re away, for example.

Or your members might be fitness addicts who don’t miss their evening workout session. They might think the Board Games night that you’re hosting would be lots of fun, but the only way to make them stay for an event would be to organize an intensive Tabata class.

These are just a few examples but you get the point. Knowing your members’ work and lifestyle will help you find the right events for your community. For inspiration about cool events, you can host, check out our article on the top coworking space event ideas.

🔹Bonus tip: Choose dates and hours wisely.

In most cases, avoiding Mondays and Fridays is a good move. Most people are too tired after the weekend and have plans with friends on Fridays so chances they’ll skip an even on these days are higher.

Also, get to know at what time the majority of your members finish work. If they’re done around 5:30 pm and you host your events at 7 pm, they won’t be much motivated to stay. And on the contrary—if most of them prefer working till late you might want to make your events later too.

Spread the word and set up the hype

Even if you organize the super mega cool event but your members don’t hear about it, your efforts were in vain. You really need to invest time and energy into spreading the word.

The truth is that people are busy, tired, having a case of Mondays, wishing it was Friday…
They sometimes don’t see notifications; they need someone to create the hype for them; they sometimes need to be invited personally. And then to be reminded because they have 54854903 things on their to-do list and it’s easy to forget about an event even if they want to attend.

Make sure you’ve used all possible offline and digital channels to promote the event and you’ve been vocal enough. If you’re interested in learning more about how to benefit from digital channels, here’s a good read on how to use online tools to improve member engagement.

Digital channels and on-site promoting such as putting signs at the reception, in the kitchen, etc, are a must but don’t neglect your most powerful weapon—face-to-face communication. Go to your members’ offices and invite them personally. Greet them when you see them in the hallways and tell them about this amazing workshop you’re hosting next week.

Of course, be mindful not to interrupt them aggressively, especially when they seem much more concentrated on a task or in a hurry, but don’t be hesitant to talk with them directly!

🔹Bonus tip: Invite the smart way

Here’s the trick—you have to “sell” the event, not to beg people to come. Rely on enthusiasm, positivity, and stress on the benefits people will get. Take a look at the following two examples:

Situation 1: “Hey, Sue, you’re coming to the marketing workshop on Tuesday, aren’t you? Come on, I’m trying to find a few more people to attend!”

Situation 2: “Hey, Sue, I’m sure the marketing workshop this Tuesday will be very useful to your startup. The speaker has been consulting tech startups for 10 years and told me he recently helped a fintech company triple their website traffic in just a month. Wasn’t that what you’re trying to achieve right now? Also, we’ll be having some nice drinks for the occasion. Will be happy to see you there!”

We bet the second sounds more attractive to you, too!

Ask for feedback

Ask your members for feedback and ideas and, if possible, do it face-to-face. Don’t rely on surveys only, unless you have that huge community that it’s just not physically possible to talk to the majority of your members.

Not that surveys are bad, but most people are extremely busy, overbooked with meetings, or simply have more important things to do, and a survey usually ends up in the never-ending to-do list or people totally forget about it…even though they are willing to share their thoughts with you.

And most of all, expressing your thoughts in a written form often gives less context and takes a lot more effort than sharing your thoughts over a coffee or a 2-minute random conversation in the hallways.

So try to have more live conversations with your members. It doesn’t need to be anything too formal—a short talk while you’re making your morning coffee or during lunch would do the job.

🔹Bonus tip: Ask members to be specific

Encouraging members to be specific will help you identify their needs. For example, when they mention they enjoyed the last networking event, ask them what exactly they liked—was it the vibe, the drinks, the people they met?

And a final tip: Be patient! Finding the right fit for your space won’t happen overnight. It’s pretty much a trial-and-error method but as long as you invest effort in understanding your community’s needs, interests and lifestyle, things will come in place.

Quick Event Planning Checklist

Detailed Timeline and Steps for Event Planning

Define objectives and goals:

  • Set a date and time.
  • Secure a venue.
  • Arrange for speakers or facilitators.
  • Plan the agenda and activities.
  • Promote the event.

Tips on Budgeting and Resource Allocation

  • Allocate budget for venue, refreshments, materials, and marketing.
  • Seek sponsorships or partnerships to offset costs.

Venue Setup and Logistics Management

  • Arrange seating and equipment.
  • Ensure accessibility and comfort.
  • Plan for registration and attendee check-in.

Promoting Your Coworking Event

Effective Marketing Strategies

Use social media, email campaigns, and your coworking space’s website to promote events. Create engaging content that highlights the benefits of attending.

Partnering with Local Businesses and Influencers

Collaborate with local businesses and influencers to expand your reach. They can help promote your event and attract a wider audience.

Creating Compelling Event Descriptions and Visuals

Craft clear and enticing event descriptions. Use high-quality visuals to capture attention and convey the event’s atmosphere and value.

Engaging Members During the Event

Icebreaker Activities and Networking Techniques

Think of some cool icebreaker activities to help members feel comfortable and encourage interaction. Use structured networking techniques to facilitate connections.

Interactive Elements and Member Participation

Include interactive elements like Q&A sessions, live polls, and group discussions to keep attendees engaged and involved.

Using Technology for Engagement

Leverage technology such as event apps, live polling tools, and social media to enhance engagement and provide a seamless experience.

Post-Event Follow-Up

Gathering and Analyzing Feedback

Collect feedback through surveys and direct conversations. Analyze this data to understand what worked well and what can be improved.

Sharing Event Highlights and Member Testimonials

Share highlights and testimonials on your website and social media. This not only showcases the success of the event but also promotes future events.

Planning Future Events Based on Feedback and Insights

Use the feedback and insights gained to plan and improve future events. Continuously adapting and evolving your event strategy will help maintain a vibrant and engaged community.

In Conclusion

  • Which are the right events for your space
  • How to use events that help you grow your business
  • How to organize events like a pro

  • The setup of your hybrid meeting space can affect employees’ experience, so it’s crucial to organize the space well.
  • With new AV equipment and an optimal AV setup, your business will improve hybrid communication and accountability and provide positive team bonding opportunities.

Why AV Conference Room Technology Is Essential for Hybrid Meetings

If you’ve ever been in a hybrid meeting, chances are you’ve experienced at least one meeting with a subpar conference room AV system. Between scratchy audio, poor visuals, and limited communication, attendees may leave feeling confused about their expectations and goals.

When you work with remote clients, inferior AV equipment can cost your company lucrative business deals. Think about it this way: If a client can’t hear or see the members in a meeting, they may misunderstand what’s discussed. Worst case scenario, they don’t come back.

With the rise of high-tech AV technology, many companies have switched to a hybrid model for their employees and clients. If your company fails to update to the newest business standards, you may lose valuable clients and hard-working employees.

The Best AV Meeting Room Equipment for a Hybrid Workspace

Here’s what you’ll need to set up the best meeting room for your in-office and remote employees:

Wireless Internet (WiFi) with an Ethernet Cable Backup

First and foremost, your company needs a stable internet connection to avoid outages during essential business meetings. A poor network will experience frequent shutdowns and connection issues — which won’t help businesses secure new clients or relay information between workers.

A hybrid model needs to be able to support anywhere from 50 to hundreds of computers working within the same area with minimal load times.

When all else fails, you’ll want a backup plan. Ethernet cables provide faster connections than WiFi, so it’s essential to have ethernet connections in your AV meeting rooms. If remote employees report issues with audio and visual quality, using an ethernet cable may stabilize the connection.

However, remote employees’ internet connections are a crucial piece of the hybrid meeting room puzzle. It may be worthwhile to offer these individuals stipends for home internet service.

Did you know you can book meeting room directly in MS Teams?

Microphones

A virtual meeting room needs high-tech microphones for an optimal meeting experience. A high-quality microphone will pick up every voice in the conference room, even when multiple people are speaking over each other.

This allows remote employees to listen to their in-person peers and acknowledge what is said accordingly.

It’s also ideal to supply high-quality microphones to your remote workers to ensure that communication on their end is also clear. If they are in charge of their own, the audio quality may vary — which can be distracting during meetings.

It’s important to note that microphones only work efficiently when the AV meeting room has an excellent speaker system. Without it, in-person participants may have trouble hearing remote employees when they speak.

Camera

Long gone are the days when remote workers looked at an aerial view of a traditional conference room and watched their coworkers interact. With today’s cutting-edge technology, remote individuals can see who’s talking in real time, with cameras that zoom in on whoever’s speaking.

One of the biggest mistakes a company can make is underestimating the need for a high-quality camera for a hybrid meeting room. Great visuals will help attendees understand the business plan and listen attentively to the speaker.

Microsoft 365, highlights remote employees’ video feeds while they’re speaking during meetings, further improving the hybrid experience.

Consider sending remote employees company-approved cameras to ensure that they are perfectly visible to in-office workers and clients. While this is an extra expense, it’s best practice if you want a hybrid meeting room that stands out from the competition.

TV Monitor/Projector

You’ve got excellent WiFi, high-quality microphones, and high-tech cameras. But now, it’s time to think about how the in-person employees will see the remote ones. Your business will need to invest in a large TV monitor or a projector so that remote employees will appear on-screen and be seen by everyone in the room.

This piece of AV equipment is vital to hybrid meeting rooms. Non-hybrid rooms may use whiteboards, but these collaboration tools aren’t always visible when some of the attendees are virtual.

Sound System

A state-of-the-art sound system combines all the essential AV elements to create a solid hybrid meeting room experience. In-person employees need to be able to hear and speak clearly across platforms to remote workers; otherwise, all of the company’s investments in AV equipment are useless.

A good sound system will filter out any background noise and allow its settings to be altered. It might also be beneficial to post a flyer in the meeting room outlining optimal control system settings to prevent valuable meeting time from being wasted configuring the control panel.

But sound systems can be finicky. It’s important to have a skilled technician check your system’s condition regularly to ensure that it remains intact for a high-caliber virtual meeting experience.

Keep Up-to-Date on the Latest AV Equipment

You can’t have a hybrid meeting room without staying updated on the latest AV equipment.

When the start of COVID-19 led many companies to make the shift to remote work, the tech industry worked diligently to improve the quality of audio-visual equipment. And there are lots of different systems out there.

Funding an entire AV workspace can be pricey, but if you already have hybrid meeting rooms, you can slowly replace your equipment as new advancements come out. This will save you money in the long run and improve communication among those who use your facility.

The Optimal Setup for a Hybrid Meeting Room AV System

You can have the best equipment possible, but without a proper conference room AV setup, your business may ostracize its clients and employees.

Suitable Camera Placement

A good-quality camera means nothing without great placement. It’s crucial that it’s positioned in a way that lets remote meeting attendees see (and zoom in on) every employee in the meeting room.

If you plan to have a TV monitor in your hybrid meeting room, consider buying one that has a built-in camera at the bottom. This combines two essential pieces of AV equipment for extra convenience.

Well-Placed Conference Table

Ideally, a meeting room conference table is placed in the middle of the room, in plain view of the camera. This allows for all speakers to see all remote employees and vice versa.

Organized Cables

With all of the high-tech audio-visual equipment available for meeting rooms, employees may find themselves swimming in cables. Of course, this isn’t ideal — one wrong move and the entire conference room audio-visual display could come crashing down.

So, consider optimal cable placement when coming up with your conference room setup, and be prepared to make any changes you need to if you have exposed wires.

Updates As Necessary

As with all technology, regular software updates are necessary for seamless AV equipment use and flawless.

Some systems use a cloud feature and install updates automatically. But it’s important to schedule these updates outside of business hours — the last thing you want is a forced software update interrupting an important hybrid meeting.

If you don’t have a cloud option, assign a tech employee to install any necessary updates while the meeting room is not in use.

Without continuous updates, the quality of your conference room AV equipment could worsen, leaving remote employees and clients with a poor audio and visual experience.

How High-Quality Audio-Visual Equipment for Meeting Rooms Improves the Hybrid Workplace

If you have a hybrid workspace, you know how poor-quality AV equipment can negatively impact the user experience. Investing in the latest AV equipment and creating an optimal conference room setup helps improve remote collaboration.

High-tech cameras and microphones help bring physical and remote workers together during meetings.

Accountability

Running a hybrid workspace requires trust in remote employees, which is one of the big reasons many companies hesitate to switch to this relatively new business model.

But top-of-the-line conference room AV equipment creates an immersive experience that helps keep employees accountable.

In-office and remote meeting leaders can easily detect inattentive workers with effective video conferencing technology.

Team Bonding

Without a proper setup that highlights open communication and collaboration, hybrid teams can feel disjointed and awkward.

Some companies provide in-person opportunities for remote workers to meet their fellow team members. However, when teams are spread across different states, in-person bonding experiences aren’t always possible.

Name: The Art Of Community Building In Coworking Spaces
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: In the world of modern work, where freelancers, entrepreneurs, and remote workers converge, coworking spaces have become hubs of collaboration and connection.
Post body:
In the world of modern work, where freelancers, entrepreneurs, and remote workers converge, coworking spaces have become hubs of collaboration and connection.

But beyond the desks and high-speed Wi-Fi sits the ingredient that can make or break the coworking experience: community.

Community building in a coworking space is the deliberate work of turning members who share a floor plan into a network that connects, collaborates, and looks out for one another.

In 2022, Harvard Business Review surveyed nearly 1,500 working professionals to measure the scope of workplace communities. The finding is hard to ignore:

When people had a sense of community at work, we found that they were 58% more likely to thrive at work, 55% more engaged, and 66% more likely to stay with their organization. They experienced significantly less stress and were far more likely to thrive outside of work, too.

This guide covers why a strong sense of belonging matters in shared spaces, and what to do about it. From practical tactics to real examples, the goal is to give you the tools to build a community that keeps members around.

Whether you’re a coworking space manager, a member trying to get more out of your space, or just curious how these spaces work, read on.

Quick Summary

  • What a coworking community is, why it matters, and strategies to build one that thrives
  • How coworking spaces can use technology to grow their community
  • Community-building examples worth copying

Why does community matter in coworking spaces?

“Community” can be defined as “a social group of any size whose members reside in a specific locality, share government, and often have a common cultural and historical heritage.”

In coworking spaces, community is the difference between a room full of strangers and a room full of people who help each other.

It’s a network of individuals who share more than a workspace. They share a sense of belonging and a common drive to succeed.

Are you using the right coworking management tool? 

A well-knit community drives productivity and sparks creativity, which makes the space more valuable to the people paying for it.

In a Workable survey of 750 US workers, respondents were asked what would attract them to a new opportunity. “Relationship with colleagues/teammates” was the top choice at 37.1%, followed closely by “overall company culture” at 34.7%, according to Workable.

Community goes well beyond having a few friends in the office. It shapes well-being more than most operators give it credit for.

Benefits of a strong coworking community

A strong community pays off in ways that show up on your member roster: richer collaboration, more networking, higher satisfaction, and better retention.

Gallup’s Q12 survey identifies the 12 factors with the most impact on employee engagement. Several of them read like a description of a healthy community:

  • “My supervisor, or someone at work, seems to care about me as a person”
  • “There is someone at work who encourages my development”
  • “I have a best friend at work”
  • “This last year, I have had opportunities at work to learn and grow”
  • “In the last seven days, I have received recognition or praise for doing good work”

The survey was built to measure engagement, but these five statements describe a supportive, connected community.

Here’s how a strong community changes what happens inside your space.

More collaboration and networking

A connected community turns a coworking space into a place where partnerships start. When members feel they belong, they reach out, share ideas, and look for collaborators.

That leads to new ventures, joint projects, and knowledge changing hands.

The conversations that happen in communal areas, the informal networking, the shared experiences: they create opportunities that go far beyond individual work.

Higher satisfaction and retention

Community is the base of member satisfaction. When people feel they’re part of an active, supportive network, they stick around.

Belonging and good experiences with like-minded professionals lift overall satisfaction.

Members aren’t just paying for a desk. They’re paying for a community that adds value to their working lives.

That satisfaction feeds directly into higher retention rates, which cuts turnover and keeps the space stable.

Better productivity and creativity

Community lifts morale, and it also improves output. Members in a collaborative network get access to different perspectives and expertise.

Exposure to other ways of thinking sparks new ideas and solutions.

The encouragement inside a strong community helps people push through challenges and stay motivated.

A positive and engaged environment leads to a more productive and creative workforce, where members are inspired to push boundaries and do their best work.

The strength of a coworking space’s community shapes its success. A supportive network unlocks a range of benefits for individuals and the group.

And that brings in new members and keeps existing ones coming back.

Creating a welcoming environment

A welcoming environment is where community starts. To get members interacting, design a space that encourages engagement while meeting a range of needs. Put simply, you need to get hospitality right.

Here’s how to build an atmosphere that supports both collaboration and comfort.

Design a space that encourages interaction

The layout of a coworking space shapes how members interact. Open layouts and common areas do a lot of the work.

Spacious communal tables and comfortable seating create natural gathering spots where people strike up conversations and collaborate.

Place these areas so interaction happens without feeling forced.

Alongside communal tables, add cozy nooks and lounge areas with soft seating where members can relax and talk more informally.

These spaces should feel inviting and easy to reach, so members are comfortable taking breaks and mingling. Arrange them well and you create flow and connection across the whole space.

Provide amenities for different needs

A welcoming space offers amenities that suit a range of work styles. Coffee stations and snack bars aren’t only about refreshments. They’re social hubs where members take a break and fall into casual conversation.

Stock them with options that cover different tastes and dietary needs. It’s a small thing that makes members feel considered.

Amenities go past pastries and cold brew. They also cover the workspace itself and what’s available to members.

Lounge areas give people a place to socialize and unwind. Quiet zones give focused, distraction-free work to those who need it.

Equip quiet zones with comfortable workstations and noise-reducing features so members can pick the setting that fits the task in front of them.

Private meeting rooms matter too. They give members privacy for calls, client meetings, and group discussions that need a controlled space. Offer a range of room sizes and setups to handle different group needs.

See this guide for the must-have coworking space amenities and this one for the amenities that help you stand out.

How do you get coworking members to interact?

Community depends on member interaction. Give members reasons and chances to connect, share, and build relationships, and the rest follows.

Here’s how to do it through events, activities, and thoughtful introductions.

Host regular events and activities

Regular events keep a coworking community alive. Run a mix, and there’s something for everyone.

  • Networking events: These build professional connections. Regular sessions where members meet, swap contacts, and talk collaborations strengthen the professional side of the community.
  • Workshops and seminars: Educational events give members a chance to build skills and share knowledge. Invite industry experts to lead sessions and you give members a look at new trends and better practices.

You can also let members speak on topics they choose. People are more likely to show up when a peer is presenting, and that opens the door to stronger relationships built on trust.

  • Social gatherings: Balance the professional events with social ones. Happy hours, game nights, and communal lunches let members relax and get to know each other as people, which builds trust and camaraderie.

Get creative. Try something new. Members notice the effort.

Use introductions and icebreakers

How you introduce new members sets the tone. Try these:

  • Welcome packages and orientation sessions: A welcome package with space info, upcoming events, and tips makes new members feel valued on day one. Orientation sessions that introduce them to the space and to other members help them settle in fast.
  • Member spotlights: Highlight members in newsletters, on social media, or on a physical wall in your space. Include short profiles, achievements, and personal interests so members find common ground and start conversations.
  • Icebreakers: Run icebreakers at events or online. Simple activities like “Two Truths and a Lie” or speed networking help members get to know each other in a low-pressure way.

Newsletters and communication channels

Clear communication keeps members informed and engaged. A regular newsletter works as a hub for updates, event announcements, and member spotlights.

It’s a good place to preview activities, share community news, and recognize member wins.

Keep active channels running too, like a Slack group or a private social page, to keep the conversation going day to day.

Facilitating collaboration and networking

Building a strong coworking community means making collaboration and networking easy.

Create chances for members to work together through skill-sharing sessions, peer-to-peer learning, and joint projects, and you tap into “The Network Effect“: the value of a network grows as more people join.

As members share expertise and collaborate, the community gets more useful to everyone in it, which drives growth.

Prioritize these connections and you build a community where everyone benefits from the collective knowledge.

Create opportunities for professional collaboration

Give members structured ways to share skills and work together:

  • Skill-sharing sessions and peer-to-peer learning: Run regular sessions where members teach what they know, from digital marketing to coding. Peer-to-peer learning builds skills and community at the same time. It’s also a good way to mark International Coworking Day.
  • Joint projects: Encourage members from different fields to collaborate. Management can kick these off, or members can. Give them a place to organize, like a project board or a recurring brainstorm, and you’ll see stronger relationships and better work.
  • Team-building exercises: Add exercises like hackathons, design sprints, or problem-solving challenges. They bring members together and get people working with those they’d otherwise never meet.
  • Internal boards or committees: Give members a say. Set up boards or committees for events, holidays, or other initiatives. Working toward a shared goal that affects everyone builds a stronger community than anything you can run top-down.

Use digital platforms for networking

Online tools extend networking beyond the walls of your space. They let members connect, share, and collaborate even when they aren’t in the building.

  • Member directories: Build a directory with profiles, skills, and contact details. It’s a go-to resource when members need expertise or a collaborator.
  • Online forums: Forums and discussion boards let members talk through specific topics, share knowledge, and ask for advice.
  • Communication tools: Use Slack or a coworking app to keep the community connected. Channels for different interests, projects, or teams make it easy to communicate. Keep them updated and encourage participation to keep members engaged.
  • Coworking intranet: An intranet may be overkill for smaller spaces, but it helps larger operations or groups with multiple locations. It pulls the tools above into one place and improves communication across members.

Bring these together and you get a space where collaboration and networking happen on their own.

Building a culture of inclusivity and support

A coworking space that runs on inclusivity and support builds a stronger community.

Promoting diversity and backing every member creates an environment where people feel valued and set up to succeed.

Promote diversity and inclusion

An inclusive space makes everyone feel welcome, whatever their background. Here’s how:

  • Celebrate different cultures and backgrounds: Run events that celebrate members’ cultures. Cultural festivals, international potlucks, awareness days. Displaying art, music, and literature from different cultures in communal areas signals that diversity is part of the space.
  • Support underrepresented groups: Create spaces and programs that address specific needs. Women in tech meetups, minority entrepreneur panels, LGBTQ+ networking events. Scholarships or discounted memberships can make your space more accessible.

A diverse member base gives professionals from all walks of life a place to be themselves.

Encourage a supportive environment

A supportive space keeps members motivated toward their goals. Mentorship programs and growth resources are central to that.

  • Set up mentorship programs: Connect experienced professionals with members who are new to their field or facing a specific challenge. Mentors offer guidance, share knowledge, and open doors. Regular check-ins keep the relationships going.
  • Provide resources for growth: Give members access to online courses, workshops, and webinars. A resource library with books, articles, and tools supports personal and professional development.

Using technology to support community building

Technology helps community happen at scale. Coworking management software and engagement tools cut admin, connect members, and keep the community active.

Coworking management software

The right software changes how you run and engage your community. It reduces admin and improves the member experience.

  • Booking systems: A solid booking system manages shared resources like meeting rooms, workspaces, and event spaces. With a clear interface, like the one in OfficeRnD Flex, members reserve spots and check availability in real time, which reduces conflicts.
  • Event management: Event features make running events simpler. Members RSVP, view details, and get reminders, which lifts turnout. Event analytics show attendance patterns and preferences so you can plan future events better.
  • Member portals: A member portal gives members one place to find information, connect with peers, and manage their membership, including directories, profiles, and billing.

Community engagement tools

Engaging members takes the right tools for communication and interaction. A few worth having:

  • Social media groups: A dedicated group on Facebook or LinkedIn keeps interaction going beyond the physical space, where members share updates, discuss topics, and network.
  • Internal newsletters: Regular newsletters keep members informed and connected. Feature upcoming events, member spotlights, community news, and useful resources.
  • Feedback forms: Digital feedback forms let members share thoughts, suggestions, and concerns easily. Review the feedback and act on it, and members see that their input counts.

Where does AI fit in?

AI has moved from talk to practice in coworking. The OfficeRnD 2025 Flex Space Tech Stack Report found that 60% of operators are considering AI adoption and 26% are already experimenting with it, most often for member engagement and operational automation.

The clearest early win is response time. Most coworking spaces don’t have a lead quality problem, they have a lead timing problem: an inquiry arrives at 9 PM and gets picked up the next morning, by which point the prospect has moved on.

AI Hub is an AI automation layer built into OfficeRnD Flex, and its first agent, the AI Sales Agent, responds to inbound inquiries from web forms and shared inboxes within seconds, then qualifies and hands off the lead. That frees your team to do the work AI can’t: welcoming people, running events, and holding the community together.

Measuring and improving community engagement

To build a community that lasts, measure engagement and adjust as you go. Collect feedback, track metrics, and adapt to keep the space responsive to what members actually want.

Collect feedback from members

Understanding how members feel is the first step. Ways to gather it:

  • Surveys: Send surveys regularly to gauge satisfaction, preferences, and suggestions across amenities and events. Keep them short, and consider an incentive to lift response rates.
  • Suggestion boxes: Physical or digital suggestion boxes give members an anonymous way to share ideas, which helps for those hesitant to speak up. Review and act on what comes in.
  • Focus groups: A focus group with a mix of members surfaces detail that surveys miss and allows for deeper discussion.

Analyze engagement metrics

Track metrics to see whether your community efforts are working:

  • Event attendance: Monitor turnout. High attendance signals interest. Low attendance may mean the events need work or better promotion.
  • Member participation: Track participation across workshops, networking events, and social gatherings. Knowing what’s popular helps you plan.
  • Satisfaction rates: Check satisfaction through surveys and reviews. High rates point to a positive community. Low rates flag what needs fixing.

Improve based on feedback

Feedback and metrics point you toward what to change. Here’s how to act on them:

  • Adapt programs and amenities: Use feedback to refine what you offer. If members want more quiet zones, reallocate space or add noise-canceling solutions. If certain events keep drawing crowds, keep them.
  • Regular updates and communication: Tell members what you’re changing and why. Transparency builds trust.
  • Iterate: Keep testing ideas, gathering feedback, and adjusting. That keeps the space relevant to member needs.

Examples of successful community building in coworking spaces

Community doesn’t happen by accident. Here are spaces and initiatives that have built it on purpose.

Hera Hub

Hera Hub is a female-focused coworking space that supports women entrepreneurs through mentorship, workshops, and networking events. It also runs a digital repository of resources for members.

What sets Hera Hub apart is its focus. By building a network of like-minded professionals, it has created an environment where women learn, grow, and share.

One member put it this way:

Hera Hub is so much more than a coworking space, it’s a thriving ecosystem of amazing entrepreneurs who are dedicated to seeing each other succeed.

One of the biggest draws is the GURU program: subject matter experts who donate their time to meet one-on-one with local entrepreneurs (members and non-members) to answer questions in their field.

It’s a chance for members to connect with each other, and for non-members to see the value of joining.

By tailoring the space to women entrepreneurs, Hera Hub has built a supportive community where members grow personally and professionally.

NextSpace / Pacific Workplaces

Pacific Workplaces, formerly NextSpace, builds community through events for its members.

The organization treats events as the foundation of community building.

Alongside lunch-and-learns, workshops, and topic-specific programming, Pacific Workplaces runs fun weekly member events.

The West Coast operator coined “The NextSpace Effect™,” describing how members get to know each other: they sit next to one another, they talk and connect, and something new happens.

Black Tech Saturdays

Black Tech Saturdays is an initiative that supports Black technologists by building a strong community. Founded in Detroit in 2023 by Johnnie and Alexa Turnage, it runs regular meetups and events focused on networking, skill development, and mentorship for Black professionals in tech.

With a focus on diversity, opportunity, and collaboration, Black Tech Saturdays gives members a place to share knowledge, collaborate, and support each other’s careers.

It isn’t a physical coworking space, but it’s a strong example of the kind of event professionals want: a recognized gathering built to serve a specific community.

An initiative like this promotes inclusion and gives other organizations a model for supporting their own communities.

Conclusion

A strong community is what separates a successful coworking space from a room of desks. It turns a location into a place people want to be.

Members who feel connected and supported stay longer, contribute more, and refer others, which drives growth.

Name: 5 Tips To Build A Successful Coworking Community
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Successful coworking communities have always been a noticeable trait that attracts people to shared spaces. The opportunity to be part of something bigger. Of something truly amazing. A reason to put on pants.
Post body:
Successful coworking communities have always been a noticeable trait that attracts people to shared spaces. The opportunity to be part of something bigger. Of something truly amazing. A reason to put on pants.

A coworking community is the network of members inside a shared workspace who connect, collaborate, and support each other’s work, turning a room full of desks into a place people actually want to be.

Research published by Harvard Business Review states that the number one reason people move from a traditional office environment to shared spaces is to have access to a community that helps them grow and create connections.

In addition, the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor shows that entrepreneurs form a kind of community, united by their networking and shared aspirations. It’s easier to grow a business when you’re surrounded by people who have similar values and interests. A place where networking and collaboration opportunities are countless.

Community remains the clearest differentiator for coworking spaces, and it matters more than ever as the sector matures. Corporate demand is now a primary growth driver, with 55% of corporations using flexible workspace. So if you’re looking to scale, how do you go about building a community that holds? After working with hundreds of coworking spaces around the world, we’ve noticed some interesting commonalities in the approach to successfully scaling a community.

Here’s what we’ve observed so far.

#1 Know your mission and define your audience

Good communities are a well-balanced mixture of shared mindset (vision, values, interests, etc) and diverse skills. When a group of people has a similar focus coupled with diverse expertise, they can complement each other by sharing good practices and exchanging know-how in a way that’s applicable.

For example, one of our clients, Alley, focuses on growing the connectivity points between individuals and entrepreneurs and adding to the value they bring to the community. They position themselves as a “connected platform for entrepreneurs”, which directly speaks to what type of members they’ll welcome in the space. The result? When you walk into any of their spaces the entrepreneurial spirit is evident.

So where do you start? Be clear on what your vision and mission are and communicate them properly. Define your target audience and make sure you understand what they care about and what you bring to the table. If this sounds a bit too broad, start by asking yourself questions like:

  • “What type of companies or individuals do I want to attract?”
  • “Why should they care about me and being part of this community?” (If your answer is because of the good location, interior design, price, etc, and doesn’t explain how you’ll help them succeed, then something is missing.)
  • “What values should they share that will increase the chance of success of each member in the space?”

#2 Think about your member journey

Consider your member journey from start to finish; from coming for a tour to becoming a member. What can you do in each stage to make sure that when the time comes, you’ll be able to point them in the right direction (or better yet, introduce them to the right person)?

The breakdown of the member journey will be different for each coworking space, but here’s an example that illustrates our point:

Pre-sales stage

You can start simply by asking potential members questions like “Why do you want to join our community?”. Alternatively, if there is high demand for your space and you have the luxury to “source” the right candidates, you can go as detailed as sending qualification questionnaires or doing “entry interviews” with potential members.

Ask them about their goals, interests, motivations to join your space, or anything else that will help you come up with ideas on how to help them down the line.

Onboarding stage

Usually, onboarding checklists come into play here. But it also might make sense to set aside some time with them to discuss all the info you gathered during the sales process. Just a casual conversation that helps you dig a bit deeper into the info they provided, so you can come up with ideas about people or events they might be interested in.

Active member stage

It’s a good practice to set up follow-up tasks and check on how your recommendations and introductions turned out, but you’ll probably need to do more than that to keep your members engaged.

It’s hard to recommend a specific set (or type) of activities that are the formula to success, as each community is unique. What we’ve noticed is that every coworking space that developed a vibrant and engaged community says that events are key.

Invest consistent effort in engaging people. In coworking, the real magic happens offline, but make sure you take advantage of online tools to engage your community as they encourage interactions and help keep your members informed.

Eventually, if you’ve made sure your community consists of members with similar interests and you’ve done your best to keep them engaged, things should start developing on their own. Just give the initial push and then make sure to provide a good environment for things to happen.

The final bit that comes into play: someone left your coworking space, but does this mean that your community is 1 person (or team) short?

Best case scenario, it shouldn’t. So we want to give special emphasis to the final stage of the member’s journey:

#3 Extend your community to people outside of your space

A community is not defined by time and space limitations but by the value and the meaning of the interactions between people. Retaining former members in your community, or establishing connections with members’ friends who share similar values and interests can be useful as they might have the expertise to help your current members (and vice versa).

Think about the people you met at college or university. Although you’re not going to classes anymore, you probably still keep in touch with the ones you’ve had meaningful interactions with. It’s not a coincidence that the best universities like Stanford, Oxford, and Cambridge have top-notch alumni associations, which are the communities that gave birth to many of the most successful companies (take Instagram for example, whose co-founders met through the Stanford alumni network).

However, once your community grows above a certain point, it becomes impossible to rely only on your memory to make such meaningful introductions. So how do you keep up?

Here’s a resource on community building worth reading.

Maintain some kind of database

Whether you’re using a coworking CRM, a spreadsheet or some kind of dedicated tool, you’ll need a way to keep track of all essential information and make it easily accessible. You can also come up with some sort of tagging mechanism to source the information you need.

Set up an online community

Think about how you can use technology to increase member visibility and let people connect with each other directly. An online community that grows on its own and can be nurtured with less effort. You have members who love dogs? Invite them and make your space dog-friendly for the occasion.

#4 Foster inclusivity and diversity

Inclusivity and diversity are now core traits of successful coworking communities. A diverse community brings together different perspectives, ideas, and skills, which lead to better collaborations. The demographic reflects this shift: the average coworking member is now 38 years old, up from 35 in 2020, and women make up close to half of members. To build a community that works for that range of people:

  • Host diverse events: organize events that cater to different interests, cultures, and professional backgrounds.
  • Promote equal opportunities: make sure all members have access to the same resources, opportunities, and platforms to share their ideas and projects.
  • Create a welcoming environment: make sure your space is accessible and welcoming to people of all backgrounds, including those with disabilities.

#5 Facilitate networking and collaboration

One of the primary reasons professionals choose coworking spaces is the chance to network and collaborate with like-minded people. To make that easier:

  • Community events: regularly host networking events, skill-sharing sessions, and team-building activities.
  • Collaboration tools: give members digital tools where they can connect, share ideas, and work together on projects.
  • Community manager: employ a dedicated community manager who actively introduces members to each other and builds connections.

How software supports your coworking community

Once your community grows past a couple dozen members, memory and spreadsheets stop scaling. This is where a coworking platform earns its keep. OfficeRnD Flex is coworking space software that helps operators manage daily operations and keep members connected in a single system.

OfficeRnD Flex makes it easy to build genuine community in a coworking space, not just manage it. Members can connect with each other, stay in the loop on events, and engage with their space right from a branded mobile app – while operators get the tools to keep that engagement running smoothly behind the scenes. It’s less about software for software’s sake, and more about giving people real reasons to show up and stick around.

Book a live demo with OfficeRnD Flex and see how you can better manage your space.

Bonus tip

Being focused on hospitality is essential for the success of coworking spaces. But be careful how far you stretch your hospitality service, as too much of it can ‘steal’ the feeling of commitment to the community. Be caring, but let people take the initiative too.

Here’s a simple example: if a member comes to you with an idea for an event that might interest other people in the space, let them actively take part in organizing it.

Conclusion

Whether it lets companies meet a new client without leaving the office, helps young startups grow, or simply gives people a chance to share knowledge, a strong community adds both human and business value.

Community is the core of a coworking space. It’s what attracts people. It’s often difficult to explain, yet it’s why we’re all in love with coworking.

Name: 7 Creative Ways To Celebrate International Coworking Day At Your Space
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: As if we needed another reason to celebrate growth, success, dedicated teams and loyal members in the coworking community, along comes International Coworking Day.
Post body:
As if we needed another reason to celebrate growth, success, dedicated teams and loyal members in the coworking community, along comes International Coworking Day.

On August 9th, coworking spaces around the world come alive as freelancers, entrepreneurs, remote workers, and creatives of all kinds gather to mark the movement that changed the way we work.

International Coworking Day is celebrated every year on August 9th to recognize the global coworking movement and the shared workspaces at its center. The first official coworking space opened on August 9, 2005, when Brad Neuberg set up San Francisco Coworking Space at a feminist collective called Spiral Muse in the Mission District. The date is now observed as International Coworking Day.

It’s a time for coworking spaces, members, and industry professionals to reflect on how far coworking has come, share success stories, and look at where the future of work is heading.

But why is this day so special? It’s not just about the free snacks and cool events (though we love those too).

International Coworking Day is a reminder of what happens when people come together to share, learn, and grow.

It’s a day to celebrate the chance encounters, the spontaneous brainstorms, and the supportive networks that make coworking spaces more than places to work. They’re places to build something.

Here are some of the best ways to celebrate International Coworking Day in your space.

Quick Summary

In this blog post, we’re exploring the 7 best ways to celebrate International Coworking Day in your space:

  1. Host a Networking Brunch
  2. Arrange Skill-Sharing Workshops
  3. Organize a Community Service Project
  4. Host a Coworking Space Open House
  5. Launch a Member Recognition Program
  6. Conduct Fun Team-Building Activities
  7. Create a Collaborative Art Project

…plus examples, tips, and practical strategies for a celebration that actually lands.

#1 Host a Networking Brunch

Bring your community together with a networking brunch. It’s designed to spark conversations and build relationships among members.

Picture a spread of pastries, fresh fruit, and a variety of drinks in a warm, inviting space. Add mingling coworkers, and you’ve got a real coworking celebration.

The brunch gives members a chance to relax, enjoy good food, and get to know one another in a casual setting.

Benefits of Networking for Coworking Members

Networking is a powerful tool for professionals in any industry. For coworking members, it offers real advantages:

  • Expanding professional networks: Meeting new people can open doors to collaborations, partnerships, or clients
  • Sharing knowledge and resources: Members exchange insights, tips, and resources that enrich their work and development
  • Building a sense of community: Regular networking creates a supportive environment where members feel more connected to the space and each other
  • Increasing visibility: It gives members a chance to explain what they do, which raises the odds of referrals and new business

Tips for Organizing a Successful Networking Brunch

Like any event, a networking brunch takes some planning. Here’s what to keep in mind:

  • Cater to various dietary preferences: Offer a menu with options for vegetarians, vegans, and those with gluten-free or other needs so everyone can eat and feel included. A buffet-style setup lets attendees pick what suits them.
  • Create a relaxed atmosphere: Set up comfortable seating, like lounge chairs or small tables, to encourage mingling. Play soft background music that doesn’t overpower conversation.
  • Encourage introductions and business card swaps: Start with a brief welcome and introduce new members or special guests. Provide name tags. Set up a dedicated area for business cards, or ask members ahead of time to bring them. Ice breakers or discussion prompts help kickstart conversations.
  • Promote the event in advance: Use your communication channels, like newsletters, social media, or a community board, to spread the word. Highlight the benefits of attending and any special features, such as guest speakers, giveaways, or special menu items.
  • Follow up afterward: Send a thank-you message to attendees. A recap with photos is a nice touch, and it’s a good moment to encourage members to connect on your space’s social platforms or join future events.

Whenever you host an event, ask attendees for feedback. You’ll learn what worked and what people want to see change next time.

A networking brunch creates a memorable experience for your community and celebrates the spirit of collaboration on International Coworking Day.

Have a dog-friendly coworking space? Invite all members and have some fun.

#2 Arrange Skill-Sharing Workshops

Skill-sharing workshops tap into the talents already inside your community.

The concept is simple: members volunteer to teach a skill they’re good at, whether it’s mastering Excel formulas or negotiating a budget, while others join to gain practical knowledge.

These workshops let members learn from each other, share what they know, and pick up new skills.

Depending on your member base, you could also run non-work skill-sharing sessions.

Let members get to know each other on a personal level by teaching a hobby or passion. How fun would it be to attend a workshop where a peer teaches you to restore old furniture, bake the perfect lemon meringue pie, or start a home garden?

Skill-sharing workshops are a great way to honor your community, their skills, and their talents on International Coworking Day.

Potential Workshop Topics

Create a signup sheet with a few pre-filled ideas to get things going, or let members pitch their own.

Here are some useful workshop topics to start with:

  • Digital marketing tips: How to use social media, SEO, and content marketing to grow an online presence
  • Time management techniques: Strategies for prioritizing tasks, staying organized, and getting more done
  • Creative problem-solving sessions: Methods like brainstorming, mind mapping, and lateral thinking to work through challenges
  • Basic coding for non-programmers: Fundamental coding concepts and tools for non-technical members
  • Effective communication skills: Practical guidance on interpersonal communication, public speaking, and negotiation

Steps to Organizing a Skill-Sharing Workshop

There are 6 steps to planning a workshop that works.

  1. Survey members for areas of interest: Use a quick survey or suggestion box to find out what topics members want. Include a spot for members to volunteer to lead a session, which saves you time later when you’re hunting for facilitators.
  2. Identify expert speakers from within the community: Review the survey results, spot members with expertise in the requested areas, and invite them to lead a workshop. Frame it as a chance to share knowledge and build their personal brand.
  3. Schedule multiple short sessions: Plan a series of focused sessions (30 to 60 minutes each, or 45 minutes with 15 for Q&A) to cover a variety of topics. Build a schedule that lets members attend more than one.
  4. Promote the workshops: Announce the lineup and schedule across your channels. Highlight the speakers and the value of each topic, and encourage early sign-ups to manage attendance.
  5. Prepare the logistics: Make sure each workshop has the equipment it needs, such as projectors, whiteboards, or handouts, and set up a comfortable space with good visibility.
  6. Facilitate networking and Q&A: Leave time for questions at the end of each session and encourage members to keep talking between workshops.

Make International Coworking Day a memorable celebration with skill-sharing workshops.

They deliver practical knowledge and strengthen the sense of community at the same time.

#3 Organize a Community Service Project

International Coworking Day is a good moment to think about the impact your community can have beyond the workplace.

A community service project lets members give back to the local area and strengthens the bond between people who started as strangers. Around 70% of employees prefer working for companies that care about their societal impact and support workplace giving and volunteering programs.

There’s a morale case too. Of surveyed corporate volunteers, 70% feel that volunteering boosted employee morale. Acts of service build a sense of purpose and shared responsibility, which reinforces the collaboration at the heart of coworking.

Benefits for Members and Your Organization

A shared service project benefits your members and your space as a whole. The main upsides:

  • Personal fulfillment
  • Skill development
  • Networking and relationship-building
  • Better morale
  • Stronger community culture
  • Positive brand image

Ideas for Community Service Projects

There are countless ways to give back. A few that stand out:

  • Local clean-up drives: Organize a group to clean up a nearby park, beach, or neighborhood. It promotes environmental responsibility and improves the area.
  • Volunteering at a local charity: Partner with a local nonprofit and give your time, whether that’s serving meals at a shelter, running a donation drive, or spending time with communities in need.
  • Fundraising events for a cause: Host a charity auction, bake sale, or fun run, with proceeds going to a cause your members care about.

Engaging Members in the Project

Not every member jumps at the chance to volunteer, but there are ways to bring people in.

Give as much notice as you can. Use newsletters, social media, and community boards to spread the word.

Explain the purpose, the benefits, and the impact to build interest. Sharing stories or testimonials from past events helps too.

If general promotion isn’t enough, try:

  • Offering incentives for participation: Small perks like discounts on membership fees, free coworking days, gift cards, or branded merchandise can encourage people to show up. Recognizing contributors goes a long way toward retaining volunteers.
  • Providing resources and support: Organize logistics like transportation, supplies, and meals to make participation easy.
  • Creating a collaborative atmosphere: Ask members to suggest ideas for this project or future ones so they feel invested. Pair members from different backgrounds so they learn from each other and make new connections.
  • Reflecting and sharing: Afterward, gather feedback and share the results, including photos and stories. It builds a sense of accomplishment and community pride.

A community service project makes a real difference locally while giving members enriching experiences and new connections.

It’s the kind of celebration that leaves a lasting impression and strengthens your community.

#4 Host a Coworking Space Open House

An open house is a great way to celebrate International Coworking Day. Inviting the local community to experience your space firsthand lets you show off its features, amenities, and community feel.

An open house can attract potential members, build partnerships, and raise awareness locally. It also gives current members a reason to feel proud of their space and invite friends, which grows the community.

Planning Your Open House

An open house takes work. You want your space looking its best so it sells itself. These tips will help:

  • Identify the focal points: Start by deciding what you want to highlight. Individual workspaces? Members presenting collaborative projects? Success stories and testimonials? Pick the core of your event and build around it.
  • Promote the event: Use social media to build buzz. Share posts about tours, refreshments, and giveaways, with eye-catching visuals. Reach out to local businesses and community organizations. Post flyers in nearby cafes and libraries, and announce it on local forums and community boards.
  • Offer tours and highlight unique features: Prepare guided tours of your different areas, including private offices, meeting rooms, common areas, and anything unusual like wellness rooms or podcast booths. Point out what sets you apart, whether that’s flexible membership options, ergonomic furniture, or a strong community culture.
  • Provide refreshments and giveaways: Offer coffee, tea, and snacks. For a more upscale event, add a small buffet and a glass of champagne. Partnering with local vendors adds a community-supportive touch.

Prepare small giveaways, like branded pens, notebooks, or mugs, or a free day pass so attendees can try the space. These small tokens leave a lasting impression.

  • Offer referral incentives: Encourage members to bring guests. Offer the first month free for each new member who joins from a referral, and a free month for the member who referred them. You can also offer free day passes. A discounted rate for anyone who signs up during the open house creates urgency.
  • Create an inviting atmosphere: Make sure the space is clean and well-organized. Add fresh flowers or banners for a festive feel. Have staff and community ambassadors on hand to greet visitors and answer questions.
  • Follow up afterward: Send thank-you emails with information on how to join, upcoming events, and any ongoing promotions. Encourage attendees to stay connected through your social channels or newsletter.

Open your doors and introduce your space to a wider audience. Showing what your community offers is a fitting tribute to International Coworking Day.

It’s also a solid way to grow your membership and reinforce your space as a hub in the local business scene.

#5 Launch a Member Recognition Program

A member recognition program celebrates the contributions, achievements, and positive qualities of the people in your community. It’s a fitting way to mark International Coworking Day.

By highlighting the efforts and successes of individual members, the program builds appreciation, belonging, and motivation.

It publicly recognizes members who embody the values of the space, which strengthens community bonds and creates a better environment.

Ways to Recognize and Reward Members

There are plenty of ways to recognize your members. A few that bring results:

  • Member of the Month awards: Recognize a standout member each month based on professional achievements, community involvement, or plain helpfulness. Feature them with a short profile on your bulletin board, website, or social media.
  • Public acknowledgement: Different from a formal title, a dedicated section in your monthly newsletter can celebrate several members’ milestones at once, such as business launches, awards, or anniversaries. Give shout-outs on social media and tag members and their businesses to boost their visibility.
  • Small gifts or perks: Offer tokens of appreciation like gift cards, branded merchandise, or free access to premium amenities. Consider exclusive perks such as priority booking for events, reserved parking, or extended access hours.

Impact of Recognition on Member Satisfaction and Retention

Recognizing members’ efforts changes their whole experience of the space.

It reinforces that they’re valued, which lifts satisfaction and morale.

HR Cloud names recognition as one of the top drivers of employee retention, noting that people respond to leadership actively listening and acknowledging their success.

Quantum Workplace backs this up. Organizations with formal employee recognition programs have 31% less voluntary turnover than organizations that don’t have any program at all.

Their research also found that when employees believe they will be recognized, they are 2.7x more likely to be highly engaged.

When members feel acknowledged, they build a stronger emotional connection to the community.

That connection leads to higher engagement and loyalty. Members are more likely to renew, which lifts retention.

A recognition program also improves your reputation as a welcoming, supportive space, which attracts new members looking for exactly that.

Launch a member recognition program to build a culture of appreciation. It enriches the experience of current members and helps you attract and keep new ones.

#6 Conduct Fun Team-Building Activities

Team-building activities build community and collaboration in coworking spaces.

Unlike traditional offices, coworking spaces are full of individuals and small teams from different industries and backgrounds.

Team-building breaks down barriers, makes networking easier, and creates a more cohesive community.

It builds communication, trust, and camaraderie, which improves the whole coworking experience. Hard to think of a better way to celebrate International Coworking Day.

Examples of Engaging Activities

HR World found that 82% of UK employees want their workplace to offer more regular team-building events to boost job satisfaction. So what are they after?

A few fun options:

  • Escape room challenges
  • Scavenger hunts
  • Group fitness sessions
  • Team hikes
  • A sporting event
  • Live entertainment
  • Lunch, dinner, or after-work happy hours

Don’t feel pressured to run day-long, off-site events. Big outings tend to draw the most interest, but you can do plenty in-house too. Don’t underestimate office bingo or yard games.

You could also run several smaller activities, one each day leading up to August 9th. That reaches a wider audience and keeps the celebration going all week.

Tips for Ensuring Participation and Enjoyment

Nothing’s worse than planning an event no one shows up to. You put in the time and energy and get tumbleweeds. Here’s how to avoid that:

  • Choose activities that cater to diverse interests: Offer variety. Some members want physical activities, others prefer mental challenges. Send out a survey or poll beforehand to gauge interest.
  • Provide clear instructions and support: Make sure everyone understands the rules and goals. Have facilitators or team leaders available to help.
  • Create a friendly, competitive spirit: Organize teams and offer small prizes or recognition for winners. Keep the focus on fun and connection.
  • Foster a welcoming, inclusive atmosphere: Make sure everyone feels comfortable joining in, regardless of experience. Ice breakers at the start help people relax and open up.

Team-building strengthens the sense of community in your space.

These activities give members a chance to interact, collaborate, and make memories. Celebrating International Coworking Day with engaging events adds to the day and to a more cohesive community.

#7 Create a Collaborative Art Project

A collaborative art project brings together the different talents and perspectives in your community.

It lets members contribute to a shared piece of art, which builds a sense of unity and creativity.

Examples of Collaborative Art Projects

Whether it’s a mural, a community mosaic, or an interactive installation, a collaborative art project turns your space into a canvas that reflects your community.

A closer look at how to run one:

  • Mural painting: Design a large mural members can paint together on a designated wall. It can depict your community, local culture, or a shared vision. The result beautifies the space and creates a lasting piece everyone owns.
  • Community mosaic: Create a mosaic from tiles, glass, or other materials, with each member adding a piece. The final image represents the diverse, interconnected nature of your community.
  • Interactive installation: Set up something members add to over time. That could be a sculpture from recyclable materials, a “wishing tree” where members hang their aspirations, or a canvas people add to. The project grows as more people take part.

Facilitating the Project

A group art project takes time, planning, and resources. Use these guidelines:

  • Secure a designated space: Pick a prominent, accessible area. Prepare it for the materials and activity, mark it clearly, and post the project’s theme and participation guidelines. A sign-up schedule or set times for different groups helps manage flow if you have a lot of members.
  • Provide materials and guidance: Supply what’s needed, such as paints, brushes, tiles, adhesive, and protective coverings. Partnering with local art supply stores or artists can help with quality materials and support.

If needed, invite a local artist or an experienced member to give initial guidance or run a short technique workshop. It helps members feel confident, whatever their skill level.

  • Encourage creative contributions: Invite everyone to take part, regardless of artistic background. The goal is to express individuality and build something together.
  • Document the process: Capture the project’s progress through photos or videos across its stages. Share it on social media or in newsletters to keep the community engaged. It might even catch the eye of potential members.
  • Showcase your work: Plan a small unveiling once the project is done so everyone can appreciate the finished piece and the effort behind it. Recognize your contributors. Consider starting early and holding the unveiling on August 9th.

A collaborative art project is a memorable way to celebrate International Coworking Day. It captures the community, creativity, and collaboration at the core of coworking.

Conclusion

International Coworking Day highlights the collaboration, creativity, and flexibility that coworking spaces give freelancers, entrepreneurs, remote workers, and small businesses working in shared environments.

The day also puts a spotlight on how coworking supports productivity, creativity, and work-life balance, which makes it worth marking for anyone in or curious about the industry.

So raise a cup of coffee (or two) to the coworking community and the future ahead. Whether you’re a coworking veteran or a curious newcomer, join us in celebrating what coworking is really about: collaboration, connection, community, and creativity.
