Name: Choosing The Right Coworking Space Furniture [Easy Guide]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Whether you’re starting a new coworking space or considering redesigning your current one, choosing the right furniture is crucial.
Post body:
Whether you’re starting a new coworking space or considering redesigning your current one, choosing the right furniture is crucial.

Providing your members with proper furniture and amenities can significantly improve their experience and keep them coming back.

But how do you know what furniture to choose?

In this article, we discuss what furniture you should buy for a coworking space and how to use your furniture choices to make your space more attractive to members.

Quick Summary

  • Choosing the right furniture is integral to a coworking space’s success.
  • When selecting your furniture, consider the needs of your members, scalability, and technology integrations.
  • Arrange your coworking space furniture and floor plans to promote optimal productivity to support your members.
  • Some basic coworking sapce furniture you should have include desks, chairs, and properly designed workstations.

What Is Coworking Space Furniture?

Coworking space furniture refers to furnishings specifically designed and selected to create a productive, stylish, and collaborative work environment for people who use coworking spaces.

Freelancers, small business owners, remote workers, and other professionals use these spaces and benefit from the camaraderie, even though they don’t always work for the same employer.

The furniture is the foundation of the coworking community feel. It forms micro-environments for individuals to meet, collaborate, or simply share space with like-minded individuals while working on their own.

Furniture in coworking spaces includes:

  • Desks and workstations with built-in power outlets
  • Chairs
  • Projectors and whiteboards
  • Sofas, armchairs, and coffee tables
  • Booths, partitions, and soundproof pods for phone calls
  • Barstools for dining areas
  • Outdoor seating and tables for outdoor areas

Why Is It Important to Choose the Right Coworking Space Furniture?

Choosing the right coworking space furniture is essential to demonstrate the quality of your services and keep customers coming back.

Furniture and the layout directly affect how people use the space and how comfortable and productive they are. Ultimately, choosing the right furniture will improve their experiences and help you retain members.

How to Choose Coworking Space Furniture

You need to consider several things when choosing furniture for your space.

1. Understand Your Members

Consider the types of professionals using the space and their working styles. Do they often have meetings, or are they mainly working independently?

  • If several of your members are part of corporate teams, you’ll likely require more meeting rooms (check out this guide for coworking meeting rooms) and collaborative furniture, such as large tables with multiple seats.
  • If you have more members who work independently, you’ll require more desks and possibly need to offer day passes for individual walk-ins.

Also, consider the type of clients you want to attract. For example, if you’re attracting corporate clients, you’ll need more tables and privacy features.

On the other hand, if you want to attract freelancers and startups, look for more inviting furniture and spaces suitable for one to three people.

The more you learn about who will use your space, the easier it will be to choose the right furniture to cater to their needs.

2. Consider Cultural and Aesthetic Appeal

To create a sense of community, incorporate furniture that reflects the local culture. This includes design elements, art, decor, themes, and colors.

  • Design elements: Use furniture and decor that reflects the local culture and heritage, including materials and patterns that are significant to the region. For example, if your space is located in Japan, use materials like bamboo to fit in with Japanese design.
  • Art and decor: Display local artwork, crafts, and cultural artifacts to create a sense of community. For example, if your space is in New York, you can display urban-themed artwork and photographs by local artists.
  • Themes and colors: Choose colors and themes that resonate with the area and your market. For example, if you cater to young professionals, opt for more colors and eclectic furniture.

3. Make Furniture Inclusive and Accessible

Choose furniture that fits different body shapes and abilities, such as desks and chairs with adjustable height options.

You can also provide chairs with good back support for people with back problems and different seating options, like ergonomic chairs and standing desks.

In addition to having inclusive furniture, you must also ensure they’re laid out correctly.

  • Have wide pathways so members can quickly move around.
  • Create designated workspaces that are easily accessible to people with disabilities, such as those in wheelchairs.

Using OfficeRnd Flex to manage your space bookings can make it easy for your members to access workstations, furniture, and amenities. Members can easily book desks, meeting rooms, and other amenities based on their unique needs.

4. Integrate Technology

People use your space to get work done, and this can’t happen without access to technology and the internet.

Make sure you choose desks and tables with built-in USB ports and power outlets so members can quickly charge their laptops, phones, and other devices. Plus, you could offer wireless charging pads.

There’s also been a significant increase in smart furniture, with a projected market growth of 12.4% from 2021 to 2028. These include systems that automatically change the lighting and temperature. These are great not only for saving costs but for boosting sustainability as well.

5. Prioritize Wellness

If your target group prioritizes their health, you can also add furniture to help them feel better physically and mentally.

Here are some coworking space furniture ideas that can enhance your space:

  • Lounges or nap pods
  • Meditation rooms and furniture
  • Yoga spaces
  • Fitness equipment
  • Spaces with lots of greenery and natural light

Learn more about the must-have coworking space amenities here.

6. Consider Versatility and Scalability

Furniture can be expensive to purchase in the beginning. So, it’s important to think about buying furniture that can be moved around for different events and uses.

You can even buy multi-purpose furniture, like desks that can be turned into meeting tables or storage units that can also be used as seats. This can help you adjust according to your changing needs instead of having to buy new furniture all the time.

If you have a small space, you can get furniture that saves space, like foldable chairs or stackable tables.

Best Practices for Arranging Coworking Space Furniture

Your coworking space’s layout can greatly impact productivity and focus. Here are some ways you can arrange your space well.

  • Perform a space analysis: Understand your space’s usage and flow. Observe how people move and work in your space and place furniture accordingly. You can use a floor plan to experiment with different layouts. You can use a powerful analytics tool such as OfficeRnD Flex’s Data Hub to analyze space usage.
  • Maximize natural light: Try to position your workstations and communal areas close to the windows to take advantage of natural light, which can improve members’ moods and happiness.
  • Create open layouts and communal areas: Make collaboration easier by designing open layouts with communal areas, breakout spaces, and shared desks. But make sure you maintain a balance between open areas and quiet zones for focused work.
  • Ensure easy technology integration: If you don’t have furniture with built-in power outlets, position furniture close to wall outlets. Also, ensure ample outlets and USB ports are available in communal areas.

Coworking Space Furniture Ideas: Modern Inspiration

If you’re struggling to get the creative juices flowing, then use these examples to help you find coworking space furniture ideas for your own space.

Common Desk is a US-based coworking company with over 22 locations across the country. It features a welcoming vibe with thoughtful layouts designed to spark human connections.

The use of a mix of comfortable lounge furniture with both individual and large tables invites members to focus on their work while surrounded by a sense of community.

WorkBetter is a one-of-a-kind coworking space in Bulgaria, Sofia. Members benefit from stylish furniture that’s also practical, including lounge chairs, phone booths for quiet work, and meeting rooms that inspire engagement.

Manage Your Coworking Space With OfficeRnD Flex

Buying proper furniture and designing an effective layout will improve your members’ experience and lead to repeat business.

Once you have your furniture in the right place, you can optimize your space for better use using coworking management software like OfficeRnd Flex, which helps streamline operations and keeps members happy. Members can book spaces, and you can receive payments, send contracts, and send communications all with one tool.

Most of today’s workers prefer having a hybrid work option over working solely in-office. In fact, recent insights from Gallup show that six in ten employees with a remote-capable job would prefer a hybrid work arrangement, with fewer than 10% preferring to work entirely onsite.

A hybrid work environment has the potential to offer the best of everything to employees — but only if the downsides are mitigated. Full-time hybrid workers cite work-life balance, efficient use of time, and higher productivity as the top advantages of hybrid work. But less resource access, reduced collaboration, and coordination difficulties rank high among the challenges of the hybrid model.

As a company with a hybrid team, you’ll need to adapt to keep your employees engaged and productive. But how?

In this article, we’ll look at how an interactive office map can help your team members maximize their efficiency and feel more connected. We’ll outline what an interactive office map is, why you should consider one, and everything you’ll need to get started with your office map template.

  • Hybrid work is popular, but it comes with challenges. An interactive office map can help keep your team on task, productive, and happy.
  • The benefits of an interactive office map include ease of collaboration and a safer workplace.
  • Creating and maintaining an interactive office map will help your team become more efficient.
  • With OfficeRnD Workplace, you can streamline the workplace experience for your hybrid employees.

What Is an Interactive Office Map?

An interactive office map is a digital representation of your company’s workspace layout. It heightens the workplace experience for hybrid employees by making it easier to view, book, and locate key office resources.

Think of an interactive office map as a customizable office directory that gives you a bird’s-eye view, showing the floorspace, equipment, and people. Put simply, it solves the problem of employees knowing which person, piece of equipment, or conference room they need but being unable to find it.

An office map that makes office navigation easier can benefit any workplace, but it’s especially helpful in a hybrid environment. If your teams often move around, use a hot desking system, and collaborate on projects with remote employees, it’s a way to help everyone make the most of their time at the office.

5 Benefits of Using an Interactive Office Map

While hybrid work is preferred by many, the structure can make it harder for employees to feel connected to their team members during their home-based days. An interactive office map lets staff reserve the spaces and facilities they need on their remote days, which can help them maximize their focused work time when onsite.

Here are some of the key benefits of implementing a digital office map template:

Meetings Are Seamless Once Employees Are Onsite

According to Gartner research, building relationships and improving collaboration are among the top reasons employees use the office. By making it easier for them to book the spaces they need, you’ll improve the workplace experience for your team, leading to higher employee satisfaction.

As an example, with OfficeRnD Workplace, your team can use desk scheduling to book spaces together and reserve meeting rooms with the amenities they need.

Working Together Gets Easier

Harvard Business Review research indicates that coordination is a key challenge of hybrid work. Beyond desk reservations and room bookings, hybrid workers can use an office directory to search for the team members they need to contact and schedule in-person collaboration for their onsite workdays.

By picking a seat close to the person they need to work with, your team members can arrange in-person brainstorming sessions from their home office and get more mileage from the time they spend with their coworkers.

With a platform that makes it simple to locate crucial colleagues, you can create a hybrid work environment that fosters cross-departmental collaboration, empowering your employees to work together and be more productive.

For example, with the OfficeRnD floorplan clustering system, booking desk space becomes easy for hybrid workers, even if they work in offices with large or complex floorplans.

You can even book desks in bulk.

A Safer Workplace

How familiar are your hybrid workers with your in-office protocols in the case of an emergency? An interactive office map is one way to help them get up to speed before disaster strikes.

A digital map gives you complete visibility of your premises. When you can see which hot desks are taken, you can manage headcounts in the event of an emergency or drill. You can then mark the emergency exits on the map for all employees to view, leading to a faster and more efficient evacuation if the worst should happen.

You can even combine this with advanced presence tracking to enhance your operational efficiency.

Optimized Onsite Time

Employees who arrive at the office prepared for their day are often more productive. Access to an office directory showing the layout ahead of time can help your team locate meeting rooms in a timely manner and easily book desks.

Plus, visitors benefit from seeing the building’s layout before their arrival. Instead of navigating a maze-like office on the fly and running late for appointments, your stakeholders, for instance, can help visitors prepare for their visit in advance.

Include a plan of the parking area to assist guests in finding a space quickly. You can even offer a contactless check-in option and add instructions for finding the badge entry area.

A Bird’s-Eye View

Creating a workplace that functions well starts with a clear and complete overview of what’s happening and where. For a facility manager, an interactive floor plan and customizable office map is a great way to keep on top of how space is being used, the occupancy status of rooms, and which areas of the office are likely to see high traffic.

For example, the bathrooms adjacent to the conference space used for quarterly sales meetings might need an extra bit of TLC ahead of the big day. An interactive map will help you to identify where your maintenance team should spend their time.

A leader in fashion design and manufacture, Dewhirst is no stranger to changing with the times. The company was established in 1880 and continues to innovate to meet the needs of modern employees.

After the COVID-19 pandemic shook up their office culture, Dewhirst turned to OfficeRnD Workplace for help adopting a reliable hybrid work model. With a simple-to-use floorplan and ease of desk and room booking, OfficeRnD helped Dewhirst get their employees back to top productivity without frustration.

4 Tips for Creating an Interactive Office Map

The shift toward remote and hybrid work continues even now, post-pandemic, according to data from McKinsey.

With many skilled employees weighing work-life balance and lifestyle aspects, such as hybrid work, heavily in their decision-making processes, getting a solid strategy in place for hybrid work in the future will help you attract and retain high-quality workers.

But creating dynamic work environments that function well isn’t easy.

An interactive office map can help you bolster employee productivity in and out of your office building by making it easier for them to navigate the physical space and make the most of their face-to-face time with colleagues.

Ready to create your office map? Take a look at these four tips:

Get to Know Your Space

Are you clear on how your space is currently being used? Creating a floor plan map is a good way to review your space management and make sure you’re getting the most out of every square foot.

It starts with collecting data on your current layout, furniture, equipment, and people. Once you have this data, you can review how your office amenities are being utilized and where you could make some changes.

For example, if a particular piece of equipment has gone unused for a while, consider placing it in storage to free up more space for the amenities your team members use more frequently.

Improve Your Space Utilization

As you prepare to create your interactive office map, assess whether the ways you’re currently utilizing your space are working or if switching things up could be beneficial.

For instance, is your furniture arranged in a way that allows natural light to enter the office? Are any breakout spaces under-utilized? And if heavily used spaces neighbor each other, are acoustics an issue?

Conduct Testing and Feedback

Once your interactive office map is ready, it’s time to test, test, test! Gather internal feedback from your teams — after all, they’ll be the ones using the office map the most. It’s a good idea to have them run through some simple tasks, like locating a colleague or booking a desk.

External feedback is also valuable. If someone external to the organization visits your office for meetings periodically, consider providing them with the map and asking for feedback on whether it makes their life easier.

And, of course, make sure to build in enough time to refine your interactive office map before you go live with it.

Update Your Map When Things Change

Building an interactive office map isn’t a one-and-done project. Sometimes, you’ll need to move things around.

And when your floor plans change, your customizable digital office map should, too.

For example, if a meeting room is closed for refurbishment, be sure to mark that on the map. Or if you’ve added an extra sofa to a breakout area, let your team know — they might plan to use it!

Getting paid shouldn’t require your team to chase invoices or manually verify bank accounts. For coworking spaces, the payment setup you run directly affects how fast members can join, book, and pay.

Our webinar, “Elevate Your Payments: Unleashing the Power of Stripe with OfficeRnD,” covered how the Stripe integration works inside OfficeRnD Flex, and what changed when Downtown Works moved to it. This recap pulls out the parts worth acting on.

The Stripe integration in OfficeRnD Flex lets coworking operators collect card and ACH payments, automate invoicing, and let members verify bank accounts and pay without staff stepping in.

If you missed the live session, here’s what came up.

Meet the speakers

David Adato; COO/CTO, Downtown Works

Downtown Works has used OfficeRnD Flex since 2018, but before integrating with Stripe, they were on PlacePay.

That provider didn’t meet their needs. Their number one goal is always “to be as operationally efficient as possible.”

They wanted members to go online and get access to everything without waiting for the Downtown Works team to respond or act. Stripe was how they got there.

Miro Miroslavov; CEO & co-founder, OfficeRnD

Miro moderated and ran the discussion with David around what it’s like to be both an OfficeRnD user and a Stripe 2.0 user.

Orlin Grigorov; Senior PM, OfficeRnD

Orlin walked through the key features of the Stripe integration and how it handles payment processing. From configuring payment method options to a live demo, he explained the benefits of using a payment service provider, and of using Stripe with OfficeRnD specifically.

Key takeaways

  • Integration: OfficeRnD Flex and Stripe work together in one place, so coworking operators manage memberships, bookings, and payments without switching tools.
  • Automated processes: Automating invoicing and payment reminders cuts down admin work. It saves time and reduces errors, so payments get processed accurately and on time.
  • Security: Stripe’s security controls, including regional parameters and risk management, mean coworking spaces can tell members their payment information is protected. Stripe keeps updating its security. See the setup guide.
  • User experience: Every speaker came back to user experience. The integration aims to give operators and members a smooth way to handle payments and financial reporting.

Behind the scenes with Downtown Works

Miro interviewed David Adato about his experience with Stripe 2.0. They covered user experience, security and compliance, and several other topics.

Here’s the conversation.

What made you switch to Stripe?

David explained that their first payment gateway, PlacePay, held back the member experience. Operational efficiency is a top priority for Downtown Works, and they wanted members to complete tasks on their own. With PlacePay, staff had to get involved in many steps of the payment process.

When the Stripe 2.0 integration let Downtown Works verify bank accounts instantly without staff involvement, they knew it was time to phase out the other provider. They ran both Stripe and PlacePay for about 3 years before deciding Stripe met all of their needs.

What payment methods are you using?

Adato sees clear value in letting members pick how they pay:

The more options you give someone to pay, the more likely they are to not only complete the checkout but continue the process.

He used Apple Pay when shopping online as an example, since it’s faster than typing in card details. Downtown Works uses all payment methods available in the United States (credit/debit cards, ACH, Cash App, Google Pay, and others) to give members options and make checkout easier.

What is the user experience with Stripe 2.0?

Admins and members both want a portal with a clean, functional UI that’s secure and looks the part. Adato said that from the member side, Stripe 2.0 is a clear step up from the Stripe 1.0 integration.

He recommends anyone still on the original version upgrade to get the newer features. One example: if members have saved payment details with other merchants that use Stripe, they can select a saved card instead of typing it again.

That saves time at checkout. On the admin side, Adato said the integration adds a lot to the overall product. Miro also talked through product updates and new features in the works.

How do you deal with security and compliance?

Stripe’s security controls, including regional parameters and risk management, let coworking spaces tell members their payment information is protected. Stripe keeps updating how it secures payment details.

As Adato put it:

There are things based on your region that they allow or they don’t allow, and in terms of just user data and user safety, I think it’s extremely important because we’re trusting both OfficeRnD and Stripe to process our members’ personal and private information.

The panel also warned against taking members’ card details over the phone. Use the automation and payment option features instead. That keeps your organization compliant.

What about pricing?

Adato said Downtown Works charges members a 1.99% processing fee for credit or debit cards, though that number varies by organization. He noted Stripe’s general rate is 2.9% plus 30 cents per transaction, which still holds in 2026 for standard US online card payments.

Both Adato and Miroslavov recommend asking your Stripe representative about lower rates. Adato said he’s happy to pay for the Stripe integration because it gives Downtown Works and their members the freedom to complete payments with ease.

Do you use a point-of-sale (POS terminal)?

Adato said Downtown Works only uses a POS for their mini-market. He asked about integrating a Stripe terminal, and Miroslavov confirmed it was on the roadmap. Adato said he’d pay for a Stripe reader to make things easier.

Final thoughts

The webinar showed what integrating Stripe with OfficeRnD Flex does for a coworking operator: less manual payment work, faster onboarding, and more payment options for members.

Automate the payment process and your team spends less time on invoices and more on running the space and serving members.

Name: How Coworking Space Owners Can Harness The Power Of Incubator Spaces
Author: asen-stoyanchev

Post body:
Launching a startup isn’t easy. Even the best ideas can fail due to limited resources and finances.

But it’s not all doom and gloom. There are many strategies business owners can use to get their ventures off the ground.

Business incubator spaces, for example, provide support from one central office location. From workspaces to tech to experts, they offer a diverse range of tools in exchange for equity or a monthly fee.

Interested in learning more? In this article, we’ll explain the differences between a business incubator, an accelerator, and a coworking space. Plus, we’ll tell you the top features the best incubator spaces have and how can you leverage that to improve your coworking space.

Quick Summary:

  • Business incubator spaces support entrepreneurs, startups, and small business owners as they get their new ventures off the ground.
  • One of the top benefits of a business incubator is that it provides physical office space in a central location. Entrepreneurs can use it for meetings and other business operations.
  • By working from a shared workspace, startups can take advantage of a coworking community. Morale and motivation improve when entrepreneurs are surrounded by like-minded people.
  • Coworking space owners can leverage incubator spaces by integrating incubator programs and resources into their offerings, creating a hybrid environment that attracts and supports early-stage startups. This strategic fusion enhances the value of their coworking spaces, fostering innovation and collaboration while increasing member retention and satisfaction.

What Is a Business Incubator?

A business incubator gives startups access to resources they don’t have the budget for. The service is usually for a limited time — specifically, until the business can survive on its own.

Entrepreneurs, startups, and small businesses all use incubators. By signing up for an incubator program, participants can run their operations from a shared workspace. In addition to physical office space, the deal may include other resources, such as mentors, technology, and training and education.

So, why does this matter?

Tracy Kitts, former Chief Operating Officer of the National Business Incubation Association, says businesses backed by an incubator have a survival rate of 87%. Compare this to those going it alone, and you’ll see a massive drop in the success rate — just 44%.

For managers who run incubator spaces, the payoff may be equity in the company. Incubators can also make money through sponsorships, partnerships, or membership fees.

What’s the Difference Between Incubators, Accelerators, and Coworking Spaces?

We already know business incubator spaces are for early startups, providing the tools they need to launch successfully. But what happens when a startup is ready for the next stage?

An accelerator or coworking space may be the right option. Let’s take a brief look at each of them:

Accelerator Spaces

  • Purpose: Accelerator spaces are designed to fast-track the growth of early-stage startups by providing intensive support over a fixed period, typically ranging from a few months to a year.
  • Programs: These spaces offer structured programs that include mentorship, education, and often seed funding. The goal is to prepare startups for growth and investment.
  • Mentorship: Access to a network of experienced mentors, industry experts, and successful entrepreneurs who provide guidance and advice.
  • Funding: Many accelerators offer initial seed funding in exchange for equity, helping startups to develop their products and scale quickly.
  • Demo Days: Programs culminate in demo days where startups pitch their ideas to a room full of investors, increasing their chances of securing further investment.
  • Focus: Accelerators have a strong focus on high-growth potential startups and work intensively with a select group of companies.
  • Time Frame: Participants join for a defined period, after which they are expected to have made significant progress and to be ready for the next stage of growth.

Coworking Spaces

  • Purpose: Coworking spaces provide a flexible, shared working environment for freelancers, remote workers, small businesses, and startups. They focus on creating a collaborative community.
  • Flexibility: These spaces offer various membership plans, from daily passes to long-term leases, catering to different work styles and needs.
  • Amenities: Coworking spaces typically provide office amenities such as high-speed internet, meeting rooms, printing services, and communal areas, fostering a productive work environment.
  • Community: Emphasis on building a diverse community through networking events, social gatherings, and collaborative projects.
  • Cost-Effective: They offer a cost-effective alternative to traditional office spaces, particularly for individuals and small teams looking for professional workspaces without long-term commitments.
  • Diversity: Members come from various industries and professions, creating a rich, diverse environment that encourages networking and cross-industry collaboration.
  • No Fixed Program: Unlike accelerators, coworking spaces do not have structured programs or a fixed duration of stay. Members can join and leave as per their convenience.

As long as the facility meets the requirements, you don’t need to choose just one service. For example, an incubator space can complement a coworking space.

Any shared setups should come with private office spaces and dedicated desks.

You can use coworking management tools such as OfficeRnD Flex to manage everything from payments to members, ensuring your coworking space runs smoothly.

The Top 6 Features of a Good Business Incubator Space

Having access to a business incubator comes with a range of perks for entrepreneurs and startups. Here are the top six features for supporting new businesses:

1. Physical Office Space

Successful companies can launch from unconventional spaces. For example, Facebook came to life in a college dorm room. Other familiar names, including Microsoft, Amazon, and Apple, started in garages.

While inspiring, these stories aren’t the norm. Business is competitive, and around 91% of startups fail without support.

Access to a physical office space can make a big difference in the day-to-day running of a startup. Business incubators provide professional office space with desks, chairs, and other amenities. With furnished offices, teams can collaborate in person.

The building should be in a convenient location, such as a city or technology hub. With a dedicated meeting space, entrepreneurs can pitch ideas and meet clients. These meeting rooms can be booked in advance using a coworking booking platform.

Depending on the types of clients the incubator program serves, the space may also offer a laboratory or creative amenities. Larger buildings may even include a cafe or restaurant.

2. Technology and Tools

Incubator programs need more than desks and bathrooms. Technology should also be part of the mix to give startups the tools they need for success.

Here are some essential tech features the best incubator office suites have:

  • Computers, fax machines, printers, and scanners
  • Telephones and noise-canceling headsets
  • Accounting, word processing, and other professional software
  • Antivirus software and encryption
  • Reliable, high-speed internet
  • Projectors and microphones for meetings
  • Analytics, goal-setting, and research tools

Remember, some business owners will also have remote workers or collaborate with international companies. Quiet zones set up for video conferencing can be beneficial for these individuals.

And because incubator spaces constantly have people coming and going, technology can help maintain security — think video cameras, mobile door access, and alarm systems.

Watch the video below to learn how to manage WiFi security in a connected space:

3. Mentorship Opportunities

It takes a team of people to run a business. New startups don’t always have the funds to hire across every department, so this is where incubators come in.

Mentorship is invaluable for those just starting out. By tapping into expertise from others in the industry, entrepreneurs can learn to avoid common mistakes and build successful brands. They can also get advice on marketing, management, human resources, and legal obligations.

Incubator spaces are designed to connect like-minded people. Mentors can offer support to entrepreneurs in person, with advice tailored to the industry and business stage.

4. Training and Education Opportunities

Skills and knowledge gaps can harm any business.

For example, if a manager isn’t up to date with local laws, they may have legal issues. Red tape can stop a business from progressing, and fines can impact cash flow.

Ongoing learning is essential for businesses that want to understand the market, improve efficiency, and reduce risk. This is why most incubation programs feature opportunities for education and training.

Training can have a mix of formal and informal options and can even be customized to each participant’s needs.

But what types of education may be relevant, you might ask? Think marketing, accounting, management, and customer research.

With a business incubator space, training sessions can be held in a central location. The building may even include a dedicated study hub. Training days can be held on-site, while remote learning can be virtual.

5. Financial Support

Some incubators invest money into startups, which can be used for a range of purposes, such as staff wages, product manufacturing, or expansion.

Investment isn’t a gift, however — and those who provide seed money get a stake in the company. Incubators have a hands-on role in making sure the venture is a success. So, before committing, it’s important for all parties to share the same vision.

Having office facilities will help ensure everyone is on the same page. Meetings can support business planning, budgeting, and growth and efficiency strategies.

Incubator spaces can also be used to connect startups with other potential investors. If the idea is good enough for an incubator to get behind, others will likely want in on the action, too.

6. Coworking Community

Coworking spaces come with perks for early-stage startups. Instead of feeling isolated, these small business communities help make everyone feel connected.

Having other entrepreneurs in the same location can be good for morale. Whether it’s a coffee “brain break” or the discovery of new role models and mentors, a space shared with others is beneficial.

And a community of entrepreneurs is only the beginning. Experts can be on-site, ready to offer business assistance. Plus, incubator spaces can be set up for formal or informal networking events. Expert speakers can share their wisdom while entrepreneurs build their professional networks.

Remember, not everyone thrives in a bustling work environment. So, make private spaces and meeting rooms available, as well.

What Are the Benefits of Business Incubator Spaces?

Business incubator spaces are beneficial for both entrepreneurs and supportive organizations. Here are some of the top benefits that come with this kind of partnership:

Flexibility

Private offices often come with long-term leases. For small businesses, this type of commitment can be daunting.

Why? Because if the business grows, it may require a bigger office. Alternatively, when money is tight, an office space in a prime location may feel out of reach.

Incubator spaces are a flexible option and a good way to test the waters. Entrepreneurs get everything they need to kick off their venture — with room to scale if they need it. Then, once the business grows, they can pivot to a coworking arrangement or take out a lease elsewhere. And if it goes the other way and becomes unviable, scaling down is much easier.

Because incubator spaces have experts and modern technology on hand, entrepreneurs can also change their goals and strategies in real-time. If an issue is flagged early, legal or financial issues may be avoided.

Research

Startups fail for various reasons — and 42% fail due to a poor market fit. Even the best ideas can fizzle out if there’s no market for their product or service.

Incubator spaces can be useful for researching everything from potential customers to product price points. With the support of in-person professionals, startups can set realistic goals

For incubators investing in the startup, the research phase will determine how successful the project may be. They can then make the necessary decisions. For example, they can decide whether more money should be invested or whether they should end their partnership.

Budgeting

Sticking to a budget can be tough for startups. The cost of manufacturing a product or starting a service is just one consideration.

Entrepreneurs need a range of experts, including those with legal, accounting, and marketing backgrounds. Add to this physical infrastructure, insurance, energy bills, and license fees, and the costs can quickly skyrocket.

An incubator space is a cost-effective solution. Instead of paying for everything separately, it’s all included in the program. It’s not uncommon for an incubator program to have a service fee, but this is more budget-friendly than the alternative.

Entrepreneurs can get support on budget creation and advice on areas where cost-cutting may be required. Experts can also give them tips to avoid overspending.

Growth

Launching a startup can be a slow process, with a lot of trial and error along the way.

But entrepreneurs don’t have to start from scratch — they can use proven strategies to grow and expand their brand. With the support of professionals, growth can become much faster.

Incubator spaces have a network of industry leaders ready to share their knowledge. By tapping into these resources, the risk of doing business decreases.

Money is also essential for those who want ‌to get ahead. Without adequate financing, the bills can pile up, causing a business to stagnate or fail. It’s also easier to secure a loan — and have more options for expansion as a result — with a healthy bank balance.

Incubator spaces keep the outgoings down for startups, giving them room to grow without the financial strain.

Whether the incubator is receiving a fee or equity, the growth and success of the startup is a priority.

Synergizing Coworking and Incubator Spaces: A Strategic Advantage

As discussed, coworking spaces and incubator spaces serve distinct yet complementary roles in the entrepreneurial ecosystem. Coworking spaces provide flexible, collaborative environments where freelancers, remote workers, and small businesses can thrive.

Incubator spaces, on the other hand, offer structured support, resources, and mentorship to early-stage startups, focusing on accelerating growth and innovation. The intersection of these two models presents a unique opportunity for coworking space owners to enhance their offerings and attract a diverse clientele.

By integrating incubator elements into coworking spaces, owners can create a hybrid environment that appeals to a broader range of entrepreneurs.

This fusion not only attracts startups seeking support and mentorship but also provides existing coworking members with access to valuable resources and networking opportunities.

For instance, coworking spaces can host incubator programs, workshops, and mentorship sessions, fostering an ecosystem of learning and collaboration.

This can lead to increased member retention and satisfaction, as well as a reputation for being a hub of innovation and growth.

Moreover, coworking space owners can form strategic partnerships with local incubators to offer joint membership packages. This allows members to benefit from the flexible work environment of coworking spaces and the specialized support of incubators.

Such collaborations can also include shared events, pitch competitions, and demo days, further enriching the entrepreneurial experience and building a vibrant community.

Incorporating incubator features can also attract investors and corporate partners interested in supporting early-stage ventures. This not only adds value to the coworking space but also provides startups with the visibility and resources needed to scale their businesses.

By leveraging the strengths of incubator spaces, coworking space owners can create a dynamic, supportive environment that caters to the evolving needs of today’s entrepreneurs, driving growth and fostering innovation.

Name: 6 Key Steps To Prepare Your Coworking Space For Sale
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Coworking spaces remain a real acquisition target. Flexible workspace now makes up a growing share of office inventory in major cities, and buyers ranging from national operators to landlords converting vacant floors are actively shopping for spaces that already have members, revenue, and systems in place.
Post body:
Coworking spaces remain a real acquisition target. Flexible workspace now makes up a growing share of office inventory in major cities, and buyers ranging from national operators to landlords converting vacant floors are actively shopping for spaces that already have members, revenue, and systems in place.

If you’re thinking about selling your coworking space, the work starts well before you list. A sale isn’t just finding a buyer. It’s getting your numbers, operations, space, and paperwork into the shape a buyer will pay a premium for.

Preparing a coworking space for sale means organizing your financials, operations, lease, and physical space so a buyer can see predictable revenue and step in without disruption. Do that well and you widen your buyer pool and push up your multiple.

A pro tip is to start thinking about the sale from the very beginning. Having a sale-focused mindset when you first open, and keeping it as you operate, puts you ahead. Clean books, transferable lease terms, and documented processes are easier to build as you go than to reconstruct under deadline.

Rather than tackling all of this in the middle of an already stressful sales process, stay on top of it and make it a priority in how you run the business.

If you’re in the process of building a coworking space, even if your intention is not to sell right away, take a look at this resource to see how you can set your business up for success right from the start.

Pre-selling helps too, though selling something that doesn’t quite exist yet is harder.

Here are the details.

Quick Summary

  • Understand the current coworking market and identify who your target buyers are and what they’re looking for
  • Prepare your financial records and legal documents ahead of time for a smoother process
  • Put organized systems in place to keep operations running before, during, and after the sale
  • Spend time improving your space to make it more marketable
  • Maximize your exposure to attract the right buyers

Step 1: Understand the market and your valuation

Before you set a price, get a clear read on the industry and where your space sits in it. A buyer will run the same analysis, so you want to know what they’ll find.

What does the coworking market look like right now?

The flexible workspace sector has kept growing since the shift to hybrid work. Coworking real estate can be profitable, but most spaces need about 24 months to stabilize, with smaller footprints reaching break even in 12-18 months and larger sites in 18-36 months. Hitting roughly 100 members is the common break-even threshold, and many operators target 70-85% occupancy to cover fixed costs and start generating margin.

Location matters more than any other single factor. Location drives profitability because submarket pricing and achievable occupancy set your desk rates, payback period, and long-term margins.

Demand has also moved outward from downtown cores. With the rise of hybrid and remote workforces, coworking space demand is also increasing. Suburban and secondary markets have seen some of the strongest occupancy growth, which is worth knowing if that’s where your space sits.

Pricing gives you a benchmark for your revenue story. As of Q3 2025, the average price for a monthly membership in the U.S. was $225, but there was significant variation based on market, according to Coworking Cafe. In New York City, for example, a monthly Manhattan coworking membership averaged $339, while smaller markets like Salt Lake City, Columbus, and Jacksonville averaged $150-$200 a month.

Know these three things before you list:

  • Who the key players in your submarket are and how they’re positioned
  • What is driving demand in your area
  • How local economic conditions and trends are shaping pricing and occupancy

10 factors that define the valuation price

Determining what your coworking space is worth takes a careful look at several factors. To understand your worth and how you compare to other coworking businesses on the market, work through the list below.

  1. Location and proximity to business hubs – spaces closer to central business districts, transport hubs, and high-traffic areas generally have higher valuations. Local demand for coworking and area economic conditions play a significant role.
  2. Physical space – the total square footage, number of private offices, open workspaces, meeting rooms, and communal areas all influence the price. Build quality, interior design, and overall ambiance matter too.
  3. Occupancy rates – current occupancy and historical data both count. Higher occupancy indicates strong demand and stable revenue, and past trends help predict future performance. Two terms to grasp here are the coworking occupancy index and the coworking revenue occupancy index (CROI).
  4. Revenue streams – have clear data on your membership fees (regular income from individual and corporate memberships) plus income from additional services such as events, food and beverage sales, virtual office services, and other amenities. Diversified revenue is worth more to a buyer than membership alone: tiered memberships, meeting and event bookings, virtual office plans, and partner services create steadier cash flow and higher margins.
  5. Operating expenses – rent and utilities (the cost of leasing the space and running it), staffing and maintenance, plus costs related to marketing and administration such as advertising, managing memberships, and other admin.
  6. Market position – brand strength and the competitive landscape drive price here. A more recognizable brand can sell for more, and the number and quality of competing spaces in the area indirectly affects the final figure.
  7. Member retention and growth trajectory – higher retention rates indicate satisfied members and stable revenue, which is attractive to buyers. Consistent membership growth improves future revenue projections.
  8. Technological infrastructure – ask yourself what technical state your space is in. Do you have reliable IT infrastructure and modern tools like access control systems that add to the appeal?
  9. Lease terms – your lease rate, duration, and sublease potential are of real interest to buyers. Longer leases with favorable terms increase stability and reduce risk, and the ability to sublease can add revenue. This is often the single biggest point in due diligence: if the lease can’t transfer, or the term is short with no renewal option, buyers will discount the price or walk. Talk to your landlord about a renewal option before you list.
  10. Community and network – community and hospitality help define a coworking space as successful. An engaged member community adds appeal, and collaboration with local businesses and regular events adds value.

Here’s what industry expert Craig Baute from DenSwap has to say about coworking space price valuation:

The valuation of a coworking space is focused on current profitability, realistic potential revenue, and the lease length or options to renew at set terms. Most profitable coworking spaces are valued 2.5 to 4x profits. Unprofitable spaces trade at a 1.5 to 3x what we call ‘optimized profits.’

As a general rule of thumb, DenSwap values a space by its annual profit, including owner compensation, times a multiple that typically falls in a 1-5x range, with the exact multiple depending on lease strength, growth, and the other factors above.

What are the common valuation methods?

Three methods come up most often.

#1 Income approach

This approach uses the capitalization rate (cap rate) to value the property based on its income. It’s usually expressed as a percentage.

The Net Operating Income (NOI) is the annual income generated by the property, minus all operating expenses. It includes rental income but excludes mortgage payments, depreciation, and other financing-related expenses. The Net operating income (NOI) divided by the cap rate gives the estimated value.

The discounted cash flow (DCF) projects future cash flows and discounts them back to present value.

#2 Market approach

This approach uses comparable sales to measure your space against similar properties that have recently sold.

#3 Cost approach

The main metric here is replacement cost. It estimates the cost to replace the coworking space with a similar one in terms of quality and functionality.

Learn more about the cost approach here.

Here’s an example calculation using the cap rate.

You’ll need these formulas:

  • Net operating Income (NOI) = Gross Revenue - Operating Expenses
  • Capitalization Rate = Net Operating Income / Current Market Value
  • Value = NOI/Cap Rate

Note that the Current Market Value is the present-day value of the property at prevailing market rates.

Take a hypothetical coworking space with annual gross revenue of $720,000 and operating expenses of $300,000.

The NOI is: 720,000 – 300,000 = 420,000.

Based on market data, suppose the cap rate for similar coworking spaces in the area is 7% (0.07).

Then the value is:

Value = NOI/Cap Rate = 420,000/0.07 = $6,000,000

Note: This information has been verified by the experts at DenSwap, who have operated coworking locations for more than 15 years.

Step 2: Get your finances in order

Your financial records tell the story of your coworking space. Keep the profit and loss statements, tax returns, and lease agreements well-organized, because this is the first thing a serious buyer asks for.

Buyers scrutinize these records to judge the business’s health and growth potential. Clean, itemized P&Ls build trust and show buyers a solid investment. Keep at least three years of financial reports, generated through accounting software or a bookkeeper, so the numbers are consistent and easy to verify.

Improve profitability before you list

Before you list, take time to boost your profitability. Small cost changes compound in a sale: at a 2.5x multiple, cutting $250 a month in expenses adds $3,000 in annual profit and roughly $7,500 to your sale price.

Cut unnecessary costs and find ways to grow revenue. To accelerate your path to profitability, focus on maximizing space utilization, implementing tiered membership options, developing multiple revenue streams beyond basic memberships, and implementing rigorous cost management practices. A little polish here makes your space more appealing when buyers decide.

Step 3: Optimize operations before the sale

Efficient operations keep the business running under new ownership. Put systems and processes in place now that show the space can operate without you.

Getting your team on board with these processes before they’re under review also shows authenticity.

Streamline day-to-day operations

Ideally you already have a coworking management system handling day-to-day operations.

If not, now is the time to put those processes in place. Buyers want an operation they won’t need to fix, so make sure things run smoothly. Document how the space works: an operations handbook, employee handbook, and written procedures let a new owner step in without disrupting your community.

Prepare your staff and management

Your team keeps the coworking space running, so prepare them for the transition to keep things continuous.

Review your current staff, keep your strong performers, and address underperformance. Make sure employment contracts are clear and current, and create a handover plan that gives the new owner continuity from day one.

Tools and technology

Walking into a business that already has tools and technology to manage and run processes is attractive to buyers.

Maintain relationships with your current vendors, and look at solutions that help you run the business more effectively.

For instance, tools such as OfficeRnD Flex help you manage your coworking space in an automated, hassle-free way. Its integrations with tools such as Stripe and Kisi automate billing and payments and support access control for coworking space operators.

Systems already in place make the transition easier and give the buyer confidence.

Step 4: Improve the physical space

A well-kept space speaks to its overall condition. Run a full inspection to find and fix any maintenance, spatial, or aesthetic issues before you show it.

Handle maintenance and repairs

Take the time and spend the money to fix maintenance and repairs before you sell. A well-maintained space appeals to buyers who don’t want to fix up the place after closing.

Aim for a functional workspace that’s safe and suited to your members’ needs. Anything broken should be repaired before you list.

Make aesthetic improvements

Give your coworking space the refresh it deserves. Fresh paint, updated furniture, and better layouts can change how a space feels.

You don’t need next year’s budget for this. Staging the space with updated furniture saves money and still gives a more appealing look.

Presenting the space is about being strategic and showing buyers what life inside those four walls would be like.

Could the layout use some quick fixes? Do them before you show the space.

Match current design trends

Keeping up with current trends and offering an inclusive, welcoming atmosphere sets you apart from other spaces on the market.

Demand has shifted toward privacy and focused work. Demand for private offices and “focus pods” has outpaced open plan seating by 3:1. If your floor plan leans heavily on open desks, adding private offices, focus pods, or relaxation zones signals to buyers that you’re tracking where the market is going, and it can lift revenue per square foot.

Step 5: Handle legal and compliance

Make sure all legal documents are current and compliant with local regulations before you list. Address potential issues early to avoid surprises during the sale.

Sort out your legal documentation

Get your legal paperwork in order. Verify that all lease agreements, zoning permits, and health and safety records are up to date. This shows buyers your space is compliant and ready for a smooth transaction.

Prepare for due diligence

Prepare for the buyer’s due diligence by having all documents and information ready. Anticipate common questions and provide clear explanations to speed the process and reduce friction. Expect the lease to get the closest look, so have your terms, renewal options, and deposit status documented and ready to transfer.

Step 6: Market the sale

Three things matter when marketing something this substantial: your target audience, the right platforms and sales strategy, and presenting the business in its best light.

Identify your target buyer

Who is going to want your coworking space? Identify potential buyers, whether investors, other coworking operators, or real estate developers who fit your space’s appeal.

Is your coworking space a green one? Market it to environmentally conscious buyers. Knowing your audience helps tailor your marketing.

Build your sales strategy

Build a sales strategy by choosing where to list and market your space. Use online platforms like DenSwap and LoopNet to reach a wider audience.

Don’t underestimate broker networks and direct outreach. Also keep your social media active and on-brand: buyers routinely check your Instagram, Facebook, and email list to evaluate a space before they ever contact you.

Showcase the space

Organize open houses and private tours to show your space.

Create high-quality marketing materials, including photos, videos, and virtual tours, so buyers get a real sense of what they’re investing in. Present the space in a way that shows its strengths and the features that set it apart.

Wrapping up

Understand the market, get your finances in order, optimize operations, improve the physical space, sort out legal compliance, and market strategically. Those are the six steps to prepare your coworking space for sale.

With these in your toolkit, you’re ready to attract the right buyer and make a profitable sale. Start today.

Name: What Is A Community Coworking Manager And Why Hire One
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: If you’re overwhelmed by the responsibilities of your coworking space and need help, now might be the time to hire a community manager.
Post body:
If you’re overwhelmed by the responsibilities of your coworking space and need help, now might be the time to hire a community manager.

In this article, we’ll cover what a community coworking manager is, how to hire one, and how to streamline the management process so that you can enhance your members’ experience and grow your business faster.

Quick Answer: A community coworking manager creates and maintains a productive community within a coworking space. They’re responsible for community engagement, operations, and space management. Management systems can enhance the customer experience and streamline mundane tasks, allowing community coworking managers to focus on higher-value activities.

What Is a Community Coworking Manager?

A coworking space manager or community manager is a professional responsible for creating and maintaining a vibrant, engaged, and productive community within your coworking space. You can see them in incubator spaces too. They’re your community members’ first point of contact.

These individuals’ roles go beyond administrative duties to focus on creating a welcoming atmosphere, supporting members, and fixing various issues within the coworking space.

4 Key Responsibilities of Coworking Managers

Community managers’ duties aren’t just administrative — they also include enhancing members’ overall experience and helping your community grow.

Let’s take a look at four of these professionals’ key responsibilities:

1. Community Management

Coworking managers must get to know your coworking space members, understand their needs, and support them wherever necessary. This includes:

  • Meeting them when they arrive
  • Addressing problems that arise
  • Resolving disputes and conflicts
  • Gathering feedback to improve services

It also includes providing personalized onboarding to build loyalty among members and organizing and hosting networking events to retain members and give them a chance to connect with others.

2. Sales and Business Development

Your coworking space manager must promote your space to potential customers through different marketing channels.

They may also be responsible for developing and implementing local and digital marketing strategies to attract new members, such as hosting free coworking days, building relationships with local businesses, using social media, and running digital advertising campaigns to attract a specific demographic.

3. Operations Management

Community space managers oversee the space’s day-to-day operations to ensure everything runs smoothly and members have everything they need.

Depending on the nature of your space, they may also perform receptionist duties, such as handling calls, scheduling tours, and organizing company mail and packages.

4. Space Management

Community managers must analyze floor plans and usage patterns to identify growth opportunities in the coworking space. They also introduce new amenities and help members use them effectively.

If you don’t use a booking system in your space, your coworking community manager may also be responsible for handling bookings and cancellations. However, remember that this takes away their time to focus on more high-level tasks that could help your space grow.

A coworking management solution such as OfficeRnD Flex allows your coworking manager to streamline mundane tasks and focus on higher-value activities, such as engaging members, taking care of strategic sales and business development planning, and building community partnerships.

Benefits of Hiring a Community Coworking Manager

Building a healthy environment for your coworking space is crucial to its success. A community manager can be of great help here for you and your members.

Here are some of the main benefits of hiring a community manager to oversee your coworking space:

Stronger Community Engagement

A community manager helps foster connections by allowing your members to network and collaborate. This enables them to work together and get to know each other, ultimately creating a strong sense of community and belonging.

Better Member Experience

A community manager can help you provide exceptional customer service, including making members feel more welcome and onboarding them properly. This can lead to more referrals since 82% of customers worldwide recommend companies based on their experience.

Efficient Operations Management

Since coworking managers oversee the day-to-day operations of a coworking space, they can ensure everything goes smoothly and handle any issues as soon as they arise. That way, minor issues don’t become big problems that are difficult to resolve later.

Increased Member Retention Rate

Your manager’s touch and attentive service can help coworking space members feel valued and increase their loyalty to your facility. By actively gaining member feedback, they can incorporate recommendations and continuously improve the space to encourage members to stay longer.

By the way, you may want to check out some other important coworking KPIs you need to track.

Essential Skills to Look for in a Community Manager

While your coworking manager must have excellent operations management skills, you’ll want to consider additional abilities when looking to hire someone for this position:

  • Problem-solving skills: Good community managers can think on their feet and find quick and creative solutions to different problems, including issues related to the facility, operational challenges, and membership conflicts.
  • Tech savviness: To operate a coworking space effectively, your manager needs to have strong technical skills and know how to use management software. They must also be able to analyze data and feedback to continue improving the space.
  • Adaptability: Circumstances may change. For example, your space may suddenly experience a higher demand for private meeting rooms due to several startups joining at once. Your community manager needs to be able to adapt to these changes to ensure your space remains relevant.
  • Relational expertise: Your manager needs good people skills to help your members feel acknowledged and valued. This includes communicating with them, listening to their suggestions and feedback, and addressing their concerns.
  • Leadership and initiative: Your manager needs to be proactive in identifying opportunities and able to motivate and inspire members to create a dynamic, collaborative environment.

How to Hire and Onboard a Community Manager for Your Coworking Space

There are several steps you can take to ensure you hire the best manager for your coworking space:

1. Determine the Job Requirements and Compensation

Do a job analysis to determine the standard practice for coworking space manager positions. You can analyze similar jobs, salaries, and responsibilities and decide on your requirements.

Think of questions like:

  • What do you need the manager to do?
  • What skills do they need?
  • What is a fair and competitive salary?

In the US, community managers earn around $47 to $65 per hour. However, this can dramatically vary, depending on their experience.

2. Write a Job Description

The job description should be no more than 600 words and have a clear structure. Include the following sections:

  • About the job: Explain the company’s role at a high level.
  • Key responsibilities: List the primary duties, including day-to-day and quarterly tasks, such as operations, space management, and quarterly analyses.
  • Skills: Mention the critical soft and hard skills the candidate needs to have. Remember to include tech-savviness as a skill, as your manager will need this if you want to incorporate management systems into your business.
  • Education and experience: Include any educational requirements, such as a specific certificate or degree, and the experience you want the manager to have. For example, you may want them to have marketing experience to effectively promote your space.
  • Compensation: Provide a salary range and details about any other benefits the manager will get, such as health insurance or a 401k.

3. Advertise the Position

Once you have a job description, it’s important to advertise it to reach the right people.

Some advertising strategies, such as job boards, are better than others because they bring in higher-quality candidates with more experience.

Places to advertise the position include LinkedIn, Indeed, Google for Jobs, Facebook, Twitter, your company’s careers page, or niche-specific job boards.

4. Evaluate Applications

Write down all the skills your coworking manager must have (the non-negotiables). These may include sales experience, a background in customer service, or the ability to use different management software.

You can determine the skills you’re looking for by deciding how you plan to operate your coworking space and what the community manager will be responsible for.

Suppose you plan on implementing tools into your coworking space to automate operations and space management (highly recommended). In that case, you’ll also need to consider applicants with management software experience.

5. Interview Candidates

After you’ve reviewed the candidate applications and identified the best ones, you can start the interview process.

Remember that you might get candidates who are great managers but have no experience managing coworking spaces specifically. So, you need to tailor your interview questions to scenarios applicable to coworking spaces.

For example, ask candidates the following questions:

  • There’s a member in the space who frequently disrupts other members. How would you handle this situation?
  • You realize that more startups have joined the space in the last three months, causing an increase in the need to book and use meeting rooms. What would you do?
  • Attendance at community events has declined. How would you plan and promote events to excite members and increase participation?

6. Onboard and Train Your Coworking Manager

Once you’ve hired the ideal candidate, you’ll need to onboard them. Here’s what to do at this stage:

  • Provide a detailed company overview and introduce them to your coworking space, staff members, and policies.
  • Tell them about your tools, systems, and processes. Note that this can be complicated if you use multiple tools. It’s ideal to use an all-in-one solution like OfficeRnD Flex.
  • Outline their daily, monthly, and quarterly tasks and responsibilities so that they know what’s expected of them.
