Name: Space Utilization: What It Is and How to Measure It Successfully
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: If your business is embracing a new hybrid work model, you might be losing money.
Post body:
If your business is embracing a new hybrid work model, you might be losing money.

Companies navigating the transition to a hybrid work model may soon find that unused office space, utilities, and parking are an unnecessary drain on resources. Not to mention, ineffective space management, like overbooked meeting rooms, can leave employees feeling less than happy.

If this describes you, don’t worry. When implemented properly, a hybrid model can actually reduce company costs by as much as 40%.

Tracking and reporting on space utilization is the key to efficiently managing physical spaces and significantly minimizing costs. And with the right tools, it’s easier than you think.

This article will guide you through all you need to know about space utilization, including what it is, its benefits, and how you can start measuring it today.

Quick Summary:

  • Space utilization refers to the analysis and optimization of using physical space within a building or environment. It involves assessing how space is allocated and used, aiming to improve efficiency and effectiveness. This concept is particularly important in workplaces, educational institutions, and retail environments, where optimal space usage can influence productivity, safety, and the overall user experience. Effective space utilization ensures that every square foot is used to its maximum potential, often incorporating elements of design, technology, and organizational behavior to achieve this goal.
  • Hybrid companies can successfully track and improve their space utilization by measuring various workplace analytics metrics like occupancy, availability, ratio, cost, density, and peak rate.

What Is Space Utilization?

Space utilization involves measuring and assessing how office users interact with meeting rooms, common areas, individual desks, and even parking spaces.

Effective space utilization is highly useful for businesses transitioning to a hybrid model, as it ensures that spaces are used in the most efficient and profitable way possible. It also helps employers gain a nuanced understanding of changing office demands while allowing them to continue providing an exceptional experience for their employees.

By tracking the usage of spaces in real time, facility managers can:

  • Gain insights into high-traffic areas
  • Identify underutilized zones
  • See where they can optimize layouts
  • Implement strategies, like need-based booking systems for desks and collaborative areas, and modify room designs to boost efficiency

Ultimately, space utilization is a vital tool for enhancing employee productivity and satisfaction, as well as cost-effectiveness in modern workspaces.

Why Is Space Utilization Important in Hybrid Businesses?

Hybrid business models have different space requirements than in-person ones. Optimizing spaces can save businesses money, create happier and more loyal employees, improve safety, and simplify operations.

Reduced office hours and flexible schedules make predicting space usage a lot more complicated, however. Failing to properly manage offices can quickly lead to unused space on one side and overcrowding on the other.

Tracking and understanding the real needs of employees based on data can help businesses save significantly. In fact, companies moving to hybrid models save as much as $11,000 per employee per year.

Instead of paying out for unused rent, utility bills, and resources, partial work-from-home systems allow facility managers to cut excess space and overhead.

Embracing better space utilization can also boost employee satisfaction and retention. Office workers prefer the flexibility of hybrid models, so offering an environment that supports this boosts employee well-being. This could look like the following:

  • Providing clear policies and systems around working from home
  • Supplying supportive furniture, lighting, and ventilation in physical spaces
  • Introducing technology and tools to effectively integrate those working digitally

Spaces with common areas for collaborating and socializing create a more productive environment and engaged community. Better utilization can even help ensure employee safety by improving layouts for improved health and fewer accidents.

Finally, an effectively managed hybrid system can simplify business operations. Downsizing spaces and implementing automated booking systems can help businesses run more smoothly and lead to better portfolio management.

Microsoft Implements a Hybrid System

Microsoft is a shining example of a company thriving under a hybrid model. The organization introduced a clear, business-wide process that allows for 50% remote work.

It has also innovated multiple hybrid systems, including specially designed hybrid meeting rooms, an app to track employee health to reduce illness, and data monitoring to determine how many people can access the worksite and when.

How Do You Measure Space Utilization?

Collecting and analyzing data is the key to determining and improving the usage of a space.

One of the most important figures companies should calculate is their current office space utilization rate. Knowing this rate for every space in a building — from desk areas to meeting rooms to restricted spaces — gives companies a full picture of their property.

You can calculate the average space utilization rate using the following formula:

(Number of employees / Total workplace capacity) x 100

So, if there were 50 people working in an office with a capacity of 100 on a given day, the utilization rate would be 50%.

Remember, the aim is not to constantly have maxed-out spaces. You must also consider the employee experience and strike a balance between comfort and efficiency. Ideal utilization rates differ from company to company, so reviewing personalized data is key.

There are many ways to gather data, from manual systems to speaking to employees to a multitude of technologies.

Tracking technologies include the following:

  • Smart badges and access control
  • Wi-Fi tracking
  • Internet of Things (IoT) occupancy ​​sensors
  • Heat mapping
  • Computer vision from security cameras

Deloitte, for example, created intelligent buildings that use occupancy trackers to measure the busyness of areas like cafeterias.

Dropbox, on the other hand, which switched to a 90% “virtual first” company in 2021, used a company-wide survey to gather data and further improve its space utilization.

After collecting data, analysis helps you turn insights into action. While one option is to invest money and manpower into an analytics team, software tools are a more effective and affordable way to aggregate and analyze data. They also automate reports to help you make informed decisions.

Click here to learn how to automate and simplify space optimization with OfficeRnD Hybrid. 

Tips for Maximizing Space Utilization

If you’re looking to maximize your space utilization in your hybrid business, here’s some advice:

Switch To Hot-Desking

Join companies like Deloitte, Microsoft, and LEGO in swapping out fixed desks for flexible ones. This allows you to dramatically reduce the number of desks needed in your hybrid workspace.

LinkedIn’s flagship hybrid office changed its pre-pandemic plan to build 1080 desks for around 1,500 employees to just 569 workstations.

Here’s a complete hot desking guide.

Create Collaboration Spaces

Collaboration spaces not only breed cooperation and innovation, but they also establish a deeper sense of community among employees and boost employee well-being.

Implement Booking Systems

An automated system for booking desks, meeting rooms, and event spaces will transform the use of your space. It will also give your employees clarity and flexibility at work, boosting their satisfaction.

OfficeRnD Workplace, for example, allows you to book meeting rooms and desks from everywhere, on an interactive office map and integrates with the tools you already use.

Make Use Of Tech

Effective space management software helps you manage your office space efficiently by organizing resource booking.

Most importantly, it allos you to make more informed decisions about your space by providing you with the needed data analytics.

Space Utilization vs Other Types of Measurement

There are various additional space utilization metrics to track in order to effectively create a profitable and future-proof workspace, including space occupancy, availability, space utilization ratio, real estate costs, and peak rates.

Here, we’ll break down each of these important KPIs to help you monitor and improve your spaces.

Occupancy

Occupancy, which is similar to space utilization rate, looks at the percentage of occupied space at a particular moment compared to its maximum capacity.

To calculate the occupancy of a room, divide the room’s total capacity by the number of occupants. For an entire building, divide the number of rooms in use by the total number of rooms.

Studying occupancy over time helps you identify weekly, monthly, and long-term trends. Occupancy sensors and trackers are necessary to do this effectively.

Variables like operational hours, workforce size, and the type of space should also be considered. For instance, meeting rooms typically have lower occupancy rates than desks.

Availability

Availability or vacancy is the other side of occupancy. It is easy to calculate once you know the occupancy rate. For example, a room with 70% occupancy has 30% availability.

A high vacancy level usually indicates that you have excess or underutilized space. While it is a good thing to have some room for growth, it might be wise to downsize or reallocate extra space for alternative use.

Understanding when and how often spaces are available is critical for optimizing timetabling and resource allocation. Identifying peak availability for meeting and conference rooms, for example, allows companies to adjust scheduling or capacity accordingly.

Target Ratio

A target ratio, typically measured per building or group of spaces, establishes a balance between occupancy and availability. This ratio serves as a goal for guiding optimization efforts, spending decisions, and capacity planning.

Achieving the target ratio ensures that the space is neither underutilized nor overbooked, allowing for a smoother working experience and higher employee satisfaction.

Actual Ratio

The actual ratio compares the balance between occupancy and availability to the target ratio. This helps companies clearly measure current performance, identify areas for improvement, and adjust strategies.

Maintaining a close alignment between the target and actual ratios helps ensure effective space utilization management.

Cost per Square Foot

Cost per square foot is a metric that evaluates the financial implications of space utilization strategies, considering expenses such as rent, utilities, and maintenance. You can calculate it by dividing the facility’s rent and maintenance costs by its usable square footage.

In 2023, the average U.S. office listing rate was $37.64 per square foot, with some cities being even more costly. Optimizing spaces can be a great way to minimize costs.

Here’s how to calculate the ideal amount of office space per hybrid employee.

Space Costs per Employee

To determine how much you are spending to provide space for a single employee, divide the total costs of rent and utilities by the number of employees working on the premises.

This amount will help you identify if you are overspending. If you are, you can tighten up your expenses and boost your profits.

Employee Density

Worker density tells you the number of employees you have per square foot of space. You can calculate it by dividing the number of employees present by the space’s total square footage.

Knowing how much space one worker needs allows you to improve the workspace’s design and layout and avoid overcrowding.

Peak Rates

It’s important to track peak rates to determine the busiest hours across dedicated workstations, meeting rooms, common areas, and other spaces.

Peak utilization indicates the maximum number of people in a room or area at one time, and peak frequency measures how often spaces achieve peak occupancy.

You can track peak rates over a certain period to determine which days of the week, times of the year, and specific hours face higher demand. With this data, you can ensure you have the space you need, implement scheduling systems, or allocate more resources to accommodate or combat busy hours.

Why Measure Space Utilization at All?

Aside from the immediate cost savings, measuring space utilization helps you make informed decisions about your business, which is vital for its future health and success.

Let’s dive into this a bit; here are some of the most important benefits of tracking your space utilization.

Improve Planning

Tracking how employees use spaces helps you do more than know how much office space you need. It assists you in accurately forecasting for the future — both short and long-term.

Regular reports let you optimize usage while still allowing for growth. This also helps you adapt quickly to stay profitable and competitive.

Reviewing utilization in company strategy meetings can help inform decisions like:

  • Adding additional meeting rooms
  • Adapting workspace layouts
  • Implementing booking strategies for shared spaces

These things, in turn, can minimize operational costs, reduce employee turnover, and boost employee health and well-being.

Get Employees for Life

Autonomy makes people 2.3 times more likely to stay with an organization.

Creating spaces that support seamless, flexible working will attract a committed and dedicated workforce. Understanding the spaces that employees value will also allow you to invest in these areas and attract and retain top talent.

Become a Greener Company

Cutting out unnecessary space, utilities, and resources will reduce your carbon footprint. In addition to saving on costs, your entire business will run more efficiently and sustainably, helping you hit the climate goals you set and comply with fast-changing regulations.

Using data to understand how you use your spaces removes the guesswork and lets you make strategic decisions for the future.

Post body:
Bulk Bookings is a feature in OfficeRnD Workplace that lets admins and team leads reserve multiple desks and spaces for a group of people in one action, straight from the office map.

If you manage seating for a team, you know the old way: open a resource, pick a desk, assign a person, repeat. Bulk Bookings replaces that with a single click-and-drag on the floor plan. Here’s what it does and how to use it.

What is Bulk Bookings?

Bulk Bookings is part of OfficeRnD Workplace. It reserves several bookable resources, such as desks and spaces, at the same time for a set of employees or an entire team.

Say your sales team is coming in on Tuesday and you want them sitting together. Instead of booking each desk one at a time, you select a block of desks on the map, add the team, and confirm. Everyone gets a desk near their colleagues, and each person receives an email invite.

You can book desks for a group in a few clicks, which saves the repetitive admin work of assigning seats individually and cuts the chance of double bookings.

Why we built Bulk Bookings

This came from direct requests by the people who run day-to-day resource management: admins, office managers, and team leads booking on behalf of colleagues.

Coordinating dozens of separate bookings by hand took time and led to mistakes. Bulk Bookings handles the whole group in one pass, so a team day out or an all-hands seating plan takes minutes instead of an afternoon.

What are the key benefits?

  1. Time saved: Book multiple desks and spaces in one action. No repetitive entries or switching between booking screens.
  2. Fewer errors: Every reservation is tied to a specific user and recorded together, which reduces double bookings and scheduling conflicts. If someone is booked as out of office or already has a reservation that day, you’re warned before you confirm.
  3. Simpler group management: Handle team days, workshops, and department seating without booking person by person.
  4. Teams sit together: Place colleagues next to each other for the days when being in the same room matters.

How does Bulk Bookings work?

A Workplace admin enables the feature first, under Settings > Organization > Booking Permissions by turning on Allow Bulk Bookings. By default you can book 15 resources at once. You can set that limit anywhere from 2 to a maximum of 25.

Once it’s on, here’s the flow:

  1. In the Web Portal, open the Office Map.
  2. Click the Bulk Booking button. This opens the full-page office map.
  3. Click or drag to select the desks and/or spaces you want to reserve, then click “Bulk Book.”
  4. Use the search field to add individual employees or a whole team (for example, the Sales team). If members are out of office or already have a reservation that day, you’ll be notified before you finalize. You can also add a message or description for the group.
  5. Choose the rest of your booking options and click “Book.” The bookings are created and email invitations go out to each attendee.

A few things worth knowing. Meeting rooms and assigned resources can’t be booked in bulk; all other bookable resources, including desks and spaces, can. Each attendee is matched to one of the selected resources. If you pick more resources than people, the extras are left free. And if any booking fails, the system tells you how many went through, how many didn’t, why, and which users couldn’t be booked.

Who benefits from Bulk Bookings?

  • Administrators and facility managers: Manage seating at scale and reduce booking errors.
  • Team leaders: Coordinate team days and make sure everyone has a desk when they arrive.
  • Office managers and executive assistants: Arrange seating for groups and events without booking each person separately.
Important: Bulk Bookings is available for Pro and Enterprise customers. Click here to check out our plans.

Frequently asked questions

How many desks can I book at once with Bulk Bookings?

The default is 15 resources per bulk booking. A Workplace admin can change that limit to anywhere between 2 and 25 in Settings > Organization > Booking Permissions.

Can I book meeting rooms in bulk?

No. Meeting rooms and assigned resources aren’t eligible for Bulk Bookings. Desks and other bookable spaces are.

Does Bulk Bookings support recurring bookings?

No. Bulk Bookings applies to a specific date and doesn’t support recurrences. For repeating reservations, use the separate recurring bookings feature in OfficeRnD Workplace.

Which plans include Bulk Bookings?

Bulk Bookings is available on the Pro and Enterprise plans.

What happens if someone in the group is already booked or out of office?

You’re notified before you confirm. If a booking still fails, the system reports how many went through, how many didn’t, the reason, and the names of anyone who couldn’t be booked.

Name: 6 Insights From Our Webinar “Transition to Hybrid Work” [Full Recap]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Hybrid work keeps shifting because the wants and needs of employees keep changing. Just when the pattern looks settled, the data moves again.
Post body:
Hybrid work keeps shifting because the wants and needs of employees keep changing. Just when the pattern looks settled, the data moves again.

Hybrid work is a model where employees split their week between the office and a remote location, usually home, instead of coming in five days a week.

OfficeRnD CMO Samantha Kenney sat down with the Akelius Team Leader of Applications and Systems, Lars Eliasson, during the “Embracing Change: Navigating the Transition to a Hybrid Work Model” webinar.

Here’s a quick look at the topics they covered and the insights from the panel. To get the full detail, watch the recording here.

Understanding the market

Leading up to the webinar, OfficeRnD ran several polls to read the climate of the workforce. The results:

  • 46% of respondents weren’t considering hybrid work at all
  • 28% were actively planning to switch to a hybrid model
  • 16% were just envisioning the idea
  • 10% needed more information to decide

It surprised the panel that so many companies weren’t moving in the hybrid direction. The caveat: the poll didn’t capture which companies or industries those answers came from.

Hybrid and remote work fit IT, sales, and other desk jobs. For manufacturing and similar verticals, they often aren’t possible at all.

The panel also polled the live audience to gauge who was in the room. 82% of attendees were already working in a hybrid model, a sign that most of these organizations see value in it.

That picture still holds. Hybrid work statistics show that among US employees in remote-capable jobs, Gallup puts 52% in hybrid roles, 26% fully remote, and 22% on-site. Hybrid is the majority arrangement for people who can work remotely, and Stanford economist Nicholas Bloom estimates about 100 million people work hybrid worldwide.

What’s the draw to hybrid work?

Eliasson spoke about the benefits of a hybrid model and how it connects to company values at Akelius.

Hybrid work has been an option at Akelius for over ten years. Their technology supported the model long before many companies thought it possible.

A good work/life balance has always been a core value at Akelius. For most of that time, the setup was in-office with the option to work remotely when needed.

As a community-forward organization, they know kids get sick and personal matters come up during the workday.

To give employees flexibility, they let people work from home when it made sense.

The idea of hybrid work was always there, but nothing pushed it forward until the pandemic hit in 2020.

That’s when the model became concrete. Not every role could run 100% from home, so Akelius moved to bring people back to the office a few days a week.

It wasn’t until they started using tools to manage remote workers and build guidelines and policies that their hybrid model worked.

How do you transition to hybrid work?

Whatever the model, fully remote, fully in-person, or hybrid, employees, stakeholders, and leadership need to agree on it. The guidelines and policies have to be adopted across the organization from the start.

Any new policy, tool, or change comes with a learning curve. Many organizations struggle to adapt to new ways of working, especially when support from the top is thin.

Good management leads by example. When actions and stated policy don’t match, adoption stalls and culture erodes.

So before you introduce hybrid work to the wider organization, get leadership and your primary stakeholders on board first.

Clear guidelines and expectations matter just as much. When the rules are loose and unenforced, the office turns into a free-for-all.

A lack of structure makes it hard for people to coordinate, and nearly impossible to track metrics or collect clean data. Define expectations at the start and save yourself the cleanup.

What technology supports hybrid work?

Technology carries a lot of the weight in hybrid work. There’s a duty of care in knowing where your employees are, and software helps manage that.

Tools keep advancing to fit how people actually work. The COVID-19 pandemic sped up that development, and software companies are now better able to follow industry trends and support what remote and hybrid workers need.

Collaboration tools show this clearly. Where teams once used Skype, they now use a single platform like Zoom or Microsoft Teams to message, video conference, and share documents in one place while staying secure.

Scheduling software has also matured. OfficeRnD Workplace lets employees book hot desks, meeting rooms, and other spaces on a visual floor plan. It gives teams desk booking, room scheduling, and visibility into who’s in on any given day, so in-office and remote colleagues can plan around each other.

Eliasson noted:

We are utilizing the desk booking system from OfficeRnD but we had another solution in the past which we started to use during Covid.

Their main goal after the pandemic was getting people back to the office.

Eliasson continued:

OfficeRnD Workplace perfectly suits the needs we have today. I know there are competitors doing similar software but we are really happy with what OfficeRnD Workplace is offering especially in this desk booking part.

Kenney also raised access control. From Wi-Fi to security clearances, access control was a piece of hybrid work that few people planned for in the early stages.

With more experience behind them, organizations now support remote and hybrid workers better and give them a smoother day-to-day.

How do you measure the success of a hybrid model?

Akelius and OfficeRnD agreed that space utilization is a key metric for hybrid work, though there are different flavors of utilization to watch.

Akelius takes a lighter touch with data, but they track occupancy rates and available spaces.

That tells the team which days draw the most demand, which rooms and spaces people actually use, and whether they need more options or can do with fewer or smaller ones.

Many companies are not renewing their original leases and are opting for smaller offices as headcount in the building has dropped. Occupancy metrics are the clearest way to see those patterns.

Utilization is now the norm, not the exception. CBRE put global office building utilization at 53% in 2025, the highest since March 2020 and up from 38% in 2024. CBRE also found that no organization now targets one desk per employee, and the average occupancy ratio sits at 111% employees per desk, since not everyone comes in at once.

Kenney shared that OfficeRnD works with hybrid companies that also factor in meeting room analytics, catering requests, and budgeting reports.

Common hybrid work objections

The panel polled attendees again on the biggest challenge in their transition to hybrid work. The results:

  • Communication and collaboration: 42%
  • Technology and infrastructure: 8%
  • Employee engagement and morale: 25%
  • Management and supervision: 25%

Kenney and Eliasson were glad management and supervision didn’t rank higher, though a little surprised given challenges they’d seen before.

They put that down to more organizations investing in middle management, senior leadership, and coaching.

On the top concern, communication and collaboration, they concluded that 1-to-1 communication is rarely the problem. The trouble starts when there are multiple channels and things slip through the gaps.

That looped back to the earlier point about tools: you need clear guidelines for how communication software gets used.

What’s next?

This webinar featured an organization operating under a hybrid model sharing what it has learned, with practical support for teams making the same move.

But these are just some of the insights, tips, and strategies discussed during the panel. Watch the full recording here to hear all of the practical tips shared by the industry experts.

Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Sustainable practices are becoming increasingly prevalent in business, leading to a significant shift in customer behavior.
Post body:
Sustainable practices are becoming increasingly prevalent in business, leading to a significant shift in customer behavior.

According to recent research by the NIH, customers of sustainable businesses are more loyal, more likely to engage in positive word-of-mouth marketing, and even willing to pay more for products and services.

So, whether you’re considering opening a new green coworking space or already have one but want to incorporate even more sustainable practices to gain a competitive advantage, you’re in the right place.

This article will give you a complete guide to creating and managing a green coworking space your members will love and be eager to spread the word about.

Quick Summary:

  • Green coworking spaces focus on sustainability and eco-friendliness, and they’re becoming more popular as customer behaviors shift. This means they offer market differentiation and can help you gain more members and profit.
  • There are several key steps to creating a green coworking space, including solidifying your location, choosing the right technology, and creating the right design layout.

What Are Green Coworking Spaces?

Green coworking spaces focus on sustainability and eco-friendliness in their design, operations, and policies. Their main goal is to minimize environmental impact while providing a calm, productivity-inducing working environment.

Typically, green coworking spaces attract groups of people who are interested in sustainability, including:

  • Local entrepreneurs: Wellness coaches, sustainable fashion designers, and green event planners
  • Corporate teams: HR teams that implement employee wellness programs and remote sales teams for green companies
  • Freelancers and remote workers: Virtual assistants, digital marketers, and remote software developers
  • Small businesses and startups: Green consultancy services, eco-friendly product manufacturers, and tech startups developing sustainable solutions
  • Educational and research institutions: EdTech startups, university research groups focused on sustainability, and green academic writers and editors
  • Community activists: Environmental advocacy groups, local non-profit organizations, and community organizers heavily focused on sustainability

And here you can see a list of the most common industries that use coworking spaces in general.

Benefits of Having a Green Coworking Space

Operating a green coworking space offers several benefits over everyday coworking spaces, ranging from financial advantages to a happier community with like-minded people. Here are the main benefits you can expect:

Financial Perks

Implementing energy-efficient systems — such as LED lighting and water-saving fixtures — will reduce your utility bills over time.

The added value of green spaces also allows you to charge premium prices. This can increase the number of members you get and help you make more profit immediately and in the long term.

Check out this free webinar to learn more about how to grow your membership by implementing green initiatives. 

Community and Networking

A coworking space focused on sustainability helps you attract like-minded people who get along well with you and have the same environmentally conscious views.

As a result, you might find it easier to communicate and collaborate, creating a happy community and a sense of belonging.

Learn more about leveraging the network effect in coworking spaces.

Market Differentiation

The coworking space market was valued at $10.81 billion in 2023 and is predicted to reach $36.92 billion by 2030. This indicates a massive increase in the need for these spaces, which is ultimately what can help set your space apart from others in your area.

According to Harvard Business Review, sustainability promotes trust, especially among Generation Z. Since they’ll soon have buying power, it’s essential to consider this demographic in your decision-making.

Another way to differentiate in 2024 and beyond is by providing exceptional hospitality.

Higher Productivity

According to research by IOP Science, poor indoor environmental quality significantly contributes to productivity losses.

In fact, in a study conducted by View on over 1,600 professionals, 50% of respondents said that air quality makes them sleepier throughout their work day. Also, 33% said they lose more than one hour of work daily due to physical and environmental factors.

In contrast, improved air quality, non-toxic materials, and natural light can help your members get more work done. This means your green coworking space can be the solution they need to increase their productivity.

7 Key Considerations to Make When Planning a Green Coworking Space

If you want to make your coworking space sustainable and eco-friendly, consider incorporating the following to help it stand out:

1. Eco-Friendly Design

The physical layout of your coworking space needs to incorporate sustainable materials, natural ventilation systems, and architectural strategies that reduce energy consumption.

For example, consider designing your space to maximize natural lighting and use low-volatile organic compound (VOC) flooring, such as bamboo.

2. Energy Efficiency

To reduce energy consumption, use energy-efficient lighting, such as LED and automated lighting systems that adjust based on natural light levels. You can also implement HVAC systems and smart thermostats.

3. Renewable Energy

Many green coworking spaces take a proactive approach to energy consumption by incorporating renewable energy sources early on. These include solar panels and wind turbines that power the workspace, leading to a more self-sufficient operation.

You can also consider partnering with energy providers that offer renewable energy options.

4. Waste Reduction

Waste reduction is a vital aspect of any green space. You can implement comprehensive recycling programs for different materials, including paper, plastic, and glass. Also, encourage your members and employees to use reusable containers and utensils in their lunches.

5. Paperless Operations

Paperless coworking offices often adopt digital tools and cloud storage, such as electronic booking and invoicing systems, to minimize the need for paper.

This is where OfficeRnD Flex can help manage your coworking space entirely online. With it, you can:

  • Manage members and their plans
  • Automate billing and payments
  • Allow members to easily book desks and meeting rooms
  • Organize and promote community events
  • Get detailed analytics and reporting
  • Seamlessly integrate with popular tools such as Kisi, Xero, and Hubspot to avoid using multiple apps

6. Employee Well-Being

Green coworking spaces can improve your employees’ health, happiness, and well-being.

Here’s what you can do to make sure this happens:

  • Provide your staff with recreational areas where they can relax
  • Implement robust onboarding processes so your employees know what’s expected of them
  • Give them other benefits, like health insurance or gym memberships

Providing your workers with a positive work environment can make them brand advocates and help your business achieve long-term success.

7. Green Spaces

What a green coworking space would be without green areas, right?

Incorporate indoor plants into your space to enhance the air quality and provide a relaxing and calming environment. You can also have outdoor green areas with gardens where members can work, such as green roofs.

How to Create and Manage a Green Coworking Space

Creating and managing a green coworking space might seem complicated, but if you take the proper steps, it becomes easier. Here’s what you can do to create a tremendous green coworking space and manage and market it effectively:

1. Plan and Research

Conduct research to determine the demand for green coworking spaces in your area. Analyze competitors’ strengths and weaknesses to create a stand-out plan.

Create a plan and vision clearly stating what features you’ll implement to make your space green, including lighting and electronic systems.

Also, remember that green initiatives can often be expensive to set up, so come up with a comprehensive budget that includes the cost of everything you want to include in your space.

2. Identify the Ideal Location and Building

If you want to start a coworking space from the ground up, you’ll need to identify a location that works well for your space.

Look for a building with green certifications, such as LEED, or one that can easily be upgraded to meet those standards. Members should also be able to access the building easily via public transportation or bike.

Once you’ve researched and identified the perfect location, you can start crafting a business plan for your coworking space.

3. Design Layout

Consider the coworking space floor plan. You can design the space to maximize natural light and ventilation and use smart lighting systems, such as smart bulbs and LED technologies.

Consider doing the following, as well:

  • Use eco-friendly materials for furniture, such as low-VOC paint and bamboo tables
  • Install low-flow faucets
  • Incorporate indoor plants throughout the space for a more comfortable atmosphere

If the building allows, you can also add an outdoor space for improved air quality and to give members a place to relax.

In addition to focusing on these “green” amenities, consider implementing other must-have amenities all coworking spaces need.

4. Choose the Right Technology

Implement digital tools for member communication, billing, and document management. You can use all-in-one coworking management software like OfficeRnD Flex to manage your coworking space online.

OfficeRnD Flex:

  • Helps you get paid faster with automatic invoicing and billing

  • Manage leads and membership contracts all in one place

5. Create Plans and Policies

Create different membership plans based on prospective customers’ needs to increase your revenue potential. Some members may only need day passes, while others want full-time access.

To avoid turning any of these members away, create different pricing plans with varying access levels. Here’s an example of how these could look:

  • Day Pass: $30 for single-day access during business hours. Members can use shared workspaces, receive complimentary coffee and tea, and access common areas.
  • Two Times Per Week: $200 per month to access the space two days per week on a flexible schedule. Members can use shared workspaces, access common areas, and get two hours of meeting room use per week.
  • Full Access: $425 monthly for unlimited access on a flexible schedule. Members get a dedicated desk, a personal locker, and unlimited meeting room use.

6. Apply for Certifications

This is an optional step, but you can apply for certifications such as LEED, WELL, or BREEAM to validate your business’s sustainability efforts. This will add to the credibility of your space.

Another option is collaborating with local environmental organizations and green businesses to become known in the market and attract even more members.

7. Market and Promote

Without members, your business won’t succeed. This makes marketing crucial. Use different marketing strategies to attract more members, including face-to-face and digital marketing.

Let’s take a look at what these mean:

  • Face-to-face marketing: Promote at local shops, host events, hold regular free coworking days, distribute business flyers, and more.
  • Digital marketing: Optimize for local SEO, promote on social media, use coworking listing websites, and implement paid Facebook and Google advertising.

Your dedication to sustainability means you and your employees can also attend or arrange green community events to promote your business to attendees.

8. Encourage Community Engagement

To retain your members, consider hosting events focused on sustainability, such as recycling workshops and green living talks. This will allow members to participate and collaborate with one another and with locals to build a sense of community.

9. Monitor and Improve

Regularly monitor your space’s energy, office supplies inventory, and water use to ensure your efforts succeed. It’s also vital to get feedback from your members so you can improve your processes and the layout of the space as necessary.

Name: Office Space Optimization For Busy Leaders [2026 Guide]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: If you’ve ever double-booked a conference room, shivered all day at your desk, or sat across the building from the rest of your team, you’ve felt what an inefficient office costs you.
Post body:
If you’ve ever double-booked a conference room, shivered all day at your desk, or sat across the building from the rest of your team, you’ve felt what an inefficient office costs you.

When employees can’t work out the basics of their own space, their focus and mood drop. Some stop coming in at all.

You can fix most of this with the right data, tools, and planning. This guide covers how to make your office space work in 2026, when hybrid is the default and most floors sit half empty on a normal day.

Quick summary:

  • A well-run office saves money and gives you happier, more productive people, including hybrid workers.
  • Before you redesign anything, address passive occupancy, ghost booking, and clunky booking systems.
  • Size your office to your busiest day, not your headcount, and the savings follow.
  • The right software helps you measure usage and gives employees a reason to come in.

What is office space optimization?

Office space optimization is the practice of using your physical office to support how people actually work: efficient layouts, flexible workstations, and technology that fits different tasks and team sizes.

The aim is an office that adapts to your workforce, supports collaboration, and stops you paying for space nobody uses.

Hybrid work is no longer the variable here. Around 53% of remote-capable U.S. workers are on a hybrid schedule in 2026, and that share has held steady for about three years. Some people come in one day a week, others three or four. Your office has to work for both.

Why office space matters to your budget

A good office keeps people healthy, focused, and willing to show up. It also protects a large line item. Wasted office space costs companies over $300,000 a year, so the space you already hold is worth using well before you sign for more.

Most hybrid offices run at 40 to 50% daily utilization. More than half the floor sits empty on an average day, and you pay rent, power, and cleaning on all of it.

People still want the flexibility. About 83% of workers prefer a hybrid setup, and most want two or three days in the office. A cramped, uncomfortable office gives them one more reason to stay home.

Benefits of a well-run office

A space that runs well gives your hybrid employees a reason to come in. Here’s what else it does.

Save your company money

U.S. office vacancy hit a record high in early 2026, with about 21% of office space vacant across 79 markets. Companies don’t need as much space as they hold, and many are paying for the gap.

Before you renew a lease or expand, use the space you have. Here’s a useful breakdown of the ideal amount of office space per hybrid employee.

Happier and more productive employees

The wrong office density lowers productivity, whether that’s overcrowding or an open plan in work that needs quiet. Good amenities, natural light, and decent common areas push it the other way.

This is worth getting right: 90% of employees say their office layout and design affect their happiness at work.

Measure and report progress

When you can show that your space is used efficiently, you give finance, leadership, and employees proof that the budget isn’t going to empty desks.

Reduce your energy use

About 30% of the energy used in commercial buildings is wasted. Cutting that lowers your bills and your emissions at the same time.

Sustainability carries weight with employees and regulators in 2026. Here’s more on the benefits of a sustainable workplace.

Challenges to address before you redesign

Start with the problems that quietly waste space. Most offices have all four.

Passive occupancy

Passive occupancy happens when people think a space is taken and avoid it, while it sits free.

An employee leaves a jacket on a desk or in a conference room, then works from home the next day. Whoever comes in skips that desk because it looks claimed.

This creates confusion and bottlenecks. Several people fight over one meeting room while another stands empty. Someone skips a fully stocked desk. An introvert sits in the middle of the floor because the window seats look taken.

Ghost booking

Ghost booking is a room that’s reserved, never used, and never cancelled, so everyone treats it as full.

Someone books a conference room, the meeting falls through, and the booking stays. Nobody else can take the room.

Like passive occupancy, this wastes space and frustrates people enough to keep them home. To stop it, use a hybrid workplace management system that lets you book resources and track whether they’re actually used.

OfficeRnD Workplace does this. You book desks and meeting rooms, give people a reason to collaborate in person, and make better calls using workplace analytics.

Clunky booking systems

Companies running a hybrid model need a simple way to book desks and rooms. A confusing or poorly connected system wastes the time it’s meant to save.

The longer people spend fighting admin, the less they get done. A clunky system also makes your job harder: you can’t see who’s in, you can’t gather clean data, and you can’t give hybrid workers a smooth reason to come in.

Future planning

Build for your current team, then plan for the one you’ll have. The cleaner your space and processes, the easier it is to grow without panic-leasing.

Look at everything: the technology you run, your energy systems, and how quickly you could add or shed desks. Planning now saves money and time later.

How much space do you actually need?

Most office sizing starts from headcount, which is why so many offices end up half empty. The number that matters is how many people come in on a busy day.

The math is simple:

  1. Start with peak-day attendance, not total headcount.
  2. Divide by your desk-sharing ratio (most hybrid teams run 1.2 to 1.6 people per desk).
  3. Multiply by your workstation footprint (6 to 10 m² per desk is typical).
  4. Add 20 to 30% for meeting rooms, kitchen, and circulation.

You can run all of this in a couple of minutes with our office space calculator. It models peak-day attendance, desk sharing, and cost savings, so you get a planning number sized to how your team works instead of a guess.

For a deeper look at the inputs, here’s our guide to how much office space you need.

Size your office to peak attendance

Attendance isn’t flat across the week. It clusters Tuesday to Thursday and drops off on Friday. Peak days run roughly 35% above the weekly average.

That gap is where sizing goes wrong. Plan around the weekly average and Tuesday turns into a scramble for desks and rooms. Plan around full headcount and you pay for space that’s empty four days out of five.

Size to the peak day instead. Your busiest day has enough desks, and you don’t carry the cost of a full-headcount office that never fills. This single shift is where most of the savings in this guide come from.

5 key tips to make your office space more efficient

You know the problems. Here are five ways to fix them.

Ask your employees what they need

Before you change anything, find out what’s working and what isn’t. Send a short survey. Questions worth asking include:

  • Open floor or a quieter setup?
  • What temperature do you want to work in?
  • Do you have the equipment to be productive?
  • What would get you into the office more often?
  • What would help you feel safer at work?

Then gather the hard data:

  • How often each person comes in
  • How many people and meetings per day your rooms need to handle
  • Your current hybrid work policy, including which teams are in on which days
  • Hiring or downsizing plans for the next few months

Pick a desk-sharing system that fits

For a hybrid office, drop permanent assigned desks and let people book a spot before they come in.

The two main approaches are hot desking and desk hoteling. Hot desking lets people grab any open desk, first come first served. Desk hoteling lets them reserve a desk in advance online.

Desk hoteling cuts passive occupancy and ghost booking, since everyone can see who’s sitting where and cancel a booking they don’t need. People can pick the desk they want, sit near their team, and skip the stress of not knowing where they’ll land.

Use software people will actually open

Good space management software helps you:

  • Let employees book desks and rooms without a fight
  • Run clear hybrid policies
  • Track how your space gets used
  • Watch your budget

Pick something that connects to the tools your team already uses, so they aren’t juggling five apps. Make sure it covers remote, in-office, and hybrid workers.

OfficeRnD Workplace connects with a wide range of platforms for exactly this reason.

Once the software is in, add IoT sensors, smart badges, and WiFi tracking to keep your occupancy data current. Also, you can check out our extensive guide on the best space management software this year.

Spend on equipment that pays off

Plenty of upgrades are cheap. LED lighting lowers utility costs and energy use at once.

Buy ergonomic chairs, mouse pads, and standing desks. People spend most of their day at a desk, so this helps both their output and their health.

Add lockers or cubbies. Hybrid workers on hot desking or hoteling have nowhere permanent to keep their things, and storage keeps the floor clean.

Some fixes cost nothing. Rearrange the layout to pull in natural light, use every square foot, and improve the flow between desks and rooms.

Lean on workplace analytics

The strongest tool you have is good analytics, giving you a clear read on space usage and how people behave.

OfficeRnD Workplace includes Workplace Analytics for this. It shows space utilization and how people use desks and rooms, with real-time updates, custom dashboards, and detailed reports.

Read the desk and room patterns and you can place resources where they’re used, support your hybrid policy, and back every space decision with data. More on Workplace Analytics here.

How to measure success

Track a few metrics so you can see what’s working and prove it to leadership:

  • Employee productivity over time
  • Collaboration frequency, measured by meetings and interactions
  • Space utilization rate: space used against total available
  • Occupancy rate: occupied desks against total desks
  • Employee density: people per unit of space
  • Meeting room utilization: how often and how long rooms are used
  • Employee satisfaction: survey scores on comfort and focus
  • Cost savings: cuts in real estate and operating costs

Get more from your office with OfficeRnD Workplace

A well-run office gives you happier people and lower costs. You need the right system underneath it to supply the data and make the office easy to use.

That’s OfficeRnD Workplace. Your team books desks and rooms, you manage resources and costs, you read space utilization, and you keep people engaged. It works with the tools you already run.

Author: asen-stoyanchev

Post body:
Coworking and retail are increasingly sharing the same floor: coffee, shopping, and a desk under one roof. That overlap is the subject here, and it’s growing for a practical reason. As stores close, landlords need tenants, and flex space operators need foot traffic. The two fit together well.

Coworking-retail integration means placing a flexible workspace inside or alongside a retail environment (a mall, a shopping plaza, or a converted storefront) so members and shoppers share the same location and amenities.

Let’s look at how this works, why it pays off for both sides, and how to run it well.

Quick Summary

  • Coworking and retail are converging as store closures free up prime, high-traffic space that flex operators can use
  • Putting a coworking space inside a retail location drives foot traffic, improves the member experience, and shares fixed costs across two revenue streams
  • Success comes down to location, thoughtful design, solid technology, and an active community
  • Marketing, local partnerships, and a plan for zoning and noise are what separate the spaces that work from the ones that don’t

How did coworking and retail spaces evolve toward each other?

Coworking and retail have both changed sharply over the past decade, and their paths have started to cross.

Coworking spaces, once a niche market catering primarily to freelancers and startups, have rapidly evolved into mainstream hubs of productivity and collaboration.

The rise of large coworking brands, corporate adoption of flexible work, and the shift to hybrid work all fed that growth. 55% of corporations now use flexible workspace.

The U.S. market keeps expanding. By the end of Q1 2026, the U.S. coworking market reached 9,136 active locations, up from 8,854 at the close of Q4 2025 for a 3.2% quarter-over-quarter increase, or 282 spaces in just three months. The sector’s growth for all of 2025 was a robust 17 percent.

Retail moved in the opposite direction, reshaped by changing consumer habits and e-commerce.

Traditional brick-and-mortar stores have faced pressure for years, pushing many owners to rethink what a physical location is for.

The numbers are stark. Following a spike in stores closures in 2024, Coresight Research expects closures to escalate further this year, to approximately 15,000. By mid-2025, roughly 6,000 store closings were announced in the first half of the year, or about 123.7 million square feet of vacated retail space, according to Coresight Research.

That vacated space is exactly what makes the coworking-retail overlap work. Empty anchor stores and storefronts are prime, high-traffic real estate, and operators want it.

The intersection started as a handful of experiments and has grown into a recognized model.

Bookstores and cafes were arguably the original coworking spaces, mixing work and leisure long before the term existed.

Today, coworking spaces are opening inside shopping malls and retail plazas, and operators are partnering with landlords to build locations that serve both work and shopping.

Mall owners have leaned into this directly. Malls are repurposing anchor spaces into gyms, entertainment venues, and coworking hubs. Industrious was an early mover here, opening coworking space inside malls to replace departed department stores, and Office Depot ran coworking hubs inside a set of its retail stores. The pattern holds: shared space, shared traffic, shared amenities.

Why integrate a coworking space with a retail business?

Mutual growth. A multifunctional location. Shared costs. Those are the core reasons to combine coworking with retail.

If you’re weighing a merger or a partnership, here’s what you get.

Increased foot traffic

Retail draws a steady stream of visitors. Coworking draws professionals, freelancers, and entrepreneurs who shop, eat, and run errands nearby.

Each side feeds the other’s audience.

Industrious, for example, has several locations inside retail buildings or plazas, which opens the door to members who saw the sign and wanted to check it out.

Shoppers see the space, wander in, and sometimes sign up. A consistent flow of visitors lifts sales for both businesses. There’s demand for the mall side too: more than two-thirds of those surveyed by Colliers said coworking space in a mall would encourage them to visit the mall’s shops more often.

A better member experience

Combining coworking and retail gives members one place to work, shop, and socialize.

Coworking members can get exclusive discounts at the retailer, and the retailer gets an on-site base of regular customers.

The mix works when it’s convenient and easy to access, with interactive spaces and a thoughtful layout that blends work areas with relaxing retail zones.

A mall location built this way pays off in daily convenience. Members can duck into a store on a lunch break or meet friends for dinner after work without driving across town. The Industrious space in Scottsdale’s Fashion Square is a clear example: with free parking, access to the food court, and stores like Nordstrom and Apple close by, members get amenities the mall already provides.

Shared resources and cost savings

Foot traffic benefits both sides while cutting marketing spend. Sharing utilities, amenities, and services lets the coworking space and the retailer both run leaner.

Office Depot showed one version of this, carving coworking hubs out of existing store space to add a revenue stream. The Workonomy Hub concept gave members access to on-site tech support, printing, mailing, shipping, and office supplies through the store. The program has since shrunk to a handful of locations, but the logic still holds: a retailer’s existing services and staff become perks for members at little added cost.

A mall food court means you don’t stock a full kitchen. Free retail parking often means lower rent than a standalone office building. Shared HVAC, security, and cleaning spread fixed costs across two businesses instead of one. That’s the financial case for the model in a sentence.

How do you integrate coworking and retail successfully?

It comes down to location, design, technology, and community. Here’s how to approach each.

Location selection

Choosing the right location matters as much for a hybrid space as for either business alone. The best spots are high-traffic: city centers, busy shopping districts, or well-trafficked malls.

Both coworkers and shoppers need easy access for the integration to work.

Worth noting: the best opportunities aren’t only downtown anymore. In 2025, the flex-space sector gained 1,000 locations nationally, which increased its share of total office inventory to 2.2 percent, and much of that growth is in secondary and suburban markets near retail. Suburban campuses with strong regional access, rail and freeway connections, and proximity to major retail destinations are drawing customers to flex spaces outside the urban core.

What to look for in a location

  • Foot traffic: City centers, shopping malls, and busy neighborhoods bring more visitors past your door.
  • Accessibility: Public transit, parking, and major roads keep the location convenient for coworkers and shoppers alike.
  • Demographics: Match the space to the local population. Proximity to universities, tech hubs, and residential areas helps.

Balance accessibility with visibility. Prominent storefronts and clear entry points do a lot of the marketing for you.

Space design and layout

A design that serves both work and retail is essential. Flexible layouts (movable walls, modular furniture) adapt to changing needs and get more out of every square foot.

A few tips:

  • Zoning: Define coworking and retail areas so each does its job without disrupting the other. Use partitions, furniture arrangements, and signage.
  • Aesthetics: Build a visual theme that works for both brands. Complementary colors, materials, and decor tie the two together.
  • Modular furniture: Pick furniture you can reconfigure for different activities and events.
  • Multipurpose areas: Design spaces that do double duty. A lounge can host casual meetings or a product showcase.
  • Storage: Add smart storage to keep the space organized. Hidden storage, shelving, and lockers handle both coworking and retail supplies.

One caution worth taking seriously: a coworking experience needs a coworking layout. What doesn’t tend to work is trying to shove a coworking experience into a non-coworking layout or form, because users have very specific expectations when they’re paying for a coworking space.

Technology and infrastructure

Solid tech keeps day-to-day operations running.

The essentials:

  • High-speed internet: Reliable, fast internet is non-negotiable. The network has to handle video calls, streaming, and large file transfers across many users at once. Extend strong Wi-Fi into the retail areas too.
  • Security systems: Cameras, access control systems, and alarms protect both coworking and retail assets.
  • Connected point-of-sale and coworking tools: Link your POS to your coworking management software to consolidate billing and invoices, understand customer behavior through analytics, and manage inventory with less manual work.

Community building and engagement

An active community is what keeps a hybrid space full. Events and activities that appeal to both coworkers and shoppers bring people back.

At its core, that means exceptional hospitality.

Ways to build community

  • Regular events: Host regular events like workshops, networking sessions, and social gatherings to bring coworkers and shoppers together.
  • Membership programs: Build programs with exclusive benefits for coworking members and retail customers: discounts, early event access, and special promotions.
  • Online community platforms: Give members a place to connect, share ideas, and collaborate through social media, forums, or a dedicated app.

Events that pull in both crowds

  • Product launches: Run launches or pop-up shops in the retail area to draw shoppers and create buzz.
  • Workshops and seminars: Cover topics your community cares about: entrepreneurship, wellness, technology.
  • Networking mixers: Get coworkers, local businesses, and shoppers in the same room.

Here’s a useful article on the network effect in coworking spaces.

Marketing and promotion tactics

A hybrid space needs marketing that pulls in both audiences and keeps them. Here’s what works.

Branding and positioning

A single, clear brand identity turns the space into a destination. Consistent branding across physical and digital channels reinforces that and builds a loyal base.

It also sets you apart and sticks in members’ minds.

Software with branded mobile apps helps here. OfficeRnD Members gives operators a white-labeled member app, so members interact with your brand, not the software vendor’s.

Basic tips for a unified brand:

  • Consistent visuals: Use the same logos, colors, fonts, and design elements across every channel, online and off.
  • Brand story: Tell a clear story about what makes your space different and how it combines coworking and retail into one experience.
  • Unified messaging: Keep social posts, email, and everything else consistent with your brand’s identity and values.

Positioning the space as a destination

  • Experiential marketing: Create experiences that fit your audience, like events, workshops, or pop-ups tied to your brand.
  • Lifestyle content: Share stories, testimonials, and behind-the-scenes looks at your community and the experiences your space offers.
  • Ambassadors and influencers: Work with local voices who fit your brand. Their endorsement brings their audience with them.

Digital marketing

Social media and online channels build visibility. SEO and content marketing pull in organic traffic, and targeted ads reach the exact demographics you want, driving foot traffic and memberships.

What to focus on:

  • Social presence: Keep active profiles, post regularly, share engaging content, and reply to your audience.
  • Content: Produce photos, videos, blog posts, and virtual tours that show off your space, events, and success stories. Show people what they’d want to see when shopping for a workspace.
  • Targeted ads: Reach your ideal customer with ads tailored to different angles: coworking, retail offerings, or upcoming events.
  • SEO and local search: Do keyword research for your community, keep a blog on relevant topics, and optimize your site for local search with your location in page titles, headings, and body copy.

Local partnerships

Experiences often do more for a space than any ad.

  • Cross-promotions: Team up with local businesses on joint promotions and discounts. Build referral programs, share marketing costs, and tie seasonal promotions to local festivals and holidays.
  • Events and workshops: Partner with local experts, artists, and businesses to run events. These bring in a wider audience and show what the space can do.
  • Influencer marketing: Work with local influencers who can promote the space authentically to their followers.

Used together, these tactics bring in customers, raise your visibility, and build an active community in your integrated space.

Strong branding, smart digital marketing, and good local partnerships are what make a space stand out in a competitive market.

What are the challenges, and how do you handle them?

There will be growing pains. How you handle them decides whether the model works.

Here are the common ones and what to do about them.

Space management and utilization

Coworking and retail serve different people with different needs, so balancing both takes planning.

Flexible spaces, booking systems, and clearly designated coworking and retail areas help you manage peak and off-peak demand.

Keeping the environment balanced

Work and retail activity need to coexist without stepping on each other, which mostly comes down to noise and privacy.

Acoustic design, soundproofing, and dedicated quiet zones or booths handle most of it.

Zoning and legal considerations

Zoning laws and lease terms make or break an integrated space. Understand the legal picture before you commit.

Research local zoning, regulations, and permits thoroughly so you don’t hit disputes later. A mixed retail-and-office use can trigger requirements that neither business would face alone.

Where is this heading?

Combining coworking with retail benefits both sides when you get location, amenities, and marketing right.

The tailwind is real. Retail keeps shedding space, coworking keeps adding it, and malls and landlords are actively courting flex operators to fill vacancies and bring people back through the doors. By adding fitness centers, medical clinics, coworking spaces, and public parks, malls are becoming multi-functional hubs. Expect more of these hybrid locations, not fewer.

Name: How To Operate 24/7 Coworking Spaces Successfully [2024]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Around-the-clock access to workspaces is becoming increasingly important for freelancers, entrepreneurs, and remote workers with unconventional schedules and diverse needs.
Post body:
Around-the-clock access to workspaces is becoming increasingly important for freelancers, entrepreneurs, and remote workers with unconventional schedules and diverse needs.

But how do you effectively create and operate a 24-hour coworking space that meets the needs of your members and stands out from the competition?

In this article, we discuss everything you need to know about creating and operating a coworking space 24/7. This includes different ways to run these spaces, member access considerations, and tools that can make managing your space easier.

Quick Summary:

  • A 24/7 coworking space is a shared office environment where members can work all hours of the day and night.
  • These spaces are becoming increasingly popular due to many employees’ and freelancers’ flexible schedules.
  • Several key steps are involved in creating and operating a 24/7 coworking space, including determining membership plans, choosing the right tools, and onboarding members.

What Is a 24/7 Coworking Space?

A 24-hour coworking space is a shared office environment that members can access at all hours, day or night. It includes access to dedicated desks, meeting rooms, private offices, and more.

The number of coworking spaces worldwide is expected to reach nearly 42,000 by the end of 2024 — more than double the number in 2018.

Increased competition in the coworking space realm will make it difficult for your space to stand out among potential customers and keep good occupancy rates if you don’t create a unique selling point — such as 24-hour access.

Who uses 24-hour coworking spaces? Let’s take a look:

  • Freelancers: Independent professionals who rent desks to get their work done in a productive environment instead of at home.
  • Remote workers: Employees of larger companies who need a local work environment but don’t need to commute to the central office.
  • Startups and small businesses: Companies that may not have big offices and need flexible office solutions to grow. Incubator spaces are a perfect example.
  • Professionals who travel often: Sales workers, company photographers, or event managers who frequently travel.

24/7 coworking spaces allow members more flexibility while giving them the working amenities and networking opportunities they need — making these spaces highly attractive.

Benefits of Operating a Coworking Space 24/7

There are several benefits to offering 24/7 access to your coworking space members. Here are a few of them:

  • Increased revenue potential: Attracting a broader range of members, including those with unconventional schedules, could lead to more customers and increased revenue since you’ll bring in full-time members and drop-ins.
  • Market differentiation: Setting your space apart from competitors who are only open during certain times of the day can be a unique selling point that helps you attract members looking for more flexible working spaces.
  • Higher member retention rates: Meet the needs of your members, regardless of their schedules and whether they’re night owls or early birds, to increase member satisfaction and retention.
  • Scalability and growth: A positive member experience, market differentiation, and word-of-mouth from loyal members can help you expand to new locations.

4 Ways to Run a 24/7 Coworking Space

It can be tricky to provide 24-hour access to your one space, let alone across multiple franchise locations. . Most 24/7 coworking spaces have four methods of making this possible:

1. With a Community Manager On-Site

This method involves having one manager oversee your coworking space. However, it isn’t often used because the high salaries can significantly impact profits.

2. Without a Community Manager On-Site

With this method, the space is open 24/7 but is not monitored by anyone. Members can check in and pay their invoices with coworking management software.

Such software, for example, is OfficeRnD Flex:

This setup is the most autonomous, saves you on costs, and frees up time for you to focus on more hands-on tasks.

3. Partly Observed

Here, the space is open 24 hours a day; however, managers only check it during certain times, such as regular business hours (e.g., from 9 to 5).

In this case, only full-time members can access the space at odd hours of the day, and they don’t receive additional support during these hours. Members with day passes and those in a low-tier plan only get access during regular hours.

4. Partly Open

Partially open coworking spaces make some parts available 24 hours a day, while other parts, such as conference rooms, are only open during regular business hours. This method can also be combined with partially monitoring the space.

What Should You Keep Accessible in a 24/7 Coworking Space?

As discussed above, some coworking operators prefer keeping parts of the space open during all hours while closing the rest after certain times. Here’s what we recommend keeping open outside of working hours:

  • Dedicated desks and workspaces: These desks are usually in open seating areas and should be available at any time of the day.
  • Private offices: Full-time members or those in your highest membership tier may have their own offices. These offices should be treated like individually “leased” spaces and accessible to such members at all times.
  • Meeting and conference rooms: Meeting and conference rooms are usually locked after business hours. However, if you realize that many of your members visit your coworking space at night, you could also consider keeping these spaces open during specific nighttime hours.
  • Printing and scanning facilities: For security reasons, you may remove access to your printing and scanning facilities after business hours. However, if you have high-paying members, consider keeping these facilities open to them after hours with special access controls.

Important Factors to Consider When Operating a 24/7 Coworking Space

As with any business, things can go wrong in coworking spaces.

However, if you make your space safe and plan for unexpected problems, you can quickly mitigate risks and resolve various issues.

Here are some of the main factors to consider when operating a coworking space 24/7:

1. Security

Security should be one of your main (if not the biggest) priorities if you operate a 24-hour coworking space. You must ensure your space is safe and secure so members can get work done without worrying about their safety.

You can make your space safer by:

  • Having well-lit entrances and exits
  • Integrating an alarm system and monitoring access to all entrances and exits
  • Installing cameras both inside and outside the building
  • Having only one door open for access after standard working hours
  • Not allowing member guests to stay after certain times of the day

One of the best ways you can provide seamless access control to your members is with a digital security platform such as Kisi.

2. Employees

Consider what staff you’ll need and when you’ll need them (such as after hours). Your staffing level will ultimately depend on your location and membership access.

If the majority of your members visit the space during working hours, you may decide to have a manager present from 9 to 5 every day and a security guard patrolling during the evenings.

Or perhaps you have members you trust and have a good relationship with. In that case, you could consider giving them additional space benefits, such as access to certain facilities, in exchange for keeping an eye on things.

Remember that if your coworking space is in an area that requires additional security, you’ll need to consider limiting 24/7 access to only your highest-paying members.

3. A Plan for Crisis Management

If you’re used to running a coworking space where the operating manager is always on-site, shifting to a 24/7 model may bring some challenges:

  • If something happens in the middle of the night, who should handle it and how?
  • How will your members know who to contact in an emergency?

You need to consider who will handle these situations and have a solid plan of action in place. Here are the steps you’ll need to take:

  1. Establish a clear emergency plan by appointing contacts and defining protocols
  2. Communicate and onboard your members effectively so they know what to do in these situations
  3. Run regular emergency drills and ask members for feedback on what can be improved

How to Create and Operate a 24/7 Coworking Space

Now that you know what factors to consider and the benefits of a 24/7 coworking space, it’s time to determine how to create and operate it. The required steps are as follows:

1. Determine Your Membership Offerings and Plans

Decide what you’ll offer to your members and at what rate. What amenities will you provide? Will all members have access to all spaces, or will you have different plans available?

Here’s an example of a tiered membership plan that provides different levels of access:

  • Day Pass: $35/day, accessible from 7:00 am to 7:00 pm
  • Starter Plan: $150/month for up to 5 visits per month, available from 7:00 am to 7:00 pm
  • Professional Plan: $250/month, offers 24/7 access with a flexible hot desk arrangement
  • Executive Plan: $400/month, provides 24/7 access with a reserved dedicated desk and additional amenities, like locker storage and priority booking for meeting rooms

Also, decide which spaces are off-limits at certain times of the day so that members know what to expect. This information will make marketing your coworking space much easier.

2. Get the Right Tools

After determining membership plans and access, consider which technology and resources you’ll need to provide for members to work effectively. This includes access control and security systems, high-speed internet, and management software.

Software like OfficeRnD Flex can help you manage your 24/7 coworking space with the following features:

  • Booking and resource management: With OfficeRnD Flex, your members can book meeting rooms easily. You can implement booking policies and, based on your membership plans, only allow certain members access to these rooms.
  • Billing and payment systems: You can automate your billing and payment processes to get paid faster and easier. You won’t have to worry about complex spreadsheets or endless paper trails.
  • Access control: You can integrate with access control systems to manage which members can access your space at which times.
  • Reporting and analytics: You can track space usage and member activity to optimize the use of your space. Plus, you can generate detailed financial reports to monitor your revenue.
  • Contract management: You can create and send contracts to your members and keep everything in one place for easy reference.

3. Create Rules and an Onboarding Plan

Establish clear rules so your members know what’s expected of them regarding the following:

  • Respect and courtesy
  • Noise levels
  • Cleanliness
  • Use of equipment
  • Access
  • Visitor policies

Ensure you notify your members of these rules and onboard them properly by sending welcome emails and digital copies of the membership agreement.

Also, make sure your staff takes new members on a tour of the space on their first day so they know where everything is. Finally, inform your members of emergency procedures.
